title: 7NEWS Spotlight: Pauline Hanson’s UK tour and meeting with Tommy Robinson exposes One Nation’s creative accounting on immigration numbers - 7NEWS
raw_text: Pauline Hanson has rarely had a better opportunity to get her facts right than in 7NEWS Spotlight’s special report broadcast on Sunday night. Months in production, with unprecedented access to Hanson, it included her first major television interview since calling for an Australian ‘monoculture’ at the National Press Club in June. The interview was conducted in London, by correspondent Liam Bartlett, midway through Hanson’s so-called fact-finding tour of the UK during which the Spotlight crew also filmed her meeting a who’s-who of Britain’s far right. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Hanson blames White Australia policy end for migration issues Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today Hanson claimed her trip provided both a warning and a political war plan for One Nation — to prevent Australia becoming the ‘sad sorry country’ she believes the UK now is. The anti-immigrant strategies she’s bringing home include a scheme for mass-deportation or ‘remigration’ drawn up by Restore Britain, which also proposes creating a ‘hostile environment’ for illegal immigrants — denying them welfare, housing, and health services to compel their voluntary expulsion. Heady stuff, if that’s where your politics run. Frightening if not. It may be 30 years since Hanson warned that Australia was in danger of ‘being swamped by Asians’ — but the message (read ‘Muslims’ for ‘Asians’) is the same. And so are the alarming statistics offered in support. But numbers that can be shouted from the fringes without regard for the facts require much greater scrutiny when the shouter commands up to 30 per cent of the popular vote and is jockeying for post of preferred Prime Minister. On a podcast with British far-right extremist Tommy Robinson, filmed ‘fly-on-the-wall’ by Spotlight, Hanson claimed Australia was taking in 739,000 migrants a year. “Every 59 seconds,” she told Robinson, “we got a new migrant in Australia.” If numbers were words, 739,000 would be a weasel. The year Hanson is quoting (2022-23), was the first post-COVID statistic, with a large catch-up factor of Australians caught abroad, family reunions postponed, and foreign students returning. But what makes the number even harder to pin down is that Hanson fails to mention the 219,000 people who left Australia in the same year. That record catch-up year added 518,000 to Australia’s population — not 739,000. And the number has fallen every year since. In 2025 it was just 301,000 — far less than half what the senator told Robinson. The $20 million Cotswolds manor of former Neighbours star Holly Valance, dubbed “radical-right royalty” by the British tabloids, is an unlikely place for earnest consideration of mass deportation. But, invited in, the Spotlight team was rolling as Rupert Lowe, founder and leader of Restore Britain, handed Hanson his party’s manifesto mapping a plan to expel nearly two million people from the UK within three years. “Pauline, I’d like to give you this,” he said. “This is a jewel of what you need to do in Australia.” A man whose far-right ideology is somewhat at odds with his crumpled country-gentleman manner, could have easily followed it up with “and please pass the sugar.” Hanson’s reply: “We’re very much on the same page.” Spotlight later confirmed her commitment. “Do you think Senator, this concept of mass deportation is a good one?” Hanson was asked. “Oh, I love it,” she replied. Lowe’s claim of nearly two million illegal immigrants in the UK is at least twice the most widely cited estimate of Britain’s illegal population. But who, in Hanson’s monocultural nation, would be in her Australian mass-deportation queue? Riding through Luton’s Muslim quarter with Robinson, she put the number at 100,000: people who “get off the airplane, destroy their identification... overstay their visas and play refugees.” The Senator’s clear suggestion — and Robinson’s even clearer assumption as they traded disparaging quips about the prevalence of women in burkas and niqabs outside the car window — was that the majority of her ‘100,000’ are in the vanguard of radical Islam. With the brevity of truth, the real number is 77,700 who stayed on after their visas expired or were cancelled, led by citizens of China, Malaysia and the US. Not one of the top three groups is from the Middle East. The typical “illegal” is not a boat arrival or a black-flag radical, it’s someone who flew in on a student or tourist visa and simply never went home. If her mass deportees are ever lined up, the third-largest contingent will be Americans. There was similar arithmetic throughout Spotlight’s behind-the-scenes coverage of Hanson’s UK tour. She told Nigel Farage’s treasury spokesman — Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick — that one imperative for removing ‘illegal’ immigrants from Australia was that “we’ve got 150,000 people that are living in cars, tents. We can’t provide the housing for them.” The closest official figure relating to that claim is in the last Australian Census, which tallied 7636 people in tents, improvised dwellings or sleeping rough. That’s one-twentieth of the Hanson homeless. When Robinson discussed the number of Muslims in Australia with Hanson — “you’ve got about 4 per cent... that’s a million? — she replied “they do breed.” In fact, Muslim families on average have three children — and the number is falling. Mark Twain wrote (quoting English statesman Benjamin Disraeli): “There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics.” Disraeli — twice prime minister and three times Britain’s treasurer — was a canny politician who clearly knew the power of numbers to convince. Hanson is a perhaps pale, but fervent, imitator. The Spotlight report captured an unguarded Hanson amidst a likeminded coterie, who share her innumerate approach to immigration statistics. All her numbers run the same way. Away from the truth. Stream free on

title: Australian man dies in immigration detention in Bali while awaiting deportation - 7NEWS
raw_text: An Australian man has died in while in immigration detention in Bali as he was set to be deported back home for overstaying his visa. Indonesia’s Ngurah Rai Immigration Office said in a statement on Saturday the 39-year-old man from Sydney passed away on Friday night while in detention. “The person concerned had received emergency medical treatment before finally being declared dead on the way to the hospital,” the statement said. Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today The man had been investigated for overstaying his residence permit by more than three months, the office revealed. “Despite being given repeated opportunities to complete his immigration process cooperatively, the person concerned repeatedly did not comply with official invitations from officers,” the statement said. The man was taken into immigration custody on Friday in Jimbaran, south of Bali’s capital Denpasar, to await the deportation process. Immigration officers were watching the CCTV cameras in the detention facility when they found “an abnormality in the detainee’s position that did not show movement for a long time in the toilet”. “Officers immediately went to the location and found the detainee in an unconscious condition,” they said. “Officers immediately checked vital signs, provided first aid including oxygen assistance, and coordinated with the nearest hospital for ambulance delivery. “The medical team who arrived at the location carried out initial treatment before taking the person concerned to Bali General Hospital Jimbaran for more intensive treatment. On the way to the hospital, the person concerned was declared dead. “The results of the initial examination by the hospital also noted a suspected heart attack as a factor at the time of the incident.” Local police are investigating the death. Head of the Ngurah Rai Immigration Office Bugie Kurniawan expressed his condolences to the man’s family, vowing to continue working with police and the Australian government. 7News.com.au has contacted the Deparment of Foreign Affairs and Trade for comment. If you need help in a crisis, call Lifeline on 131114. For further information about depression contact beyondblue on 1300224636 or talk to your GP, local health professional or someone you trust. title: Amanda Rishworth and Nat Barr clash over tradie ranking in skilled migration scheme - 7NEWS
raw_text: Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth has refused to say whether tradies should be prioritised over economists and animal trainers under Australia’s skilled migration scheme, despite the country’s housing crisis. The minister was grilled by Sunrise host Nat Barr over the government’s migration priorities on Wednesday and was pressed on why construction workers remain in the same priority tier as a range of other occupations despite Australia’s desperate need for more homes. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Tradies ranked equal to actors in migration scheme Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today Under the current Skilled Migration Scheme, nurses and health professionals are listed in tier one, teachers sit in tier two, while construction trades are ranked in tier three alongside occupations including actors, dancers, economists, animal handlers, and animal trainers. Rishworth defended the government’s approach, saying it had significantly increased the number of construction workers entering Australia. “We’ve had three times increase in the number of construction workers since we’ve come to government taking up those jobs,” she said. “But importantly, we’re also fast-tracking the recognition of those skills. So not only can those construction workers come here, but they can actually work on construction sites.” Rishworth said an additional 20,000 people had their skills recognised through the fast-tracking measures, allowing them to begin working sooner. However, when Barr repeatedly asked whether tradies should continue to be ranked alongside occupations such as animal trainers and actors, the minister stopped short of giving a direct answer. “I want to see more tradies, I want to see more doctors, I want to see more nurses, people that we need, and of course what we’ve had is the opposition play a very sneaky game of talking down our skilled migration, telling us that skilled migration isn’t important but not being clear about who they would cut,” she said. “What I would say is that when it comes to making sure we’ve got more construction workers in the country, I absolutely support that and I also want to see those skills recognised… so they can get to work quickly.” Shadow Defence Minister James Patterson accused the government of failing to prioritise the workers Australia needs most during the housing crisis. “Only a Labor government, which is beholden to corrupt unions like the CFMEU, would think, in the middle of our worst-ever housing crisis, that they [animal trainers and actors] are equally important to bring to Australia right now,” he said. “Labor thinks that we should bring in as many economists and actors as we should bring in sparkies and carpenters and plumbers and other critical trades.” Rishworth rejected Patterson’s claim that unions were influencing the government’s migration settings, arguing the tier system had not changed since the previous Coalition government. Barr immediately challenged the explanation. “Why not?” she asked. “We’ve got a housing crisis now, so why hasn’t it changed in four years?” Rishworth again declined to directly address why tradies remain in the same migration priority tier, instead saying the government continues to receive expert advice on skilled occupation lists. title: Pauline Hanson meets with UK far-right figure Tommy Robinson - 7NEWS
raw_text: Pauline Hanson has met with UK far-right figure Tommy Robinson to record a new podcast interview. Robinson, 43, took to social media to share news of their sit-down, and what is to come. “Had a fascinating time chatting to one of the bravest lady’s (sic) on the planet,” the controversial activist shared on X. “Fearless, relentless, consistent, fighting for the Australian people and hopefully the next leader of her nation. Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today “Podcast coming soon...” Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, founded the far-right Islamophobic group the English Defence League in 2009. He has multiple criminal convictions and has previously been denied a visa to visit Australia. Just last month, he appeared on an episode of The Karl Stefanovic Show to talk about “free speech, censorship, immigration and the direction he believes Britain should be heading in”. The interview was removed from online platforms and led to Stefanovic’s high-profile exit from Nine. It was later reuploaded to Hanson’s Please Explain account. “Tommy Robinson has a lesson for Australians,” the account said. “If we don’t learn from the UK’s mistakes on immigration and radical Islam, we are going to face the same destruction. “This is exactly what Karl was trying to bring to Australia’s attention.” News of the Hanson-Robinson podcast episode comes after the One Nation leader enjoyed a drink with former Neighbours star Holly Valance. “Nothing like a beer with your mate at the pub on a hot day,” the soap star posted online, sharing a picture from ex-Top Gear presenter Jeremy Clarkson’s pub in the UK. The Senator’s Please Explain Account said Valance had been a longtime supporter of “true conservatives”. “While here in England, I took some time out to catch up with Holly Valance who has been a staunch backer of true conservatives both here in the UK and myself in Australia,” the post read. “Some big meetings lined up this week. I’ll have more to say about those discussions later in the week.” Stream free on

title: The Issue Podcast: Demographer says the tax system is ‘unfair’ for families amid the great population debate - 7NEWS
raw_text: Leading demographer Professor Peter McDonald says the tax system is “unfair” and the Albanese Government should be “looking at better ways to support families with children”. The professor once described by former Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull as “arguably the world’s leading demographer”, has discussed migration and population with 7NEWS Podcast The Issue. Australia previously had universal, non-means tested, allowances for families like the Child Endowment scheme from 1941 and the Family Allowance policy from 1976. Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today The nation’s current system is the Family Tax Benefit which is income-tested and capped. 7NEWS can reveal the latest figures for the fortnightly payment scheme, designed to help families with the cost-of-living. In 2022-23 only 42 per cent of Australian families were in receipt of Family Tax Benefit Part A, which is paid per child and is adjusted for income. Thirty-five per cent of Australian Families were in receipt of Family Tax Benefit Part B, which is an extra benefit for single parents, grandparent carers or couples with one main income. “We’ve been taxing away the family tax benefit and I’m a pro-child person so I think that’s unfair,” Professor Peter McDonald told The Issue Podcast. “We should be looking at better ways to be supporting families with children. “These policies are not just about increasing the birth rate, they’re making life more comfortable for Australian couples, they’re providing education to Australian children and so on.” Australia’s fertility rate is currently at a record low of 1.5 children per woman. But among Australian born women the fertility rate actually rises to 1.7 children per woman. Income splitting 7NEWS has asked the three most popular political parties in Australia about the nation’s family tax system and the comments by McDonald. One Nation supports a tax policy for couples known as income splitting. In simple terms, the total income of a couple could be divided between both parents before calculating tax, which would reduce the overall amount of tax paid to the government. The Parliamentary Budget Office costed an income splitting policy by former Senator Gerard Rennick at $12 billion per year. “Of course it comes at a cost, but it also comes at a saving because if a person’s at home looking after their children then they don’t need that daycare position to look after their children,” One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce told 7NEWS. “As a nation we have to have more babies. If you don’t have babies, then you’re going to have to import them, which means that that comes in the form of immigration.” McDonald doesn’t support income splitting as he says it discourages Mothers from working. “Sure there are some women who would prefer to stay at home and look after the children, they’re usually people whose husbands aren’t making a lot of money,” McDonald said. “But today women are more highly educated than men, they are career oriented, they want to work.” Coalition’s families package Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume says the Coalition is working on a comprehensive package of policies for families to take to the 2028 federal election. But the Liberal Senator wouldn’t go into further detail when pushed by 7NEWS. “The best thing a government could do to encourage people to have families, expand their families, is to reduce the cost of living,” Hume said while speaking in Melbourne on Saturday. “When families feel that next year isn’t going to be any better than this year... of course they’re going to hesitate before they have another child, before they have another mouth to feed, another child to educate.” Labor’s childcare agenda The Prime Minister has stated he wants universal childcare to be his legacy. The Albanese Government’s Child Care Subsidy helps families with the costs of child care. All eligible families can now get three days of subsidised childcare per week. Parents earing more than $538,520 are not able to access the scheme. Cabinet Minister Chris Bowen says the decision to have a child is an extremely personal one. “In relation to childbirth and birth rates, Australian couples are making those decisions every day and they are highly personal decisions,” Bowen said. “Tony Burke is working very hard to ensure our migration settings are correct and he’ll have more to say.” Migration debate Australia’s population debate is experiencing a flashpoint. Immigration Minister Tony Burke was due to announce changes to Labor’s migration policy but postponed the speech to the National Press Club. Burke is yet to announce a new date for the address, and there is speculation he was told to toughen up his plan by the Cabinet. Energy Minister Chris Bowen has denied that report saying, “No. Tony Burke will make announcements when he’s ready.” Labor is aiming to reduce annual net overseas migration to 225,000 by 2027-28. The Coalition wants to lower migration under 200,000 per year. One Nation’s policy is to cut the amount of temporary and permanent visas to 130,000 a year. Temporary visas are the issue McDonald says permanent visas should be prioritised over temporary visas. He argues temporary migration is adding to Australia’s productivity problem. “It’s a very, very unpopular statement to make, but I think that permanent migration should be higher,” McDonald says. “Churning over temporary migrants is a reason for the decline in labour productivity. “We’re continually replacing experienced workers with inexperienced workers. That is not just aged care where that happens, it is also in construction and in other industries as well.” You can catch more of The Issue on Listnr or watch full episodes on our YouTube channel. raw_text: There are fears a bumper multibillion-dollar harvest in WA is at risk because of a new crackdown on backpacker and temporary visas. An army of workers arrive to help on the land every year but farmers say they are now being blocked or delayed in a bureaucratic nightmare. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Visa delays threaten WA’s bumper harvest season Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today “Farmers are distressed trying to work out who’s going to operate all their big machinery this year,” farmer Mic Fels told 7NEWS. The Esperance farmer says the Federal Government’s decision to slow down approvals is another blow to the industry. “We have three Danish skilled farm workers, they’ve got university qualifications, they’ve got years of experience operating exactly the same machines that we own,” he said. “They’re sitting on hold — have been since July — waiting for their visas to be processed.” Harvest has made an earlier than expected start in WA, and grain farmers are eyeing off a crop of 23 million tonnes. A visa approval which used to be just days or even minutes can now take up to three months. “It’s like they’re picking on farmers now,” Fels said. “Farmers have had to deal with a lot this year. “There’s been the risk over whether there was going to be fertiliser, whether there was going to be diesel. “We got through that, but the uncertainty is the big cause of stress, and now it’s the uncertainty over workforce.” National Farmers Federation vice president John Hassell said working holidaymakers “stay in accommodations on farms” and “don’t put pressure on all those sorts of things”. “I think this is a very ill-informed response to calls by One Nation and the Liberal Party to reduce immigration,” he said. The federal government has now agreed to fast track some urgent visa requests but approvals are not guaranteed and farmers say time is already slipping away. “Every day that a harvest is delayed, it decreases the value and the quality of the crops,” Hassell said. title: Labor immigration crackdown: Warning to foreign students, family visas and working holiday extensions - 7NEWS
raw_text: International students will be restricted from hopping between visas and bringing family members to Australia as part of a major government crackdown on migration. Immigration Minister Tony Burke used his speech at the National Press Club in Canberra on Thursday to reveal how Labor proposes to hit its target of getting net overseas migration to 225,000 by 2027/28. The Albanese Government will strengthen compliance measures to ensure people without valid visas leave the country. Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today ’Australia welcomes people who make a genuine contribution to our country,’‘ Burke said in a statement. ‘’Australia does not support people who seek to rort or defraud the system. We’re making changes to give us more control over who arrives, who stays and who leaves.’‘ The skilled migration program will be tweaked to prioritise applicants in healthcare, construction, education, law enforcement, defence, resources, agriculture, aquaculture, and fishing. Tourists will be prevented from extending their stays in Australia with the introduction of a ‘‘no further stay’‘ condition on visitor visas. Working holiday maker visas, which the agriculture and tourism industries heavily rely on for staff, will also be changed. A ballot system will be introduced for years two and three and an additional regional work requirement introduced. The current freeze on processing of working holiday visas will come to an end, with processing times for applications to be stabilised at three months. Ministerial Direction 110 will also get an update — used to combat hate and criminal behaviour by better protecting children who are victims of crime, better protecting victims of domestic and family violence, and reflecting modern Australia’s commitment to stamping out hatred. The government will also stabilise processing times for Working Holiday Maker applications to three months. Burke said Australia would continue to be strong on borders and maintain the integrity of its migration system, while treating people with the fairness and decency that Australians expect. “The government supports immigration but is opposed to anyone rorting the immigration system,” he said. “Almost everyone who comes to Australia is a good guest in our country. These reforms are to ensure that our migration system can be better targeted to the current needs of Australia.” New migration figures released Net overseas migration was 292,100 in the year to March 2026, a 5.6 per cent decrease in people since the previous year. There were 557,500 people immigrating to Australia and there were 265,400 people emigrating from Australia That’s the lowest rate of migration in nearly four years. All states and territories had positive population growth over the year ending 31 March 2026. Western Australia had the fastest growth rate (2.1 per cent). Tasmania had the slowest rate (0.6 per cent). Criticism from One Nation and the Coalition One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who wants negative net overseas migration, says she was the one to force Labor to reduce their migration policy. “But it’s not going to work,” she said. “It’s all smoke and mirrors. “Labor continues to lie to the people with the hidden agenda, I don’t trust them.” One Nation released its migration plan on Monday, which would cut three-quarters of a million migrants over three years and impose even more strict restrictions on international students, family visas, along with promises of widespread deportations. The Coalition is yet to reveal its plan, but will aim to get net overseas migration under 170,000 to match the construction rate of new houses. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Labor had never reached its immigration targets. “Young Australians are not able to get into a home because the immigration numbers have been too high,” Taylor said. “There’s no change to the targets, and Labor’s never reached its targets anyway.” Burke revealed the long-awaited changes to the migration system on Thursday, following weeks of delay and speculation. The suite of policy changes, which does not include new legislation after negotiations with the Coalition broke down, will also strengthen compliance measures forcing people without a valid visa to leave the country. Burke said the changes would help bring net overseas migration from 292,100 to meet budget forecasts of 245,000 in 2026/27 and 225,000 each year thereafter. Burke’s plan did not detail the integrity measures that would stop student visa hopping, nor did it say how the government would crack down on rogue migration agents who knowingly supported visa applications without merit. It’s the immigration minister’s second run at announcing migration changes, six weeks after canning his first due to cabinet disagreements over the extent of the shake-up. The Australian Bureau of Statistics revealed net overseas migration fell from about 299,000 in 2025 to 292,100 in the year to March in a population update released one hour before Mr Burke’s scheduled address. Australia’s total population grew by 1.4 per cent in cent in the 12 months to March to 27.9 million. Migration by the numbers — International students and those on graduate visas will no longer be allowed to bring family members with them to Australia, with some exceptions including for PhD students — Only 45,000 working holiday-makers will be able to stay in Australia for a second year, and only 5000 for a third year — down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively, but a slow-down to the processing of those visas will end for everyone except British citizens — Migrants coming to work in construction, farming, fisheries, mining and teaching will be prioritised — Only foreign students transferring to higher-level courses (bachelor’s to master’s for example) will be able to extend their visas — People who overstay their visa, of which there are about 77,000, will be sent to detention centres, with the government now on the hunt for more facilities, compliance officers and beds — The points test, which determines which skilled migrants come to Australia, will be revamped to consider construction-related qualifications as equivalent to university degrees — Powers to punish and de-register dodgy migration agents, who help foreigners get Australian visas, will expand Why the changes to migration? — The government is trying to bring Australia’s population growth due to migration down from 292,100 to 245,000 in the year to July 2027 and 225,000 each year thereafter, and to curb visa-hopping, “rorting” and “gaming” the system — That figure has stubbornly exceeded Labor’s forecasts since the party came to power in 2022, but Immigration Minister Tony Burke said migration was now tracking in line with its targets * The coalition believes the figure should descend to 170,000 in line with housing construction, and One Nation wants a 130,000-person a year cap HOW ARE THEY BEING IMPLEMENTED? * The changes may not be law because negotiations between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor broke down in the week before Mr Burke’s address, dooming hope of getting reforms through the Senate * Without parliament’s approval, the government cannot proceed with a desired crackdown on phoney asylum-seekers’ claims * But Mr Burke insisted negotiations with the coalition were ongoing and productive, and said “we have put nothing forward that is a wedge to them”. title: Military called in as more than 40,000 migrants from Morocco pour into Spanish border territory - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: Spanish officials say more than 40,000 people crossed from Morocco into Spain, via the North African enclave of Ceuta. Footage showed hundreds of migrants swimming from the Moroccan side, and others breaking through a gate on land. What's next? At least 18 people died during the crossing and Spanish government has deployed military units to reinforce police at the border. Spanish military units are being deployed to reinforce police in the city of Ceuta after migrants in Morocco broke through fences, overwhelming the local force. Spain's interior ministry estimates more than 40,000 people swam, with 18 people declared dead from the process. Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers association representing Civil Guard officers, said some migrants drowned in the crossing, and some are believed to have been killed in the stampede exiting the water. Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain, on the North African coast, and has been the scene of previous mass migration events in recent years. Ceuta, on the northern African coast, would be a 5-kilometre swim from the Moroccan town of Fnideq. Video footage showed hundreds of migrants swimming or floating on inner tubes from the Moroccan side, and others breaking through a gate on land and running into the city. "It was very tough. The police tried to stop us. But our will and determination allowed us to come here," migrant Jadid Zacaria, his hair and shirt still wet from the ocean, said in an interview as migrants streamed through a border gate nearby. Nine people were found dead, local authorities said, adding to a toll of 60 migrants who have died attempting to cross into Ceuta in recent months. The Spanish government said 200 specialised police officers and 60 troops had arrived from the Spanish mainland to reinforce the enclave's regular forces. The scene was reminiscent of 2021, when about 10,000 people from Morocco and sub-Saharan Africa, many of them minors, entered the enclave of 85,000 people in days. Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez will travel to Ceuta today with Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska for meetings with security forces and local authorities, his office said. Morocco's Interior Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 'Entering from the sea' Earlier, a Guardia Civil spokesperson said migrants were "massively entering from the sea" around the Tarajal breakwater, a border seawall that migrants can swim around to enter Ceuta. The spokesperson said police were overwhelmed. Many local shops were shuttered. Enrique Serrano, who runs a women's clothing store in central Ceuta, said business owners were organising self-defence because they believed police resources would be insufficient. "I'm not opening this afternoon because the situation is extremely tense … The first thing I have to do is protect my business and my family," he said. Ceuta and Melilla — another Spanish autonomous city located in North Africa — have the European Union's only land borders with Africa. Both cities periodically experience surges in attempted crossings by migrants seeking to reach Europe. Local government seeks state of emergency Spain's Socialist government stands out in Europe for its pro-migrant stance, and it has recently launched a program to provide legal status for some 500,000 undocumented migrants, triggering an influx of applications double that number. Right-wing parties criticised the drive, arguing it would attract more migrants to Spain, and were quick to blame Mr Sanchez for allowing the situation in Ceuta to reach crisis proportions. Conservative opposition People's Party leader Alberto Nuñez Feijoo said in a post on X: "The situation in Ceuta is desperate. The government cannot look the other way… because we are facing a national security crisis." Ceuta Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas had urged the national government to declare an emergency over the mass arrivals. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on X that the images from Ceuta showed that Mr Sanchez's migration policy was "misguided". A source told Reuters that Italy was exploring reintroducing border controls for people travelling from Spain to Italy, which normally falls in the European Union's passport-free Schengen zone. 'An explosion' Earlier this month, Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants intercepted at sea while attempting to reach Ceuta or Melilla could not be summarily returned under the enclaves' special "border rejection" regime, which allows authorities to immediately send back people caught crossing the border fences. Spain's government said it was the "exploitation by mafias and criminal organisations" of this ruling that had triggered the migrant surge, not its bid to give legal status to some undocumented migrants. Loading... "It has been a slow trickle since the Supreme Court's ruling, but today has been an explosion," the Guardia Civil spokesperson told Reuters. The Interior Ministry said it was working closely with Morocco to address the surge in irregular arrivals, having prevented thousands of migrants from illegally entering Ceuta in recent days. Migrant rights activist Zakaria Zarroqui said people were still flocking to the adjacent Moroccan city of Fnideq in an attempt to cross into Ceuta and the situation was still out of control. Mauricio Valiente, director of the Spanish Commission for Refugees, which has lawyers working in Ceuta, said the migrants crossing into the enclave were of Moroccan and sub-Saharan origin, including families. Reuters / AP / AFP

title: Home Affairs asks DV survivors to prove abuser relationship 'genuine' - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: A federal government safety net for migrant domestic and family violence (DFV) victim-survivors has been criticised as a stressor and barrier. Lawyers and experts say the Department of Home Affairs needs to rethink a process that requires documentary proof a relationship was "genuine" as part of family violence provisions. Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke says he has taken the "unprecedented" step of cancelling the visas of DFV perpetrators. For women on temporary visas experiencing domestic and family violence (DFV) in Australia, their perpetrators are often also their visa sponsors. Returning to their home countries is usually unthinkable, as many are terrified of being separated from their Australian children, or they know they will face stigma or abuse over the ended relationship. The Department of Home Affairs has family violence provisions under the Migration Act, but the application asks for proof the relationship was "genuine" via documents that usually do not exist. title: How Pauline Hanson's winning the migration debate - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: Two months since Pauline Hanson's Press Club address calling for monoculturalism in Australia, new polling shows more Australians prefer her stance on immigration than that of either of the major parties. Today, Tony Barry, a former Liberal party strategist and director at Redbridge Group on One Nation's appeal. Featured: Tony Barry, former Liberal party strategist and Redbridge Group director Subscribe to ABC News Daily on the ABC listen app. Sam Hawley: Two weeks since her press club address where she called for monoculturalism, Pauline Hanson has had a win with voters. New polling this week shows more Australians prefer her stance on immigration than that of either of the two major parties. Today Tony Barry, a former Liberal Party strategist and director at Redbridge Group, on One Nation's appeal. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Tony, you've been involved in politics, well, for a pretty long time now. And so you know that immigration has always been a touchstone issue for voters, hasn't it? Tony Barry: Yeah, immigration is always an issue that animates voters. And in the current political environment, we've got cost of living pressures, but also housing affordability, whether it be renting or buying. And in the era where politicians like Pauline Hanson readily identify as grievance, you have this perfect storm brewing. Sam Hawley: Yeah, but I mean, you kind of think back to the Howard years, it was sort of key to his leadership because who can really forget, "we will decide who comes to this country." John Howard, former Prime Minister: We have a proud record of welcoming people from 140 different nations, but we will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come. Tony Barry: Yeah, the 2001 election was fairly unique insofar as we had September 11 earlier in that year, and then shortly after that, Tampa. News report: Well, it's been a day of high drama on the high seas. A Norwegian freighter carrying more than 400 mainly Afghani asylum seekers has been refused entry to Australia and is still anchored 70 kilometres from Christmas Island. Tony Barry: And so that spoke to sovereignty and the key value there that was driving vote considerations was sovereignty. And so that was a unique situation, but it does frequently happen in politics where particular cycles immigration will be elevated as an issue. Sam Hawley: And the Howard years were really a lot about stopping the boats, of course, although just noting migration numbers overall increased when he was prime minister. But just tell me since then and up until now, it doesn't seem to have been such a key issue in voters' minds. Is that fair to say? Tony Barry: Yeah, I think Tony Abbott's prime ministership, while it sort of lacked a lot of highlights, the one thing you have to give him credit for was his tow back the boats policy did actually kill the issue. And so it sort of forced a bipartisanship between both parties. And obviously that wasn't an issue where Labor wanted to have a fight. And so consequently it was sort of neutralised as an issue. But now in the current environment, we have had record numbers of immigration post COVID and there's reasons for that. But in an era where people are hurting and are looking for explanations as to why things aren't working out as well as they'd have hoped, you have this politician who's been talking about it for 30 years comes along. And we've done a lot of polling on this. And one of the reasons why people are voting One Nation is because of what they describe as Pauline Hanson's authenticity. The fact that she has been talking about these issues for so long. And there's a political reward for that. Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader: At the centre of this crisis is the utterly flawed policy of multiculturalism. We cannot be a multicultural society. We are a multiracial society, but we must be monocultural. Sam Hawley: So, Pauline Hanson and One Nation, they're ensuring, I suppose, that immigration, the issue of immigration and debate around it is gaining traction again. And Tony, this week we had a Resolve political monitor poll, which showed that 35% of voters think that Pauline Hanson is best placed to manage immigration and refugees. Just tell me how significant is that number? Tony Barry: Well, it is significant. We've got similar numbers on our research that we did for the AFR. Immigration is currently the fifth most salient issue to voters. 28% of voters put it in their top three and about 8%, 9% rated it their number one. So a significant number, but not a huge number. Cost of living is the most dominant issue. Around 75% of Australians have it in their top three and almost half of all Australians put it in their number one issue. So the next election will probably be decided on who voters think is best to manage the economy and its relationship to housing affordability. Now, immigration will play a part in that. And I'm sure Hanson will try her hardest to keep the conversation there because she keeps the conversation there, she's got a huge lead over the two major parties. The art of politics is to control the narrative. Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader: I'm always listening. And that's why my policy to slash immigration reflects what most Australians want. Tony Barry: I think in the case of immigration, because of Hanson's strong lead, and she has on our polling a 40% of voters say she is the best person to handle that issue. And Labor and the Coalition are on 17% each. So even combined, they still don't match One Nation. But the challenge for the major parties is to bring the conversation back to their strengths. That is the art of politics is playing to your strengths. Sam Hawley: All right, well, Tony, let's consider then why it is that voters feel this way, why they like what Pauline Hanson has to say on immigration. What exactly is One Nation's policies on immigration? It's not actually that clear, is it? Tony Barry: Well, for a lot of voters, she's the anti-establishment candidate. And we asked One Nation voters in our last poll, why? Why are you voting One Nation? And of course, at the moment, it's around 30% of the electorate. So it's a very significant number. For about 16% of those currently supporting One Nation, they say it's because Hanson represents change, and they want change. For another 16% of those One Nation voters, it's their anti-establishment credentials. They're sick and tired of the major parties. For another 14% say they think she's authentic. And 11% say it's her immigration policy. And a lot of it is not so much because of immigration per se, although that is a component, it's that they feel the current political model isn't working for them, and they want to smash it up. Sam Hawley: So not so much the nitty gritty of the immigration policy. That's not really on voters' minds. But if you go to their website, the party says it would cap visas at 130,000 per year. Now if it did that, that would lead to zero or even negative migration. I don't know that voters understand that. Tony Barry: And I think that's the point. I think that a lot of voters don't understand that because Labor, they control the microphone. And yet I'm not really sure what their immigration policy is. Now I'm a high volume user of media. And if I don't understand what their objectives are, then I think you'll find most voters also don't understand. And I think there's been a failing of both sides to explain the importance of immigration, particularly skilled immigration. John Howard, as you mentioned before, actually increased immigration, and he changed it from family reunion and skewed it more towards skilled. And he explained why that was important. About 10% of the healthcare workforce in Australia are migrants. So there's been a failing of the major parties, particularly the government at the moment, to explain why good immigration program is important for Australia. In that environment, it's very easy for an anti-establishment party like One Nation to undermine the credentials of that campaign. Sam Hawley: Yeah. All right. Well, Barnaby Joyce, he was asked about this 130,000 figure. He said it really only applies to the net intake of migrants. Pauline Hanson, she was grilled about it on News 24, formerly Sky's Sunday Agenda. Again, not clear at all. News24 journalist: What's your permanent number? What permanent number do you want to see here? Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader: Well, I want to see 130,000 as the permanent number that are here. So there are people, look, there's people that come in, they come in on visas. So we have the palm workers, we have backpackers, we have short term workers. If you've been here for over 14 months or 16 months, you're basically classified can be a permanent into the country. Yeah. But we've allowed people... Pauline, sorry News24 journalist: to interrupt. I just want to clarify this. Sam Hawley: But as you say, we also had this issue with Tony Burke, right? He was meant to have this major address at the National Press Club. He cancelled it. So really, as you say, voters are not really clear where they stand with any of these parties. Tony Barry: Yeah, I think that was obviously a very untidy episode for Tony Burke having to cancel it. But I think he made the right decision strategically because you've got to get these things right. And rather than sort of going in and sort of walking it back and then having this sort of very convoluted position, they've basically caught their breath. They're obviously going to try and recalibrate and then do some positioning on it. Because at the moment, that's a really important issue for them to neutralise. Because whilst only fifth most salient issue on voters' hierarchy, the more you talk about an issue and the more oxygen it gets, then it has the potential to increase in salience. And Labor would be very concerned about that. They can't afford to be trailing or not competitive in the issues that voters will consider when they go into mark their ballot card. Sam Hawley: Yeah, the ABC reported that Tony Burke, he had postponed that speech because the cabinet couldn't agree on the detail. But what you're saying is really what the government and Labor wants to do here is, well, come up with some figure for immigration that neutralises this issue or neutralises the topic as an issue. Tony Barry: Yeah, and also they've got to pre-position their policy. You know, the great failing of many policies in governments, whether it be Labor or Coalition, is a failure to sort of execute the idea. You just sort of drop it on the table like a raw piece of steak and you expect voters to digest it. You do need to position these policies. Sam Hawley: All right, and what about the Coalition? How does it play into all of this? The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, he seems to want to link new houses to net migration. Angus Taylor, Opposition leader: A coalition will cap immigration numbers based on the number of homes constructed each year. Hear, hear. Never again will a government be able to bring in more people than our housing can support. Hear, hear. That's our commitment. Tony Barry: Well, I think the problem for the Coalition at the moment is their primary vote is so low, they're not even in the conversation. Their job strategically is to get over the top of One Nation, so you can't win when you're coming third. There's just no universe where they're going to be competitive with the primary vote in the low 20s. Sam Hawley: All right, well, Tony, as you mentioned, One Nation seems to be elevating the issue of immigration. So do you think that is a tactic that will be successful and beneficial to the party in the end when it comes to election time? Tony Barry: A lot of it's going to depend on how the two traditional major parties respond and are they able to communicate differentiated policies on salient issues. And there's no more salient issue than cost of living and housing and healthcare. So if they can articulate an agenda that voters can digest and believe in, then I think they'll effectively neutralise One Nation. How do you control the One Nation vote? You look back at the Howard government. In 2004, One Nation did not win a cent spot. In fact, the coalition won four Senate seats, including a newcomer at the time, Barnaby Joyce, and the coalition won four, which is unprecedented for a major party to win four out of six Senate spots in a half Senate election. But such was the success of Howard and Costello on a macro level and the late Ron Boswell on the ground arguing against One Nation that they were able to basically neutralise One Nation as a political force. But a large part of that was that under the Howard government at the time, wage growth was around 24.6% and interest rates generally fell one or two points or more every year. And so there wasn't as much grievance in the electorate because people were quite happy. And the greatest measurement of that is we always ask a diagnostic test. Do you think Australia is heading in the right direction or the wrong direction? Now, I remember polling in 2007, the right direction was 65%. 65% of Australians said we're heading in the right direction. And the most recent poll we did for the Fin Review, 54% said we're heading in the wrong direction. So there's been a significant shift over the last 19 years in people's assessments of how the country is travelling, and that's building the grievance. And that is why One Nation is able to identify that grievance and speak to that grievance. Sam Hawley: And it's got hold of the narrative and it's driving it, right? And that counts for a lot. That's what every political party wants to do. Tony Barry: Exactly. Exactly. You want to control the microphone because you get to drive the narrative and the opposition typically responds. But Hanson is in the position where in some cases she actually drives the narrative and the government is responding and the opposition is responding.

Sam Hawley: So not so much the nitty gritty of the immigration policy. That's not really on voters' minds. But if you go to their website, the party says it would cap visas at 130,000 per year. Now if it did that, that would lead to zero or even negative migration. I don't know that voters understand that. Tony Barry: And I think that's the point. I think that a lot of voters don't understand that because Labor, they control the microphone. And yet I'm not really sure what their immigration policy is. Now I'm a high volume user of media. And if I don't understand what their objectives are, then I think you'll find most voters also don't understand. And I think there's been a failing of both sides to explain the importance of immigration, particularly skilled immigration. John Howard, as you mentioned before, actually increased immigration, and he changed it from family reunion and skewed it more towards skilled. And he explained why that was important. About 10% of the healthcare workforce in Australia are migrants. So there's been a failing of the major parties, particularly the government at the moment, to explain why good immigration program is important for Australia. In that environment, it's very easy for an anti-establishment party like One Nation to undermine the credentials of that campaign. Sam Hawley: Yeah. All right. Well, Barnaby Joyce, he was asked about this 130,000 figure. He said it really only applies to the net intake of migrants. Pauline Hanson, she was grilled about it on News 24, formerly Sky's Sunday Agenda. Again, not clear at all. News24 journalist: What's your permanent number? What permanent number do you want to see here? Pauline Hanson, One Nation leader: Well, I want to see 130,000 as the permanent number that are here. So there are people, look, there's people that come in, they come in on visas. So we have the palm workers, we have backpackers, we have short term workers. If you've been here for over 14 months or 16 months, you're basically classified can be a permanent into the country. Yeah. But we've allowed people... Pauline, sorry News24 journalist: to interrupt. I just want to clarify this. Sam Hawley: But as you say, we also had this issue with Tony Burke, right? He was meant to have this major address at the National Press Club. He cancelled it. So really, as you say, voters are not really clear where they stand with any of these parties. Tony Barry: Yeah, I think that was obviously a very untidy episode for Tony Burke having to cancel it. But I think he made the right decision strategically because you've got to get these things right. And rather than sort of going in and sort of walking it back and then having this sort of very convoluted position, they've basically caught their breath. They're obviously going to try and recalibrate and then do some positioning on it. Because at the moment, that's a really important issue for them to neutralise. Because whilst only fifth most salient issue on voters' hierarchy, the more you talk about an issue and the more oxygen it gets, then it has the potential to increase in salience. And Labor would be very concerned about that. They can't afford to be trailing or not competitive in the issues that voters will consider when they go into mark their ballot card. Sam Hawley: Yeah, the ABC reported that Tony Burke, he had postponed that speech because the cabinet couldn't agree on the detail. But what you're saying is really what the government and Labor wants to do here is, well, come up with some figure for immigration that neutralises this issue or neutralises the topic as an issue. Tony Barry: Yeah, and also they've got to pre-position their policy. You know, the great failing of many policies in governments, whether it be Labor or Coalition, is a failure to sort of execute the idea. You just sort of drop it on the table like a raw piece of steak and you expect voters to digest it. You do need to position these policies. Sam Hawley: All right, and what about the Coalition? How does it play into all of this? The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, he seems to want to link new houses to net migration. Angus Taylor, Opposition leader: A coalition will cap immigration numbers based on the number of homes constructed each year. Hear, hear. Never again will a government be able to bring in more people than our housing can support. Hear, hear. That's our commitment. Tony Barry: Well, I think the problem for the Coalition at the moment is their primary vote is so low, they're not even in the conversation. Their job strategically is to get over the top of One Nation, so you can't win when you're coming third. There's just no universe where they're going to be competitive with the primary vote in the low 20s. Sam Hawley: All right, well, Tony, as you mentioned, One Nation seems to be elevating the issue of immigration. So do you think that is a tactic that will be successful and beneficial to the party in the end when it comes to election time? Tony Barry: A lot of it's going to depend on how the two traditional major parties respond and are they able to communicate differentiated policies on salient issues. And there's no more salient issue than cost of living and housing and healthcare. So if they can articulate an agenda that voters can digest and believe in, then I think they'll effectively neutralise One Nation. How do you control the One Nation vote? You look back at the Howard government. In 2004, One Nation did not win a cent spot. In fact, the coalition won four Senate seats, including a newcomer at the time, Barnaby Joyce, and the coalition won four, which is unprecedented for a major party to win four out of six Senate spots in a half Senate election. But such was the success of Howard and Costello on a macro level and the late Ron Boswell on the ground arguing against One Nation that they were able to basically neutralise One Nation as a political force. But a large part of that was that under the Howard government at the time, wage growth was around 24.6% and interest rates generally fell one or two points or more every year. And so there wasn't as much grievance in the electorate because people were quite happy. And the greatest measurement of that is we always ask a diagnostic test. Do you think Australia is heading in the right direction or the wrong direction? Now, I remember polling in 2007, the right direction was 65%. 65% of Australians said we're heading in the right direction. And the most recent poll we did for the Fin Review, 54% said we're heading in the wrong direction. So there's been a significant shift over the last 19 years in people's assessments of how the country is travelling, and that's building the grievance. And that is why One Nation is able to identify that grievance and speak to that grievance. Sam Hawley: And it's got hold of the narrative and it's driving it, right? And that counts for a lot. That's what every political party wants to do. Tony Barry: Exactly. Exactly. You want to control the microphone because you get to drive the narrative and the opposition typically responds. But Hanson is in the position where in some cases she actually drives the narrative and the government is responding and the opposition is responding.

title: Guilt and isolation: Genocide survivors on adjusting to life in Australia - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: The United Nations calls them "the most persecuted minority in the world", but now 10 years on from a genocide, members of the Rohingya people are rebuilding in Australia. The Rohingya, a Muslim ethnic group, have lived in mainly Buddhist Myanmar for centuries, where they have suffered killings, forced evictions and other atrocities. As the community in Australia continues to grow, some live in constant fear about the state of their loved ones who remain abroad. In 2017, the Myanmar military marched into northern Rakhine — a Rohingya territory — beginning a sustained campaign of violence, forcing more than 700,000 people to flee for nearby Bangladesh. Saddam Hossain was one of them, escaping over the Bangladeshi border amidst the chaos. President of the Rohingya United Youth Network and community spokesperson Robi Alam translated for Mr Hossain as he described to the ABC how Myanmar's military surrounded his village in 2017. "They started attacking anyone, shooting everywhere," he said. Concerned for his cows, Mr Hossain went to release them so they could escape, putting himself in the firing line in the process. "When [I] was cutting the rope to release the cows [I] was shot on [my] right upper thigh and by the time [I] was looking to see the wound … [I] had got another two shots on [my] left thigh," the translator said. The family escaped to a nearby village, but after three days with badly injured legs and no medical treatment, they decided to flee the region. "Usually ... to go to the borderline, it takes about an hour on transport," Mr Alam said. "It took them seven days, because two people had to carry him." Finally canoeing into Bangladesh, Mr Hossain found himself at the refugee camp in the port city Cox's Bazar, which has become home to more than one million stateless Rohingyas. After four years in and out of the camp's hospital, Mr Hossain secured a UN humanitarian visa and joined a Rohingya community in Australia, which advocates estimate is made up of about 5,000 people. Despite his new home, Mr Hossain said the pain hasn't gone away. "[I feel] that … [I look] alive on the outside … [I don't] feel that on the inside at all," Mr Hossain said. Mr Hossain is thankful that he is now in a place where he can express his suffering, and grateful to his wife for taking care of him. But after losing his father and two uncles, he is still concerned for his brother, who remains in the Bangladesh camp. "What he wants is for the Australian community to know about the injustice against his family and community, and he wants justice," Mr Alam said. Fears for family still in camp Shofika Begum also came to Australia on a humanitarian visa after spending time in the Bangladesh camp, and remembers her family being killed when the military surrounded her village Arakan in 2017. She said she was forced to watch her sister's murder. "She had this sort of valuable hijab, and they took it off from her and just smashed her skull with that thing," Mr Alam said, translating for Ms Begum. "And she doesn't remember anything afterwards." Now safe in Australia, Ms Begum shares Mr Hossain's fears for those left behind. "She's got one more sister in the camp, two brothers [also in the camp] and two brothers in Malaysia," Mr Alam said. "And she's just very worried for them because they're still not receiving any sort of help." While Ms Begum is grateful her children won't grow up in perpetual fear, the mental scars from her ordeal remain. "[I] can't sleep at night, [I] feel that [my] mum is right next to [me]. [I] feel that [my] sister is playing next to [me]," she said. "There's just so much in [my] head." Speaking out to keep identify alive Mr Alam was born in the Bangladesh refugee camp, and after 10 years his family came to Australia as part of the humanitarian assistance program. He started community work when he was 14 or 15 and hears stories like Mr Hossain's and Ms Begum's "almost on a daily basis". "Every Rohingya that we meet has stories like this and it's getting to a point where it's normalised and sometimes you just get so dehumanised that … your emotions don't react as it should after hearing such horrific stuff because of how normal it is in our community," he said. "It just breaks you and sometimes you feel hopeless. "But you also know that you've got to do something, and you just can't stand still." Mr Alam said he didn't want to see the community lose its identity. "The most fundamental thing for me is, and a lot of Rohingya people feel this, is that because of the genocide that our community has been going through over the last four or five decades, we feel that our identity is almost becoming extinct," he said. "That's why it's a strong sense of responsibility for me to be able to do whatever I can in my capacity, because we don't want to lose who we are as a community. "And I don't want to lose who I am as a Rohingya as well." The Rohingya community is hosting a Genocide Remembrance Day event later today in Kingston in Logan, organised by community organisations Rohingya United Youth Network, Australia Rohingya Council, Burmese Rohingya Association in Queensland and Rohingya Community of Queensland.

title: Inside Papua New Guinea's secret political refugee crisis - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: Each election cycle in PNG sparks conflicts and tribal violence leading to mass displacement of thousands of people around Papua New Guinea, but especially in the highlands. You'll hear from a journalist who borne witness to this violence, a human rights advocate walking alongside the refugees, and a police commissioner trying to negotiate peace. Talent: Rebecca Kuku, PNG Journalist Ruth Kissam, President Advancing PNG Women Leaders Joseph Tondop, Acting Assistant Police Commissioner Highlands Western End Presenter: Scott Waide This edition of Politok was a repeat of the program broadcast on the 6th of May 2025 Credits Image Details Scott Waide: Election time in Papua New Guinea is tense and chaotic. News clip: Escalating violence has engulfed the Papua New Guinea elections with reports of up to 18 people being killed in the Enga Highlands. Scott Waide: Millions of people in more than 20 provinces turn out to vote, but it's not always free and not always fair. Rebecca Kuku: We literally saw kids voting and there was no privacy, like you couldn't just cast your vote. All the scrutineers of candidates that were contesting would stand at the ballot, where the ballot box was and where you were supposed to vote. And they would all see you put that mark. Scott Waide: In 2022, journalist Rebecca Kuku was in the highlands of Papua New Guinea, in Enga and Hela provinces, reporting as voting chaos turned to terror. Rebecca Kuku: So it was very scary. There was no law. There was no respect for law. They didn't follow the election laws. Scott Waide: In the highlands, tribal rivalries have people on edge and ownership of illegal guns is on the rise. And when election comes around, this can mix quickly and turn deadly. Rebecca Kuku: During the election, one tribe supported one candidate and the other tribe supported the other candidate. All the supporters of the candidates were there, fully armed, you know, sweaty. You could just feel the tension in the air. Scott Waide: Hi, I'm Scott Waide and this is Politok, a show taking you behind the scenes of Pacific politics and how it affects us. Over the coming episodes, I'll be speaking with politicians from across the Pacific region and with everyday people about the political experiences that shape us. I'll uncover the stories and unpack the big questions. Today on PoliTalk, every election cycle in Papua New Guinea, thousands of people are displaced and many are killed. And I want to know why this keeps happening and why isn't anyone talking about it? And a warning, this episode contains mention of sexual violence. Rebecca Kuku has seen it all. She's an experienced journalist in Papua New Guinea and she's reported on everything from dodgy politicians to sorcery accusations. But even still, in 2022, while reporting on that year's election, she was shocked at what she saw. Rebecca Kuku: So the 2022 elections was crazy. We literally saw kids voting. There was no privacy, like you couldn't just cast your vote. All the scrutineers of candidates that were contesting would stand at the ballot, where the ballot box was and where you were supposed to vote. And they would all see you put that mark so they can record it on their books. Scott Waide: Across many parts of the country, chaos reigned. There were delays to polling schedules, ballot boxes weren't arriving on time, and there were allegations of vote buying. The mistrust in the process, coupled with underlying tribal tensions, saw buildings burn to the ground and women and children massacred. Rebecca Kuku: It was really frustrating to see all the stuff that happens during the elections. We just had to stand there and watch them do whatever they wanted to do. Scott Waide: Rebecca, violence during election time is common because there's a level of distrust in the government and the election process. But you were in the highlands where there's also a big link between tribal violence that bleeds into election time. How does that link work? Rebecca Kuku: So, for example, let's talk about Poguera. So in Poguera, there's an existing tribal fight there. Between about 20 to 25 clans break it down into four tribes or three tribes, and they have this land dispute tribal fight that was already there. So when the election came about, it just, it just added up again. During the election, one tribe supported one candidate and the other tribe supported the other candidate. And then it just led into an all-out war again, tribal war. So there were about, I think, over 20 clans clashed. And people were displaced and a lot of families, especially the public servants that were serving in Poguera, like doctors and service teachers, they had to get their families and they had to get out of there. They had to travel in the night back to Hagan to find refuge. And those that couldn't afford to travel or didn't have any relatives in Hagan that they could stay with just went into the bushes and they were living in the bushes. Scott Waide: What triggers the violent outbreaks during elections? Rebecca Kuku: Most of the fights broke up during the ballot box picking. There was tension, there were arguments, there were a few fistfights and all that during the campaign period and during when the ballot box was inserted into the voting areas. But the fights broke up when officials went in to pick up the ballot boxes. In some cases they bent ballot boxes and in other cases they didn't want people to vote and they just hijacked ballot boxes. Scott Waide: In the 2022 election, the United Nations estimated that 90,000 people were displaced because of the violence that broke out. When people in the highlands had to flee, what did that look like? Rebecca Kuku: The mothers and the children, especially the old, they would go up into the mountains and they'd hide in the bushes. There was no way for them, they couldn't seek refuge anywhere. So the only thing they did at the time was to hide in the bushes. And those who had intermarriages close by villages in Anga, they went there to seek refuge. But even so, when they went to seek refuge in the nearby villages, it was very difficult for them. When you go into someone else's territory, they got bullied again. So it was very hard, especially for the girls. There were so many girls that were sexually abused, assaulted and there was nothing done about it. There was no justice sought for them. Scott Waide: The violence and the displacement comes during election time can have a huge impact on children in particular. Is there a story about how it's affected children that stuck with you? Rebecca Kuku: So one of those stories that I heard that really left an impression on me was how a young boy tried to save his mom. So the father was a supporter of a candidate. He was very vocal in supporting him. So the other candidates, supporters, they went to their house and they burned down their house. They pulled women and girls and this little six-year-old boy took his mom and they went up into the bushes and he hid his mom up in the bushes. That was very tough to see that a child so used to the violence knew what to do and how to protect his mother because the father wasn't there. There have also been stories of school children that were raped during the election violence, especially girls in high school, secondary schools, who were just caught up in between them. I mean, from going to school and coming back, some of them were caught up in the election violence and they were sexually assaulted, but nothing was ever done about it because it was just chaos out there and police had their hands full. All these young girls, they were just assaulted. Scott Waide: In the media, there are lots of headlines and reporting about tribal violence, but there isn't a lot of coverage of election violence and the displacement that comes with it. Why is that? Rebecca Kuku: Well, it's very sad because most of the stories don't get published. It doesn't get the coverage it needs to be in order to raise that issue. In PNG, because of the most of these people that were displaced, they just go on to live with relatives or go on to live with their in-laws from the nearby villages. And despite the challenges they face there, they have nowhere else to go. So they just stay and make a new place their home. It's been very tough trying to get those stories out. Scott Waide: The picture Rebecca paints is of a crisis that's being swept under the rug. Tens of thousands of people, families, women and children must flee their homes, their customary land, every time there's an election because of tribal tensions and a distrust of the electoral system. There's also the growing threat of illegal firearms, adding fuel to a raging fire. And for decades, Ruth Kisam has been trying to put that fire out. Ruth Kissam: I'm Ruth Kisam. I call myself a community organizer, human rights activist, but I am currently the president of the Advancing PNG Women Leaders Network, an amazing network of community-based organization across 15 provinces. Scott Waide: Ruth is a peace-building activist, and over the course of her career, she's stood by the side of women and families in the region, advocating for an end to violence. Ruth Kissam: You don't set out to be a peace-builder, but your work actually draws you into it. Scott Waide: Ruth is from the Highlands in Enga province. She's also well-known for her work around sorcery accusation-related violence, which began after a chance encounter at a hospital. Ruth Kissam: I ended up at the hospital, taking my dad to the hospital, and then I saw this notice that was put up on the notice board, followed the prompt on the notice board to claim a body that was unclaimed for some time, and then claiming the body and burying her, later finding out that she was killed on accusations of sorcery. Fast forward three years later, I found out that she had a daughter, and the daughter was also tortured on accusations of sorcery. So that also now sort of dragged me into it after the rescue, and I basically took my work home, and my work is my daughter. So I have a vested interest now, it's a personal one, to be in this space and to do what I do. Scott Waide: Ruth, you witnessed firsthand the election violence that happened in 2022. What was it like for you? Ruth Kissam: It was one of the worst elections that I've ever witnessed, and it caused a lot of displacement when people started turning violent. All villages, all tribes were wiped off their land. Even to this day, there's people that have not even gone back to their homes, and they're living in other provinces. They've set up camps in other provinces. What land in other provinces? Mosby has some of those, Leah has some of those, Hagen has most of those. So people are living internally in Papua New Guinea as refugees within the country. Scott Waide: Can you explain how tribal allegiances influences elections? Ruth Kissam: The interesting thing about politics in Papua New Guinea is no one is interested in policies, because it becomes a tribal matter. So people will affiliate with you because of their tribal affiliation, or in other parts, yes, it's your policy, but it's also your party affiliation. So it's more along the lines of who I know than what I want to know about that person. If I know that person, if I know someone that knows him, then I will align with him. And from my experience, especially up in the highlands where I'm from, it's always to do with how your tribe is linked to this person or your family. Unfortunately, in these circumstances, a lot of people that are running for elections usually go by their rest houses or where the polling booths are. So if this person has about two or three polling booths in his tribal land, now they don't care about the ward or the LLGs. For them, it's how they're affiliated to a tribe, whether it's from their mother's side or their father's side. And if that's the case, then the ballot boxes are there. So then it usually ends up being a tribal block vote. Scott Waide: And how did you see this play out in the 2022 elections? Ruth Kissam: One classic example is one up in the recent 2022 elections up in the Ambon-Kompiem district where it pretty much affected the whole of Enger province was what they call the seven in one. So seven tribes actually ganged up against one tribe because of displacement happening well over 8,000, 9,000 people simply because of tribal affiliation. So the displacement is coming about because of tribal affiliation. Those elections are now proving to be the triggers. So once the elections are coming about, sometimes it resurfaces old tribal wars. Scott Waide: Although the 2022 election was bad, election violence happens every time people go out to vote. How have you seen this kind of violence impact people over the years? Ruth Kissam: So one of the stories of a family member, a family that I married into. So back in 2012, a house was burned, election related. She rebuilt it. 2017, the house got burned. She rebuilt it. 2022, the house got burnt again. All of the times the house got burnt was not a tribal fight. It was election related. So this is a woman that was highly traumatized. But in 2022, she had her granddaughters with her, two granddaughters. I think one was five and I think the other one was three or something. They actually ended up at a creek and not only herself, but she and other women as well. And this creek actually housed them for two or three nights, three days. They couldn't even get out. They couldn't move around because people were rampaging through their village, burning down, killing, mutilating people and raping women and children. So for them was that they just, and they survived by the creek, you know, drinking from the water, just not going anywhere because that was the only place that they could find refuge. And then they walked for another day or so just to reach safety. Now, this is just one and this is a woman in her late 50s, early 60s. And that's just one. You can imagine what's happening with others, women and children. For some, the mother said she couldn't find her daughter, later found out that the daughter drowned while trying to cross the big river. And she wasn't the only one. Others also. Scott Waide: Thousands of people flee this violence each time there's an election and these political refugees are moving to other provinces, other tribal lands. What's the experience like for them? Ruth Kissam: So, you know, the thing about internally displacement of people is culture plays also a very critical role. In a culture like Gela, they'll never even get a branch from another tribal land without permission for firewood. So when people are internally displaced and given refuge by another tribe, they can only get what is allowed to them. They will not get anything that is not allowed to them. So when they don't have food, when they don't have water and all of that, it makes it really hard. So now they will have to look for something better for themselves. So people will now, because they need to be able to access health, will start to move. Likewise with schools, parents will start to move if the school closes down because of the threat of violence or because of violence. People will now start to move in order to look for better options for their children. What are the consequences of the internal displacement that is happening on other provinces that they're going to? The strain on education, the strain on health, the strain on all the other services. When people in bulk move from one area to another without proper coordination, without proper facilitation by authorities, you can now drive in cities like Port Moresby. And you'll see families sleeping on the sidewalk. It never used to be like this before. Where are they coming from? Where are these people coming from? A lot of them are, like I said earlier, they're leaving their tribal lands because they cannot be able to survive on their tribal lands. They have no other place to go within that province. Scott Waide: And what role do you think politicians play in all of this? Ruth Kissam: So when that happens and then it causes displacement, it's incumbent on them to look for any way possible to bring peace back into the land. It will not be easy, but then that's what leaders are for. We vote you whether or not our tribe wiped out your tribe, it doesn't matter. When it comes to resettling people, everyone is your constituent. And because of that, the mandate is yours to make sure your people go back. raw_text: A big part of the problem with housing in Australia, and the rest of the economy, is a slow-moving collision that began under the Howard government between the regulation of housing and the effective deregulation of migration in the early 2000s.
