The NCC then picked up new EV rules, with a requirement that buildings accommodate electric vehicle charging, and tightened wet-weather details such as a minimum 15mm freeboard height for valley gutters. Adding to this was the simultaneous growth of land use zoning and planning regulations at the state level, with no connection to national housing supply needs or construction feasibility. On top of that was progressive deregulation and a complete lack of control over temporary migration, which has resulted in 2,807,322 temporary migrants currently living in Australia — a million more than five years ago — while construction productivity and the size of the construction workforce have sunk to record lows. The crisis was inevitable. Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That’s Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor. title: NSW Premier Chris Minns tells Indian community 'we've got your back' on first official visit - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The NSW premier's first day of his trade mission to India included a visit to the Asha community centre and the official launch of Western Sydney University's India campus. At the centre, he met young people who had grown up in poverty in Delhi, describing his visit as a "humbling" experience. He said the Indian community was "hugely important" for the future of NSW. The premier says the New South Wales Indian community should feel proud of its contribution to the state, despite continued debate about Australia's immigration numbers. On the first day of his official visit to India, Chris Minns met young people who had grown up in poverty in Delhi only to be accepted into Australian universities. They included 22-year-old Madhu. "I'm from a south Delhi slum. My home is a one-room home," she said. "We don't have a proper kitchen and toilet [so] we have to go to the public toilet." Madhu said nobody from her family had left India before. However, next year she will begin a master's degree in public health at the University of Sydney, thanks to support from the Asha society, which offers health and education opportunities to some of Delhi's poorest children. "It will change my whole future and my whole family's future as well," Madhu said. "I will help my community to grow … and do something good in their life." The premier said his visit to the Asha community centre was a "humbling" experience. "[It's] one I don't think I'll ever forget," he said. "There is a real strength of character and dignity within those communities, even though they're doing it incredibly tough." Mr Minns, who joined some of the children for a game of street cricket, said he hoped the recent debate about student visas would not affect Australia's reputation as a welcoming destination. "We need to make sure that education, which is the second-biggest export industry in New South Wales … is open, warm and acknowledges the economic benefits for our community," he said. Earlier this year, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson called for an Australian "monoculture", saying multiculturalism had failed. While the premier said he would not use the trip to rebuke One Nation, he would seek to highlight the benefits Indian migrants brought to their communities. "I want to make Indian-Australians proud of the relationship," he said. "The New South Wales government and its leadership has got their back. "We believe they're hugely important for our future and we think that they're proud Aussies who love our country." A piece of Western Sydney in India The premier, and Treasurer Daniel Mookhey, also officially launched a new India campus for Western Sydney University. The facility is still being built in Uttar Pradesh, but will start taking students in February next year, with a focus on agricultural technology, sustainability and business administration. The Vice-Chancellor George Williams said the university was committed to "admitting students from all backgrounds, on merit". "We want this campus to be accessible to the best and brightest in India," he said. However, the university's ability to accept foreign students at its Australian campuses could be affected by looming changes to Australia's immigration system. The number of student visas increased from 383,910 in 2017 to 528,999 this year, according to the Department of Home Affairs. One Nation has already vowed to slash student visa numbers and the federal government is now considering tweaking eligibility settings to bring Australia's overall immigration intake down. Professor Williams warned that reducing foreign student numbers would have negative consequences for the state's economy. "If you're in aged care, there's a good chance it's a Nepalese student," he said. "If you're blood's being taken in Western Sydney, there's a good chance it's a Filipino international student who studied at Western Sydney University." The construction industry was also heavily reliant on foreign students, he said. "We depend on international students for our prosperity and I'd love to have a debate that actually started with recognising their contributions," he said.

title: Labor was poised to reveal massive migration cuts, then suddenly delayed - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has postponed a scheduled appearance at the National Press Club. He was set to unveil sweeping cuts to migration, which the ABC understands were internally contentious. What's next? The speech is to be rescheduled. A spokesperson for the minister said the decision was made because some details would not be finalised in time. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has postponed a speech at the National Press Club where he was expected to unveil far-reaching changes to Australia's migration settings in a bid to quell public anger and growing support for One Nation. Mr Burke was due to appear tomorrow but withdrew yesterday afternoon. A government source said the speech would be rescheduled in the near future. A spokesperson for the minister told the ABC the speech would "deal with the migration system as a whole". "Yesterday it became clear that some elements of the speech would not be finalised by Thursday. We're working with the press club to find a new date," the spokesperson said. Three sources familiar with the government's thinking told the ABC the minister had been preparing a package of measures to achieve a quick and drastic cut to net migration. It is understood the proposal was considered by cabinet on Monday. Among the measures canvassed were tougher family visa rules, a cap on the number of backpackers in the country and restrictions on the work and appeal rights of asylum seekers. Several sources said internal deliberations had been highly contentious. One senior government source downplayed the extent of internal disagreements and said the elements that were yet to be finalised were minor, but confirmed that the changes would be wide-ranging and designed to give the government greater control over net migration figures. The government has endured sustained criticism from One Nation and the Coalition since a post-pandemic spike in net migration, which exceeded half a million people in 2023. That figure tracks arrivals and departures of both Australians and migrants. The spike was caused in part by a glut of demand which had accumulated during the pandemic, when migration was effectively halted, and also because of pandemic-era measures to encourage migrants who were already in Australia to stay for longer. Before the 2025 federal election, the Albanese government moved to restrict international student numbers. Net overseas migration has fallen to just over 300,000 on the latest figures, but has repeatedly exceeded Treasury projections. Net migration is hard for governments to control because most of the temporary visa categories are driven by demand and not formally limited. Many of the policy suggestions understood to form part of Mr Burke's package would give the government more control over that number, at least in the short term. Quiet changes leading up to speech Last month, Mr Burke quietly made a series of changes likely to further reduce net migration. They included a substantial across-the-board increase in visa application fees, which was never formally announced but seems to have been decided in the early months of this year, and took effect on July 1. Budget papers published in May showed the budget would collect an extra $1.2 billion in visa fees this financial year alone, compared to what had been forecast in the December mid-year budget update, and equating to an increase of 24 per cent. Mr Burke also made two ministerial directives, ordering officials to prioritise onshore applicants over offshore applicants for permanent skilled and family visas. There were limited exceptions for those working in law enforcement and defence. The direction to prioritise one pile of applicants over another is a similar strategy to the one the government deployed to reduce the number of international students. Given the large backlog of applications, it effectively amounts to a short-term pause for applicants who are de-prioritised, which would in turn reduce the number of overseas arrivals. Further sweeping changes expected Mr Burke's proposed reform package was also expected to prevent the spouses, children and parents of Australian citizens and permanent residents from applying for family visas while they are in the country as tourists. This has been a common approach for many families seeking to stay together in Australia while they wait for their permanent visas to be approved. Australian law requires that permanent family visas be granted to all those who apply, provided they meet the criteria. But the number of applicants far exceeds the number of permanent visas the government allocates each year, creating a years-long backlog. Partners who apply while they are tourists are typically moved onto bridging visas while they wait, granting them the right to work and access Medicare. If this avenue were removed, they would have to wait overseas until their permanent visas were processed, and may also have their applications de-prioritised under the recent ministerial directive. Also expected was a restriction on the rights of humanitarian visa applicants to work while their claims were assessed, and to appeal rejections of their claims. A similar proposal has been floated by the Coalition and One Nation, premised on a longstanding concern that some migrants make false asylum claims so that they can work in Australia while those claims are processed and repeatedly appealed. Mr Burke was also expected to reveal details of how the government planned to expand the use of lotteries for working holiday-makers, as flagged in the May budget papers. Lotteries are already used for applicants from China, India and Vietnam, but one source said the government was considering caps on backpackers from all countries who sought to extend their stay into a second or third year. Currently, eligible backpackers can extend their stay if they complete a regional work placement, although British backpackers no longer have to do this. It is unclear whether the government plans to change that preferential arrangement. Energy Minister Chris Bowen will address the press club on Wednesday, the day before Mr Burke was scheduled to appear. It is unclear whether the delay relates to internal disagreement over what Mr Burke was planning to announce, but the ABC understands the final content of the speech has not been settled. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese returns from leave on Thursday. A senior government source said the remaining concerns were over "fine details", with risks that those seeking to exploit loopholes in any migration changes would be advantaged if the speech was made with any element not yet airtight. One Nation and the Coalition have both declared their intention to drastically reduce net migration if elected. The story has been updated to clarify this applies only to partners and that work rights and Medicare access are granted at that point, not retained. Loading...

That figure tracks arrivals and departures of both Australians and migrants. The spike was caused in part by a glut of demand which had accumulated during the pandemic, when migration was effectively halted, and also because of pandemic-era measures to encourage migrants who were already in Australia to stay for longer. Before the 2025 federal election, the Albanese government moved to restrict international student numbers. Net overseas migration has fallen to just over 300,000 on the latest figures, but has repeatedly exceeded Treasury projections. Net migration is hard for governments to control because most of the temporary visa categories are driven by demand and not formally limited. Many of the policy suggestions understood to form part of Mr Burke's package would give the government more control over that number, at least in the short term. Quiet changes leading up to speech Last month, Mr Burke quietly made a series of changes likely to further reduce net migration. They included a substantial across-the-board increase in visa application fees, which was never formally announced but seems to have been decided in the early months of this year, and took effect on July 1. Budget papers published in May showed the budget would collect an extra $1.2 billion in visa fees this financial year alone, compared to what had been forecast in the December mid-year budget update, and equating to an increase of 24 per cent. Mr Burke also made two ministerial directives, ordering officials to prioritise onshore applicants over offshore applicants for permanent skilled and family visas. There were limited exceptions for those working in law enforcement and defence. The direction to prioritise one pile of applicants over another is a similar strategy to the one the government deployed to reduce the number of international students. Given the large backlog of applications, it effectively amounts to a short-term pause for applicants who are de-prioritised, which would in turn reduce the number of overseas arrivals. Further sweeping changes expected Mr Burke's proposed reform package was also expected to prevent the spouses, children and parents of Australian citizens and permanent residents from applying for family visas while they are in the country as tourists. This has been a common approach for many families seeking to stay together in Australia while they wait for their permanent visas to be approved. Australian law requires that permanent family visas be granted to all those who apply, provided they meet the criteria. But the number of applicants far exceeds the number of permanent visas the government allocates each year, creating a years-long backlog. Partners who apply while they are tourists are typically moved onto bridging visas while they wait, granting them the right to work and access Medicare. If this avenue were removed, they would have to wait overseas until their permanent visas were processed, and may also have their applications de-prioritised under the recent ministerial directive. Also expected was a restriction on the rights of humanitarian visa applicants to work while their claims were assessed, and to appeal rejections of their claims. A similar proposal has been floated by the Coalition and One Nation, premised on a longstanding concern that some migrants make false asylum claims so that they can work in Australia while those claims are processed and repeatedly appealed. Mr Burke was also expected to reveal details of how the government planned to expand the use of lotteries for working holiday-makers, as flagged in the May budget papers. Lotteries are already used for applicants from China, India and Vietnam, but one source said the government was considering caps on backpackers from all countries who sought to extend their stay into a second or third year. Currently, eligible backpackers can extend their stay if they complete a regional work placement, although British backpackers no longer have to do this. It is unclear whether the government plans to change that preferential arrangement. Energy Minister Chris Bowen will address the press club on Wednesday, the day before Mr Burke was scheduled to appear. It is unclear whether the delay relates to internal disagreement over what Mr Burke was planning to announce, but the ABC understands the final content of the speech has not been settled. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese returns from leave on Thursday. A senior government source said the remaining concerns were over "fine details", with risks that those seeking to exploit loopholes in any migration changes would be advantaged if the speech was made with any element not yet airtight. One Nation and the Coalition have both declared their intention to drastically reduce net migration if elected. The story has been updated to clarify this applies only to partners and that work rights and Medicare access are granted at that point, not retained. Loading...

title: Licence loss, fines for companies hosting migrants in shoddy housing - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The Victorian Labour Hire Authority has tightened regulation of businesses that provide accommodation for their workers. Labour hire providers that do not comply with standards could lose their licence and face fines of more than $160,000. What's next? Migrant advocacy groups hope the rules can be applied in other states and territories. Labour hire companies that house migrant workers in substandard accommodation will risk losing their licence as part of a new crackdown. The Victorian Labour Hire Authority has launched new licence conditions after a series of cases in which migrant workers were housed in poor conditions. The authority, which works to prevent the exploitation of labour hire workers, brought in the conditions for businesses that provide housing for their workers. The conditions have been put in place for providers in industries such as horticulture and meat processing, which have high rates of worker exploitation. In addition to losing their licences, businesses that do not comply face fines of more than $160,000. The authority's director of intelligence, compliance and enforcement Erin Barlow said the changes were aimed at protecting vulnerable workers. "We know that when accommodation is tied to employment, workers can feel unable to complain because they can be fearful of losing both their job and their housing," she said. "These workers are especially vulnerable to exploitation." Ms Barlow said the new conditions were in response to substandard worker accommodation the authority had seen. In December 2025, the authority found 22 migrant workers were housed in unsanitary conditions in a single home and a granny flat in Gippsland. The accommodation in Warragul, about an hour east of Melbourne, had sewage pooling in the front yard and black mould covering doors, windows, ceilings and curtains. "In that case, we saw some of the worst accommodation that we had experienced," Ms Barlow said. "Providers can expect to see us out and about inspecting that accommodation more now that we are introducing these conditions. "Accommodation is a clear focus for the Labour Hire Authority in the next year." 'Not fit for an animal' Migrant Justice Institute co-executive director Bassina Farbenblum has welcomed the change. "We've seen for a long time that migrant workers are subjected to really appalling accommodation," she said. "It's terrific to see that the Victorian Labour Hire Authority is now ramping up. "The proof will be how well it is enforced. Hopefully we will see really strict enforcement." Ms Farbenblum said living in unhygienic and overcrowded accommodation was "incredibly demeaning". "We've heard from many migrant workers … the ability to sleep and function is diminished, there's issues with privacy and especially for women there are real safety issues. "I had one migrant worker describe [their accommodation] as 'not fit for an animal'," she said. "I'd hope that other states like New South Wales will follow and that we will start to see a real shift in the impunity of labour higher providers that don't provide habitable, decent accommodation to vulnerable migrants." Industry backs new conditions Victorian Farmers Federation horticulture president Michael Crisera said the change was a good step for the industry. "We're definitely supportive of improving conditions for our workers," he said. "Any industries with labour hire involved definitely need some more compliance." Mr Crisera said there needed to be education for labour hire providers about what the standards were, as well as education for workers. "Everybody needs to play a part in making sure that it's a win-win for the staff and also for the farmer," he said. Accommodation standards already existed but sat with other bodies, such as local councils and Consumer Affairs Victoria. The standards are now a part of some labour hire licence conditions, which allows the Labour Hire Authority to take action against businesses that do not comply. The conditions are being applied to new labour hire licences in the horticulture, meat and poultry processing, commercial cleaning, and security industries and will be rolled out to existing licence holders in those sectors in coming months.

title: PM rules out British backpackers being forced to work in regions - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The government was considering imposing regional work requirements on British backpackers to make the scheme less attractive in a bid to bring down migration numbers. The prime minister has publicly poured cold water on that idea, heading off a diplomatic stoush. What's next? No date has been set for the government to unveil its changes in migration policy after Tony Burke postponed a National Press Club address earlier this month. The prime minister has vowed not to make British backpackers work in regional areas as part of a looming migration overhaul, defusing a potential diplomatic stoush with the United Kingdom. British citizens on Working Holiday Maker, or backpacker, visas are allowed to live in Australia for up to three years without any specific work requirements under a free trade deal which came into force in 2023. Working holiday makers from all other countries must work in regional or remote areas to have their visas extended beyond a year. The favourable treatment has led to a steep increase in the number of UK backpackers coming to Australia, up from 47,238 in 2023/24 to 79,412 in 2024/25 according to Home Affairs data. Under pressure to clamp down on temporary visas and reduce overseas arrivals, the government was considering a plan to impose regional work requirements on British backpackers to make the scheme less attractive. But some in the government were concerned that would clearly breach the free trade agreement between Australia and the United Kingdom at a time when the government had positioned itself as an international champion for trade rules. Anthony Albanese quashed the proposal on Wednesday afternoon, ruling out any changes to the deal. "The UK situation is a separate agreement as a result of the UK free trade agreement which we are certainly honouring," Mr Albanese said. He intervened not long after UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on the sidelines of a Five Eyes meeting in Sydney. After that meeting, Mr Burke did not deny the issue had been canvassed. "We talk regularly about all migration issues, about the issues we are managing in each of our countries," Mr Burke told reporters in Sydney. "In terms of anything coming forward, as to any changes we'd made to the migration program, those are decisions that would be made by the Australian cabinet." The possible change to UK arrangements was one of several under consideration as part of a wider crackdown on immigration which Mr Burke was due to announce three weeks ago before being forced to postpone. No new date has been set for the policy announcement, which is designed to ensure Labor meets its own target of cutting net overseas migration (NOM) from the current 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028. Backpackers are a significant contributor to the NOM with a record 321,116 visas being issued last year, up from 234,556 the year before. Mr Burke last month paused the processing of applications from 24 countries including Argentina, Chile, Spain, Poland, Thailand and Malaysia, and pushed workers applying for overseas skilled visas to the back of the queue. "The processing of backpacker visas across the entire program is happening more slowly than it was," Mr Burke said. "And similarly there are changes we've made to the permanent program in preferencing, at the moment, onshore positions rather than offshore." The far-reaching directive is designed to stop, or dramatically slow, the number of overseas arrivals but has created an enormous amount of confusion and concern within the business, hospitality and tourism sectors which rely on migrant workers. As one business figure told the ABC, "everything has ground to a halt". One Nation and the Coalition are promising dramatic cuts to migration, but both have ruled out any cuts to backpacker visas given their popularity in regional areas.

title: Country cafe mounting costly battle to retain beloved barista - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short A country cafe is desperate to keep a Taiwanese traveller in town, but Australia's migration pathways are proving challenging. Balingup cafe owner Brian Foster says the costs of securing a temporary skilled migration visa are prohibitively high. What's next? The federal government has foreshadowed plans for sweeping migration changes to further reduce net overseas migration. A cafe owner in southern Western Australia is facing an increasingly expensive battle to retain a valued worker amid uncertainty over the federal government's pending changes to the migration system. Penny Hung has become part of the fabric in Balingup, about 231 kilometres south of Perth. The town has a population of about 560 people and is thousands of kilometres from Ms Hung's home in Taiwan. She has become a mainstay employee at one of the few cafes around, where she works as an all-rounder. "I think for my personality, I prefer the country life," she said. "Balingup is very special; people here are very caring. "It's very hard work to try to stay here." Keeping qualified staff 'impossible' Cafe owner Brian Foster said Ms Hung was a core part of the cafe, filling an important role in a town where it was hard to secure long-term hospitality employees. "Keeping qualified people is impossible," he said. "Penny's done so much training over the years, and she's an integral part of the business, and she wants to stay here." Mr Foster said he had begun the process of applying to sponsor Ms Hung, but the processing costs and minimum salary rate made it prohibitively expensive for a small business. It comes as the government moves to reduce net overseas migration, shifting its priorities for onshore visa applicants from skilled workers in regional communities to law enforcement and defence. Balingup is about a 10-minute drive from the world's largest hard-rock lithium mine, Greenbushes, where Talison Lithium employs more than 1,500 people. "Why would you work in a cafe in a village like this when you can earn that sort of money?" Mr Foster said. "It's hard keeping staff when you're competing with something like that." Ms Hung is working to secure a solution so she can remain in Australia long term, having already used her working holiday visa. Pay thresholds increasing In 2023, the Australian government increased the threshold employers have to pay sponsored employees for the first time in about a decade, from $53,900 to $70,000. Since then, the threshold has risen further to $79,423. Under the South West Designated Area Migration Agreement (DAMA), some concessions are offered to the threshold, as well as concessions for minimum standards of English or skills and experience. That agreement is due to expire in December. If Mr Foster were able to secure a concession under the DAMA, the minimum salary rate would be about $71,480. "When the original income was about $50,000, that was very doable for a small business," he said. "It's a bit of a kick in the guts as far as immigration goes and sponsorship." Sponsorships 'expensive' South West migration agent Maaike van der Zon said the increases to minimum salaries for sponsored employees in recent years had been significant. "It's very difficult for some people to find sponsorship because it is too expensive or the salary level is just too high and especially for regional businesses," she said. A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson told the ABC that skilled visa income thresholds were indexed annually, in line with average weekly earnings. "Indexation of income thresholds reduces risk of exploitation of skilled migrants, which could occur if there is a lack of wage growth and greater gaps between their wages and those of Australian workers," they said. The full details of the government's looming overhaul of the migration system are not yet known, but the spokesperson said the latest ministerial direction would prioritise onshore applicants in order to retain migrants already contributing to communities. "Under the new Ministerial Direction 119, employer sponsors in regional Australia in healthcare, education and now construction retain priority processing for applicants who are in Australia," they said. Ms van der Zon said while a move to prioritise onshore applicants was welcome news for skilled migrants in Australia, she wanted to understand the impact on visa processing times. "At the moment we're looking at seven, eight, nine months for those particular visas to be processed which are only temporary skilled visas," she said. "We don't know yet where processing times are heading even with this new ministerial direction where they say they're prioritising onshore applications. "We still have to see if that's really going to make an impact on visa applications that are currently in the system."

title: One Nation MP leaves door open to slashing citizens' family visas - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: One Nation MP David Farley says his party is open to cutting visas for family members of Australian citizens. On Monday, One Nation unveiled its policy to reduce Australia's temporary migration intake by 750,000 people over three years, including a ban on families of temporary skilled workers and international students. What's next? Mr Farley said One Nation had commissioned "extensive" economic modelling of its migration plan and would reveal more of the party's immigration strategy. One Nation MP David Farley has left the door open to "potentially" cutting visas for family members of Australian citizens, as the party prepares to reveal more details of its immigration plan within coming weeks. Mr Farley said whether the party considered preventing citizens from bringing family members to Australia to live would be dependent on the availability of services, including housing. "It's a hypothetical question, but can we grow our health system, our education system and other infrastructure we need to make sure the existing population that's here … are not under pressure?" he told the ABC. On Monday One Nation revealed its plan to reduce Australia's temporary migration intake by 750,000 places over three years, partly by barring the families of temporary skilled migrants and international students from entering the country. Mr Farley, who previously stated One Nation's migration policy would be "not too different" to Labor's, rejected suggestions that cutting family visas would deter the skilled migrants needed to plug critical workforce shortages from coming to Australia in the first place. "It is 2026. People have the ability now to work remotely … the reaches of the world are all 12 or 14 hours on a flight, and ultimately in an employment contract of skilled labour, everything is negotiable," he said. The minor party did not detail what its permanent migration intake would be, but Mr Farley said its immigration plan would be rolled out "completely" within the next fortnight. Caps on family visa intake 'illegal' Former deputy secretary of the Immigration Department Abul Rizvi said it would be illegal to cap family visas issued for Australian citizens. Despite that, Labor's current intake of permanent family visas is limited to 52,460 per year. "Under section 87 of the migration act, the government doesn't have the legal power to cap visas for the partners and dependent children of Australian citizens and permanent residents," Mr Rizvi said. "Regardless, successive governments have administratively — and illegally — limited the number of such visas issued." Mr Rizvi said, as a result, the backlog of partner visa applications was now about 120,000 and growing. "None of the parties have indicated what they will do about this illegal behaviour," he said. The government has been contacted for comment. One Nation to reveal 'complete' migration policy Meanwhile, One Nation is also facing calls to reveal the economic impact of its proposal to send Australia into "net negative migration" for three years. Labor frontbencher Murray Watt said the plan would destroy regional economies and likely send Australian into recession, while Shadow Immigration Minister Jonno Duniam demanded to see the party's costings. Mr Farley said One Nation had commissioned "extensive" economic modelling of its migration plan. "We've done the modelling and we will roll our strategy out on immigration completely over the next fortnight," he said. Weeks after Immigration Minister Tony Burke was forced to shelve a speech in which he was expected to unveil sweeping changes to Labor's migration settings, pressure is mounting on the government to unveil its policy to the Australian public. "I think they're going to be two years too late, but it's critical," Mr Rizvi said. "Part of the reason for One Nation's strength is because the government has failed to explain its policies, and the merit of those policies, to the Australian public." Senator Duniam said the Coalition would release its policy, with full costings, within weeks.

title: 'Unbearable emotional weight': Partner visa delays come at high personal cost - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: Each day feels like a window is closing for Nadine Chamas, who wants to start a family but is facing indefinite separation from her husband, Aboudi Alsaidy, in Lebanon. The 44-year-old's doctors had advised her to remain in Australia if she planned to become pregnant due to her medical condition. However, Mr Alsaidy has been waiting for a partner visa so that they could be reunited in Australia. "That stress of undergoing complex fertility planning while constantly worrying about my husband's safety in a conflict zone, it's an unbearable emotional weight," she said. They are among couples urging the federal government to hear their stories and reconsider its decision to prioritise partner visa applicants living in Australia over those who applied offshore. After they married in June last year, Ms Chamas hoped to stay with her husband in Lebanon, but they had to change plans when war erupted in the Middle East early this year. "That's when we decided we needed to be in a safe place together," Ms Chamas, who is an Australian citizen, said. She returned to her home city Melbourne and her husband applied for a partner visa in March. They are now waiting for the outcome of an Australian visitor visa application submitted last month. In a submission to Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke this week, a group of partner visa applicants and their Australian sponsors have urged him to explain his decision in July to deprioritise the processing of offshore partner visa applications. Applicants face waits of more than three years for subclass 309 visas, with 90 per cent of cases processed in up to 39 months, compared to 29 months for onshore partner visa applicants. "The relationships are no less genuine. The Australian sponsors are no less Australian," the submission says. "Yet one group receives more favourable administrative treatment, while the other carries the greater human burden of separation." Sasha Bellamy, who helped write and coordinate the submission, said the minister's decision to prioritise onshore over offshore applications was "fundamentally unfair". She was motivated to act partly because she had been separated from her own partner for a year as he awaited a partner visa in Belgium, and she felt she could use her experience as a lawyer to put the submission together. "I don't believe there has been enough transparency on the why or how, the modelling under which such a big decision has been made that's had massive human consequences." A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson told the ABC while offshore partner visa applications would have lower priority, they would still be processed and granted "in accordance with the planning levels and priorities set by the government". "An onshore-focused program will support timely transitions to permanent residency for migrants already living, working and contributing to Australia, and further reduces the program's impact on net overseas migration." 'Go back to video calls' Emily Hill-Ogbonnaya's husband Nick applied for a partner visa from Nigeria in March last year and was later able to secure a 12-month visitor visa in December. When she became pregnant, wait times were shorter and the couple did not expect to face a prolonged separation if Mr Ogbonnaya's partner visa didn't arrive before their baby's due date in January. "Suddenly in the last month or so, they've [wait times] just jumped so much since this new ministerial direction has come in," Ms Hill-Ogbonnaya said. "He might not be back until mid-2028 if they don't give him another visitor visa." Ms Hill-Ogbonnaya has a six-year-old daughter from a previous relationship and is concerned about how she would take Mr Ogbonnaya's departure. "That's going to be so destabilising for her to just have one of the most important people in her life just disappear and go back to video calls." Another Australian sponsor of a partner visa applicant, David Elms, is working long hours to be able to visit his wife and daughter in the Philippines every few months while they wait for a decision after lodging in June last year. The uncertainty combined with the additional financial pressure from travel and other costs has impacted his health. "I always try to remain positive, but it does affect you. You get these little bouts of depression here and there," he said. Mr Elms said because he was the sole provider for his wife and daughter, he believed their chances of proving strong ties to the Philippines and securing a visitor visa to Australia were low. He said it seemed there was "no hope" the partner visa would be granted soon after the government's decision to deprioritise overseas applications. "Hopefully someone who has some power or control over things might be able to look at it and maybe change things." 'More Australians fall in love with people overseas' Department of Home Affairs data shows the number of onshore and offshore partner visa applications increased from 52,479 in 2019–20 to 68,105 in 2024–25. In his National Press Club address last week, Mr Burke acknowledged demand for partner visas had grown. "We do have a situation now where more Australians fall in love with people overseas than they used to," he said. Mr Burke said planned changes imposing a "no further stay" requirement on visitor visas would lead to more being issued to offshore partner visa applicants wanting to spend time with their spouses in Australia. "The practice that we've had of people being able to, from visitor visas, automatically transfer on to bridging visas has meant a whole lot of these visas don't get issued at all," he said. Department of Home Affairs documents show 10,000 offshore applications had been on hand for more than 12 months in March, while a further 2,500 had been on hand for more than two years. The Home Affairs Department spokesperson said migration laws did not allow capping but provided "scope in administering migration programs to consider planning levels and prioritise processing accordingly". They allowed the minister to "consider visa applications in such order as he or she considers appropriate", the spokesperson said. "All visa programs, regardless of whether there is a planning level in place, are subject to limited resourcing which can result in delays in application assessment, especially in programs with high demand." Australian National University Migration Hub director Alan Gamlen said the "planning levels" worked as an effective cap. "They can choose which order to prioritise visas in. Once they reach a certain number of visa grants, they can decide to stop processing the partner visas and go and prioritise other visas," he said. "If that approach were challenged successfully in court, it would have an impact on other areas where the government is using this approach to regulate migration. "It probably will be a court case at some time, and it probably should be tested in court." Peter Van Vilet, chief executive of peak body for migration agents and lawyers, the Migration Institute of Australia, said the government's decision to prioritise onshore applications put offshore partner applications "at the bottom of a very long caseload". "It is very unclear when and if offshore partner visas will be processed under this direction," he said. "It will blow out the already long processing times even further." Meanwhile, he said the impact of partner visas on net overseas migration was small. "Partner visas should not be a part of the population debate. Australians living with their life partners is a basic human right and governments should not get in the way of this." Loading...

title: Love when you don't know when you'll meet again - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: After Mohammad "Mo" Mohammadi's brother died in 2020, he wanted to honour his memory with a portrait. That's when he came across Iran-based artist Fereshteh Ahmadi on Instagram. He never expected that a simple message would lead to a love story shaped by distance, war and agonising immigration struggles. These are Mo's words. Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us. After I reached out to Fereshteh on Instagram, she told her father. He recognised my name. It turned out we were from the same village in Afghanistan, and our families had been neighbours. It was a complete coincidence. We were both Afghan refugees who had ended up in Iran; Fereshteh's father had fled there many years before, and it was in Iran he got married and started his family. I had moved to Iran with my uncle as a young child. Throughout 2021, Fereshteh and I spoke on Instagram, and we quickly became friends. Fereshteh offered to send the artwork she'd drawn of my brother to me in Australia. I'd relocated there in 2010. But I was already planning to visit Iran the following year and wanted to collect it from her in person. When we met in real life, I could instantly feel she was a really nice person. When you find the other half of yourself, you just know Soon after that first meeting, we decided to get engaged. We had a little party with our families and got our marriage certificate from the Embassy of Afghanistan in Tehran in 2022. Five weeks later, I had to return to Australia for work. We were hoping to get a visa for Fereshteh to join me. But because she's an Afghan refugee in Iran, it's difficult for her to get the paperwork she needs. I had no idea when we would see each other again, so a few years ago, I asked Fereshteh to send me some of her artworks in the mail. I didn't tell her what I wanted them for, but I submitted them to a local art gallery in Bordertown, South Australia, where I now live. They all sold. People really loved them, and even asked for commissioned works. Fereshteh was really excited about all the support and used the money to purchase new art supplies. It's been almost three years now since we last saw each other in person We miss each other a lot. We're really just at the start of our relationship, and we should be spending time together. I was planning to visit Fereshteh earlier this year, but the week before I was due to depart, Israel and the US attacked Iran. My flight was cancelled, and I could not go. When the conflict started, I lost contact with Fereshteh for nearly two months. No phone calls, no text messages, no nothing. I had no idea where Fereshteh and her family were, or what they were going to do. It was really hard. I was always thinking about her and what was going to happen. Were they going to get bombed? Were the missiles going to drop directly where they were? Once the internet was restored, Fereshteh and her family texted me saying they were OK. I was really, really happy to hear that they were safe, at least. There was nothing I could do, because there were no flights, and everything was closed. Thankfully, Fereshteh and I can speak often now, but the internet is very poor, and we cannot video call. Still, at least we can talk. She's alright, and her family's alright. Loading... Still, we're hopeful about our future together My dream is to meet Fereshteh back in Iran so we can do the ceremony and celebrate with our families, before returning to Australia. Then we can finally build our lives together, and hopefully have children some day. I hope that she continues with her art when she arrives in Australia. But I'll support her with whatever she wants to be or become. She might want to study, or maybe even teach her own art class. In Australia, she'll have the freedom to do that. In Iran, she can't study or go to university. She can't work, and she can't even sell her artworks. It's too difficult, especially with the conflict happening now. I've bought a house in Bordertown, and it's like home to me, so I hope she'll like it here too. I can't wait to be together again, going out for dinner, going for holidays — even going camping. title: 'Not fair and quite sad': Cohort of workers being underpaid by billions - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: Cash-in-hand is no longer the preferred strategy some employers are using to underpay migrant workers, researchers say. Those business owners are instead asking prospective staff to create an Australian Business Number (ABN) with the aim of avoiding paying entitlements under the Fair Work Act. What's next? The Department of Home Affairs has a temporary visa allowing people to remain in Australia longer to pursue workplace exploitation claims but there are concerns uptake is very low. International student Mai was full of pride when she landed her first job in Australia. "At that time I was really happy because now I can live by myself, be more independent, not rely on my family and actually can afford the renting," the Australian National University student said. But she said her employer at a Canberra hospitality business began to call her day and night, asking her to work at short notice, for which she was paid a flat rate below the minimum wage, even on weekends. "Even sometimes when I saw my check-in and check-out sheet it was often rounded down, and I mean that's not fair and quite sad," Mai said. "Everything was so hard to afford and even paying rent is now more difficult and you're actually working for a lot of hours but like your effort is not anywhere, it's not showing." Mai, who has chosen that name to protect her identity, said she was "really afraid to speak up". "And I was scared that my parents would be worried for me. So I would stay by myself, try to go get through all of it by myself," she said. Passports taken, no breaks, threats Associate Professor Bassina Farbenblum, who founded the Migrant Justice Institute, said the underpayment of temporary visa holders, such as in Mai's case, was often a clue that those businesses were committing other forms of exploitation. She has co-authored a major study into migrant worker exploitation commissioned by the Commonwealth attorney-general's department, finding: "International students alone may be short-changed by around $3.18 billion per year," the report said. "Not by accident, and not by a few rogue employers." Associate Professor Farbenblum said they had found "that the more that people were underpaid, the more likely they experienced conditions like having their passport confiscated or being made to work very long hours with no breaks, often two weeks in a row". "And in some cases threats of harm or violence," she said. "One of the things we see, particularly for migrant workers, is a threat to report the worker to immigration if they speak up or if they do anything. "They're really fearful of losing their visa and they need to pay for food and pay their rent." How ABNs are used for exploitation Associate Professor Farbenblum said one of the biggest insights from the report, which heard from close to 10,000 migrant workers in Australia, was that cash-in-hand was no longer the preferred strategy to underpay employees on temporary visas. "So we used to see that the way of keeping migrant workers off-the-books was to pay in cash. We're still seeing one in four paid at least some of their wages in cash, but what we're seeing now is increasing use of ABNs," she said. "Then there's no record of these people as employees and their pay can't be compared against their entitlements under the Fair Work Act." Workers can pursue exploitation claims The Department of Home Affairs introduced a temporary visa in 2024 to allow people to remain in Australia for up to 12 months to pursue a workplace exploitation claim after their previous visa had expired. The Commonwealth also has a Strengthening Reporting Protections Pilot which promises the Department of Home Affairs "will not cancel your visa if you have breached a work-related visa condition, and there is a link between that visa breach and workplace exploitation" that is reported. But there are concerns very few temporary visa holders ever report workplace exploitation. The ABC has asked the Department of Home Affairs what the uptake has been for its migrant worker protections but the department has not yet responded to the questions. Mai said she believed almost no one came forward. "A lot of my friends around me, they also get underpaid ... because we are international students, we just want to have the income, so we accept the situation and just follow it," she said.

title: Hundreds of migrants flood into Spain’s Ceuta exclave from Morocco - News.com.au
raw_text: Hundreds of migrants flood into Spain's Ceuta exclave from Morocco Madrid said on Thursday it would despatch soldiers to Ceuta to ensure security after hundreds of migrants entered Spain's north African exclave from neighbouring Morocco and hundreds more headed there. The Spanish government's delegation in the enclave told AFP that the bodies of nine migrants who died while trying to reach Ceuta by swimming had been recovered. Migration from Morocco into Spain's two north African territories, Ceuta and Melilla, has long been a politically sensitive issue between the two countries, as thousands cross the border at times. Italy called on Thursday for Spain to be suspended from Europe's open-borders Schengen zone, prompting a backlash from Spain, which summoned the Italian envoy to Madrid. AFP reporters saw a stream of adults and children, most of them soaked, entering the town of Ceuta after having swum there. Discarded flotation rings and clothes were discarded on the shore near where the border barrier meets the sea. "The armed forces will reinforce the Civil Guard in the exercise of its powers and any others that may be necessary to maintain security in the city of Ceuta," Spain's interior ministry said. It did not specify how many soldiers would be sent to the small territory of 18.5 square kilometres (seven square miles) but said the Civil Guard's strength there would be nearly doubled from the current level of 80. It will also send diving teams and coastguard ships. - Spain 'profoundly wrong' - Italy said on Thursday Spain should be suspended from the Schengen zone -- a system of open borders spanning 29 European countries that have officially abolished controls at their common borders. "I am in favour of closing the Schengen area with Spain," Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani wrote on X. "Irregular and uncontrolled immigration poses a danger to national security," he claimed. "The images coming from Ceuta show how the Madrid government's decision to grant Spanish, and therefore European, citizenship to over 500,000 irregular immigrants is profoundly wrong and encourages human trafficking," he argued. Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Luis Albares responded by accusing Tajani of weaponising immigration for political ends; He said such remarks were "improper" for "a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery". title: ‘Wild’: Shock as Aussie visa fees skyrocket - News.com.au
raw_text: ‘Wild’: Shock as Aussie visa fees skyrocket for students, backpackers and Kiwis International students, backpackers and Kiwis have hit out at “wild” visa fee increases of nearly 200 per cent which came into effect this week. From July 1, most visa applications have increased by 25 per cent, with student visas (subclass 500) rising by $500 to $2500 and temporary graduate visas (subclass 485) jumping $1150 to $5750. Among the largest increases were to partner visas, which shot up to a whopping $11,710 — an increase of $2345 from $9365 — and the New Zealand family relationship visa, which almost doubled — up 198 per cent – from $445 to $1330. “I’ve never been so grateful for being on top of applying for my visa, because what do you mean it’s now $1000 as of today?” one working holiday-maker shared on TikTok. “Yesterday it was $670. That is wild.” Another TikToker called the New Zealand visa increase “crazy”. “I would have thought a couple hundred … I was just so surprised,” she said. “I feel so grateful that I got mine in when I did. I also feel so terrible for the people who haven’t got it in yet.” The increase to the temporary graduate visa fee comes just three months after it was doubled from $2300 to $4600. “TR fees increased again! Jesus, what an absolute jaffa,” one TikToker said. Former Immigration Department deputy secretary Dr Abul Rizvi said the fee increases were “really poor policy”. “They’re going to have to do something about net migration [to meet Anthony Albanese’s target], but this won’t get them there,” he said. “Australia’s visa fees were already amongst the highest in the world by a long way, particularly the student visa fee. “The UK student visa fee, for example, is about $1000, ours is now $2500. “The question is what is the government trying to achieve with such high fees, including for partners? “Why penalise Australians who have married foreigners with such a huge fee? What is the public policy objective? “I think it’s primarily a revenue-raising thing, they’re probably hoping it will bring down net overseas migration a bit but I don’t think it’ll do much. “If you think about partners, it’s probably not going to have much effect — if you’re a genuine partner, [the increased fee] is not going to mean you’re not going to get married. “It just means some people will have to scrimp and save a bit longer.” Dr Rizvi said the student visa fee increase would only have a “marginal” impact on bringing down numbers. “The bigger impact on student numbers is the refusal rate,” he said. It comes after Australia’s peak business body raised the alarm at the surprise visa fee hikes. Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar said on Thursday the increase far outpaced inflation and risked making Australia less attractive to skilled workers and international students. “Australia already had the most expensive student visa fees in the world,” he said in a statement. “Lifting that charge so dramatically in such a short period sends a poor signal to the global market.” Mr McKellar said higher visa costs would make Australia “a harder sell for visitors”, which could potentially impact tourism operators and educators. “Many businesses rely on skilled migrants, international students working in key sectors, and graduates who choose to stay and build their careers here,” he said. He added it was disappointing the government imposed these changes without consultation and without a public announcement. “Sneaking in major changes that carry drastic consequences is a poor way to treat the business community,” he said. Increases to various income thresholds for skilled migrants also came into effect on Wednesday. “Income thresholds are indexed annually so wages for skilled migrants increase at the same rate as Australian workers,” the Department of Home Affairs said in the announcement. “This ensures that people cannot use skilled migration to undercut Australian workers.” Mr McKellar said the visa increases come on top of other policy decisions making it harder for businesses to grow. “Visa charge hikes on top of a capital gains tax increase, new tax on trusts, minimum wage costs increasing beyond inflation, and employer incentives being cut — the government burdens are piling up,” he said. “The government cannot keep asking businesses to lift productivity while making it increasingly difficult to be productive.” It comes as Labor, the Coalition, and One Nation seek to assert their immigration credentials. Labor has dismissed criticism of booming immigration over its tenure as a result of Covid backlogs, while cracking down on character-related tests in the aftermath of the Bondi Beach terrorist attack. The Coalition, meanwhile, has sought to tie migration levels to housing completion, while One Nation has blamed immigration for the country’s housing and cost of living crisis. The latest figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) last month showed annual net overseas migration as of the December quarter 2025 was 300,960 people, down 9 per cent on the previous year. — with NewsWire

title: Bombshell new One Nation proposal - News.com.au
raw_text: One Nation unveils shock plan to reset net migration to zero One Nation has revealed a dramatic overhaul of Australia’s migration system, with hundreds of thousands fewer arrivals and a warning for those who don’t comply. EXCLUSIVE One Nation has unveiled a shock plan to “reset” Australia’s net overseas migration levels to zero by slashing the number of arrivals by more than 750,000 people. The major plan would take Australia’s current net overseas migration figure, which has a target of 225,000 in coming years, down to zero in a temporary measure lasting three years. It would then be reviewed and resettle at around 130,000 people a year. Labor’s current NOM target is 245,000 for 2026-27 and 225,000 for 2027-28. Want the latest political news? Download our new app so you never miss a headline. The temporary measures mirror radical reforms adopted in Canada that slowed a post-pandemic immigration surge by slashing overseas students and other arrivals. “Vested interests and elite economists will shriek at the prospect of these cuts,’’ Senator Hanson said. “But Canada has shown you can cut migrant numbers, take pressure off rents, and still grow the economy.” Plan to ‘restore living standards Senator Hanson said the plan would restore living standards, ease pressure on housing and essential services, and bring population growth back to a sustainable rate. “I know Australians are doing it tough. Families are competing with hundreds of people for rental accommodation,” she said. “Patients are stuck in ambulances because there are not enough hospital beds. Young Australians are being locked out of home ownership while wages and infrastructure fail to keep up. “Under Labor, the number of temporary visa holders has surged from 2 million in 2022 to roughly 3 million in 2026.” What is Net Overseas Migration? The net overseas migration figure is a poorly understood measure of the net gain or loss of population through immigration to and emigration from Australia. It is based on an international traveller’s duration of stay being in or out of Australia for 12 months or more over a 16-month period (the 12/16 month rule). It measures the difference between the number of incoming international travellers who stay in Australia for 12 months or more within 16 months and the number of outgoing international travellers. ‘Net negative’ migration reset One Nation’s plan aims to return the temporary migrant population to around 2017 levels and the international student population to 2015 levels. “Over the three years, net overseas migration will be net negative,” the One Nation policy document states. “Following this, One Nation’s net overseas migration ceiling of 130,000 per year would remain in place. “We will crack down on illegal migrant employment, cutting off illicit income and encouraging departures. Illegal migrants will be given three months to leave Australia. “Those who depart will be allowed to apply for a visa in the future. Those who remain unlawfully after this period will face immigration enforcement and a lifetime ban from re-entering Australia.” How the 750,000 reduction would work One Nation’s reduction in the temporary migrant population of approximately 750,000 would be achieved through restricting visa numbers and tightening eligibility criteria for temporary student and student graduate visas It aims to substantially restrict the ability of temporary students, graduates and skilled workers to sponsor family and dependants to Australia Crackdown on Overseas Students Under One Nation’s plan: -Overseas students must leave after completing their studies unless eligible for the targeted graduate pathway. -Graduate visa holders may move to an eligible employer-sponsored temporary skilled visa, but cannot obtain another graduate visa or switch back to a student visa from within Australia. -Temporary skilled workers may renew or replace their work visa if eligible, but cannot switch onshore into student, graduate, visitor or other temporary categories. -Visitors cannot apply for another visa from within Australia, apart from the specified exception for family-sponsored applications. Bridging visas would remain available for legitimate applications that are permitted to be made in Australia. Restricting onshore applications and visa switching aims to reduce the number of people entering and remaining in the bridging visa system. One Nation anticipates this will reduce the current bridging visa population from approximately 413,000 to 300,000 by year three. One Nation said universities would still be able to enrol more than 100,000 international students per year. “The temporary skilled migration program will remain available and be driven by employer demand,” the document states. “One Nation will maintain the existing seasonal worker programs, such as PALM and the working holiday maker program. “Employers will still be able to sponsor skilled migrants, but temporary skilled migration will no longer operate as a sham family migration pathway.” Divisions within One Nation One Nation has been criticised for its “incoherence” on migration policy after new MP David Farley suggested the party’s plan wasn’t that different to Labor’s policy. He argued the 130,000 NOM target excluded other forms of migration, including temporary workers from the Pacific Islands, skilled workers, and backpackers. The remarks sparked a rebuke from Senator Hanson. “The cuts will come from fewer international students and dependants, a dramatic reduction in temporary graduate visas and their dependants, and a much more targeted skilled migration program focused on the skills Australia genuinely needs,” she said. Opposition home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam said that One Nation was struggling to “get its story straight” on migration. “It is one thing to have a (NOM) number out there. It is another to go around and point at certain groups of visa classes and say we’ll reduce this,” Senator Duniam said.

title: ‘Tank the economy’: One Nation alert - News.com.au
raw_text: One Nation’s immigration plan will ‘tank economy’ to scale not seen since 1890s depression One Nation’s plan to slash immigration by 750,000 over three years would ‘tank the economy’, a prominent political commentator warns. One Nation’s plan to cut immigration by 750,000 over three years would “tank the Australian economy” on a scale not seen since the 1890s Depression, a prominent political commentator and author has warned. Speaking on ABC National Forum, George Megalogenis said the controversial policy would be disastrous, pointing out no government had ever purposefully caused a net outflow of migrants. Mr Megalogenis said One Nation was proposing to do something that had only happened four times in Australia’s history. Twice during the depressions of the 1890s and 1930s, and twice during the deployment of troops during the First and Second World Wars. “We’ve never had a period over the long run of our history where more people have left than have come the other way,” he said. “If you’re going to take 766,000 people out of the Australian economy and society for three years, you have tanked the Australian economy in a way that is on the scale of the depression of the 1890s and 1930s.” Net overseas migration has been falling from its post-COVID peak in 2023, when international borders reopened after the pandemic. Net overseas migration was 306,000 in 2024-25, down from 429,000 the previous year but still above the pre-COVID number of 241,000 in 2018-2019. One Nation’s plan would take Australia’s current net overseas migration figure down to zero for three years. It would then be reviewed and settled at around 130,000 people a year. Labor’s current target is 245,000 for 2026-27 and 225,000 for 2027-28. One Nation will follow ‘will of the people’, Joyce says One Nation treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce appeared alongside Multicultural Affairs Minister Anne Aly and opposition frontbencher Andrew Hastie on ABC’s National Forum on migration. Mr Joyce defended One Nation’s proposal, saying the party’s policy would focus immediately on the 3 million temporary visa holders as a way to drastically reduce net migration. “We’ve said quite clearly that you can’t have 3 million temporary visa holders walking around Australia; that means it’s going from a country to a caravan park,” Mr Joyce said. Mr Joyce was pressed by host David Speers on how much the proposal would cost in jobs, income and the budget. “The issue of what it is going to cost I think is contentious, but I have no concern about following the will of the Australian people,” Mr Joyce said. “I think the Australian people are sort of tired of the fact that you have to go to an economist to come up with public policy, to go to the Parliamentary Budget Office, and, to be quite frank, I have been around this game for a while and I have never seen a forward estimates in any budgetary paper be even close to the mark. “The will of the Australian people is so pronounced, this has to be dealt with, we will deal with it.” Mr Joyce said he wasn’t worried about what the Parliamentary Budget Office or another office might conclude about the policy, saying “they’re not elected, I am.” Ms Aly agreed migration numbers had been too high, particularly post-Covid, but said the challenge was how to bring those numbers down in a manageable way. “The difficulty is doing it in a way that preserves the integrity of the migration system, but that creates a system that is fair for everybody and one that responds to the needs of Australia and in the national interest of Australia,” she said. Mr Hastie said the Coalition was committed to tying net overseas migration to the number of homes being built each year. “Last year we built 170,000 homes and the net overseas migration figures for the last four years have been well above that and we’re now seeing the consequences of that with Australians not being able to find homes,” he said. “I’ve seen people waking up in their cars down on the beach in Western Australia. I know of children who are living in tents and caravans because our housing stock has not kept pace with the growth of immigration.” ‘Kill the economy’ Since the announcement on Monday, One Nation’s plan has been slammed by the government, opposition, farmers and business groups. Environment Minister Murray Watt said the plan would “kill the Australian economy and kill regional economies in particular”, pointing to early industry responses including farmers. “I mean, I don’t know when the last time Barnaby Joyce or Pauline Hanson walked into a doctor’s clinic, a hospital, an aged-care facility, to a construction site, to a country pub, to see the number of migrants who are working in these populations,” he said. Senator Watt said Labor understood “that we do need to bring down the number of migrants coming into Australia”, and that the Albanese government had been “doing that since we came to office and we intend to do more”. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the policy raised more questions than it answered. More Coverage “I am deeply concerned about what it means for individual farmers, for individual businesses, for builders, for pub owners, for cafe owners,” he said on Monday. The National Farmers Federation said the plan would hurt regional Australia, where temporary workers “help put food on tables, with backpackers alone filling roughly one in seven farm jobs nationally”. The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry also warned “major cuts that reduce skilled migration” would put the economy at risk.

When Prime Minister Anthony Albanese likened Narendra Modi to Bruce Springsteen in 2023, it captured more than the spectacle surrounding the Indian leader's visit. Addressing a lively crowd at Sydney's Qudos Bank Arena, Albanese remarked that the rock legend was the last person he'd seen on stage there, adding that "he didn't get the welcome that Prime Minister Modi has got". It reflected the cordiality between the two leaders, who have helped transform a relationship once seen as rich in untapped potential into what both now describe as a "comprehensive strategic partnership". But Albanese's comments also drew sharp criticism from some parts of the Indian diaspora and human rights advocates, who argued that the glowing reception glossed over allegations of human rights abuses under Modi's leadership — claims he has strenuously denied. The response captured the stark divide in public opinion about Modi, who is widely celebrated by supporters for driving economic growth and India's global profile, but whose leadership is also the subject of sustained international scrutiny from human rights organisations and democracy monitors. Now, as the Indian prime minister returns to Australia for his third visit in nearly 12 years, the setting has shifted to Melbourne, where another large diaspora gathering is expected to showcase the public enthusiasm that has become a defining feature of his overseas outreach. Beyond the flags, crowds and political theatre, the visit comes at a more complex moment for the relationship between the two nations. Experts say it will test whether Albanese and Modi's close relationship can translate into concrete outcomes as both navigate a changing regional environment, domestic pressures and more difficult conversations around visa policies and migration, trade, and differing approaches to global issues, including sanctions against Russia and Iran. The visit also offers an opportunity to examine a relationship that has become one of Australia's most important in the Indo-Pacific — shaped by geopolitics, economic ambition and the realities of a growing diaspora, including the opportunities and challenges that come with closer ties. Although diplomatic ties with Australia were established before India's independence in 1947, the two countries spent decades navigating differences over the Cold War, nuclear policy, migration and Australia's engagement with Asia. The legacy of the White Australia Policy and disagreements among earlier leaders also affected bilateral ties at various points. Modi's 2014 visit, the first by an Indian prime minister to Australia in more than three decades, marked a turning point in resetting ties beyond the familiar territory of cricket and community links. Since then, cooperation has expanded through trade, the Quad — the strategic grouping of Australia, India, Japan and the United States — alongside defence engagement, critical minerals and supply chain partnerships, with both countries seeing each other as important partners in a more contested Indo-Pacific. Teesta Prakash, a research fellow in security and geopolitics at the Australia India Institute, says Modi's repeated visits reflect how significantly Australia's role has grown in India's strategic thinking. "This is the most amount of times any Indian prime minister has visited Australia, which underscores just how important Australia is to India's strategic imagination," she tells SBS News. Prakash says Modi's first visit was largely about resetting the relationship after he came to office. Twelve years on, with the broader strategic framework now established, the focus has shifted towards implementation. "So this trip is less likely to focus on announcing new strategic frameworks, but more on delivering concrete outcomes, in defence, defence industry, critical minerals — uranium included —technology partnerships and supply chain resilience." What to expect from Modi's visit With Modi scheduled to be in Melbourne on Wednesday evening, his third visit is expected to focus on delivery. Pradeep Taneja, a senior lecturer in Asian politics at the University of Melbourne, says Australia has described India as a "top-tier" security partner and expects the visit to build on existing areas of collaboration. "In terms of concrete outcomes, it is possible that some agreements may be signed that build on the ongoing collaboration in critical minerals and energy security," he tells SBS News. But I don't expect any big bang announcements during this visit. Economic ties are also expected to feature prominently. The Australia-India Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement, which came into force in late 2022, substantially lowered tariffs and expanded market access across a wide range of goods and services, opening Australia's market to Indian exports while giving Australian businesses improved access to India. Negotiations are continuing on a broader Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement, which aims to deepen the economic partnership. Agriculture, however, remains one of the more sensitive issues. Australia has long sought greater access to India's agricultural market, while India's government has resisted opening sectors such as dairy, wheat, rice and sugar, arguing they are critical to the livelihoods of millions of small farmers. The differing scales and structures of the farming sector across the two countries mean agriculture is expected to remain one of the more challenging areas in negotiations towards a comprehensive trade deal. Defence will be another key area to watch. Cooperation has expanded through military exercises, maritime engagement and deeper coordination in the Indo-Pacific, with both countries seeking to move from strategic alignment towards practical collaboration. Lisa Singh, CEO of the Australia India Institute at the University of Melbourne, says the visit will ultimately be judged by whether commitments translate into action. These prime ministerial visits are such a significant moment to move the relationship forward. "New commitments in defence are one important area that both nations can show they are doing that, highlighting that our trusted partnership is not just words but actions that will help make our nations and region safer," Singh said in a statement to SBS News. What's driving the partnership The transformation in India-Australia ties reflects a broader shift in the Indo-Pacific. China's growing military and economic influence has heightened strategic competition across the region, and concerns over supply chain resilience have pushed Canberra and New Delhi into closer alignment. Through the Quad and other bilateral initiatives, the two countries have expanded cooperation on defence, maritime security, critical minerals, clean energy and technology as they seek to strengthen regional stability and reduce dependence on any single partner. Albanese has also framed the relationship through the lens of India's growing economic weight. In an address to the parliament in May, he described India as "a global economic powerhouse" and said it was on track to become the world's third-largest economy this decade, calling it "an extraordinary opportunity for us in our region". Taneja says uncertainty over the future strategic role of the US has prompted Australia to diversify its strategic partnerships. "India is now seen as an important partner because the interests of the two countries align more closely than they did in the past," he says. Taneja says while both governments frequently speak of shared democratic values and a free and open Indo-Pacific, the relationship is ultimately shaped by strategic interests. The visit also comes as Melbourne debates the proposed 'Little India' cultural precinct in Docklands on the western end of the CBD, which supporters say would recognise the Indian community's contribution to the city. Nationally, the timing is significant. But the relationship between diaspora and diplomacy is unfolding alongside a more contested migration debate in Australia. The Albanese government has tightened student visa settings and sought to reduce net overseas migration, while visa scrutiny has intensified and anti-immigration rhetoric has become more prominent in domestic politics. Prakash says while migration is ultimately a sovereign policy decision, it is one of the issues Modi could raise with Albanese, much like he raised concerns over the vandalism of Hindu temples during his 2023 visit. "Migration specifically is a sovereign domestic decision, and while obviously it impacts Indian potential students or migrants who were looking to move to Australia.
