Modi faced accusations over his handling of the violence but was later cleared of personal wrongdoing by Indian investigative bodies and the courts. Critics continue to cite the riots as emblematic of broader concerns about accountability and minority rights in the Hindu-majority country, while supporters argue the matter has been thoroughly examined and legally resolved. Those debates resurfaced internationally following the 2023 BBC documentary, India: The Modi Question, which examined the Gujarat violence and its political aftermath. The documentary was banned in India, while the Indian government dismissed it as biased and rejected its conclusions. The BBC said the documentary was "rigorously researched" and featured a range of opinions and experts. The broadcaster said in a statement that it had given the Indian government a right of reply, but the government had declined to respond. India has also fallen sharply in global press freedom rankings, with Reporters Without Borders placing it at 157 out of 180 countries, citing increasing risks to journalists and concerns about political pressure on media independence. Modi's own engagement with the media has also drawn scrutiny. Since becoming the prime minister in 2014, he has not held a traditional solo press conference and has rarely taken unscripted questions from journalists during his foreign jaunts. Human Rights Watch's (HRW) latest report on India states the country's "slide to authoritarianism under the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party-led government continued [in 2025], with increased vilification of Muslims and government critics". The BJP's performance in India's 2024 general election also changed the political landscape, with Modi losing his outright majority and returning to power as the head of a coalition government after the party lost 63 seats compared with the previous election. Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at HRW, says these concerns are not confined to India's borders, with political tensions also being felt within parts of the diaspora. I think it is important to see that there is a growing sort of muscular nationalism and politics of hate [in India]. "That is also being exported among the diaspora. So even the communities that lived in far greater harmony before are feeling those tensions when they're living abroad because of what is happening in India," she tells SBS News. Following Modi's 2023 visit, Albanese dismissed suggestions he had shared a stage with a "tyrant", saying India was "a great democracy". The push for strategic cooperation These debates are happening at the same time as a broader foreign policy conversation is unfolding. India's strategic autonomy continues to shape its international relationships, including its ties with Russia and Iran. India has maintained defence and energy links with Russia and has not joined with Australia and other Western nations in imposing sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The government has also maintained its relationship with Iran despite documented evidence of severe human rights violations under the Iranian regime, citing its importance for India's energy, connectivity and regional interests. India is also part of BRICS, a group that includes countries like Russia and China, reflecting its non-aligned approach to global politics. For Australia, these uncomfortable differences exist alongside a growing push towards strategic cooperation. When asked about India's relationship with Russia ahead of Modi's 2023 visit, Albanese acknowledged the different histories shaping the two countries' foreign policies. "We have very different histories, of course ... India has been a leader of the Non-Aligned Movement for such a long period of time," he said at the time, referencing the group of more than 120 countries that are not formally aligned with or against any major international power bloc. A partnership entering a new phase Returning to the moment Albanese welcomed Modi on stage in 2023 stirs mixed feelings for some. "Prime Minister Modi is 'the boss'," he declared, referencing the colloquial nickname for US rock legend Springsteen. However, for many in the Indian diaspora, who may not be Springsteen fans, it likely resonated differently — reflecting the power wielded by a leader who has become central to India's global image. Beyond the symbolism, the Australia-India partnership is stronger than it was a decade ago — and far more complex. It now involves defence cooperation, supply chains, migration, education, diaspora politics and a growing debate about how democracies engage with each other in a more uncertain world. Singh says the next phase will depend on whether both countries can turn alignment into lasting cooperation. The question now is how both nations navigate their future partnership amidst the current backdrop of global uncertainty. "I hope new investment opportunities are created and that we work further on building trusted supply chains in goods and technology that will overcome the shocks of the future," she says. As Modi arrives in Melbourne, the scale of the community event will once again highlight the strength of the people-to-people connection. But the future of the relationship will be defined by what happens after the applause fades. The challenge for both countries is whether they can continue expanding a partnership that has become strategically important while managing the tensions that come with being closer than ever. raw_text: In brief - Several parties have announced migration policies in the past year. - Labor says housing construction needs a chance to "catch up", while One Nation says it plans to end "mass migration". After weeks of headlines dominated by One Nation, the federal government has unveiled its long-awaited migration reforms. Notably, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke did not name Pauline Hanson's party during his 35-minute National Press Club speech on Thursday, and he was quick to point out the policy had been in the works since last year. "It's simply demonstrably wrong to suspect that somehow this is a recent bit of work done to deal with a political climate; it's not," he said. Yet some analysts say it's difficult not to see the government as responding to the rise of One Nation, which has overtaken Labor on the primary vote and is the favoured party on immigration, according to some polls. Nine newspapers reported Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was concerned about the optics of using a forum like the Press Club to draw more attention to an issue being dominated by One Nation — a claim Burke rejected on Thursday. News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. One Nation announced its migration policy earlier this week, promising to end "mass migration" by cutting temporary visas by 750,000 over three years and delivering net negative migration to ease pressure on housing, healthcare and infrastructure. That follows the Coalition's plan announced in April, while the Greens' policy platform is the same one it took to the 2025 federal election. With the political battle lines drawn on one of the most major issues facing Australia, where do these parties stand on migration? Labor The government wants to reduce Australia's net overseas migration (NOM) figure from its current level of 292,100. It has forecast figures of 245,000 for 2026-27 and 225,000 each year thereafter. Burke acknowledged in his address there were housing pressures, but rejected claims Australia was experiencing mass migration. "We need immigration to soften enough that housing has a chance to catch up," he said. He outlined three parts to the reform: who arrives, who stays and who leaves. Among the most consequential changes are those affecting students, backpackers, visa overstayers and "visa hoppers". International students will no longer be able to bring their family members to Australia, though there are some exceptions, including for PhD students. title: ‘Heard the popping’: Man shot dead by US immigration agents in Maine - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Washington: Snap protests have erupted in the US state of Maine after immigration enforcement agents were involved in another fatal shooting, with a 26-year-old Colombian man killed, according to immigration advocates. It is the second such fatality in seven days after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and killed 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a pursuit in Houston last week. The incident occurred early on Monday morning (US time), and the Department of Homeland Security did not issue a statement until Monday evening. It said ICE was conducting targeted surveillance on the last known address of an illegal alien who had been ordered to leave the country. “An illegal alien departed the residence in a vehicle. ICE law enforcement attempted to conduct a vehicle stop. The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and, fearing for public safety, an officer discharged his weapon,” DHS said. The person was struck and later died of their injuries. The DHS statement did not claim the man tried to use his vehicle as a weapon. “Like all discharges of firearms, this will be investigated.” However, there was still some confusion over the victim’s identity and whether he was the target of the ICE arrest warrant. A witness, Lucas Scott, told the Portland Press Herald that he was driving through the intersection at the time of the fatal shooting and that the driver was “trying to hit the ICE officer”. “The ICE agent was yelling and drew his weapon,” Scott told the newspaper. “He kept yelling and yelling and warning the person driving, which is when the car was put into drive and was trying to hit the ICE officer. “He fired, I would say probably four shots, at him ... I just heard the popping, but I did see him draw his gun at the windshield.” Angus King, an independent senator for Maine who caucuses with the Democrats, said he spoke with DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin, who had promised a full and transparent investigation. He also said the agents involved were not wearing body cameras, meaning it was uncertain whether the investigation would give a clear picture of what happened. “We’ve been told that body cameras would be widely distributed,” King said. “I am concerned. They should have been having body cameras two years ago when all this started.” King initially said that in his conversation with Mullin, the DHS secretary indicated the person shot was being arrested and removed from the country because he was not there legally. But he later said updated information from Mullin indicated the man was not, in fact, the target of the warrant the officers were executing. The Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition and Presente! Maine, both immigration advocacy groups, said the man killed was a 26-year-old from Colombia who “was authorised to work in the United States and had been issued a social security number”. “We are grieving, we are furious, and we will not allow his death to be treated as routine or inevitable,” MIRC executive director Mufalo Chitam said. “How much more harm must our communities endure before those with the power to act acknowledge that this has gone too far?” The consecutive deaths of people fleeing arrest by ICE come six months after the US was rocked by the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both American citizens who were protesting ICE raids in Minneapolis during an enforcement blitz. Those killings were a turning point in public attitudes, and prompted US President Donald Trump to send his border tsar, Tom Homan, to Minnesota and to scale back operations in the state. But ICE has continued to execute the administration’s mass deportation agenda. The Associated Press reported the agency arrested 10,000 people over five days at the end of June – a substantial increase in enforcement. In Maine, protesters gathered at Mechanics Park in Biddeford on Monday, and outside the office of Republican Senator Susan Collins, carrying signs that said, “F--- ICE”, and chanting: “Vote her out.” Collins, who has broken with Trump on several issues and is up for re-election in November, said on X: “The shooting in Biddeford requires a full and impartial investigation of what happened. It is my understanding that the Biddeford police have secured the site and that the FBI is investigating.” Maine’s Secretary of State, Shenna Bellows, a Democrat who is running to be the state’s next senator, said at least 11 people had been shot dead by ICE or Border Patrol since Trump’s crackdown began. That figure is also cited by immigration advocates. “It’s time to get ICE off our streets,” Bellows said. title: Australian tackled, handcuffed by ICE officers in Las Vegas - SMH.com.au
raw_text: An Australian man was left partially handcuffed on the ground by two Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents after they attempted to arrest him in a Las Vegas airport. A video of the incident posted on social media showed the man, in a light blue shirt, screaming “I don’t know what they’re doing” while one of the officers pinned his arm behind his back. One of his shoes had fallen off and his suitcase had been left to the side. The two plainclothes ICE agents – a man and a woman – were both wearing hooded sweatshirts, with the woman also sporting a mask. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it is making “urgent enquiries” following reports of the arrest. The man who filmed the altercation can be heard asking “what’s going on?” while approaching the two agents. When the male officer realises he’s being recorded, he swipes at the camera. An airport employee then steps between the two and holds his arms out wide, declaring “they’re law enforcement”. Immediately after, the two officers, who have both put their hoods over their heads, walked off and left the distressed man behind, still partially handcuffed. A woman in the video can be seen running after the agents and yelling at them. The incident is reported to have happened on Monday night in Terminal 3 at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas. NBC News reported that the Department of Homeland Security identified the man as 57-year-old Phu Nguyen, an Australian citizen who overstayed his visa. The two agents left without arresting Nguyen “to de-escalate the situation and for officer safety” after a crowd formed, a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to NBC News. ICE arrested him at the Los Angeles International Airport on Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security told CNN. Nguyen is being held at the Adelanto ICE Processing Centre in California. “The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is making urgent enquiries following reports of an Australian citizen detained in the United States,” a DFAT spokesperson said in a statement. “The Department stands ready to provide consular assistance to any Australian citizen, should it be requested.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world. title: Labor recruits ex-Liberal premier to champion multiculturalism - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Former Tasmanian Liberal premier Peter Gutwein has been appointed, by Labor, as chair of Australia’s peak multicultural advisory council, warning that rhetoric from parts of the political right is fuelling hatred and vilification. Gutwein, himself a migrant, said One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s call for Australia to become a monocultural society should have been met with “appropriate disdain”, saying it was disappointing that Opposition Leader Angus Taylor didn’t immediately condemn the remarks when first asked about them. On Monday, the Albanese government revealed Gutwein, who led Tasmania between 2020 and 2022, had been appointed chair of the Australian Multicultural Council, the independent body that provides advice to the government on multicultural affairs and social cohesion. His appointment comes amid fierce debate on the political right over multiculturalism, and a surge in support for Hanson who last month warned Australia must exist as a “monocultural society”, warning high migration had caused the country to lose its values and identity. Former Liberal prime minister Tony Abbott has since claimed that multiculturalism has failed, prompting frontbench Liberal Andrew Bragg to reject his comments and say that it was not a view shared by elected Liberal members in parliament. In his first interview as chair, Gutwein told this masthead that Australia had benefited from decades of bipartisan support for multiculturalism and that such an approach provided certainty and confidence in the system. “Quite obviously that’s not occurring at the moment,” Gutwein said. “Unfortunately, the leaning towards the right, especially some of the national narrative that we are seeing at the moment, is very unhelpful ... both for the country but also for the communities in which people live. “There has been green-lighting of an opportunity for those that might seek to do others harm through inciting hatred or vilification, that green lighting’s been occurring by voices on the right at the moment. I don’t think that’s good enough, and it needs to be called out.” He said political leaders had a responsibility to reject rhetoric that risked dividing Australians rather than allowing multiculturalism to become another source of division. Gutwein said Australia’s success had always depended on leaders resisting attempts to turn multiculturalism into a partisan issue. “I believe that as a country, we need to govern from the centre,” he said. Gutwein said Australia remained one of the world’s strongest examples of a successful multicultural society. “You have to work hard at it. You need to lean into it. You need to accept it and embrace it.” In 2024, Gutwein led a 330-kilometre walk to highlighted the contributions of Tasmania’s migrant and refugee communities to the state’s social and economic wellbeing. The former premier said Australia had to spend more time highlighting the contribution migrants make to communities, businesses and public life. “One thing that I think we have to do, and be very loud about, is the need to celebrate the contributions more that people make.” Born in England to a British mother and an Austrian-Yugoslav father, Gutwein migrated to Tasmania as a child in 1969. He said his own family experience had shaped his belief that immigration had made Australia stronger. “We are a multicultural country. We have been for a long period of time,” he said. “As a former migrant myself ... through my own lived experience, I know that if provided with opportunity, people can do wonderful things both for themselves and for the communities they live in.” He also pushed back against attempts to harness community frustration over housing affordability by blaming immigration, saying it had become a political scapegoat, pointing to Tasmania’s experience during the pandemic. “We had negative net migration. We increased supply, we reduced migration and house prices still went up,” he said. “To have a strong, growing economy, especially at a time when you have low unemployment, we require immigration to fill those skill gaps.” Assistant Multicultural Affairs Minister Julian Hill said Gutwein brought “strong leadership” and would help guide the council as it worked to bridge communities and build a more cohesive Australia. “He brings a track record in strong leadership and a demonstrated commitment to speaking out against racism and standing in support of the rights of all Australians to participate in our national life. “Shared values, mutual respect and a genuine sense of belonging is the foundation of success in modern, multicultural Australia.” Minister for Multicultural Affairs, Dr Anne Aly, said the council’s work helped ensure that people of all backgrounds felt valued, connected and able to contribute to Australia’s future. title: John Howard neutralised Pauline Hanson 30 years ago. What’s changed since then? - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Who are we becoming as a nation? The question of our political identity as voters had a simple answer before Pauline Hanson finally cracked the populist code in 2026, after almost three decades on the electoral fringe. Before this year, Australia’s democracy was defined by the absence of extremism. Liberal prime ministers sat consistently to the centre-left of their Conservative and Republican peers in Britain and the US, while Labor’s were to the centre-right of British Labour and less ideological than the US Democrats. The flipside of our gold coin of moderation was the leaders and parties that Australians rejected. The Liberals lost winnable elections when they imported American agendas, to deregulate the workplace or to wind back Medicare, as John Howard learnt twice, from opposition in 1987 and in the defeat of his government in 2007. Labor failed when it tried to redistribute income, most recently under Bill Shorten in 2019. Our system of compulsory preferential voting had reinforced our egalitarian and obedient national temperament by pulling the major parties towards the centre while creating a barrier to entry to those on the hard right. So what changed this year to elevate One Nation above the Coalition and up to level-pegging with Labor in the national opinion polls? How did One Nation suddenly break out of its Queensland-centred political identity to seize its first House of Representatives seat at the byelection for Farrer, in southern NSW, and come within a single win of claiming the formal opposition from the Liberals in South Australia, the state traditionally considered one of our most socially progressive? All this before the Victorian showdown in November, where the polls, if they are to be believed, point to the first three-way contest since the early years of federation when the establishment side of politics was represented by two competing Liberal parties, the Protectionists and the Free Traders, while the trade union-backed Labor was the rising political force on the left. Understanding Hanson’s late career surge, and the implications for both our politics and our sense of self as a nation, starts with a reminder of her role as an electoral wrecking ball in the late 1990s, when she threatened Howard’s first-term Coalition government. For Howard, Hanson was an accident waiting to happen. Liberal Party pollster and strategist Mark Textor explained it to me long after her insurgency had passed into political history: “Why did Hanson flatfoot Howard? Because Howard, after attacking Paul Keating from the right, was being attacked from the right.” Hanson had caught the anti-incumbent wave that wiped out the Keating Labor government in 1996. Preselected by the Liberal Party to run for the safe Labor seat of Oxley, south-west of Brisbane, she had her endorsement withdrawn after she ignored repeated warnings to tone down her comments to the media. She said, among other things, that the government had created racism “by looking after Aborigines too much”. Howard said her removal from the Liberal team proved that his party would “govern for all Australians”. title: ‘Fake agents’: Migration operators stripped of credentials in crackdown - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Three migration agents have been suspended or stripped of their registrations after allowing unqualified people to use their credentials to provide immigration advice, in a crackdown exposing further misconduct within Australia’s migration industry. The cases include hundreds of visa applications in which registered migration agents allowed unregistered individuals to provide migration assistance using their government-issued identity numbers, commonly known as “front agent” arrangements. The action marks a more aggressive approach by the federal government after years of criticism over the handling of misconduct complaints and a damning Commonwealth auditor-general report that identified a host of failures in supervising the migration agents who facilitate the arrival of vulnerable people into the country. The Office of the Migration Agents Registration Authority (OMARA) cancelled one agent’s registration after finding hundreds of applications lodged through three business ImmiAccounts – the department’s online portal – involved either undeclared immigration assistance or work performed by people who were not registered migration agents. In another case, an agent was suspended after admitting his son, who was not registered, had provided immigration assistance through the business. Investigators also identified allegations that clients had been given falsified departmental correspondence, creating the impression their visa applications had been lodged when they had not. A third agent was suspended after knowingly allowing another business director to lodge visa applications using his registration number until the person became qualified as a migration agent. Assistant Minister for Citizenship Julian Hill said migrants paying for professional advice should be able to trust the person handling their case was properly qualified. He compared the practice to allowing an unqualified person to operate using the registration of a doctor, lawyer or financial planner. “When people pay a migration agent they rightly expect a qualified person will do the work, not an untrained, unregistered fake agent,” Hill said. OMARA, which sits within the Department of Home Affairs, can caution agents, suspend or cancel their registrations and bar former agents from re-registering. Its investigations team can take disciplinary action when agents breach professional obligations or are found not to be fit and proper to provide immigration assistance. Only registered migration agents, Australian legal practitioners or exempt people can legally provide immigration assistance in Australia. In March, the federal government announced migration agents would have to undertake yearly ethics training and regular refreshers on their obligations to continue helping people obtain Australian visas. A 2024 Australian National Audit Office report found Home Affairs’ regulation of migration agents was not effective, with inadequate monitoring and failures to take timely action on complaints. The audit found the department had failed to properly investigate an agent suspected of involvement in sex trafficking after being alerted by Australian Border Force. It also found an automated renewal system had approved agents despite complaints alleging fraudulent behaviour. One complaint took five years to resolve, while allegations involving cash-for-visa arrangements were dismissed over a technicality. The audit’s findings came after then-home affairs minister Clare O’Neil pledged to overhaul the integrity of the migration system following a series of reports in this masthead exposing the way criminals were hijacking visa schemes for their own gain. Migration Institute of Australia chief executive Peter van Vliet said this year that despite more than 4000 registered agents nationwide, only a “very small” number were sanctioned each year. He also warned that negative media narratives were contributing to migration agents becoming “punching bags” in public debate despite their role in helping migrants and businesses comply with Australian law. A spokesman for OMARA said the sanctioned operators damaged the reputation of the broader profession and undermined confidence in migration advice. “While the vast majority of [registered migration agents] act with integrity and professionalism, there is a small cohort who intentionally seek to undermine the migration program for personal gain,” the spokesman said. title: Is Hanson’s rise Albanese’s fall? Not so fast - SMH.com.au
raw_text: A month ago, Anthony Albanese gave a remarkably sanguine admission of the fact that sometimes there is nothing you can do to stop political decline. “I firmly believe that if you govern in the right way, and you get the policies right, then the politics will look after itself,” he told The Saturday Paper. “And if it doesn’t, due to circumstances beyond your control, well, that’s OK.” Is Labor in political decline? The opinion of pundits right now seems drastically split. On one hand, there is acceptance that Labor is very likely to win the next federal election – because it starts with a huge seat majority and the conservative vote is split between teals, One Nation and the Coalition. At the same time, there is a growing hum of commentary suggesting the government is in trouble, Albanese is unpopular and fighting back could be tough. Saturday’s result in the byelection for the West Australian state seat of Secret Harbour will amplify that hum. The WA Labor government suffered a huge swing against it, its MP’s primary vote being almost halved. One Nation won decisively. Albanese would have had a good sense this was coming: context for the fact that last week, visiting the state, he gave a clear indication he is aware that anything might happen between now and the next federal election. That indication came in the form of a clear commitment to continue the ridiculously generous deal WA gets on the GST. This undermines his first point from last month – that if policies are right, the politics will look after themselves. The WA GST deal is bad policy, hugely expensive and unfair to all other states and the people who live in them – as the Productivity Commission’s recent interim report made clear. But the commitment shows Albanese is entirely genuine when he refers to the possibility of circumstances running beyond you. The only good reason to keep the GST deal is the knowledge that the moment Labor breaks its word, every one of its opponents in WA will move in for the kill. And the only reason that matters is if you believe it is possible that, at the 2028 election, those WA seats might turn out to be essential. Albanese is not betting Labor will be in political strife by 2028, but he is obviously taking out insurance just in case. On the politics, this is understandable. The Secret Harbour byelection means little federally. First, it’s a state seat. Second, byelections indicate nothing about the future. They are not full elections, which people know: voters are free to lodge a protest without having to worry about changing the government. This has been true in most of One Nation’s recent successes: in the Farrer byelection in NSW and in the South Australian election, when everybody knew Labor would win. But then Albanese, who is always thinking ahead, will be cognisant this is a real risk in 2028, too. If voters believe Labor is guaranteed victory, they might feel free to vote One Nation, whatever their reservations about the party’s seriousness. Or perhaps One Nation will become more serious – something it is clearly attempting. Recently, it hired one of Scott Morrison’s former advisers. He had been working at the Australian Banking Association. Then it hired another ABA employee. About the same time, it announced it would cut tobacco taxes. That policy had potential cut-through – everybody knows about illegal tobacco – and aligned with calls from some economic experts. This move towards seriousness will be undermined if its Farrer MP, David Farley, ends up leaving the party, as is rumoured. Last week, a higher-than-expected inflation figure came in, leading to speculation about a rate rise in November or even September. It is true that a rate rise will be bad for the government – and may help One Nation. But the signals are hugely mixed, with some economists advising caution while we wait for more data. And this should give the political class pause. A significant factor in Labor’s struggles last term was inflation. Poor(ish) polls were often read as a sign of broad trouble, rather than simply what happens to every government during an inflationary surge. By the election, inflation had fallen and the government won. And despite the entire political class having lived through this, there is a fair bit of amnesia around. It could be that some of Labor’s current polling troubles (which, it must be said, its opponents would kill to have) are the result of wider dissatisfaction. But it is also possible they are largely traceable to inflation. In which case, if inflation begins to slide again, Labor could see a recovery similar to 2025. There is every chance that will happen. The Reserve Bank, in its August monetary statement, observed that its May prediction – that the Middle East conflict would rapidly drive up prices – had been incorrect. Predictions aren’t lasting long. But the government will face other hurdles. As inflation comes off, voters are likely to sharpen their focus on the government’s achievements – a focus Albanese has invited. In the same interview in which he accepted the role of circumstance, Albanese made the point that seeing everything through the prism of One Nation could distort things. “You can get swamped by, ‘What are we doing about Hanson?’ No, no, no, no. It is the wrong question. ‘Are we governing properly?’ is the right question.” That is a good reminder for those of us writing about politics. As the government prepares to release its immigration policy, it may be a useful reminder for Labor, too. Last week, it seemed the government was cutting the country’s refugee intake – before the prime minister made clear it would remain where it was. If the GST deal was a sign that sometimes the politics comes ahead of sensible policy, the refugee decision was a welcome sign that One Nation isn’t yet quite as influential as it sometimes seems to be. The truth is that none of us really know what type of immigration policy is likely to stop One Nation’s rise. The focus – for Labor and everyone else – should be on whether the policy is a good one. Sean Kelly is an author and regular columnist. He was an adviser to Labor prime ministers Julia Gillard and Kevin Rudd.

title: One Nation’s ‘vibe’ adds to its confusion over migration policy - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Having spent 36 years as a social science teacher, I thought I had a reasonable grasp of migration issues. Intrastate, interstate, net and gross migration, various classes of visas, the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility system and even the Colombo Plan found their way into my classrooms. Now I feel I must apologise to my students for having got it all wrong, as One Nation has clarified the issue to the point where I am totally confused (“Five days on, Hanson still finds it hard to explain migration policy”, August 28). On the same subject, Waleed Aly is absolutely correct when he says “the devil has convinced us the details don’t matter” (“One Nation policy all about the vibe”, August 28). I can’t wait for further enlightening policy announcements from “our future prime minister”. Peter Cooper-Southam, Frenchs Forest Like Waleed Aly, I have been fascinated by the Goldilocks figure of 130,000 net migrants. Assuming some arrive with families of three or four, does this mean they have calculated that only about 60,000 new migrants will be available to fill vacancies in high-demand sectors such as aged care, hospitality and healthcare, given that not all dependents in family units take part in the workforce? The reason Pauline Hanson has not yet been able to arrive at a scientifically defensible migration figure is that population planning and labour demand require deep analysis, projections, assumptions and, more importantly, data gathered from the ground up. Simply plucking numbers from the air as part of a bidding war for votes may attract support because of the “vibe”, but it will not produce workable solutions for the nation. Cultural grievances may be part of the conversation, but they cannot be the sole lens through which complex policy problems are viewed, however tempting that may be. Manbir Singh Kohli, Pemulwuy Waleed Aly demonstrates very clearly that One Nation’s policy, whatever it is, is a circular argument, designed to make people feel rather than think. This is not news, just a clarification. It’s been obvious for some time that no one in One Nation seems to understand its own policy position, let alone be able to explain it. David Farley tried to calm the waters and explain that we still need migrants in his electorate. George Christensen doesn’t want the cat let out of the bag. Hanson can’t explain, because it can’t be explained. Barnaby Joyce is all about nonsense policy, presented as common sense. The figures in this alleged policy cannot be defined, capped or clarified because that is not the point. The point is that Hanson presents a nebulous group of people to blame for all our woes – “migrants” – regardless of why they arrive or how long they intend to stay. Geoff Nilon, Mascot Remember when the Reverend Fred Nile was receiving undue coverage with his evangelical rants? Pauline Hanson is pretty much in the same boat, only Fred did no harm and made us laugh with his prayers for rain on the eve of the Mardi Gras. Hanson, on the other hand, has the potential to do considerable harm with her xenophobia and her far right-wing leanings. Fortunately, Herald correspondents this week have put her blusters into true perspective. Ray Alexander, Moss Vale For someone in the political arena for over 30 years; a leader who put immigration front and centre of her party’s manifesto, Pauline Hanson has consistently and remarkably failed to master the policy basics. The so-called national conversation is fraught enough without confusing and straight-out incorrect information swamping us. Please explain, Ms Hanson. Cathryn Callaghan, Croydon Climate denial Mike Keene explains the problems climate change causes in ski resorts perfectly (Letters, August 28). He says: “For climate deniers, the easiest way to solve a problem is to deny it exists.” This is why we deny that world overpopulation is the No.1 problem humans face. So many other real problems stem from it. We live on a planet with finite resources, and denying it won’t help our children. Please speak up. Henry Schneebeli, Moree Parking mad The push to reduce apartment parking makes sense, particularly when more than 40 per cent of existing spaces sit empty overnight. Sydney’s rapid growth in apartment living has also contributed to worsening traffic congestion. As your editorial argues, the transition away from car dependency will work only if we improve public transport (“Homes can do without car parks but only if there’s great public transport”, August 28). Bikes, and particularly e-bikes, can then play an important supporting role, allowing people to cycle to and from stations and extending the reach of buses and trains. But if we want to encourage their use, we need to address where all these e-bikes are going to be parked. Sydney’s councils should collaborate to develop sensible standards for secure bike and e-bike parking at transport hubs, in apartment developments and around shopping centres. Reducing car parking is only part of the equation. If we want people to leave their cars at home, we need to make the alternatives practical and that includes giving e-bikes somewhere sensible to park. John Kempler, Rose Bay Inner West Council will allow some developments without parking spaces. Maybe NSW needs the system that applies in Tokyo, which requires a car buyer to prove they have a parking space before they are allowed to register a car. Steven Lee, Faulconbridge Yes to red tape More of the same self-serving offerings from the business elites of the Business Council of Australia (“‘Consume, be silent, die’: that’s the PM’s message, say fed-up business chiefs”, August 28). Decades of neoliberalism have increased corporate profits and overly generous executive remuneration while they snatched any productivity gains for themselves and watched wages stagnate or go backwards. But that is still not enough for them. They want more profit and less red tape. On the contrary, I say more red tape to stop large companies avoiding income tax. I say more red tape so that when companies collapse, they are not a maze of shell companies specifically designed to hide the true state of affairs of the principal corporation. There would be no red tape at all if all businesses operated ethically, but they don’t. Graeme Finn, Campsie GST hurts all Tony Martin says raising the GST is a fairer strategy for the Reserve Bank to employ instead of rate rises for mortgage holders, spreading the pain to all (Letters, August 28). How many times do they employ this strategy, once? Or every time it’s needed? One could ask, why should those without mortgages, or those on pension, or welfare payments, et cetera, subsidise wealthy property owners who have large mortgages and who are struggling to service them? The cost of living is already rising to alarming levels and families are struggling. The GST affects almost everything we rely on to survive, and it should not be used to make life harder for all. Lynn Nadjarian, Forster Powerhouse mystery The back door on Powerhouse Parramatta has finally opened a crack (“Powerhouse Parramatta chief Lisa Havilah departs just weeks from opening”, August 28). It would be a travesty if the Powerhouse Ultimo tragedy does not also get an airing. In brief terms: A budget of $300 million was set in March 2023 for the so-called revitalisation of the Powerhouse Museum. A year later, the museum closed its doors and its entire collection of objects, including the priceless and fragile B&W steam engine, was carted off to that giant warehouse in Castle Hill. This year, without any legitimate public consultation, the Wran Building and the Galleria, both of them the very essence of the Powerhouse Museum, were turned into landfill. It can’t be physically confirmed, but all evidence indicates that the heritage-listed Powerhouse building itself has been gutted and is now just an empty shell. Yet to this day, the government has not corrected the myth that this project is on budget and will deliver a revitalised applied arts and sciences museum. The reopening date remains in limbo. Garry Horvai, Pennant Hills The news today that the Parramatta Powerhouse is in chaos is not surprising. Not really since the days of Neville Wran has there been any government that has understood what heritage is. The state’s heritage is in chaos – the Harbour Bridge is rusting away and so is Cleveland House, Australia’s oldest house, in Bedford Street, near Central Station. The Ultimo Powerhouse has been demolished and its historic collection has been taken away. Heritage is something we should be proud of, but we seem only to be ashamed of it. Clive Lucas, Neutral Bay Cashing in Ted Bush (Letters, August 28) insinuates that US Democratic politician Nancy Pelosi is comparable with US President Donald Trump without presenting any evidence that she or her husband traded using confidential government information, whereas the correlation between White House decisions and the trading patterns of Trump and his family are well documented. Pelosi and her husband’s increase in wealth of $230 million happened over 40 years, not outside the norm for an astute share trader. Trump’s increase has been about $4 billion over two years. Stein Boddington, St Clair Heed disasters’ lessons Through no fault of their own, villagers and their homes are swept away by a terrifying ice avalanche (“A terrifying roar, then came the fury of the flood: How disaster unfolded in Nepal”, August 28). As UN chief Antonio Guterres has said: “The rooftops of the world are caving in.” Hard on the heels of record heatwaves and wildfires across the northern hemisphere, some of which are still burning, the warning for humanity is absolutely deafening: “Stop burning fossil fuels!” Rob Firth, Red Hill (ACT) The folly of placing financial gain above the care for our planet has been horrifically demonstrated in Nepal. Through climate change, nature has demonstrated its power and exposed life’s fragility and our hubris. And not just this event but catastrophic and record-breaking bushfires, floods, heatwaves and severe weather events around the world. When will governments react comprehensively and decisively to climate change, as they do to its resultant disasters? Stop opening new gas and coal mines, stop the diesel subsidy, tax the gas giants, introduce a climate trigger, expand the transmission network, promote clean energy exports, financially support EV purchases and infrastructure and improve home thermal efficiency. A major duty of our government is to protect its citizens. So do it! Rowan Godwin, Rozelle Europe’s on fire. Glaciers are collapsing in the Himalayas. Grass is growing in Antartica. Hey Tony, Matt and Pauline, tell us about the “climate hoax” again, will you? Phil Bradshaw, Naremburn Degrees of knowledge A friend once admitted that despite having two degrees in economics, he still didn’t understand it. He said it was all based on assumptions, and to highlight that impracticality, he told a joke that economists tell about themselves. Three people are marooned on a desert island: an engineer, a doctor and an economist. They have one can of baked beans between them. The engineer says, “Let’s smash it against that rock.” The doctor says, “Let’s sharpen that stick on that rock and pierce it.” The economist says, “Assume we have a can opener.” Malcolm McEwen, North Turramurra Name games In the 1960s, our geography teacher taught us to remember the names of the Great Lakes of North America by the words “Sydney Morning Herald Early Order”. How dare Mr Trump mess that up (“Trump orders Lake Ontario to be renamed ‘Lake America’ amid Canada trade war”, August 27)? Margaret Swinbourne, Drummoyne I don’t understand why Donald Trump hasn’t changed the name of New Mexico yet (Letters, August 28). Brendan Jones, Annandale I can’t wait for Trump to rename Earth. Maybe “Planet America”? Kevin Farrell, Beelbangera - To submit a letter to the Sydney Morning Herald, email letters@smh.com.au. title: ‘Could see myself sitting here’: One Nation MP Farley gatecrashes Liberal meeting - SMH.com.au
raw_text: One Nation MP David Farley has fuelled speculation about his future in Pauline Hanson’s party after accidentally walking into a private meeting of more than 20 Liberal MPs – then telling them he could see himself sitting with them. The extraordinary encounter happened in Parliament House last Wednesday when Farley wandered into a regular meeting of Liberal MPs from marginal seats. Several Liberals present said the Farrer MP took a while to realise he was in the wrong room before turning to leave. “I could see myself sitting here,” Farley told the MPs, before walking out. “We were all taken aback, to be honest,” one Liberal MP said. “It was a very loose thing to say.” Farley confirmed the incident on Monday, but portrayed it as an off-the-cuff joke after accidentally entering the room. He said the Liberal MPs had a “who-hit-John” look on their faces, silent with their mouths open, before he “filled the empty space with my quip” and left. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said Farley was currently a member of One Nation “but certainly let’s see what the future holds”. “He’s a decent fellow, I’ve met him a couple of times,” Hastie told ABC’s 7.30. The remark comes at an awkward time for One Nation, with Farley again publicly at odds with Hanson over one of the party’s central political issues. The Farrer MP told ABC’s Insiders that while One Nation wanted to reduce net overseas migration to 130,000, it would allow another 100,000 migrant workers through skilled visas, backpacker programs and the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. That would put the effective number at about 230,000 – broadly in line with Labor’s forecast of 225,000 by 2027–28. Hanson moved quickly to reject Farley’s interpretation, insisting One Nation’s policy was to cut net overseas migration to 130,000, with some short-term agricultural workers excluded from the official measure. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce was then sent out to clean up the mess, telling Sunrise that Farley had simply got it wrong. “Show me a political career where people haven’t made a mistake, and I’ll show you a person who’s not told the truth.” Joyce said One Nation had seemingly raised the matter with Farley but refused to elaborate. “Oh, look, I’m not going to throw anybody under a bus,” he said. “When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect, and that’s what happens. God knows I’ve done it enough.” “I think [Farley] would have been offended by [One Nation’s head of operations] James Ashby going on News24 last night with a mop and essentially mocking what I thought were his thoughtful contributions on [ABC’s] Insiders yesterday,” Hastie said. Hastie was referring to Ashby’s appearance on News24 on Sunday night where he brandished a mop and clarified One Nation’s migration policies, stating he’d spoken to Farley and that “people make mistakes”. “For a new member of parliament, it’s always difficult getting your head around those [net overseas migration] numbers,” Ashby said. Farley’s comments were also savaged by online news site One News Australia, which branded his appearance a “rookie blunder” and claimed his “clueless” performance had given Labor an “escape route” from its migration policy. The criticism is notable given One News Australia’s origins as the One Nation Supporters Network before it was rebranded as a news organisation. The site and the party say they have no affiliation, although its coverage is strongly pro-One Nation and Hanson. Farley was previously counselled by Hanson during the Farrer byelection campaign after he agreed a net migration figure of 306,000 last year was “probably not” too many. The pair also exchanged harsh words after it was revealed that he’d previously tried to seek preselection with Labor for the seat and not informed anyone within One Nation before it was revealed by this masthead. Farley has already shown he is prepared to depart from Hanson’s position in the parliament. Last week he voted with the Coalition on an amendment to Labor’s wagering legislation, despite Hanson having previously committed to supporting the government’s ban on foreign matched lotteries. His growing independence is being watched closely by Coalition MPs, particularly given his conservative and agricultural background. Sources in the Coalition said Opposition Leader Angus Taylor knew Farley from his time as an agribusiness leader and could potentially use the relationship to court him in future, although there are no immediate plans to do so. “He is a Nat or a country Liberal, not a populist,” one Liberal MP said. Farley told Insiders he came from the conservative LNP tradition, joined the Nationals after returning to Farrer and later explored joining Labor and running as an independent. He ultimately chose One Nation because he said it offered the “political courage” and “tenacity” he wanted. “I have the full support of the party to pursue what I’m doing, especially for Farrer,” he said. title: One Nation denies fringe influencer is a member after he supports neo-Nazi rights - SMH.com.au
raw_text: A right-wing influencer who interviewed Pauline Hanson has described the fight to overturn a ban on the neo-Nazi White Australia party as “the last stand” for Australian democracy. A week after distancing himself from neo-Nazi figures, an online influencer known as Ausmaxx has posted videos condemning the various criminal charges against National Socialist Network leaders. Ausmaxx, whose real name is Andre Mamet, interviewed Hanson at the CPAC summit in London in the same week she met with anti-Islam activist and criminal Tommy Robinson, raising questions about her associations with fringe figures. This masthead reported last week that Mamet had recently joined One Nation, a point that neither Mamet nor One Nation disputed. But late on Wednesday, after questions about Mamet’s later remarks, the party issued a statement saying: “This individual has not been a member of One Nation since May.” This masthead has learned that Mamet joined One Nation around May, raising questions about how his membership lapsed around the same time. Mamet spoke about NSN founder Thomas Sewell in a livestream on X on Friday. He defended Sewell, who was born in New Zealand, against a judge’s accusations that he was un-Australian. “It’s actually insane… He’s a perfect example of an Australian because he’s from the collective of what is the Anglosphere,” Mamet said. Sewell founded the NSN, which the federal government banned along with radical Islamists Hizb ut-Tahrir. He also punched a security guard in Melbourne before performing a Nazi salute after he was found guilty of recklessly causing injury. Mamet also posted a video on Saturday about neo-Nazis including Joel Davis and Michael Nelson. Davis was part of a delegation who held a large banner on the steps of NSW parliament that said, “Abolish the Jewish lobby” and chanted “blood and honour”, a Hitler Youth slogan. Davis was later charged over a post calling on NSN members to “rhetorically rape” MP Allegra Spender. Nelson was jailed for 21 days for performing a Nazi salute in Melbourne and wearing a meme T-shirt about the Holocaust which said “6 million? That’s a bit much mate”. Mamet said of Davis and Nelson: “Political speech is being treated as a criminal offence.” Mamet’s comments feed into a broader complaint from some on the right who say that laws are increasingly used to shut down debate on issues such as migration. The NSN’s successor, the White Australia party, has been subject of a High Court case. White Australia has also been trying to register as a party. The High Court will hold a two-day hearing in September on the constitutionality of anti-hate speech laws. “This is the final stand. In September, the fate of Australian democracy is decided on the banning of this political party,” Mamet said in the stream on X. As Hanson’s party attracts supporters worried about ethnic diversity in Australia, One Nation will receive more scrutiny over the limits of its tolerance for hardline views. Hanson previously told the Inside Politics podcast that she feared her party was “infiltrated by extremists”. One Nation retains a big lead on the Coalition in the polls. Mamet, who is promoting “March for Australia” rallies later this month, said he did “not support Nazism at all, but the purpose of democratic rights is not to protect only popular opinions.” “I completely reject the ideas of ‘hate speech’ and ‘hate groups’. I don’t believe it is acceptable to ban a political group based on the government’s perspective… The hate speech laws empower the government of the day to ban anyone they don’t like”. “That’s why this [High Court] case is so important: it will determine whether Australians holding views some find extreme can organise politically and be judged by the voters. What the government considers hateful today could be the White Australia Party, and tomorrow it could be One Nation.” Some experts have argued that banning extremist parties can push networks underground and make them more difficult to monitor. In 1951, a referendum to ban the Communist Party was defeated in Australia. Mamet said it was important to defend “the policing of free speech is a slippery slope which, if left unchecked, will lead to the criminalisation of all nationalists.” “The concept of hate speech was literally invented in Stalin’s Soviet Russia. Does The Age support the atrocities of Stalin’s regime?” Mamet’s support for Hanson’s party reflects its growing support among Australians worried about Australia’s rate of migration, which has been well above peer democracies over the past 20 years and is the subject of new proposals from all major parties to reduce numbers. One Nation was forced to clarify its signature migration policy earlier this week. A proposal previously described as capping visas at 130,000 has turned into the party’s net migration figure, meaning the number of visas issues would be tens of thousands more than 130,000. Adding to the confusion, new One Nation MP David Farley told The Conversation that there would be about 40,000 more migrants on top of the 130,000 because certain visa classes such as Pacific workers and nurses should effectively be exempt. Asked if he had differences with Hanson on migration policy, Farley said: “Oh, there’s definitely a difference.” But he later said he had convinced Hanson of the merits of his positions on the need to retain migration in agricultural communities. “We matched our positions. We negotiated our position to arrive at it,” he said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

title: How a conspiracy theory embraced by Trump became mainstream in Australia - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Talking about the far-right immigration narrative that’s moving ever further into Australia’s political mainstream is about as much fun as having a colonoscopy but is similarly necessary and urgent. With One Nation leading federal polls and the Liberal Party’s announcement that it wants to bring migration down to its lowest level since 2009, now is probably the wisest time to peek into the future that they aspire to for Australia, before we wake up in late 2028 to discover there’s a shortage of nurses and we’re all eating government-mandated traditional British food like spotted dick, which is a dessert made with mutton fat that sounds like it’s contracted a venereal disease. The story that the far-right is telling is a compelling one: the West, and particularly the left, needs to wake up to the threat of invasion by brown and black people, before it leads to the erasure of Anglo-Celtic culture and the extinction of the white race. (I believe I might be part of the invasion vanguard. Still awaiting orders, if so.) Their story has three distinct acts. There is the problem, which is the threat of immigrant invasion; the cause, widely believed to be an organised conspiracy named the great replacement theory and the solution, known as remigration. While the concept of invasion is familiar, the great replacement theory and the term remigration have only relatively recently entered the political mainstream. The central claim of the great replacement theory is that changing demographics in the West are evidence of a conspiracy by leftist and Jewish elites to commit “white genocide”, through immigration policies that would allow new non-white, and particularly Muslim voters, to ultimately control political and cultural power. Tony Abbott, who is back in charge of the Liberal Party as federal president and, who has a long history of buying into this narrative, recently dog-whistled to this theory, writing: “To green-left, cultural Marxist governments, mass migration from the ‘global south’ is not a problem; it’s the plan.” Conservatives who are genuinely afraid of co-ordinated political interference by religious groups could start by answering the call that’s coming from inside their house, given the secretive campaigning efforts of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church on behalf of the Liberal Party at the last federal election. They’re not wrong, however, to claim that the great replacement theory is terrifying, only they completely misidentify who has the most reason to be fearful of it. The theory has become one of the primary drivers of racially motivated mass violence events globally, with Muslims and Jewish people comprising the overwhelming majority of victims. Since 2017, believers in the theory have been responsible for over a dozen mass murders, including the Australian Christchurch killer, who murdered 51 Muslims in 2019 and titled his manifesto “The Great Replacement”. The theory leads to its proposed solution: remigration. This refers to the forced, mass removal of non-white immigrants and their descendants from Western countries, even if they’re citizens or legal residents. In 2025, One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts told an anti-immigration conference in Brisbane: “Remigration is the second part of my speech. Take the people who are not fitting in or that we don’t need and send them home.” When Pauline Hanson was asked in July if she agreed with a UK far-right party’s policy of mass deportations, she replied “I love it.” Should One Nation end up governing Australia, they may follow the example of their MAGA friends in the US. In 2025, the Trump administration quietly set up an Office of Remigration in the State Department, with WIRED reporting: “There’s no mention (of the Office of Remigration) on the department’s social media feeds or even on the official website. There aren’t many details about when it was established, who is running the office, or what work it is carrying out.” How remigration will Make America Great Again is also unclear, with Forbes reporting: “The Trump administration’s policies on immigration may reduce the projected number of workers in the United States by 6.8 million by 2028, lower the annual rate of economic growth by almost one-third, harming US living standards … and substantially increase the federal debt.” Back in Australia, the math ain’t mathing for Hanson either. During a July podcast, Hanson stated that Australia is taking in 739,000 migrants a year. She didn’t mention it, but the figure (737,000) was from the 2022-23 financial year when there was an anomaly of post-COVID returnees. Nor did she mention the 219,000 people who left Australia during that period, meaning the net migration figure was really 518,000. It’s telling that Hanson misused a statistic that she must have known was outdated. The problem for Abbott and One Nation’s narrative is that since 2023, Australia’s migrant intake numbers have been on a downwards trajectory. In 2024-2025, Australia’s net migration number was 306,000. Over half of that was international students on temporary visas, who do not have voting rights, which means another 157,000 people can be discounted from the scary migrant-takeover-from-within story being told to anxious voters. So if you know someone who is angry or frightened by immigration conspiracies, invite them over for afternoon tea. Gently remind them that they’re worrying about less than 150,000 annual migrants – about 0.5 per cent of Australia’s population – many of whom are the skilled workers that Australia desperately needs. This includes the migrants who make up 40 per cent of our healthcare workforce, with this figure even higher in regional areas. Then offer them a slice of spotted dick. If facts don’t change their mind, maybe that will. Melanie La’Brooy is a novelist who writes on politics and social justice issues. title: Labor quietly pauses working holidaymaker visas as stoush over backpackers brews - SMH.com.au
raw_text: The Albanese government has quietly paused working holidaymaker visa applications from 24 countries as it seeks to wrest control of the migration system while a political stoush brews over whether to curtail the number of backpackers who come to Australia. Migration and travel agents have told the tourism industry they have been detecting delays in processing times for countries with uncapped backpacker places since the beginning of July, while the pause on applications from countries with caps was introduced without notice in the last month. Backpacker and Youth Tourism Advisory Panel chair Peta Zietsch said this would have a knock-on effect for tourism operators and regional employers who relied on backpackers for seasonal work, and who would usually expect young Europeans to arrive in Australia soon for the summer period. Zietsch said it also risked deterring backpackers when combined with the recent rise in visa fees, which increased from $670 to $840 for first visas and $1000 for second- and third-year visas last month. “Rather than placing barriers in the way of the working holidaymaker program, we should be looking at ways to attract more young international travellers here,” she said. Working holidaymakers, who have surged in number since the pandemic, were drawn into the political debate over immigration this week as both Labor and the Coalition fine-tune their plans for lowering Australia’s migrant intake. title: The moment Australia’s immigration program went off the rails - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Three major factors are driving Australia’s immigration intake to record highs. All of them start in the centre of Australia’s largest cities. The CBDs and surrounding suburbs of Melbourne and Sydney are where universities are filled with international students, as well as bars, offices and delivery services that thrive on the backs of foreign workers – and where most backpackers first land. Australia’s permanent migration intake has barely changed over the past decade, hovering around 200,000 a year under Labor and the Coalition. But the temporary intake has exploded. Last financial year, more than 1 million visas were delivered to students, working holidaymakers, and skilled migrants. There are now more than 3 million temporary visa holders in Australia, effectively creating an underclass of migrant workers who now count for more than 16 per cent of the working-age population. Martin Parkinson, former head of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, says voters would never have agreed if the government had explicitly said it was going to have a guest worker program. “What we ended up with was this underclass of the permanently temporary,” he says. Like many poor policies, the situation is not the result of a single piece of legislation, but a patchwork of shifting regulations that are now very difficult to unravel. On July 1, 2014, parliament’s attention was not on the prime minister’s courtyard. It was on Christmas Island, 5000 kilometres from Canberra, in the middle of the Indian Ocean: 153 Tamil asylum seekers had just been handed over to the Sri Lankan navy. Immigration minister Scott Morrison was in the midst of Operation Sovereign Borders, a military-led forced deportation scheme of asylum seekers that would decimate the people-smuggling trade and rocket secrecy over “on-water matters” to the top of the national agenda. But behind the headlines, a little-known legislative instrument was implemented that would have a much larger impact on Australia’s immigration program. Business lobby groups had spent years criticising the Rudd-Gillard Labor governments over their crackdown on skilled worker visas. The Australian Hotels Association and the National Farmers Federation wanted the minimum income threshold for skilled migrants reduced. They had built on the lobbying of Neville Roach, the former managing director of Fujitsu Australia, who argued in the 1990s that Australia had to get workers into jobs as quickly as possible. The Howard government under immigration minister Philip Ruddock balanced this campaign for speed by implementing thresholds on the minimum incomes migrants could earn and tying them to inflation. “I was not prepared to expand skilled migration by weakening the very criteria that made it valuable,” says Ruddock. “The answer was to sharpen the targeting and hold firm on minimum thresholds.” On July 1, 2014, Morrison froze the threshold at $53,900. It would stay there for the next decade. By 2016, the temporary skilled visa program almost tripled, growing from 98,000 to 260,000 by allowing more workers to fill jobs that paid below-average wages. Morrison was contacted for comment. In May of that year, a government review by Deloitte partner John Azarias recommended pegging the threshold to wage growth. The Coalition government ignored it, driving cheaper workers into more jobs. By the time it was unfrozen in 2023, 90 per cent of Australian full-time jobs were paid more than the minimum threshold. Parkinson, who led a review into the immigration system in 2023, says the threshold freeze was a key driver behind the surge in lower-skilled migrants into Australia. “The subsequent introduction of labour market agreements provided even greater flexibility to undermine the previous arrangements, allowing for the payment of wages below the Temporary Skilled Migrant Income Threshold and easing other requirements such as English language,” says Parkinson. Labor’s former home affairs minister Clare O’Neil unfroze the threshold in 2023, taking it above $70,000 and re-pegging it to inflation. But the damage had been done. Once they were in Australia, many workers stayed by jumping between visas. The backlog of bridging visas exploded. When bridging visas were introduced in 1994, they were designed to fill brief administrative gaps. They have now overwhelmed the department, leaving Home Affairs unable to process visas in time and keeping temporary migrants in Australia far longer than initially expected. “I remember a meeting in the Department of Immigration in 1993, where we discussed whether we should have bridging visas at all or not,” says Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the Department of Immigration. “The conclusion was that there will always be circumstances where we need a bridging visa [for exceptional reasons], but we should never allow the number of people on bridging visas to get much above 10,000. Well, we now have over 400,000 people on bridging visas. “This is just eye-watering stuff.” Successive governments cannot say they were not warned. In 2011, immigration researcher Peter Mares said in a lecture delivered in the Senate that Australia was in danger of mirroring Germany through its use of Gastarbeiter, referring to migrant guest workers mostly of Turkish origin who could work in Germany, but did not have political rights, fuelling social and cultural isolation. Mares said Australia “called for labour power and people came”. “[But] we are in danger of focusing on the Arbeitskräfte – the labour power – and losing sight of the Mensch – the human being,” he said. “The problem is that human beings cannot be reduced to units of production in the mining industry or export dollars for the education sector.” In Melbourne and Sydney, those workers brought in on skilled visas now staff offices, restaurants and hospitals. They are often supported in those roles by international students who are working while studying. They gravitate towards the centre of our biggest cities for work and for play. “Density creates the vibe,” says Howin Chui, the head of business development at Castle Group, a property developer that also runs venues. Chui says his venues in the centre of Sydney would struggle to survive without international students as both staff and customers. “People like to go to one place where they can get everything.” During the COVID pandemic, the government also removed any restrictions on student work hours (previously capped at 40 hours). Businesses became increasingly reliant on cheaper labour even as the pandemic receded. Students can now legally work 48 hours a fortnight, and illegally a lot longer, making Australia more attractive to those who also want to be able to send money home to their families while studying. In 2013-14, the number of student visas granted was 292,000. Last financial year, that number exceeded 371,000. “Over the last two decades, the Australian government has cut its contribution to universities to a point where they only cover around a third of the cost of educating a student,” says Parkinson. “So essentially, how we cover that is through student fees, domestic and international. Fees from international students also help replace the shortfall in government funding for research. So if you suddenly remove the international students, you are basically going to threaten the financial viability of the university sector, with consequences for student access and support, staffing and Australian research.” The challenge for Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is keeping universities alive without taxpayers footing the bill. That’s left him targeting partners and parents, who will be restricted from being able to join students on visas, as well as students who hop from one course to another. Ruddock has urged him to go further, arguing international students should have to leave Australia after completing their degrees, then reapply for visas to re-enter the country. Burke will also take out a chunk of the 300,000 backpackers in the country by introducing a ballot system. Until Pauline Hanson’s One Nation put them back at the top of the news cycle this year, many of the other recommendations in Parkinson’s review met the fate of countless other inquiries: filed away in the cupboard, gathering dust. Burke disputes this, arguing he has been working on solutions since he was appointed Home Affairs Minister in 2024, but accepts that politics is the prism through which the media and the public may view the immigration policy overhaul. Hanson has proposed cutting international student places by 40 per cent, a figure that Universities Australia has warned will see campuses shut down and research decimated. Now even Burke’s modest changes may have more far-reaching consequences than initially anticipated, as tighter regulations combine with anti-immigration sentiment to drive more people out of the country and stop more people from coming in. The government had planned to bring net overseas migration down from 300,000 to 225,000 a year. “Net overseas migration is now poised to significantly undershoot,” Timothy Hibbert from Oxford Economics said on Wednesday. “It is forecast that NOM will fall to 160,000 in 2028-29, slowing the national population growth rate to 0.95 per cent – the lowest figure since 1993.” Australia has a long history of migration boom and bust. “Migration: Crisis Point” screamed the headline in this masthead on September 10, 1967. The crisis former editor Max Suich raised in these pages was not about too many migrants; it was about too few. “The large and rapidly growing number of immigrants who are leaving Australia should not be tolerated,” Suich wrote. “This leak can be plugged.” By the end of the next decade, the leak had not just been plugged; the ship had been refloated. The White Australia policy had been abandoned. The country welcomed Tran Hue Hue, who, after fleeing Vietnam, survived five months marooned on a coral reef by eating seagulls. In Melbourne, a decade later, they celebrated Eritrean refugee Kongit Abdulmalik Mohammed joining Melbourne University’s medical faculty as one of the state’s top-scoring high school students. And in Sydney, Chui’s father Andy Chui and uncle Terrence Tang emigrated from Hong Kong to open Tang Dynasty: the Hurstville institution that would go on to serve generations of Australians. His mother, Annie Tang, became the deputy mayor of Kogarah, and Australia would go on to have the longest unbroken period of economic growth in the developed world. Chui has opened half a dozen venues under his Urban Agency banner, including the Hong Kong-style Kowloon Cafe and the modern Australian-adjacent Touch Wood at the Sydney Fish Market. “My Western friends think I’m too Asian. My Asian friends think I’m too Westernised,” laughs Chui. Urban Agency merged with Castle Group, a developer started by Sri Lankan migrant Ritchie Perera that is building hundreds of new homes across Austral and Rouse Hill in the outer suburbs of Sydney. Chui says many migrants feel like they have to prove themselves. “I think one of the strongest things that we have inside us is building the community and building the people around us,” he says. When his father founded Tang Dynasty, it was one of the few yum cha restaurants in Hurstville. Now the suburb is filled with food from Xinjiang to Beirut. “I think we’re the only country that I’ve been to where you can enjoy culture and food with such diversity,” says Chui. “You can’t go to Hong Kong and have a nice kebab.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
