title: 438 rejections, $55,000 and a years-long-wait: How international talent is turned away - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Dr Maha Selvanathan applied for 438 jobs in Australia before a rural NSW clinic offered her a role as a general practitioner. It took another three years and $55,000 before she was allowed to start working there. As the federal government struggles to find politically palatable ways to reduce the number of overseas arrivals, a parliamentary inquiry into skilled migration has exposed the growing challenges Australia faces in retaining foreign talent in crucial fields such as medicine. Australian Medical Association president Dr Danielle McMullen told the joint standing committee on migration on Friday that some doctors were going homeless while waiting on a complex and lengthy approvals process. She said highly specialised professionals would be poached by other nations with more streamlined systems, and Australia needed to address its duplicated layers of administration and a lack of support for new arrivals. Selvanathan, an AMA member who also appeared before the inquiry, told this masthead she began her job hunt in Adelaide after moving from Malaysia in 2011 to be with her husband. For months, she sat exams, proved her qualifications and demonstrated her English proficiency. Almost two years later, she was granted permanent residency. But she still didn’t have a job, and she had become subject to the 10-year moratorium, which requires migrant doctors to work in areas of high need for a decade. “I got rejection after rejection, and I got one offer from Armidale,” she says. Then there were more exams, and the regulator had to give its approval. Plus, the one clinic that had offered her a job was not already classified as being in need. For six months, the clinic advertised for a doctor to prove it could not get one. Selvanathan waited, barred from working in her field. She uprooted and moved to Sydney, ready to relocate again to Armidale. Her husband followed her there, but he could not get a job in the city of less than 24,000 people for almost eight months because he worked in IT. Throughout the process, she squirrelled away funds to return to Malaysia so she could keep her clinical skills up to date. “It was very depressing because I don’t know what my future holds,” she said. “There was always this praying and waiting whether this will go through, ‘will my registration go through, will my supervision go through’. So it was just very upsetting and a lot of money.” McMullen said more than half of Australia’s GPs were international medical graduates, who prop up rural medical services. They should be celebrated rather than being treated as a “temporary fix for poor workforce planning”, she said. She pointed to a lack of rural housing as a significant barrier. Logistical challenges were compounded by a “deep-set culture” of racism that meant migrant doctors were often forced out of roles, or lived in fear of speaking up against discrimination because their visa was tied to their employer, she said. “It is deeply concerning that we’ve got doctors essentially living in even short periods of homelessness. It is not, I think, what the community would expect,” she said. Liberal MP Leon Rebello, the migration committee’s deputy chair, said the housing challenge was a recurring theme across Friday’s testimony from numerous industries, from law to medicine and science. “That nexus between housing and immigration is going to be critical going forward,” Rebello said. “You can’t set migration numbers without giving due consideration to the infrastructure and the housing that Australia could take, and that’s ultimately the key.” As Prime Minister Anthony Albanese scrambles to get the Coalition onside for laws that will help the government hit a forecast 225,000 net migration target in two years time, Labor premiers have split. title: ‘You know a racist when you see one’: The premier’s balancing act on migration and One Nation - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Mumbai, India: States should have a greater say over the mix of skilled migrants who come into the country, Premier Chris Minns says, arguing the Commonwealth should be more responsive to the skills needed by individual jurisdictions to help target problems such as the housing shortage. During a four-day trade trip to India this week, Minns is walking a line between vocally supporting Australia’s Indian diaspora while throwing his weight behind the federal government’s mooted crackdown on net migration. While Minns is realistic about the prospect of states having greater control over migration, he made clear that he wants the Commonwealth to listen to the states. In the most recent federal budget, the government reduced the quota of workers individual states can nominate to work in specific industries, and the premier said he’d like to see “greater understanding from the Commonwealth” of the needs of individual jurisdictions. “If we could get, you know, more who are suitably qualified in the residential housing construction sector, that would really help … approvals are up, the capital’s there … but we find it very hard to get labour,” he says. Asked whether states should have a larger say over migration numbers, Minns says: “The short answer is yes. Will it ever happen? No. “You know, state and federal governments are in their lanes, but you’re going to hear from the premiers. They’ll have their say.” As the federal government prepares to announce tougher migration laws, such as limiting visas for international students, as it tries to lower net migration from 300,000 to 225,000, some, such as Premier Peter Malinauskas in South Australia, have warned against significant cuts. Last week he said, “we don’t have a migration crisis – we’ve got a housing crisis”. Minns, however, believes the rate of migration post-COVID did “overwhelm” housing and other services, and supports net migration in line with the 225,000 target. “I think the circumstances in Adelaide and Sydney are different,” he says of his divergence from Malinauskas, pointing to the states’ vastly different housing markets. “If [net migration] meets the federal government’s stated targets, I think that’s about right. But we keep overshooting that number.” However, Minns pushes back hard against the protectionist instincts of One Nation, and the more troubling fringe of the migration debate. While Minns dismisses the notion his trip to India is an appeal to the large diaspora in key western Sydney seats such as Riverstone, he’s willing to accept that the broader discourse over multiculturalism and immigration that One Nation’s rise has prompted is the backdrop. Calling for lower migration while backing multiculturalism are not mutually exclusive, he says. “When people say it is contradictory, I think that they shut down a whole bunch of legitimate debate and make people angry. What I’m trying to say is, you know a racist when you see one.” While in India, Minns has faced attacks from right-wing influencers such as the anti-immigration populist Chris Katelaris, aka “Big Chocky”, who recorded a video attacking the premier over the trip. “Wake up Mr Minns that’s exactly what we don’t want. We don’t want more f---ing immigration out of India,” Katelaris said. Minns is not shy about attacking that sort of rhetoric, saying Indian Australians had been unfairly targeted. “What have they done wrong, other than open businesses, work their asses off, educate their kids, pay taxes, commit no crime? I mean, what more do we want from Australian citizens?” Whether he likes it not, Minns knows he’s facing an election next year at which bread-and-butter state political issues – transport, education, health – are being subsumed by a broader debate about immigration, and he wants to take on the isolationist instincts of One Nation. The two-way trading relationship between India and NSW is worth about $7 billion and the country’s young, increasingly affluent population is the fastest growing on the planet. Every premier since Barry O’Farrell in 2011 has made the trip, and, as Minns has made clear, the relationship can’t be taken for granted; India is not short of trading partners. “What’s the end game to this? Is it the dislocation and the dismantling of a relationship with the fastest-growing economy in the world? We are an export nation. The reason we’re wealthy and prosperous is because we sell goods and services to the world,” he says. “Let’s just play this out to its end conclusion. People like me are gone. Those of us that are looking for trading relationships, we’re out. The politics changes, and these guys take the reins of power. What does our community look like? What does our economy look like? I think it looks far worse than where we’re at today. We want a growing economy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: Pub test: Albanese faces dire warnings that migration plan risks shuttering hotels - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is facing blowback from industry groups over his migration overhaul amid fears that regional pubs will shut down and food security will be compromised without enough foreign workers. As Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke scrambles to work out how to rein in migration without damaging the economy, junior international education minister Julian Hill has used new powers to kill a dodgy graduate diploma course being used by tens of thousands of international students to visa-hop and extend their stay by years. Labor is aiming to bring net overseas migration from 300,000 down to its target of 225,000 after years of missed forecasts. A suite of changes to tighten up the system was abruptly delayed last month after ministers said the policy needed more work. One Nation and the Coalition are proposing large cuts to the inflow of migrants as fresh national accounts show the economy struggling to keep up with population growth. Separate to measures likely to be announced in coming weeks, this masthead revealed last month that Labor had quietly paused working holidaymaker visa applications from 24 countries. Two dozen peak bodies wrote to Albanese on Wednesday about those changes, which they said could hurt industries and test Australia’s arrangement with Asian nations to provide fertiliser in return for food. Backpackers make up around 44 per cent of the horticultural peak harvest workforce. “We are collectively calling for immediate clarity on your government’s intent concerning proposed reform of the [working holidaymaker] program, the extent and effect of current administrative actions, and a commitment to consult,” the industry chiefs said. Groups including the National Farmers Federation, Council of Small Businesses of Australia, Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association, and a range of agricultural groups said the backpacker scheme performed a dual role. As tourists, they argued, working holidaymakers spent more time in regional areas than other visitors. As workers, the letter said, “restaurants, cafes, hotels, pubs, catering operators, retail and the care sectors, including childcare and early learning, rely on [backpackers]”. “These are precisely the services that make a regional community liveable,” they said. The business groups’ decision to unite against changes to backpacker visas reflects the economic trade-offs involved in the migration debate. This masthead previously reported that ministers were concerned about the effect of proposed changes on the budget bottom line and labour shortages in critical industries. Australian Hotels Association chief executive Stephen Ferguson said pubs and clubs relied on backpackers and international students because the system for training locals was broken. He criticised the government for de-prioritising hospitality training even though the sector contributed $74 million to the Skilling Australians Fund. “If they helped us train our own, we’d be far less reliant on immigration at least as it relates to the kitchen, which is our chronic problem,” he said, noting it took nine months to a year to bring a worker into the country after their application was approved. Cathal Leslie, a former economist at the Productivity Commission, rubbished the concerns of big business on Thursday, writing that Australia could drop the ATAR score required to study to be a doctor, increase wages for aged care nursing to attract locals and stop using cheap labour instead of innovating. “Our lacklustre productivity performance has coincided with a migration program that is less skilled than advertised,” he said in the Australian Financial Review, arguing for net negative migration. Backpackers have proved a divisive issue. Both the Nationals and One Nation have pledged to protect the streams of visitors into regional areas. There is bipartisan support for moves to reduce the number of international students. Labor has been working behind the scenes to rein in student numbers, raising visa fees well above the peer nations to $2500 and rejecting a record-high 40 per cent of applications in the most recent time period. Hill used ministerial powers to cancel a graduate diploma course, the Graduate Diploma of Management, that has been used to game the visa system. His action on Thursday represented the first use of powers enacted by parliament last year. “The Coalition left behind a shocking mess in 2022, with unsustainably high growth in student numbers in the least reputable parts of the sector, and our high-quality student visa being degraded into a low-rent illegal work visa and misused by shonks,” Hill said. Nearly half of Australia’s 900 vocational education providers are now offering the course, which has no prerequisites. The government says its graduates add little to Australia’s skilled workforce. Nearly half of the people who enrolled in the course – 18,340 – did not study. The government’s statement of reasons claimed: “High non-commencement rates among international students, low completion rates, significant course transfer activity, high visa refusal rates, and rapid growth that appears disconnected from demonstrated skills demand. “Widespread non-completion of the course may undermine confidence in the quality, purpose and reputation of Australia’s education system.” There are more than 41,000 international students enrolled in the course. Students will not automatically have their visas cancelled but will need to prove to officials how they plan to satisfy their visa conditions. title: ‘One of the great Australian achievements’: Howard praises immigration - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Former prime minister John Howard says immigration has been one of Australia’s great success stories and that the best way for politicians to deal with the rise of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson is to not pay her too much attention. In a call for calm after months of increasing hostility over Australia’s immigration intake, driven by One Nation’s surge to a historic high, Howard said everybody, irrespective of their ethnic background, should feel they are a part of Australia. “We wanted migrants who would embrace this country. We didn’t require of them that they forget the country of their birth. Nobody wants you to do that,” he said. “If your parents were born in Italy, or if they were born in Lebanon, if they were born in China, why should you ask of them that they give up affection for the country of their ancestry? We did require of them that they become fully part of the Australian community.” Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on Thursday announced a series of measures aimed at curbing temporary migration, including limits on partner visas for students, and a backpacker ballot. The measures have been broadly accepted by the university sector and they have drawn condemnation from farmers alarmed about workforce shortages to pick crops, highlighting the challenges of making even small changes to the immigration intake without a backlash from a range of lobby groups. Burke said Australia was facing a much broader challenge over the structure of its immigration program, which has become reliant on temporary migration and is at risk of creating a guest worker economy. “This is one of the things I’m very worried about,” Burke said in an interview. “I don’t have an immediate fix to it.” The temporary migrant workforce now accounts for more than 16 per cent of the working-age population, filling offices, farms and restaurants across the country without the rights of permanent residents or citizens. The government does not have the legislative tools to address the demand-driven system without support from the Coalition. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has echoed Hanson’s claims that Australia has a problem with “mass migration” and he rejected Labor’s attempts to legislate new powers to tackle the demand-driven system without a “serious cut to the numbers and a serious improvement in the standards”. Howard’s 2001 slogan, “We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come”, came to define decades of refugee politics. But his government also turbocharged the demand-driven temporary migration system by handing control over temporary migration to business, allowing employers and universities to sponsor staff and students with minimal government oversight. The policies under the old 457 visa were designed to fill labour shortages, reduce taxpayer funding for universities and drive economic growth. They also created the foundation for the current explosion in temporary migration. More than 1 million temporary migrant visas were issued last year, based on business and education demand, not government regulation. “It’s important to have a migration program that caters for reasonable expectations of a number of things, including shortages of skilled migrants,” Howard said. Australia’s second longest serving prime minister would not comment on the long-term implications of his government’s temporary migration policies. “The Labor Party is obviously the government now, and there’s always more pressure for the government party, but it’s a community issue and I want Australia to be a happy family.” One Nation is polling well above the Coalition and just one percentage point lower than Labor on first preference votes, according to the latest Resolve Political Monitor. Howard was the Liberal leader when Hanson was first pre-selected as a Liberal candidate in 1996, before she was disendorsed after offensive comments against Indigenous Australians. Hanson, at age 41, entered parliament as an independent, beginning an almost three-decade career in politics based largely on anti-immigration policies that have now resulted in her party eclipsing the Coalition as the dominant challenger to the Labor government. “What I said was that we shouldn’t pay too much attention to her and I think that was a sensible approach then,” Howard said. Howard said Australia had become more divided. “It only, in my view, started to go off the rails when we started talking in tribes,” he said. “What I know is that the policy we followed for decades worked. It’s been one of the great Australian achievements that we’ve taken people from all around the world.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: Budget loses billions, nation in deeper debt: The cost of cutting migration - The Age
raw_text: Any cuts to Australia’s overseas migration intake will cost the federal budget’s bottom line and plunge the country into deeper debt, complicating the equation for political parties as they promise to significantly slow the flow of immigrants into the country. Fresh costings released by the independent Parliamentary Budget Office on Tuesday show the budget’s underlying cash balance would improve by $80.6 billion in a decade if the annual migrant intake increased by 40,000 more people than current assumptions. But cutting the assumed annual net migration figure by an extra 40,000 people would deteriorate the bottom line by about $79.1 billion. The reason higher overseas migration improves federal coffers is that migrants are generally younger and arrive in Australia at working age, after most of their education costs have been covered, meaning they deliver more in personal income tax and economic activity than they cost in government spending over time. The PBO said its report was seeking to assess just how sensitive the federal budget is to changes in net overseas migration, which tracks long-term arrivals to the country minus departures. “This trend shows the fiscal improvements to the budget of higher net migration into Australia,” it says. But immigration has become a political debate in Australia since the net intake it surged to a record high of 550,000 immediately after the pandemic, before falling to about 300,000, which is significantly lower than the 2022-23 peak but still above the long-term average of 230,000. Immigration expert Abul Rizvi said the fiscal benefits of migration, particularly skilled and temporary migrants, had been well understood for 30 years – but the considerations in establishing migration settings went beyond their fiscal impact. “Of course, there are other things to consider here: demography, housing and infrastructure, service delivery. If you press a net overseas migration accelerator too much, which is what happened immediately after COVID, other problems will arise. This is what we’ve seen,” he said. “It’s not that simple as ‘they’re a budget positive’. There is a balance, and a point where benefits outweigh the costs. title: Police injured as protesters descend on homes for asylum seekers in England - The Age
raw_text: Thetford: Angry residents have turned on police in a clash over asylum seekers in an English town where homes have been used to house migrants, with some protesters trying to break into a property to force the new arrivals to leave. A crowd of about 100 residents gathered in the Norfolk town of Thetford over two nights to try to stop local homes from being used to offer emergency accommodation for asylum seekers, including many who cross the English Channel by boat. Authorities had to evacuate at least five of the migrants when the protest turned violent on Wednesday night, the second night of the protests, as residents threw eggs and rocks at the house as well as the police. The town was calmer on Thursday night (early on Friday, AEST) after police applied public safety powers to require people to remove balaclavas and other face coverings or risk being arrested. While dozens of people gathered on the third night of protests, police issued 10 dispersal notices to prevent any violence. The unrest is the latest example of violence over migration after years of growing anger at the arrival of thousands of asylum seekers, many of whom are housed in hotels or homes in residential areas. Around 36,000 people arrived by small boat over the year to the end of May, straining the government’s capacity to house them despite plans to turn former military bases into asylum seeker camps. Tempers in Thetford, halfway between Cambridge and Norwich, were already raw over government plans to house about 1000 migrants at an air base south of the town. Opponents are planning a public rally against the plan later this month. The angry scenes over the past few nights included men in black balaclavas confronting police in the apparent belief that authorities were protecting the asylum seekers rather than the community. While the gatherings were largely peaceful on Tuesday night, they turned violent on Wednesday night when police stopped protesters trying to break into the ground floor of a home with asylum seekers living upstairs. “As police intervened, members of the group became physically aggressive towards officers,” Norfolk Police said. “Two were taken to hospital after a male officer was struck with a rock and a female officer was seriously bitten, breaking the skin. A third officer was also spat at.” Police said one man, 68, a resident of Thetford, was charged with possession of an offensive weapon – a wooden bat – on Wednesday night. He was released on bail and is due to appear in court on August 25. Another man, aged in his 30s, was arrested after the first night of unrest on suspicion of a public order offence, but was released and issued with a conditional caution. Two men, both in their 40s, were arrested on the third night of the protests. One was detained on suspicion of inciting racial hatred the previous evening. The second was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly. Assistant Chief Constable Julie Dean said the police supported the right to peaceful protest but would act against violence, intimidation or criminal behaviour. “Our role is to keep people safe. We have a duty to protect everyone in our communities, maintain public order and prevent harm,” she said on Thursday afternoon, local time (about 10.30pm AEST). “We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties.” One protester drew a direct link with recent violence in Belfast, where local residents burned homes being used to house asylum seekers, according to the Eastern Daily Press. “They got them out, kicked them out, and the ones that didn’t go, they burned the house down,” the woman told the local newspaper. “I’m not saying that we would do it, I’m not an arsonist. “At the end of the day, we got them removed.” A video shared on TikTok showed dozens of police escorting a small group of asylum seekers while protesters jeered, with some yelling: “Get them out.” Reform UK councillor Scott Hussey, a cabinet member at Norfolk County Council, highlighted the scale of the police response in a post on X that said “half of Norfolk police” were guarding the house with migrants. A key issue in public debate is how a residential property can be converted into a “house of multiple occupancy” (HMO), in which each room can be rented under a separate tenancy. Companies including Serco have used HMO properties to provide housing services to the Home Office to help with the arrival of asylum seekers, but this is controversial in residential areas where local people oppose the new arrivals. The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, condemned the violence and said some local residents told him they feared for their safety. Jermy, a former mayor of Thetford, said he opposed the plan to turn the air force base at nearby Barnham into a camp for asylum seekers. About 193,000 people crossed in small boats to reach the UK over the seven years to 2025, according to the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford. Citizens of six countries – Iran, Afghanistan, Iraq, Albania, Syria and Eritrea – made up 65 per cent of those crossing. Asylum was granted to 62 per cent of all those who came by small boat. “Around 36,000 people arrived by small boat in the year ending 31 May 2026, 13 per cent less than in the same period the year before,” it said. The fall in arrivals has been much steeper over the first five months of this calendar year. Only 9000 crossed in that period, down 38 per cent on the same period last year. The data is likely to change because boat arrivals generally increase over the northern summer. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world. title: ‘Total disregard’: Top officials warned Labor of NZ rules before Kiwi migrants surged - The Age
raw_text: The Albanese government overlooked internal warnings there would be an influx of New Zealanders under plans to give them easier access to welfare and citizenship, which has turned into one of Labor’s thorniest challenges in driving down the migration rate. The burst in Kiwis coming to Australia has been one of the biggest blowouts in the net overseas migration rate since the pandemic, a prospect that was raised by top officials at the time Prime Minister Anthony Albanese made the key policy move early in his first term. Sources familiar with cabinet deliberations at the time, not permitted to speak in public, said officials from Treasury and Home Affairs expressed serious concerns that the move would create too big an incentive for Kiwis to move to Australia, particularly if Australia had a healthier job market and economy. New Zealand subsequently went into recession, sparking more movement. The net intake of New Zealanders surged to 38,000 per year in the two years after Albanese widened benefits and citizenship pathways in July 2023 – compared to about 8000 or fewer before the pandemic. Consistent demand and uncapped places meant New Zealanders on special visas made up 12.5 per cent of the net migration figure in the 2024-25 financial year. Labor is now scrambling to find ways to reduce net migration after consistently overshooting its targets, while the Coalition and One Nation have tied themselves in knots advocating for more drastic cuts. As migration and its interplay with the cost of living rise to the top of the political agenda, this masthead revealed in recent days that the government is mulling increasing deportations for visa overstayers. It also quietly paused backpacker visas from 24 countries. Treasurer Jim Chalmers warned about the costs of lowering migration on Monday, arguing the Coalition was intent on “dividing the country” and crashing the economy. The New Zealand surge coincided with Albanese’s decision in 2023 to reverse a Howard-era policy by allowing New Zealanders to gain citizenship after four years without becoming permanent residents first. It also gave New Zealanders quicker access to Medicare and the family tax benefit once they arrived. Albanese said at the time that the Howard-era changes had made citizenship harder for Kiwis and that the 2023 change harmonised rules between the nations. But department officials feared that even if the economies were about as healthy as each other, the relaxed rules would still create a large incentive for New Zealanders because Australia is a bigger and wealthier country. Labor warmed relations with Jacinda Ardern’s government after the progressive leader sparred with Scott Morrison over deportations of criminal dual citizens. The Albanese government policy to grant access to Medicare stopped short of offering the same access to the NDIS and other welfare items. Migration expert and former department official Abul Rizvi said the 2023 policy change was “made with total disregard to the impact on [net overseas migration].” Asked about the bureaucratic alarm bells, a spokesman for Burke said Labor reversed the Howard-era rules because the old settings created “intolerable circumstance where young people would spend their whole life in Australia only to reach uni and discover they were ineligible for HECS.” Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows around 30,000 New Zealanders were arriving each year before the pandemic, while between 22,000 and 27,000 left. This meant their overall impact on the net migration figure was small – between 2.5 per cent and 3.5 per cent of the annual migrant intake. Numbers surged from July 2023. In the two years since then, more than 50,000 Kiwis have arrived annually on a special 444 visa, while fewer than 15,000 departed. It means that New Zealanders as a share of the net migrant intake has increased – from 4.9 per cent in 2022-23, to 8.7 per cent in 2023-24, and 12.5 per cent in 2024-25. Even as the government has lowered arrivals under other temporary visa classes, consistent and uncapped demand from Kiwis has offset these efforts to drive down the net overseas migration rate. The 2024-25 net intake of Kiwis was 30,200 above the 2018-19 level, which is the largest increase in raw numbers during that period of any individual visa class, just above backpackers and students. Students remain the largest migrant group, comprising 32 per cent of the net intake last financial year. But while many of them live in special accommodation, New Zealanders tend to live in the mainstream part of the housing market where supply is strained. But the Australia-New Zealand arrangements would be difficult to reverse for Labor given the close relationship between the nations. Albanese has tasked Burke with finding new ways to cut net migration from 300,000 to 225,000 as Hanson surges off the back of anti-establishment sentiment and voter anger about migration. Treasurer Jim Chalmers used question time on Monday to highlight the sharp trade-offs in the mission to cut back on migration, which Labor is balancing against the need to attract tradies, farmworkers, and doctors. “You can get net overseas migration down as we are doing, at the same time as you can recognise and not diminish the really important role played by migrants in our economy and in our society,” Chalmers said, referencing RBA research showing that migrants were beneficial to the economy. Working holidaymakers have been another area where migration has blown out since the pandemic, this time under Morrison government changes that expanded age eligibility and added a third year visa. Their contribution to NOM in 2024-25 was up 29,400 compared to the pre-pandemic intake. Labor has slowed down backpacker visa processing and quietly paused applications from 24 countries, while the Liberal and National parties have been at odds on backpackers, which are key to Nationals’ agricultural seats. Backpackers made up 17.5 per cent of the net migration figure last year, up from 10 per cent in 2018-19. Former Labor adviser Henry Sherrell on Monday raised the alarm on Australia’s migration program, cautioning that “a few tweaks and some sentimental rhetoric will do little to win hearts and minds.” Sherrell noted that about 30 per cent of people aged 25 to 29 living in Australia were temporary visa holders, underlining the explosion in backpacker and student visas. The researcher called for a cap on population growth stemming from migration of one per cent per year, after Australia’s yearly growth outstripped all similar nations this century. “Without immigration, today’s populists would be impotent. To some, this reality has meant simply ignoring the topic, and attempting to elevate other issues in order to dominate the public debate. This approach is failing. Keeping our heads in the sand will only delay the inevitable backlash,” he said in an article published by Inflection Points. “These people are not racist. A full 46 per cent of overseas-born Australians say that immigration is too high. They are making a judgement about the pace of immigration and whether the system is working for them.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. title: Labor pushes to boost Pacific workers as Joyce says some Australians ‘bung lazy’ - The Age
raw_text: Labor is telling regional businesses to boost their workforces with Pacific migrants as it fights complaints from One Nation and industries who warn their operations will be crippled under government plans to cut thousands of working holidaymakers. Barnaby Joyce on Monday insisted that backpackers should be quarantined from cuts under Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke’s migration changes since they worked jobs that Australians would not perform. “There are a lot of jobs that just cannot be filled with Australians because … they’ve basically risen above the bottom level. Or they’re just bung lazy and are not capable of work,” he said. The fight over working holidaymakers began when Labor quietly paused visa processing in August and escalated this month when Burke unveiled his plan to cut second- and third-year visas by 38,000 places. Young foreigners must complete three months of regional work to qualify for their second visa, and six months for their third, although British backpackers are exempt. The new lottery system for those who want to stay in Australia longer is one way Burke will reduce Australia’s annual migrant intake as Labor comes under public and political pressure to deliver on lower targets. Working holidaymaker numbers have climbed to record highs over the past three years and made up 17.5 per cent of the net migration intake in 2024-25. However, the plan has prompted backlash from tourism, accommodation, commerce and farming peak bodies who say Labor’s plans will deter young people from working in the regions, compromise $1.65 billion in visitor spending and cost 11,000 regional Australian jobs. “The uncertainty created by the ballot is a massive disincentive for backpackers to travel and work in regional Australia,” said Australian Tourism Industry Council chief executive Erin McLeod. Treasurer Jim Chalmers, questioned about the impact on industry on Monday, conceded that construction, the care sector and seasonal parts of the economy were facing worker shortages. However, he insisted that Burke’s plan had the balance right. “We’re managing the migration system in the most responsible way that we can,” he said. “There will continue to be a role for backpackers, for working holidaymakers in the [agriculture] sector and elsewhere. There is, I think, more potential in the PALM Scheme as well for Pacific Island workers.” About 30,000 Pacific Islanders work in regional Australia under the PALM scheme, which remains demand-driven, but some businesses have preferred to employ backpackers because the PALM scheme is more tightly regulated. title: Migration fix could hit parliament next week – but these sticking points remain - The Age
raw_text: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor have held talks on migration as Labor seeks a pathway to get its fresh crackdown through the Senate, but the Coalition’s demands on how to crunch the overseas intake means a deal is not yet in sight. If the two major parties can resolve their differences, government sources said Labor’s highly anticipated migration plan could be put to parliament as early as next week. A planned National Press Club speech to announce the policy from Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, which was spectacularly cancelled last month, is unlikely to be the method by which Labor announces measures to reduce the net overseas migration figure from 300,000 to 225,000. Barring any belated change, Labor is expected to reveal its plan in a more low-key manner rather than a set-piece speech, which may create an unwanted sense of theatre as Labor comes under pressure from One Nation and the Coalition after years of overshooting migration targets. Labor is highly unlikely to secure the Greens’ support for any reduction in migration, so Albanese sought a meeting with Taylor in parliament on Wednesday to discuss potential points of agreement. But Coalition sources said the parties remained far apart. Opposition MPs are concerned about any perception that the Coalition would support Labor on migration, which could fuel Pauline Hanson’s talking point on the Labor-Coalition “uni-party”. Labor, under political pressure to act on migration without offending the left and migrant communities, is prepared to use regulation rather than legislation to make as many changes as possible if it cannot secure support in the Senate. It needs either the Greens or Coalition to pass bills as it does not hold a majority. Taylor wrote to Albanese on Wednesday saying Australians had “lost confidence in your government’s ability to protect our borders” and said the net overseas migration figure should be about 50,000 fewer than Labor’s target. He set 10 red lines for any legislation, including making it illegal to repatriate ISIS families; establishing a UK-style safe-country list to stop sham asylum applications; removing legal aid for people appealing visa decisions; restricting access to graduate courses to students seeking in-demand skills; deporting the 77,000 unlawful non-citizens; and turning the Australian Values Statement into a visa condition. This masthead has previously reported that Labor was considering a heavier focus on deportations, visa-hopping, bogus asylum claims, and aligning the international education system more closely with the need of the economy. But Taylor’s hard line on the saga surrounding ISIS brides presents as one potential sticking point that may preclude a deal. Taylor, who is well behind Hanson in the polls, could claim to be controlling the debate on migration if he helped Labor formulate a tough package. But he would open himself up to One Nation criticism that he had gone soft by working with the government in a critical area of policy to conservative voters.

title: ‘A big chunk of positive energy’: Green Man celebrates 10 years of training refugees - The Guardian
raw_text: For many young people growing up in Britain, their first music festival is a rite of passage; watching live music in a field with thousands of others, sleeping under the stars, and spending time with friends old and new. Green Man festival in Wales has been extending that formative experience to refugees and asylum seekers – who are offered training placements that help them develop valuable skills as they work to build new lives in Britain. Now in its 10th year, the refugee training programme, part of the Green Man Trust, the festival’s charitable arm, has worked with 191 refugees and asylum seekers. Most are between 18 and 28 years old, but the oldest have been in their late 50s. “It’s a proper training scheme, so the idea is that they learn about communication, integration, they learn front of house work, so dealing with the public, they’re giving directions, they’re asking questions,” said Fiona Stewart, who owns and runs the festival. “Some of them were working for a while running their own food stall as well, so they had to learn about health and safety and food management, money management, it’s been a kind of a crossover of a lot of skills.” Mina, who was a cyclist in Afghanistan, fled the Taliban in 2022. She said working at Green Man had helped her “feel more connected to life in the UK”. She took part in the programme because she “wanted to learn more about British culture and also I wanted to connect with people”. After studying politics at university, she will graduate this summer. A few weeks later, she will return to Green Man – which is this year headlined by Wolf Alice, Mogwai, Wilco and Four Tet. “I really enjoyed being in the festival,” Mina said. “It was my very first experience of being in a festival, and my very first experience of camping. “I got to know basically a few other refugees, similar backgrounds, but from different countries who were displaced, asylum seekers and refugees,” she added. “And I could build connections with them, get to know them, and now we are still friends.” Javid, also from Afghanistan, said the festival in the idyllic Bannau Brycheiniog national park had been his first ever experience of a music concert. Under the Taliban, he said, “there is no music and it’s banned to listen to any music. So if someone is spotted with a musical instrument, the person would be prosecuted just because of having a musical instrument.” “Visiting Wales was really exciting,” he said. “Camping, festivals, those things are new for me. All those are first-time experiences for me, and yes, they all got me excited. “I enjoyed the music. I enjoyed the camping – before that I had some anxiety on how to camp, but the whole experience was really good.” He had also learned about Welsh culture, as well as some Welsh language, he said – and the communication skills he learned have helped him with his current work as an interpreter. “The psychological benefit of participating in Green Man was that usually for people in my situation, sometimes there is bad news, and it’s like a big chunk of negative energy would affect other parts of my life,” he said. Before participating in the programme, Javid had had some bad news, which had stopped him doing things he enjoyed, such as running. “And then participating in Green Man, it was again a big chunk of positive energy,” he said, “and it did help me to start running again.” Refugees and asylum seekers from 52 different countries have trained at Green Man. Last year the festival had participants from Afghanistan, Libya, Sudan, Pakistan, Syria, Nepal, Yemen and Ukraine. They are provided with everything they need for the festival, such as camping equipment and warm clothing. “Overall, it’s really like something to give you a fresh start and I’m pretty sure when we return back home it will be very positive vibes. And you can spread this back,” Olga, from Ukraine, said. “The crew entertainment was such good stuff and you felt like, you know, part of the crew. I think this group is very special – and it actually feels that way.” “It’s very rewarding to get such a good opportunity,” Sophia, another Ukrainian participant said. “So it’s quite a good idea, so you can contribute back. We are really happy not to get this for free but to contribute.” While not every festival would provide a safe enough environment, Stewart said, Green Man did just that. “I’ve worked at other festivals where this just wouldn’t be possible because of the noise level, or behaviour issues, or whatever,” she said, “but I think it does work at Green Man, so we’ve had the best opportunity to enable that to happen.” Stewart said the programme felt particularly important at a time when communities are so divided, and refugees and asylum seekers have faced hostility. “I know from feedback that some of them have felt quite intimidated by what they see, what’s going on,” she said. “I think it’s horrible hearing some of the media coverage of these things. “When you meet people like this, they’re trying to make the best of their lives. No one is going to be going through what they went through if what they’re leaving is amazing. They just want to be accepted, and they can offer a lot as well, they can bring so much to our culture as well.” M, from Egypt, said: “When I first came here, my English wasn’t great and I wasn’t comfortable to speak with strangers, random people.” Participating in the project had helped him to “get out of my comfort zone to speak with people”, he said, and he now has a job in a cafe. “I’d never been to a music festival before in my life,” he said, but he now sings in a choir and is “really interested in the arts”. He is returning this summer for the fourth time, and said: “One day maybe I will perform at Green Man.” “For us, it’s a wonderful thing to do, but it’s also incredibly inspiring to see,” Stewart said. “Just from the point of view of seeing them out integrating with the rest of the team is a lovely thing, but also for the team as well.” “I mean, no one necessarily knows when they’re part of the wider team that they’re refugees or former asylum seekers unless they want to bring it up,” she added. “I think it’s that feeling that they’re just a kid in a field with everyone else.”

title: Israeli siblings who fear breaking law in Gaza under IDF owed protection by Australia, tribunal finds - The Guardian
raw_text: Three Israeli citizens facing conscription into the Israel Defense Forces have been granted the right to reapply for protection visas in Australia, after a government tribunal found they held a genuine fear they would be forced to break international humanitarian law in Gaza. The Administrative Review Tribunal found the punishment the young adults could face from the state of Israel – including imprisonment as conscientious objectors – would amount to persecution. Part of a family group, three siblings faced mandatory national service if they were returned to Israel, and held a genuine belief they would be forced to “engage in breaches of international humanitarian law”. The tribunal found there were “credible allegations that Israel’s military operations in the Gaza Strip are in breach of international humanitarian law” and that international opinion was that the IDF’s actions in Gaza were disproportionate. It found the three siblings were refugees facing persecution from the state of Israel, and Australia had a legal obligation to protect them. The family’s case went before the tribunal in October last year. The decision was published in March. The family – a husband and wife and their children – arrived in Australia on the husband’s working visa a decade ago. That visa expired, and the family applied for protection visas in 2024, six months after the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023 sparked the current conflict in Gaza and Israel. Their application for protection was rejected by the government. On appeal to the tribunal, the family claimed they were not safe from terrorist attacks anywhere in Israel and had “lost faith in the ability of the state of Israel to protect its citizens”, citing previous terrorist attacks by Hamas and being forced to live in bunkers for sustained periods. This argument was not accepted by the tribunal. While the tribunal found the family was at risk of being injured or killed by a Hamas rocket attack, it said any harm they suffered would not be the result of “discriminatory conduct aimed at them”. “Rather, it would be because they were a casualty of the armed conflict between Israel and Hamas. The applicants do not meet the refugee criterion in relation to this aspect of their claims.” However, the couple’s eldest child – who, along with two siblings, had reached the age of 18 – told the tribunal she and her siblings had vowed to refuse the national service compulsory for Israeli citizens. “She gave evidence that she and [her two siblings] had made a pact between themselves that they would refuse to serve in the Israel Defence Forces (the IDF). “The basis of their refusal to serve in the IDF was that they would be required to serve in the Israel-Palestinian conflict on the Gaza Strip, and as part of that conflict may be forced to engage in breaches of international humanitarian law. The tribunal accepts that these views are genuinely held.” The tribunal said it accepted that the three adult siblings “would be liable to terms of imprisonment of up to two years for refusing to serve in the IDF”. The tribunal noted that arrest warrants had been issued by the international criminal court against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the former defence minister Yoav Gallant on allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder. The tribunal also noted the United Nations Commission of Inquiry had reported that “Israel authorities and Israeli security forces have committed and are continuing to commit genocide against the Palestinians in the Gaza Strip”. “The International Criminal Court arrest warrant and the United Nations Commission of Inquiry report contain credible allegations that Israel’s military operations in the Gaza Strip are in breach of international humanitarian law,” the tribunal said. “This is a situation where Israel’s military operations are not currently considered by the international community to be proportionate in the means used to achieve a legitimate national objective of Israel.” The tribunal said it was not required to express any “concluded views” as to whether Israel had engaged in acts of genocide and noted Netanyahu and Gallant were “entitled to a presumption of innocence” before the ICC. The tribunal argued that the enforcement of Israel’s national service laws – and the expected punishment for refusing to serve – “would amount to persecution” of the adult siblings in the family. “The tribunal is satisfied that the risk of imprisonment faced by the [siblings] for refusal to do military service would involve a real chance of serious harm to them. The essential and significant reason for this persecution would be the political opinion underlying their refusal to do compulsory military service. “There are no reasonable steps the [siblings] could take to modify their behaviour to avoid the threat of serious harm. As the risk of persecution comes from the state itself, the tribunal finds that state protection is not available. The risk of harm also extends to all areas of Israel.” The tribunal ruled the three adult siblings facing conscription into the IDF met Australia’s obligations for protection under the refugees convention: that is, they faced a “well-founded fear of persecution” in their home country. The entire family should be afforded protection, the tribunal found. The tribunal ordered that the family’s application for protection visas be reconsidered. The Guardian sought comment from the Department of Home Affairs.

title: Australia to ditch paper arrival cards for incoming travellers | Australian immigration and asylum - The Guardian
raw_text: The days of filling out paper arrival cards are to end for millions of travellers arriving in Australia on international flights. The Albanese government has announced it will roll out digital passenger cards to all Australian international airports and seaports after a “successful” trial on Qantas flights into Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne. The paper forms, which ask passengers arriving in Australia for personal information and to declare any food, plant or animal products, have long been an annoyance for travellers arriving on long-haul flights. The government said it would spend $56.1m over four years to modernise airport systems and introduce the digital Australian travel declaration. The trial program run by Qantas will be expanded to other capitals including Perth and Adelaide by the end of 2026. A digital declaration will then be phased in for all airlines and at seaports over the next 12 to 18 months. The minister for trade and tourism, Don Farrell, said a simpler and quicker arrivals process would mean “visitors can spend less time filling out forms and more time enjoying everything Australia has to offer”. The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said the modernisation was “essential to Australia’s prosperity and national security” and would create a “seamless border process” for international visitors and Australian travellers. Digital systems for incoming passengers operate at many airports globally, including major hubs in Japan, Singapore and New Zealand. The Albanese government said the declaration would initially be accessible via a webform option but it aimed to work with the industry to make the form accessible through airline apps. The Qantas trial was made available through the airline’s app, with travellers completing the form digitally before flying. The government said the broader rollout would reduce manual processes for passengers and enable digital collection of information ahead of time. It said it would also “increase data quality for risk assessments, allow for rapid updates and management of global risks and events, such as biosecurity outbreaks, and meet passenger expectations for a biometric-enabled, seamless digital border experience”. Julie Collins, the agriculture minister, stressed that the government would “never compromise on biosecurity”. “Modernising our border is an important part of maintaining that protection,” she said. A 2024 report by the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry called Australia’s paper system “antiquated” and warned that it risked damaging Australia’s reputation as a desirable tourist destination. The report called for the paper cards to be abolished and said efforts to modernise incoming and outgoing passenger systems could bring an additional $50bn to the Australian economy every year.

title: ‘Get rid of them’: One Nation senator claims party will ‘remigrate’ illegal visa holders in resurfaced interview - The Guardian
raw_text: Senator Malcolm Roberts claims One Nation wants to deport at least 200,000 people and has repeatedly referred to the far-right concept of “remigration” in podcast interviews and speeches to niche platforms. In two recent podcasts, Roberts said One Nation wanted to deport 100,000 temporary residents as well as 100,000 international students – a total much higher than the party’s published policy. The senator said after those people were removed, he wanted to “start working on the higher numbers of people we need to get rid of”. One Nation’s policy website states the party would seek to “deport 75,000 illegal migrants”, specifically noting “visa overstayers, illegal workers, and unlawful non-residents”. The website also pledges to “end the student visa loopholes that turn study into a backdoor to permanent residency or low-wage labour”. But Roberts, in an interview with the 2 Worlds Collide podcast in November 2025, suggested One Nation wanted to deport or “remigrate” a far higher number. “We would also deport immediately anybody who’s here illegally, and that’s 100,000 people now … on contravention of their resident visas. That’s 100,000 we would deport, remigrate. Call it what you want. Get rid of them straight away,” he said. “Then we’ve got about an estimated 100,000 international students who are here illegally. They’ve either graduated and not gone home or they’ve breached their legal visa. So we would send them home.” In another interview with podcaster Brodie Buchal, published in June, Roberts repeated those sentiments. “We have 100,000 people here on temporary resident visas illegally. We would deport them, remigrate them, send them home,” he said. “We’ve got 100,000 students who are here illegally, and we suspect it’s much, much more. Send them home.” “We’d tighten the entry requirements, remigrate, deport, and then start working on the higher numbers of people we need to get rid of.” One Nation was contacted for comment and clarification of its deportation policy. One Nation’s hardline immigration policy has come under renewed scrutiny after Pauline Hanson’s appearance on Channel 7’s Spotlight program, where she met Rupert Lowe, leader of hard-right party Restore Britain. Lowe gave her a pamphlet titled “mass deportations” and Hanson replied they were “on the same page”. Seven reporter Liam Bartlett asked Hanson whether she thought “this concept of mass deportation is a good one?” She replied: “I love it.” However One Nation has consistently declined to detail how it would enact such a policy. MP Barnaby Joyce on Monday said people would be deported “as it becomes apparent that they’re not supposed to be here”, including “as people present themselves for medical issues”. Abul Rizvi, former deputy secretary of the immigration department, said it would be “eye-wateringly expensive” for a system to deport such numbers of people from Australia, or a Trump-style mass deportation operation like the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He said recent figures showed only about 2,000 people were apprehended, detained and deported from Australia last year, with another 6,000 voluntarily leaving. “It would cost a fortune and unless you did it carefully, it would result in massive errors and all sorts of problems,” Rizvi said. “There is a sensible policy in this space to be developed, but you need to do it in a careful, well-targeted way that doesn’t increase in huge errors, huge numbers of people detained and clogging up court systems.” Roberts’ recent comments have also repeatedly referenced “remigration”. The term has featured in Trump administration immigration policies, including an “office of remigration” to oversee deportations and “voluntary return of migrants” – Trump himself tweeted about his plan to return “illegal migrants to their home countries (also known as remigration)”. But remigration has also become a buzzword for the global far right. The Global Project Against Hate and Extremism described remigration as “a white supremacist policy concept that calls for the forced removal of immigrants, refugees, and their descendants — including legal residents and citizens — based on race, ethnicity, culture, being perceived as ‘non-white,’ or a failure to ‘assimilate’.” One Nation was contacted for comment regarding Roberts’ understanding of the term. In addition to mentioning “remigration” on the 2 Worlds Collide and Brodie Buchal podcasts, Roberts also advocated for it during a speech to a conference organised by conservative campaign group Firebrand. Photos from that conference, posted to social media, show Hanson was also in attendance. The conference host, welcoming Roberts onto the stage, praised him as “one of the only MPs yet to mention the magical, unmentionable word ‘remigration’”. In his address, Roberts said: “Remigration is the second part of my my speech. Take the people who are not fitting in or that we don’t need and send them home. “We need to put Australia first. Stop immigration, deport people, remigrate.” In that speech, Roberts said he was “opposed to mass immigration, the swamping of our culture” but was “not opposed to immigrants”. Roberts’ speech was praised by a white supremacist news outlet, The Noticer. The outlet said “remigration” had been popularised by German and Austrian far-right parties and activists, who frame the term as meaning the mass removal of non-white citizens. Dr Kurt Sengul, a research fellow at Macquarie University who studies far-right ideology, called remigration “an extreme and dangerous” position. “It’s important to note that remigration refers to the forced repatriation of all non-white people, not just so-called illegal or undocumented migrants or reducing ‘mass migration’. It’s an extreme position rooted in ethnic cleansing and white supremacy,” he said. Asked if he thought there was any other way to interpret the term “remigration” in this context, Sengul said no. “I don’t think there is any other way to see it; there’s not a friendlier or more moderate version of remigration … it sends a powerful signal to far-right activists that One Nation are embracing the term,” he said.

title: Green-led council plans to ban cooperation with Home Office on immigration raids - The Guardian
raw_text: A Green-led London council is planning to ban its officials from working with the Home Office on immigration raids, after uncovering evidence suggesting government officials wanted to use environmental health data to target restaurant workers. Councillors on the Lewisham borough council are due to vote next week on a motion that would review its systems with a view to ending any cooperation with the government’s attempts to deport people without the right to remain in the UK. The vote comes after council officials uncovered an email from the Home Office’s immigration enforcement team asking for help with conducting “joint operational visits”. Ministers have boasted about conducting more immigration raids than the previous Conservative government, but Green-led councils are now promising to defy the Home Office with a “green crescent” of sanctuary boroughs across the capital. Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, said: “I’m proud of brave, compassionate Green councils in London working to create a corridor of sanctuary where nobody, no matter where they’re from or what papers they have, has to live in fear of being snatched away from the place they call home.” A Home Office spokesperson said the department had a “collaborative relationship” with Lewisham council, adding: “While all immigration enforcement visits are intelligence-led, we make no apology for joining forces with local authorities to enable information sharing and ultimately fighting criminals who fuel immigration crime.” Labour has increased immigration raids to historic numbers since entering government two years ago as the party comes under pressure from voters and Reform UK to take a harder line on the issue. The Home Office said in January there had been a 77% increase in the number of raids on businesses such as nail bars, car washes, barbers and takeaways since the 2024 election, with an 83% rise in arrests. This is despite mixed evidence for their success. Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory, said: “There is evidence that workplace enforcement makes employers think twice about hiring people without the right to work. “But with an unauthorised population likely in the high hundreds of thousands, raids can only ever touch a small share of the businesses involved, and reporting has tended to suggest that they remain expensive, resource-intensive and reliant on tipoffs of variable quality.” The Greens won sweeping victories in the local elections in May, in part by winning over progressive voters in urban areas who had been angered by Labour’s migration policies. The party now runs councils in Southwark, Haringey, Hackney, Lewisham, Lambeth and Waltham Forest. Lewisham became a “sanctuary borough” in May 2021 under a Labour administration, announcing it welcomed all migrants, asylum seekers and refugees. However, an email from 2023 seen by the Guardian shows the Home Office asking the council to cooperate on raids, with an official at the department’s immigration enforcement team writing to the council’s food standards team to ask for assistance. “I am trying to establish some contacts within the council of whom we as a team can share findings with that may be of interest to the Local Authorities,” the person wrote. “Also with the possibility of carrying out joint operational visits.” That year the Observer also uncovered evidence that child protection services in Sussex were working with immigration enforcement to gather data on unaccompanied child asylum seekers. The Green party in Lewisham now wants to review all of its spending and data-collection systems to stop any cooperation with the Home Office on raids, as a first step to creating a corridor of sanctuary boroughs across London. Party sources say the review will also include any contracts the council has with organisations that have themselves helped facilitate raids. That could include the homelessness charity St Mungo’s, which in 2019 apologised for sharing information about migrant rough sleepers with the Home Office. Councillors will vote on the move at a meeting next Wednesday, with the motion expected to pass given the Greens have 40 of the council’s 54 seats.

title: Asylum seeker in UK as part of ‘one in, one out’ scheme says it is unfair on those deported - The Guardian
raw_text: An asylum seeker brought to the UK by the Home Office has said it feels unjust that he was allowed into the country only because someone else was deported. The individual benefited from the “one in” part of the controversial “one in, one out” scheme, where one asylum seeker who reached the UK on a small boat is forcibly returned to France in exchange for another being brought legally to Britain. In the first interview with an asylum seeker brought to the UK legally, the man said: “I am very happy to be here, but it’s not fair that another asylum seeker who may have a very similar case to mine but arrived in a small boat has been sent back to France so I can come here legally,” the asylum seeker, who the Guardian is not naming to protect his anonymity. “I don’t support sending some people back to France so that others like me can come to the UK.” More than 900 people have been allowed into the UK to apply for asylum under the scheme since it was announced last July, with a similar number who arrived here irregularly moved out. The charity Safe Passage, which supports asylum seeker families in France trying to come to the UK legally, condemned the policy as “not a genuine route to protection”. The asylum seeker acknowledged that his legal journey to the UK – by plane from Paris – was much safer and speedier than the crossings made by people risking their lives in small boats, but said he is in limbo here while he waits for his asylum claim to be determined. “We are waiting for our main asylum interview and have nothing to do while we wait,” he said. “I applied for a university scholarship, but was told I am not eligible because I am an asylum seeker. I am doing some volunteering, but by not allowing us to work or study and just waiting, the Home Office is teaching us to be lazy.” He added: “I am in a hotel with others brought to the UK legally, and I have only seen other single men like me.” The asylum seeker said that he applied for the “in” scheme online. “They took our biometrics and passports in Paris and then we were taken to a hotel and told to wait until 5pm to find out if temporary visas had been approved for us to travel to UK by plane,” he said. “Those who were approved were taken to the airport in Paris and flown to the UK.” He said that on arrival in Britain, he and the rest of the “in” group were taken to a Home Office building. “They took us from a parking basement into an elevator for the Home Office interview so I don’t know exactly where it was.” He said Home Office staff dealt with the process in a diplomatic way and were “so nice and friendly”. Gunes Kalkan, head of campaigns at Safe Passage, said that while the charity welcomed the provision of a safe route from France to the UK, challenges with the scheme – such as the length of time it takes to process applications on arrival – were “preventing it from being a genuine route to protection in the UK”. Earlier this year, the French national assembly’s commission of inquiry into arrangements between the UK and France to manage migration at the Anglo-French border heard that, as of February 2026, 89% of people brought to the UK under “one in, one out” were single men aged between 20 and 39. The inquiry also heard that, while small boat crossings are down, the scheme had not yet acted as a deterrent. More recent figures show that Channel crossings in the first five months of this year are down by more than a third on the same period last year. More than 2,000 people crossed last month, compared with 3,665 people in June 2025. A Home Office spokesperson said: “Multiple families have made a successful application under the UK-France agreement, and applications continue to be processed with thorough consideration. “All individuals transferred to the UK under the agreement are subject to robust security and identity checks before travel. Those who do not pass these checks will not be transferred to the UK.”

title: French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since spring - The Guardian
raw_text: The French authorities have halted small boats at sea in the Channel on 10 occasions since the spring, officials said on Friday. Despite claims from the Conservatives and Reform that the French were refusing to intervene in small boat crossings, maritime prefect officers were using “intervention tactics” to board or control vessels at sea and take asylum seekers back to France. The disclosure comes as political parties are once again attempting to seize the initiative over small boats over the summer. Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, last week confronted French police on a beach near Boulogne and uploaded footage to X of an officer saying: “Our order is to let them go. We just have to say to them, ‘Don’t do that. It’s dangerous.’” Earlier this week, Reform MP Lee Anderson visited Calais and said the French police were “literally waving these people on to boats”. In an unusual intervention, the director of maritime and small boats at Border Security Command, Charlie Eastaugh, said: “The incidents we have seen in the Channel over the last few weeks are a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting people for profit. It is easy to look at out-of-context images and think little is happening to stop these crossings – this is simply not true. “I know personally how tirelessly French officers have been working to disrupt launches before they reach UK shores. Their efforts include facing violent people with weapons, dispersing huge crowds, arresting smugglers, seizing equipment and collating vital evidence to help our prosecutions.” Every confrontation with asylum seekers was assessed by commanders as well as individual police officers and gendarmes, who were expected to balance the safety of their officers with that of the public, including large groups of often agitated people and gang members, officials said. On Sunday, when Andy Burnham visited HM Coastguard in Dover, Border Force officers had been warned that it was a “red day”, when conditions were calm enough for several small boat crossings. Two small boats attempted to launch from France, but one was intercepted at sea, while the other was halted on land. Small boats crossing the Channel were down by 43% compared with January to mid-July 2025 – from 21,690 people who crossed last year to 12,469 over the same period this year. The drop has come despite hot and dry conditions, which are usually associated with an increase in crossings. title: Home Office could be blocked from deporting trafficking victims to Albania | Immigration and asylum - The Guardian
raw_text: The Home Office could be blocked from deporting many young male trafficking victims to Albania after a major court ruling. Thousands of Albanian males have been identified as potential trafficking victims in the UK in recent years. Many are sent back to their country even if they are potential or confirmed victims of trafficking, as the Home Office contends they will be safe there. The ruling is likely to come as a significant blow to the government, which is trying to increase the number of people it removes. Albanians have been the most common nationality forcibly removed from the UK in the last five years, with 2,247 deported in the 12 months to the end of March, accounting for a quarter of enforced returns, according to UK government figures. Data disclosed in the court case shows that while Albanian females were previously major victims of trafficking, in their case into the UK sex industry, they have been overtaken by males – mainly boys and young men – who are trafficked into the drugs trade, either to distribute illegal drugs or to work as “gardeners” in cannabis farms. In 2022, 4,107 Albanian males were referred to UK services over potential trafficking, in comparison with 502 women. In 2023, the figure was 3,463 males and 588 females. The legal challenge was brought by a 21-year-old victim of trafficking from Albania who was first exploited by an Albanian gang in Belgium when he visited the country with his father at 16. He was sold to another Albanian gang, who brought him to the UK and forced him to work cultivating cannabis plants. He later escaped and was recognised as a victim of trafficking, but was denied asylum because he was told it would be safe for him to return to Albania. A panel of three senior judges in the upper tribunal of the immigration court accepted his asylum claim and found that even though five years had passed since he was first trafficked, he remained at “real risk” from his traffickers and could not safely move back to Albania. The judges issued new country guidance to the government, which must be considered by the Home Office before deciding whether to send male trafficking victims back to Albania. The judgment found that while Albania has made progress on tackling corruption, it continues to be a widespread problem and that there are no dedicated shelters for adult male trafficking victims, while the risk of victims being retrafficked if returned to Albania is significant. Islington Law Centre, which has particular expertise in representing Albanian trafficking victims, highlighted many concerning practices that gangs subject their victims to. These include deliberately videoing sexual abuse including rape of child trafficking victims and threatening to release the footage on social media; they also show videos of loved ones in Albania to young people to let them know they know who their families are; and the gangs also inflict physical injuries such as broken bones on children and young people. Esme Madill, a solicitor at Islington Law Centre specialising in representing young Albanian trafficking victims, welcomed the judgment: “This measured judgment has been reached by a court which had the benefit of significant and detailed evidence as to the worrying issue of trafficking of boys and young men by organised Albanian criminal networks. The profiles of trafficking survivors and the risks recognised in the judgment accord strongly with what we see in our work with deeply brutalised and traumatised young survivors every week.” Home Office sources said they were considering whether to apply for permission to appeal.
