title: US halts all immigrant visa applications amid tightening restrictions - The Guardian
raw_text: All US immigrant visa applications have been paused by the Trump administration as the state department moves to tighten restrictions and limit access to applicants who they deem could end up relying on US assistance, a state department official confirmed on Tuesday. The agency launched the initiative at all embassies and consulates in early August, according to the official and visa appointments had to be adjusted to accommodate “in-depth training”, according to the official. The state department has been working on updated guidance and training since early this year, “to ensure all consular officers are fully equipped to evaluate every visa applicant comprehensively and consistently”, they added. The Financial Times reports that applicants with interviews already scheduled were sent emails that their appointments had been canceled and that they would be informed of a new date and time. Agency officials claim this will ensure visa applicants will not end up relying on US public benefits. But it’s part of a slate of strategies the Trump administration has employed to crack down on both lawful and undocumented immigration and create a more selective process for who can gain entry into the system. This week the Trump administration also announced plans to revoke visas from asylum seekers who initially entered the country for tourism or business. Up to 200,000 people currently seeking asylum could be affected, marking what would end up being the largest mass pulling of visas in the history of the US. The action is being taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security. Under Donald Trump, visa applicants have also faced new restrictions, including review of their social media histories and added costs for processing, the Associated Press reported. The pause on new visas and training program follows an attempt by Trump to block applications on a similar “public charge” basis, which included a block on applications from 75 countries selected by the administration, which was recently overturned by a federal judge. “The court made clear that immigration laws cannot be used to justify discrimination,” said Joanna Cuevas Ingram, a senior staff attorney at the National Immigration Law Center, in a statement last week. “We are determined to ensure every person and family this ban harmed receives appropriate relief and will continue to hold this administration accountable to its obligations under the law.” In February, a federal judge overturned the president’s attempt to suspend the US refugee system entirely. Federal agents, under Trump, have been allowed to block asylum seekers from entering the US, a move that human rights advocates said undermines international asylum laws. The latest attempt to restrict access will cause immediate obstacles for those who have lawfully abided by an already challenging process, according to immigration law experts. Many applicants impacted by the pause likely “spent thousands of dollars and disrupted their lives to attend scheduled interviews, only to have their appointments cancelled at the last minute”, Brian Simmons, an attorney at immigration law firm Fragomen in Washington, told FT. It’s unclear when those appointments will be rescheduled.

title: Trump signs new orders targeting birthright citizenship - The Guardian
raw_text: Donald Trump has made a second attempt to restrict the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship, just weeks after the US supreme court rejected his initial, more sweeping bid to deny automatic citizenship to the children born to undocumented immigrants and temporary foreign residents. Trump on Thursday signed two executive orders that seek to broaden the categories of children ineligible for automatic US citizenship and ban so-called “birth tourism”. The directives are expected to face legal challenges. Trump has long sought to dismantle birthright citizenship and has made the effort a centerpiece of his second-term immigration crackdown. He has thus far been unsuccessful. On Thursday, the president lashed out at the supreme court over what he called “a very unfortunate decision in the supreme court concerning birthright”. “It was close, but a very, very unfortunate decision,” Trump told reporters. “So we’re making adjustments because it’s very unfair.” A first new order seeks to expand the definitions of children who would not be able to receive birthright citizenship. Historical exceptions to the citizenship clause of the 14th amendment have included children born in the US to foreign sovereigns and diplomats; children of occupying foreign forces; children born on foreign ships; and children of Indigenous Americans. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff and chief architect of Trump’s anti-immigration agenda, said the order aimed to expand the categories to include children of members of “foreign terrorist organizations” as well as “large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments”, though it is unclear who would fall into the latter category. The order also seeks to broaden the exception of children born to foreign ambassadors to include more foreign government employees, and refers to people born in “a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute” as ineligible. At the moment, that only includes American Samoa. The order would also deny birthright citizenship to children whose parents “engaged in fraudulent activity to obtain citizenship”. The second order targets “birth tourism” – travel to the US with the intention of giving birth so that the child will acquire US citizenship. Trump claimed on Thursday, without pointing at any evidence, that “hundreds of thousands” of people had undertaken this practice. “They’ve taken birthright citizenship and they’ve made a joke out of it,” Trump told reporters. “People are building businesses around it. That’s not the way it’s supposed to work. It’s a disgrace. They’re buying their way in, and we’re not going to let it happen.” According to the Migration Policy Institute, the highest census-based estimate “puts birth tourism at 22,000 to 26,000 babies born annually on US soil, although government data show just 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024” – less than 1% of all the babies born in the United States each year. The second order directs federal agencies to target “birth tourism operators” who arrange such travel to the US. Traveling to the US under the guise of tourism while actually intending to give birth so the child automatically obtains citizenship constitutes visa fraud and is already illegal, raising questions about the practical implications of the new order beyond existing law. Thursday’s executive orders will almost certainly be challenged in court. On 30 June, the US supreme court voided his day one executive order denying automatic citizenship to children born to parents in the United States illegally or on temporary visas, reaffirming that the constitution guarantees citizenship to nearly everyone born on US soil. Trump’s new directives aim to test the boundaries of that ruling by expanding the categories of people the administration argues fall outside the 14th amendment’s citizenship guarantee, while separately directing agencies to intensify their efforts to stop birth tourism. The American Civil Liberties Union on Thursday said the orders were another unconstitutional attempt to undo birthright citizenship after the administration’s defeat at the supreme court in June. “The supreme court already decided this issue: birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the constitution. No additional executive order can change the meaning of the constitution,” said Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “Any executive order that tries to rewrite birthright citizenship will meet the same fate as the last one.”

title: ‘What they’re doing qualifies as torture’: new details of ICE force-feeding revealed | US immigration - The Guardian
raw_text: One hunger striker in an immigration detention center was force-fed for almost six months. One detained immigrant with mental health problems was about to be force-fed, until his attorney intervened and stopped the process. And another hunger striker was almost force-fed, but gave in and broke her hunger strike as coercive procedures loomed. These are among 10 separate cases the Guardian found, since Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, in which Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has attempted to subject detained hunger strikers to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding. Of those, ICE subjected at least three – but probably five – who were protesting against the conditions of their confinement, to the procedures. Human rights organizations have widely condemned force-feeding as torture. Now, as ICE detains more immigrants nationwide, immigrant rights organizations and medical experts worry more people will be subjected to involuntary medical procedures. Among the 10 cases, the Guardian can exclusively reveal, are an Afghan man who was force-fed for months in Texas, a Ukrainian man with mental health problems in detention whose looming force-feeding in Florida was stopped by his attorney, and a Saudi Arabian woman who ended up in hospital while on hunger strike in Louisiana and eventually broke her strike in Texas before she was subjected to the procedure. The process to engage in force-feeding is quick and secretive. After a detainee has spent a certain amount of time on a hunger strike, which varies, ICE will request emergency court orders from federal judges allowing them to quickly force-feed them. In six of the cases reviewed by the Guardian, detained immigrants did not have any legal representation during the court proceedings. Most records are sealed, giving the public only a glimpse at the process. ICE detention center guards will then restrain the hunger striker, while medical staff insert a tube through the nose and down the throat and pump nutritional liquid into their bodies, according to court documents and the Guardian’s reporting – a painful, traumatizing and potentially harmful procedure. The Department of Homeland Security and its ICE agency, and the US attorneys offices for the southern districts of Texas and Florida did not respond to requests for comment. As part of the Guardian’s reporting, we tracked specific cases in ICE detention centers nationwide. The following three cases give vivid insight into what is going on behind the walls of ICE facilities. Case one: prolonged force-feeding An Afghan man in ICE detention was force-fed daily for nearly six months, starting in September 2025 and lasting through March 2026, enduring repeated nasogastric tube insertions under restraint. “What they are doing qualifies as torture,” said Dr Kate Sugarman, a family practice doctor based in Washington DC. Sugarman is not familiar with the man’s specific case, but she has worked with immigrant communities around the US and is familiar with healthcare practices in ICE detention. “Hunger striking is an act of desperation. They don’t do it because it’s fun. They do it because they’re desperate,” she said. Sugarman is also active in Doctors for Camp Closure, an organization of physicians and healthcare professionals “who oppose the inhumane detention of migrants and refugees arriving to the United States of America”, according to its website. According to court records filed in the southern district of Texas federal court, the Afghan man began his hunger strike at the El Valle detention facility, a privately run ICE facility in south Texas, on 11 September 2025. Four days later, he was transferred to the Port Isabel processing center, another privately run facility in Los Fresnos, south Texas. He told facility staff through a translator he was striking “due to his discontent with his case” and indicated that if there was no resolution he would continue “until he is removed from this country”, according to declarations submitted in court. The Guardian is choosing not to name him because he is still detained by ICE and repeated efforts to contact him and his legal team were unsuccessful. There are limited public records related to the man’s case, so background information on his immigration history is unknown. However, another hunger striker at Port Isabel, who met him while in detention, told the Guardian that the Afghan man spoke limited English. He was seen frequently being taken to the facility’s infirmary from the segregation unit they were both in. On 19 September, eight days after the Afghan man began his hunger strike, federal judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr ordered ICE to force-feed him, without a hearing or any input from the hunger striker. Nearly a month later, Rodriguez found the man to be “indigent” and assigned him legal assistance. After nearly three months of the man being force-fed, a doctor working at the Port Isabel facility named Shauna Kincheloe, according to a court document seen by the Guardian, submitted a declaration to the court claiming it was “medically necessary” to continue force-feeding him. Officials by this point had begun to force-feed him twice a day, she added. And the months of hunger striking had taken a toll, forcing him to use a wheelchair while remaining “frail in appearance”, the doctor said. Kincheloe added in her declaration that although the Afghan man was not compliant with orders, he was “not combative” when made to comply by the “use-of-force team”. The “use-of-force team” is usually made up of detention facility guards, who physically restrain hunger strikers while they are force-fed. The Guardian attempted to reach Kincheloe via phone, email and ICE but did not receive a response. The private prison company that runs guard services at Port Isabel, Akima Global Services, did not respond to a request for comment. “Are they tearing up his esophagus? Are they tearing up his stomach, by shoving in that nasogastric tube? How are they even doing it?” Sugarman asked. “From what I understand, it’s very painful, very traumatic. There’s certain cases in the ER [hospital emergency room] where sometimes you have to do it because something very dire is going on, but it’s not something you do for six months.” Attorneys representing the Afghan man consulted an independent doctor, who testified in court on his behalf. Court records related to the hearings are sealed, shielding many details, but docket entries show Rodriguez extended the force-feeding order several times. Rodriguez’s staff at the southern district of Texas did not respond to a request for comment by the deadline. Eventually, records from 3 March of this year show the US government requested the case be dismissed because the case had “been resolved”, suggesting the man broke his hunger strike. Case two: the significance of legal representation Andriy Shepitsen, a Ukrainian man detained by ICE, has a doctorate in a computer science-related field. But he struggled for years with mental health problems. According to court records, Shepitsen, 46, has severe bipolar disorder, which, according to Katie Blankenship, an immigration attorney who worked on his case, contributed to mental health crises and subsequent arrests. After an arrest, the criminal court recognized Shepitsen’s mental health problems and sent him to receive psychiatric care, Blankenship said. But he was arrested by ICE and was taken to the now-closed “Alligator Alcatraz” state-run immigration jail in the Florida Everglades and then another ICE facility, where his attorney says he was denied medical care for his bipolar disorder, leading to suicidal ideations. Shepitsen was transferred to the privately run Krome Service processing center in Miami on 20 February this year and began a hunger strike to protest against his continued detention. Blankenship said officials refused to give Shepitsen his bipolar medication, citing his hunger strike, while Shepitsen refused to end his hunger strike until he received medical care – leading to an impasse. In April, 44 days after he began his hunger strike, ICE requested a court order to restrain and force-feed him. Blankenship said that by that point, Shepitsen’s lack of food had led to physical and mental distress. Meanwhile, Blankenship submitted motions in immigration court to try to get him released, which were unsuccessful. “He was deteriorating very rapidly,” Blankenship added. “At that point, his wife and I were trying to get him out of the hunger strike, but he was in such a mental state that he just really couldn’t hear that.” Dr Manuel E Lopez Diaz, a Florida-based doctor working at the Krome facility, wrote a court declaration requesting permission to force-feed Shepitsen, adding that the man’s bipolar disorder diagnosis was not a factor in the case. Lopez said it was his “informed medical opinion” that force-feeding “through a nasogastric tube” was “medically necessary”. According to records reviewed by the Guardian, Lopez has been involved in five separate forced procedure cases since August 2024. When reached by phone for comment, Lopez refused to answer questions or speak about his participation in requesting court orders to force-feed detained immigrants and hung up. On the day ICE requested to force-feed Shepitsen, Blankenship intervened, pointing to Shepitsen’s mental health problems as a factor in the case. The following day, a court filing outlined the next steps: Shepitsen would be taken to a hospital and receive an independent psychological and medical evaluation before ICE took further steps. Five days later, the case was dismissed. In a court filing, attorneys wrote that Shepitsen began to eat in the hospital. In total, Shepitsen was on hunger strike for 68 days. The prolonged hunger strike affected his body. Shepitsen is still unable to regularly eat, drinking only coffee with milk, and nutritional shakes, according to his attorney. Now, Shepitsen is awaiting his removal by the US authorities to Poland, where he will be reunited with his wife. Case three: looming threat with no representation The Afghan man’s and Shepitsen’s cases are outliers, in that they had attorneys representing them during court proceedings related to their force-feeding. In the majority of the cases reviewed by the Guardian from 2024 through 2026, detained immigrants did not have attorneys advocating for them in court. One of those cases was for a Saudi woman on hunger strike, who had to face off against US government lawyers alone in federal court. The Guardian is choosing not to name her because she has no legal representation and, according to ICE records, she is still detained. Efforts to contact her in detention were unsuccessful. In late June 2025, the Saudi woman launched a hunger strike to demand her release while locked up at the Richwood correctional facility, a privately run immigration jail in northern Louisiana. In the weeks that followed, she was sent to the emergency room and diagnosed with malnutrition, a urinary tract infection, a fever and low sugar and potassium levels. After nearly a month on strike, she was transferred to the Houston Contract detention center, another privately run facility, in Texas, where other force-feeding cases took place in 2024, according to court records. title: Far-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UK | US immigration - The Guardian
raw_text: Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US after being detained on Thursday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New Orleans in connection with what the agency said was expired authorization to be in the country and a deportation order. Yiannopoulos’s deportation to the UK occurred on Friday, said a statement on Saturday from a spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE. A DHS spokesperson on Friday said that Yiannopoulos, 41, had been arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport. The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”. The spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”. The spokesperson added: “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” Yiannopoulos – who has previously been a vocal supporter of ICE and immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency – was believed to have been arrested while heading to a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West. West performed at New Orleans’s Caesars Superdome on Friday. In 2022, Yiannopoulos worked on West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working for a company of the rapper. Yiannopoulos, a former editor of the conservative media outlet Breitbart News, previously served as an intern for the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene. He eventually became locked into a feud with fellow far-right commentator Laura Loomer, a Trump administration ally who claimed on Friday that she had reported Yiannopoulos to ICE over his immigration status. At the peak of his influence, Yiannopoulos was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency. He fell out of favor in conservative circles after the publication of a video in which he condoned sexual relations with boys as young as 13. Yiannopoulos claimed that his experiences as a victim of teenage sexual abuse gave him license to comment on the subject. He soon resigned as a senior editor at Breitbart. Yiannopoulos was also banned from Twitter, now called X, in 2016 for directing racist and misogynistic tweets against a Black actor in a Ghostbusters remake. His account was reinstated to the platform in 2022 after it was acquired and renamed by multibillionaire Elon Musk. A little more than a year before his detention by ICE, a social media post from Yiannopoulos called on immigration checkpoints to be set up at California “supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersection and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”. He had also sarcastically asked whether it was impolite for one “to masturbate” in public rather than in private “if you are going about your business and find yourself observing an ICE raid” amid the mass deportation campaign that Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency.

title: Cutting immigration to the UK means billions less for the Treasury. Can the country really afford that? | Zoe Williams - The Guardian
raw_text: Every 100,000 immigrants lost to the UK costs the treasury £7bn, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility. That figure is unsurprising if you’ve been concentrating at all – the calculation was made in 2024 – but at the same time completely staggering. Nobody ever says, “The chancellor’s going to be in trouble because of all those lost immigrants”; few people remark on, let alone decry, the very large numbers of migrants who have been lost due to policy decisions. And then, as budget day approaches, brute facts and mathematical realities assert themselves: migration numbers have been falling faster than anticipated. And if you take all the measures you can to discourage international students, skilled workers, all imaginable young, mobile people who work and don’t get ill, while at the same time preventing with all your might any legitimate employment opportunities for asylum seekers, you will suffer a hit to the national coffers. That’s another word I haven’t seen in a while. We used to talk about coffers all the time, these metaphorical chests of cash that would be added to, in the good times, by a bustling economy in which people worked and made and sold things. If these things were good enough, other countries might even want to buy them. It probably slipped out of usage around the time of Brexit, when we decided by that overwhelming majority that money wasn’t important any more – or, at least, not as important as taking back control of our borders. If we had to poleaxe our export industries in order to prevent the arrival of healthy people who might contribute to the economy, then so be it – coffers be damned. If this were working in the other direction, it might almost be charming. If money were no object in the matter of human dignity, if no price were too high for functioning social care because that was the society we wanted to live in, then it would be beautiful, although there would definitely still be people saying: “Guys, money actually is an object. It’s both a trust metaphor and a real thing.” But we’re only prepared to jettison practicality in the interests of a particular set of higher objectives: securing our borders; assuaging formless anger (but only of a certain kind, from certain people); sending a message to the rest of the world – you might think this looks like a good place to live, but think again. I’ve never been especially attracted to rational economic arguments in politics: they usually seem to serve the interests of the establishment. But now that the establishment has become so emotional, I realise I miss the days when it could, at least, count.

title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US - The Guardian
raw_text: Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under Donald Trump’s hardline immigration policy. However, Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial details. Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to about half a dozen African nations as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of dollars. In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections. Mutoni said preparations were under way to arrange accommodation, living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said. “If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship. Burundi aimed to both strengthen diplomatic relations and provide hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson added. The US state department did not immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

title: Britain knew about the Holocaust as it happened. A new exhibition reckons with that truth - The Guardian
raw_text: The “complex and unsettling” story of what Britain knew during the Holocaust is being explored amid plans to create a new permanent national memorial. An exhibition highlighting how news of the atrocity reached Britain much earlier than is commonly understood will tour the country after being viewed privately by MPs at Portcullis House on the parliamentary estate at Westminster in September. The research draws upon newspaper reporting, broadcasts, academic scholarship, witness testimony and government archives. The exhibition is a sample of a more extensive, permanent exhibition for the national Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which is planned for a site in London. Martin Winstone, the senior historical adviser to the Holocaust Educational Trust, said: “There’s a feeling today that Britain really only found out about the Holocaust at the end of the war. But in 1942, the year in which most victims of the Holocaust were murdered, you couldn’t really escape this information in Britain. It was in every newspaper. It was on the BBC. “The Manchester Guardian was the newspaper that reported most extensively on the Holocaust, taking a crusading position that there was more the British government and allied governments could be doing.” For years, the Manchester Guardian, which was banned from Germany in 1933 for highlighting Adolf Hitler’s antisemitism, called for immigration restrictions to be lifted for Jews, lobbied for pressure to be applied to neutral nations to open their borders to refugees and for special rescue measures, realising that “the Nazis were aiming at the complete elimination of an entire group of people”. Much of the information about the Holocaust, including the locations of death camps, was smuggled out of Poland – where the murders were “happening in plain sight” – by couriers to the London-based Polish government-in-exile. Winstone said: “It was a challenging situation. There were lots of things the government had to deal with. And for much of that war, Britain was on the defensive. “On one level, the government’s response was always, ‘we’ll win the war, that’s how we stop this’; while critics said, ‘there’ll be nobody left to save, if that’s what you’re waiting for’.” During the second world war, the government commissioned reports on antisemitism in Britain, with agents opening people’s mail and recording conversations overheard in air raid shelters to gauge public opinion. In what Winstone described as a “complex and unsettling story”, Ministry of Information bulletins revealed that while there was mass public sympathy for Jews in occupied Europe, it contended with anti-migration and antisemitic sentiment. Winstone added: “Nearly everybody in Britain was disgusted about these mass murders, but at the same time you start getting more antisemitic discourse about Jews in Britain – that Jews were running the black market, avoiding military service and spreading panic. “Even before the mass murder began, during the 1930s, there was a significant body of opinion which felt Britain should not be admitting refugees.” Winstone said UK immigration laws in the 1930s were highly restrictive, in part because of antisemitism earlier in the 20th century. But after the Kristallnacht pogrom of 1938, Britain relaxed restrictions to some extent, allowing Jewish children to come from Europe without visas. The Manchester Guardian reported how Jewish communities and Quakers in the city set up organisations to support refugees. British women – from MP Eleanor Rathbone, to grassroots fundraisers and those who found themselves interned alongside Jews in France – were at the forefront of humanitarian efforts, Winstone said. A 2021 survey by Claims Conference found 21% of the British public knew the UK government was aware of the mass murder of Jews as early as 1941. UK Holocaust Memorial Foundation is co-chaired by the broadcaster and former Labour politician Ed Balls and the Tory peer Eric Pickles, who said the exhibition would give an early insight into the work being developed for the forthcoming memorial. The exhibition will be at the Northern Ireland assembly from 30 October until 13 November; the Scottish parliament from 7 to 10 December; before travelling to Cardiff from 16 January to 4 February 2027, coinciding with Holocaust Memorial Day on 27 January. It is also expected to visit Manchester, with a date and venue yet to be confirmed. The UK Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which would be at Victoria Tower Gardens, Westminster, does not have a confirmed opening date yet, as a planning application is being redetermined by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. The Holocaust Memorial Act 2026 received royal assent this year, granting legal clearance and government funding for the project.

But after the Kristallnacht pogrom of 1938, Britain relaxed restrictions to some extent, allowing Jewish children to come from Europe without visas. British women – from MP Eleanor Rathbone, to grassroots fundraisers and those who found themselves interned alongside Jews in France – were at the forefront of humanitarian efforts, Winstone said. A 2021 survey by Claims Conference found 21% of the British public knew the UK government was aware of the mass murder of Jews as early as 1941. UK Holocaust Memorial Foundation is co-chaired by the broadcaster and former Labour politician Ed Balls and the Tory peer Eric Pickles, who said the exhibition would give an early insight into the work being developed for the forthcoming memorial. The exhibition will be at the Northern Ireland assembly from 30 October until 13 November; the Scottish parliament from 7 to 10 December; before travelling to Cardiff from 16 January to 4 February 2027, coinciding with Holocaust Memorial Day on 27 January. It is also expected to visit Manchester, with a date and venue yet to be confirmed. The UK Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which would be at Victoria Tower Gardens, Westminster, does not have a confirmed opening date yet, as a planning application is being redetermined by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. title: Anika Wells accused of treating voters like ‘3-year-olds’ after using Ooshies to explain housing crisis - 7NEWS
raw_text: Communications Minister Anika Wells is facing backlash for using Ooshies to explains Australia’s housing crisis. The minister took to Instagram and Facebook on Sunday afternoon, sharing a video that drew parallels between the popular supermarket collectibles and Australia’s housing crisis. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Minister uses Woolies Ooshies to explain housing crisis Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today “What do (Ooshies) and the Australian housing market have in common?” she questioned. “Both the Ooshie market and the Australian housing market are dictated by supply and demand,” she said with dozens of Ooshies in front of her. “The problem right now is that supply of Ooshies and supply of housing is not keeping pace with demand. “To fix that problem and increase supply, at the last budget, Labor told housing investors or Ooshies collectors, you can keep using the tax system to buy Ooshies, but only new ones. “In turn, that means more new Ooshies to rent and more existing Ooshies for first time buyers.” The video has drawn the ire of her followers, who likened the explanation to “Play School” and slammed the minister for treating Australian voter’s like “three year olds”. “Actual Budget planning footage,” one follower commented. “Had to explain it in Ooshies so Jim and Albo could understand and relate,” another said. Chief Executive Officer of Cheek Media, Hannah Ferguson, defended the minister’s tactics on Sunrise on Tuesday, saying she understood the attempt to engage audiences on social media. “I’m someone on social media. I’ve done some different things to try and beat the algorithm and get people engaging with difficult political concepts. title: Why superannuation may have become more tax-effective following budget changes - 7NEWS
raw_text: While everyone was arguing about negative gearing, superannuation became one of the biggest winners of May’s tax overhaul, and almost nobody noticed. That’s the take from Motley Fool Chief Investment Officer Scott Phillips, speaking on 7NEWS’ latest episode of Money Talks, powered by Vanguard. Take the Vanguard SmartRetire quiz at vanguard.com.au/smartretire to discover the building blocks of a more confident retirement. Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today “Before the budget, super was still better than investing in your own name because of the tax advantages that come with it,” says Motley Fool Chief Investment Officer Scott Phillips. “The changes they made make investing in your own name less attractive than it was, and that makes super far more attractive relatively than it used to be.” Inside super, contributions are taxed at 15% instead of your marginal rate, and the capital gains tax rate is reduced and untouched by the reforms. With the tax perks of investing outside of super now smaller, that gap just got wider. You might also like to read: - Natasha is 28 years old with $310,000 in shares and a $1 million net worth - these are the rules she swears by - Melissa Browne is one of Australia’s leading finance experts but her shocking divorce decision still haunts her - The $250 rule: Finance expert Melissa Browne on the small habit every teenager should be doing “I’ve already had people all over the place tell me they’re shoveling more money into super than they were last time, because they want the extra tax benefit,” Phillips said. The strategy inside your fund doesn’t need to change. What’s worth revisiting is how much you’re putting in, and how much you’re paying to do it. Phillips’ rule: fees are the one variable you actually control. “You can’t control the returns. You absolutely can control your fees. Every time you save a dollar on fees, it’s a dollar in your pocket, and that dollar compounds for decades into your future.” Find a reputable, low-fee fund, check your investment option actually matches your age and risk appetite rather than defaulting to whatever sounds safest, and don’t be put off by the admin. “It’s one page these days,” Phillips said. “The super funds don’t deserve your donations.” Investors panic-selling properties they didn’t need to sell Own a negatively geared property bought before 7.30pm on budget night in May? You’re grandfathered. The old rules apply to that property for as long as you hold it and for as long as ownership doesn’t change. Yet Phillips says he’s watched investors sell anyway, convinced they were about to lose a benefit they’d already locked in. “That’s completely unnecessary,” he said. “That’s a rash move.” Sell now, and that tax benefit is gone for good, you won’t get it back on a new property. A tax rule nobody’s talking about As Phillips explained on 7NEWS’ latest episode of Money Talks, powered by Vanguard, buried in the changes is a new 30 per cent minimum tax rate on capital gains, no matter what you earn. Someone on the 16c tax bracket, who’d normally expect to pay tax at that rate, will now pay 30 per cent on any capital gain instead. “That is new,” Phillips said. “It wasn’t in place in the original capital gains tax regime.” The trap hiding inside your own home Your primary residence is currently exempt from capital gains tax, and that exemption can even survive up to six years if you move out and rent it elsewhere. But move out, rent your home for the negative gearing benefit, and you give up that CGT-free status on the property itself. It’s a straight trade-off, negative gearing now versus a tax-free sale later, and Phillips says to get an accountant to run both scenarios before deciding, not after. What’s actually changed, in plain English New residential property purchases from budget night can no longer claim negative gearing losses against personal income. Existing investors keep the old rules. From 1 July next year, the flat 50 per cent capital gains discount disappears, replaced by indexation, meaning investors only pay tax on the gain above inflation, not the whole profit. That’s on top of the new 30 per cent floor described above. Family and discretionary trusts face a crackdown too, aimed at structures used purely to minimise tax rather than for legitimate business or estate planning. There’s also a fix coming for the so-called “widow’s tax”, where moving a property from joint names into a single name, say after a death or relationship breakdown, has been treated by some banks as a change of ownership that strips away grandfathered negative gearing. Phillips says legislation is set to correct that. Negative gearing benefits also remain available for brand new dwellings, part of a government push to boost housing supply. A knockdown-rebuild generally doesn’t qualify. A genuinely new dwelling, or land never built on before, does, though Phillips says to get advice before relying on that distinction. The good news nobody mentioned Small personal income tax cuts are landing this year and next, along with a cut to the lowest marginal tax rate. It didn’t make headlines, because good news never does. Where to actually get answers Start with the ATO website for the basics. For anything involving six or seven figures, the couple of hundred dollars for a session with an accountant or financial adviser is cheap insurance. An accountant can tell you the tax obligation of a decision; only a licensed financial adviser can tell you what to actually do about it. The timeline to watch Legislation is still being finalised, with government aiming to pass it by the end of the calendar year. Phillips’ advice for anyone tempted to move before then: “Make haste slowly.” The rules that are locked in, are locked in. The rest could still change. title: Albanese Government defends falling house prices as Labor MPs celebrate property market downturn - 7NEWS
raw_text: The Albanese Government has defended falling house prices as a “deliberate result” of its housing policies, as Labor MPs face accusations of celebrating the property market downturn. The political fight over housing affordability intensified after Labor MP Jerome Laxale shared an annotated headline about struggling Sydney sellers, changing an auctioneer’s assessment that conditions were the “worst” he had ever seen to the “best”. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: MPs clash over first home buyer scheme integrity Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today The story detailed a first home buyer couple who secured a two-bedroom Sydney apartment after finding themselves the only bidders at auction. Laxale’s post has sparked controversy, coming just days after Housing Minister Tanya Plibersek declared on Sunrise there had “never been a better time” to be a first home buyer. Labor defends ‘deliberate result’ but opposition not convinced Speaking on Sunrise on Friday, Health Minister Mark Butler defended the government’s position, arguing its housing policies were giving first home buyers a better chance of competing at auctions. He said first home buyers were increasingly taking centre stage at Saturday auctions instead of having to compete with investors benefiting from tax concessions. “That’s a good thing. That’s a deliberate result of the policies that we’ve put in place. We want to see first home buyers able to get into the market easier,” Butler said. He did, however, acknowledge buying a home remained difficult, with property prices still historically high compared to wages. “As a ratio to income, they’re higher than they certainly were when Jane and I were the age of most first home buyers,” he said. “That’s why we’re doing so many things, to help them get a crack at the Australian dream of home ownership,” he said. Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume hit back at the government’s rhetoric, arguing Australians should not be celebrating falling property prices. “Only Labor seems to do this. And you don’t make housing more affordable by making Australians poorer,” Hume said. Hume argued 15 interest rate rises under Labor, combined with rising taxes, had made it harder for Australians to buy a home. Potential first home buyers eligibility loophole sparks concern The clash comes as another key component of the government’s housing strategy, the 5 per cent deposit scheme, faces scrutiny over who can access taxpayer-backed assistance. Economists have urged the government to close a loophole allowing Australian residents who own property overseas to potentially remain eligible for the scheme. Butler defended the scheme, saying applicants were required to declare all their assets, including those held overseas. “If those assets would allow them to put together a deposit of 20 per cent, then they’re not eligible for the scheme,” he said. Hume also took aim at non-citizens accessing the scheme and its use by some buyers who later turn properties into investments. “This is a taxpayer-subsidised scheme. No wonder Labor is running out of money and increasing taxes if they’re using taxpayer money to subsidise what is a failing housing market,” she said. She argued the government instead needed to address housing demand by building more homes and “managing migration” before moving to “fix” the economy by lowering taxes and energy prices. Butler defended allowing permanent residents to access the program, pointing to essential workers such as doctors and nurses who had moved to Australia and were filling critical workforce shortages. Hume maintained taxpayer-funded housing assistance should be reserved for Australian citizens, arguing “citizenship should have its privileges”. Stream free on

title: Housing expert’s verdict after major Adelaide announcement at the former Hampstead Barracks - 7NEWS
raw_text: A plan to build up to 400 homes at Adelaide’s former Hampstead Barracks has drawn praise from housing advocates, though experts say it is unlikely to make a significant dent in the affordability crisis. The federal and state governments on Tuesday unveiled plans to fast-track housing on the inner-north site, with apartments and townhouses planned just 6km from Adelaide’s CBD. WATCH ABOVE: Prime Minister jets into Adelaide to announce new housing estate at old defence base Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said there was “no more important infrastructure than housing” as he announced the proposal alongside Premier Peter Malinauskas. But Gatton Institute researcher Matthew Bowes said Adelaide needed to go much further by allowing more apartments and townhouses throughout established suburbs. “Allowing more townhouses and apartments is key to boosting housing supply, but these kinds of homes shouldn’t just be limited to former defence sites,” Bowes said. “South Australia should be looking to remove the planning restrictions that block well-located homes across its existing suburbs.” The Gatton Institute recently warned that Adelaide has become one of the least affordable housing markets in the country relative to local incomes. According to a recent report by the institute, the city’s house prices have jumped more than 90 per cent since the COVID-19 pandemic, while rents on newly advertised properties have risen by at least 50 per cent since 2020. The report argues Adelaide has allowed less housing growth in its middle suburbs than Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth, despite strong population growth and worsening affordability pressures. Instead, development has largely been pushed to the urban fringe. Bowes said planning rules remained a major barrier to increasing supply in suburbs close to jobs, schools and public transport. Research by the institute found more than 80 per cent of residential land within 30km of Adelaide’s CBD is zoned for low-density housing. “That means most of Adelaide’s residential land simply doesn’t allow for the kinds of entry-level townhouses and smaller homes that are affordable for first-home buyers,” Bowes said. The report calls for three-storey townhouses and apartments to be allowed across residential-zoned land, higher-density developments around major transport hubs and taller apartment buildings in high-demand locations. “Removing these kinds of blockers to new supply would put downward pressure on rents, and help more South Australians into homeownership,” Bowes said. The Hampstead Barracks redevelopment forms part of a nationwide plan to sell surplus defence land. Early concepts for the site include apartment buildings, two and three-storey townhouses and community facilities centred around a large public park. Albanese said the project would deliver much-needed homes in a well-connected location. “It’s this infill development that’s so important,” he said. Malinauskas said increasing housing supply was critical to supporting South Australia’s growing economy. “We’re at full employment, and we’ve got a lot more work that is coming our way, which means we need more workers. But you can’t have more workers without more homes,” he said. The state and federal governments are also investigating future housing opportunities at Keswick Barracks, with defence operations expected to leave the site by 2030. Stream free on

title: Housing market eased 'more than anticipated', RBA says - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The Reserve Bank governor says the world has become more shock-prone in recent years, and the latest oil spike is a complication for the central bank's policy. Michele Bullock told a Sydney function the RBA was "prepared to act as required" to achieve its inflation target "including by increasing the cash rate further if needed". What's next? The Reserve Bank's interest rate-setting board next meets in a fortnight. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock says the world has become more shock-prone in recent years, with the latest spike in oil prices another complication for monetary policy. She said the recurring shocks had been occurring against a backdrop of persistently weak productivity growth in Australia, which had been weighing on real incomes and wages for years already. She warned, with continued weak productivity growth, that Australia's economy would not be capable of growing strongly without putting upward pressure on inflation, and that would limit the choices of policymakers in the coming years. "This is the fundamental challenge for the Australian economy over the next few years," she warned. "When the growth of potential supply is constrained, inflation is higher for any given level of demand, sharpening the trade-off between our dual objectives of price stability and full employment. "In a more uncertain and shock-prone world, navigating those trade-offs has become more challenging for central banks." Ms Bullock said one thing monetary policy could not do was address Australia's slow productivity growth, and while the problem persisted, workers would probably keep experiencing limited growth in real wages. But she said if inflation kept rising from here, the RBA's Monetary Policy Board would be prepared to lift interest rates even higher, if it was necessary to achieve its inflation mandate. She made her comments in her speech to the Anika Foundation in Sydney on Tuesday. The title of her speech was Monetary Policy in an Era of Shocks. Bullock says economy more resilient than in past Ms Bullock's speech was broadly about the similarities and differences between the oil shocks of the 1970s and today's recurring waves of supply shocks. She said thankfully, even though the world had been more shock-prone in recent years, Australia's economy was more resilient than it was in the past, for a few reasons. She said the adoption of a credible inflation target by the RBA in the 1990s had played a "key role" in Australia's improved resilience. Another key difference, she said, was that Australia's economy had become less dependent on oil than it was in the 1970s. "This means a given increase in oil prices has a less direct and less pervasive effect on inflation today than it would have in the 1970s," she said. "[But] this doesn't mean we're immune from adverse supply shocks. They can constrain growth, reduce real incomes and add to inflationary pressures. "In this environment, our job is to keep inflation expectations anchored and make sure that shocks don't lead to lasting increases in inflation. With inflation and capacity pressures already elevated, recent shocks have added further to the inflation impulse. "That is why we tightened monetary policy earlier this year and why we remain focused on returning inflation sustainably to target." Ms Bullock said five months have passed since the United States and Israel began bombing Iran, and since the outbreak of the conflict oil prices have been highly volatile and, as recent days and weeks have demonstrated, conditions can change quickly. "While the effect on fuel prices and headline inflation has so far been smaller than initially feared, headline inflation remained well above target at 4 per cent in May," she said. Housing market weaker than expected, more unemployment needed Staying with the Middle East conflict, she said business confidence in Australia fell sharply at the start of the conflict but has "rebounded somewhat" over recent months. Ms Bullock said the decline in business conditions and capacity utilisation had been less pronounced, while business investment had been stronger than expected, largely driven by investment in data centres. But she said Australia's housing market had been a little weaker than expected in recent months. "We had expected conditions to ease in response to the changed outlook for monetary policy and the rise in the cash rate earlier this year," she said. "But the housing market has eased by more than we had anticipated in May. "This appears to reflect a range of factors, including recent policy developments affecting the housing market, and a general softening in housing market sentiment. "Even so, the easing in established housing prices has so far been modest, following a period of strong growth. "Price declines have been concentrated in the Sydney and Melbourne markets, but prices in these markets remain around where they were before interest rates started to rise in February this year. "Furthermore, the most recent data suggest that, notwithstanding the price falls, negative equity remains very limited, affecting less than 1 per cent of borrowers." Ms Bullock said while the RBA expected property prices to be affected when interest rates rise, monetary policy did not target housing prices. "Rather, what matters for monetary policy is how changes in housing prices affect household spending, investment decisions, and, ultimately, inflation," she said. She said the labour market had also "eased" a bit more than expected in recent months, with the unemployment rate rising a little faster than expected. But even still, she said, the labour market probably needed more unemployment or underemployment to bring inflation back down. "Overall, we continue to assess that some further easing in labour market conditions will likely be required to bring inflation back to target," she said. The national unemployment rate is currently 4.4 per cent. The RBA is forecasting the unemployment rate to be 4.6 per cent by the end of next year. Loading...

title: Why are Sydney house prices falling in some areas, but rising in others? - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The downturn of Sydney's house and unit prices are "less likely" to impact first home buyers, a residential economist says. Data released by Domain shows the city recorded the lowest drop in the country, but mainly in "premium locations". A real estate agent in a traditionally affordable area of Sydney's west says buyer confidence is at "an all-time low". First home buyers are "less likely to be affected" by Sydney's housing price and unit downturn as historically affordable areas have increased, a property expert says. Figures released by real estate company Domain showed a turning point for the city's house prices, which saw the largest drop in the country of 3.3 per cent on the last quarter. Domain's chief residential economist, Nicola Powell, said it was the first quarterly fall in about 3.5 years for house prices, and the first quarterly fall for units. "The fall for house prices in particular was quite sharp. It means that about $60,000 was shaved from the median house price in three months," Dr Powell said. However, she said the downturn had impacted "premium locations" in Sydney's north and east, not necessarily making it easier for first home buyers. "Those areas that are outer suburbs that are much more affordable, these are areas that are actually still rising in price," she said. "At the outer south-west as an example, house prices there are up almost 13 per cent over the past year." 'It ripples out' The quarterly data shows usually affordable suburbs Penrith and Fairfield have seen a $12,000 increase in unit prices compared to last quarter. But, Dr Powell does expect the shift could eventually make it to those traditionally more affordable areas, including Western Sydney. "What you tend to find when Sydney moves into a downturn, what moves first and what sees property prices fall first are the premium locations," she said. "Then what happens over time is it ripples out. It ripples to those middle suburbs and often you tend to find those very outer suburbs either don't see a fall, or if they do see a fall, it's much more marginal." Andrew Partners Real Estate director Gary Attard, who has worked in and around Fairfield for almost three decades, said uncertainty was changing how buyers approached the market. "Buyer confidence is at an all-time low," he said. "We had a combination of the budget announcement, the tax reforms, and obviously with the cost of living at an all-time high, we are seeing the market affected in a negative way." Mr Attard said there was still demand for units due to affordability, but houses and properties with land were "unfortunately still out of reach for a lot of first home buyers". "We're seeing first home buyers hesitant to buy, they're waiting for the bottom-end of the market," he said. "Young first home buyers have got their savings to invest in a property, and that deposit that they initially outlay with falling prices, are scared to lose that." NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson said the change in the market was in its relatively early stages. "I don't want to read too much into it. I still think housing is really expensive in Sydney, so the average house price is still up close to $1.7 million," she said. "When you talk, as I do to people who are on the social housing waiting list, who are looking for affordable housing, they still see house prices as a huge issue." Investors 'sitting on their hands' Dr Powell said a convergence of factors, including three rate hikes this year, had caused the slowdown in one of Australia's most exposed markets. "We've also got ... weak consumer confidence, and when you do see consumer confidence low, it does slow down transactions across the housing market," she said. "It [Sydney] has a higher proportion of investor activity compared to other state and territories and I think what we've got at the moment is the sentiment has changed dramatically." Mr Attard said the investment market in Fairfield had come to a "complete stop". "Investment is not on the radar. Property investors are sitting on their hands," he said. "They're scared to make a move at the moment because of so much uncertainty." Dr Powell said the cash rate had hit its peak, but warned any rate reductions were a "far distance away". "It's important to remember that this is the normal dynamics of a property price cycle," she said. "We have gone through a period of strong growth and you then tend to find a period of weaker growth."

title: Ep 29 - Take a rent hike - Media Watch - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: And now, Australia’s long suffering renters in for a rude shock: JAYNE AZZOPARDI: Rent prices are projected to surge over the next two years. Economists from NAB say they could jump by 30 per cent as landlords look to make up for the loss of property tax breaks abolished in the federal budget. - Today, Nine Network, 18 Aug 2026 A one-third increase in rental payments in just 24 months, all thanks to Labor’s property market reforms: HARNSLE JOO: The debate about Australia’s rental markets sparked by a National Australia Bank report that says gross rental yields will need to rise … - Ten News First (Syd), 18 Aug 2026 The news on everyone’s lips: landlords weighing up a big squeeze: MARK LEVY: Rents are projected to soar by as much as 30 per cent over the next two years to compensate many landlords for the loss of property tax concessions … - Mornings with Mark Levy, 2GB, 18 Aug 2026 And from where did this earthquake originate? Why, the mighty Oz of course, which warned readers to assume the position and: Brace for an extra 30pc on your rent Rents are projected to soar by as much as 30 per cent over the next two years to compensate many landlords for the loss of property tax concessions that Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese abolished … - The Australian, 18 Aug 2026 And where did it come upon this astounding number? This note from NAB, which told its clients the loss of tax benefits for investors will naturally prompt a market response: “For investment properties in Sydney and Melbourne, a rise in the rental yield … to around 4.5 per cent implies an increase in rents of 25 to 30 per cent, assuming the current level of house prices is unchanged.” - The Australian, 18 Aug 2026 Rents needing to climb for investors to make up for lost tax benefits. But is there any other way landlords might make up the difference? By joves, yes, because the bank went on in the very next sentence of its report to explain: In the end, the adjustment … will likely require a combination of both higher rents and lower dwelling values. - Macro Monday, NAB, 17 Aug 2026 In plain language, rents need not go up as much if property prices come down, and what’s more likely according to NAB is a combination of the two. But that sentence was not included anywhere in The Australian’s report, prompting the Treasurer himself to line up for a free kick: JIM CHALMERS: Well a couple of points about that story in The Australian today. First of all that’s not a forecast from the National Australia Bank … - Sunrise, Seven, 18 Aug 2026 JIM CHALMERS: I think people see beyond the kind of clickbait headlines that they're reading … - Today, Nine, 18 Aug 2026 The bank itself, no doubt after a phone call from Canberra, appeared to agree, its note to clients the following day offering a shade of remorse: In yesterday's note, we outlined one possible scenario … This was not a forecast … In reality, the adjustment will likely take place via a combination of lower dwelling prices and higher rents … and should have been more clearly stated … - Data React, NAB, 18 Aug 2026 So what happened next? The Australian gathered around its conference table and planned a careful, nuanced follow up article acknowledging it might have over-egged the pudding. Nah: RENTAL DISORDER - The Australian, 19 Aug 2026 The splash dismissed NAB’s update as only a "supposed clarification" and turned to another trusted, independent arbiter of property forecasting, real estate agents, for back up: Australia’s largest rental property manager has affirmed that Jim Chalmers’ budget could lead to a 30 per cent spike … - The Australian, 19 Aug 2026 But did that property manager, Ray White, really "affirm" rents could soar 30 per cent? title: More than 1,500 Brisbane children listed as experiencing homelessness - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: New data from Brisbane Zero shows last financial year there were 984 families, including 1,539 children, who were identified by name as experiencing homelessness in the city. The snapshot is used to understand the scale of homelessness in Brisbane, and to recommend ways to improve the situation. Caitlyn Wheatley, a youth ambassador with the Foyer Foundation, reminded people to remember that a person sleeping rough is "someone's someone". More than 70 per cent of families listed by name as experiencing homelessness in Brisbane last year had a single mother as the sole parent, new data shows. Between July 1, 2025 and June 30 this year, 984 families, including 1,539 children, were identified by name as sleeping rough on the city's streets, in parks, in cars, in motels, or in emergency accommodation. Of those families, 715 had a woman as the sole parent. The list of people accessing services is compiled by Brisbane Zero, a group of 32 organisations committed to ending homelessness. The snapshot is used to understand the scale of homelessness in the city, identify gaps in support and track changing needs over time. The data shows the number of families surveyed by Brisbane Zero almost doubled in the last year. Salvation Army Acting Regional Manager Jonathan Dyer described the situation in Brisbane as "quite dire", with the number of children experiencing homelessness particularly alarming. "We know that experiencing homelessness as a young person increases your risk of experiencing homelessness across your life span," he said. "It is all about breaking cyclical homelessness experiences and taking people out of that system into a life where safe and stable housing is a trampoline into everything else that's positive." Of the families recorded, 321 identified as being homeless for the first time, 268 identified as First Nations and 56 had been experiencing homelessness for more than 12 months. Brisbane Zero data shows 318 of the families identified through the list were housed, including 558 children. Of those housed, 41 per cent were in social housing and 35 per cent were in a private rental. During the same period, 2,326 individuals were listed by name as experiencing homelessness, with the number surveyed almost doubling in a year. Of those, 985 were homeless for the first time and 604 identified as First Nations. Micah Projects acting chief executive Bridget Kinch said there were more people with significant health and wellbeing needs. "This reinforces that homelessness isn't just a housing issue," she said. "It takes health, housing and community services working together to make a real difference." The data shows 54 per cent of individuals surveyed had experienced violence within the past year, 52 per cent did not feel safe where they sleep and 23 per cent had interacted with police five or more times in the past year. Since October, fewer individuals have been added to list, however, MrDyer said this did not reflect a drop in those experiencing homelessness. "It means services have less capacity to reach everyone who needs help," he said. "The strength of Brisbane Zero is that organisations don't work in isolation. They share information, coordinate support and focus on getting people housed as quickly as possible." Ms Kinch said the limited availability of rentals and affordable housing was hitting hard. "The cost of living is making it really hard for people to make ends meet so they are moving into homelessness because they can't afford the rent they were paying," she said. Micah Projects was among the organisations to have top-up funding from the state government for its emergency hotel program cut. Ms Kinch said the focus for the organisation, and other services, was on working with transitioning people from hotels to sustainable long-term solutions. "As much as the reduction is a lot to work with at the moment, we are working really closely with the government around that, particularly around housing pathways," she said. Caitlyn Wheatley, who has experienced homelessness and now works as a youth ambassador with the Foyer Foundation, said she would urge people to remember when they see a person sleeping rough that they are "someone's someone". "Every time you see someone out on the street, just remember that is someone's brother, someone's sister, someone's mum, someone's dad," she said "Would you like the world to look at your sibling or your mum like that? "I would tell the world to break the stigma." Want to have your say? Go to www.abc.net.au/yoursay

title: Some states waive stamp duty for existing homes. One minister says the idea is 'stupid' - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The Property Council in SA says the government should consider waiving stamp duty for first home buyers purchasing established homes. South Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory do not offer stamp duty concessions for first home buyers on houses that are not new. What's next? The Property Council is calling for stamp duty reviews and young people fear they are bearing the brunt of the housing crisis. First home buyers in three Australian jurisdictions are being slugged tens of thousands of dollars in taxes when buying established homes, as a property industry lobby says now is the time for concessions. South Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory are the only Australian states that do not offer stamp duty waivers or concessions on houses that are not new. According to RevenueSA's stamp duty calculator, a $700,000 established home in SA would cost a first home buyer an additional $32,330 in taxes. Bruce Djite, South Australian executive director of the Property Council, said stamp duty concessions for established homes should definitely be on the government's agenda now. "On the back of the federal budget changes recently, clearly investors have vacated the space when it comes to established dwellings, so I think the state government absolutely should look at pulling all levers, as they always tell us, here's a lever that is yet to be pulled," he said. "Investors aren't buying existing stock, that market has really gone dormant and what a great opportunity for first home buyers to be able to buy something where they've grown up, where their jobs are, where their family is." SA housing minister Nick Champion said he was against a policy change as adding more demand to existing homes was "an incredibly foolish thing to do". "It would be idiotic to do that, what we do is give tax concessions to new builds," Mr Champion said. "It's stupid, other state governments shouldn't do it." Young people in favour of reform Architecture student Clementine Cooke-Hall, 20, was in support of the stamp duty change and said buying a house in Adelaide was "out of the question for most young people". "If you are on welfare benefits, there would be almost no properties in the entire country that you could afford," she said. "We need houses to be built for human need instead of profit." University student Sam Menadue said having to pay stamp duty on established homes was unfair. He also feared that young people would be forced to move further from the city as they search for new builds. "By moving young people away you're kind of taking away from the nightlife, all the 20-somethings obviously enjoy Hindley Street so how are they going to do that when they live so far up north they can't get there," he said. "You got to think about the young people, they're the future of the state, you want them to stay here [in SA]." Mr Menadue also said young people were scraping by while saving for a deposit. "The cost of rent, the cost to pretty much do everything is just not that much fun, even going to the footy is really expensive." Glenelg renter Jordan Armstrong said students were paying hundreds of dollars to live in "share houses in despicable living conditions". Mr Armstrong said the entire housing market was "completely rigged for the rich" but "housing should be a human right that everyone has access to". "People are told you can grow up and be able to get a house one day," he said. "But the reality is for a whole bunch of people that's not been the case, that the cost-of-living crisis and the housing crisis has meant it's not an option for a whole bunch of people." Here's how different states and territories assist first home buyers First home buyers in SA are not eligible for stamp duty relief on established homes. Stamp duty relief is available for a new home, an off-the-plan apartment or vacant land to build a new home on. No property caps have applied after June 2024. A first home buyers grant one-off payment of $15,000 is available for applicants buying or building a new home. First home buyers are eligible for a full stamp duty exemption on new or existing homes valued up to $800,000. Homes valued over that figure and under $1 million may qualify for a concessional rate. The $10,000 first home buyers grant is available for new or substantially renovated homes. First home buyers can claim exemptions on stamp duty if the new or established home is valued up to $600,000. A reduced stamp duty amount is offered for properties between $600,001 and $750,000. A $10,000 first home buyers grant is available to people who buy or build a new home. For established homes in QLD, first home buyers can receive a concession on homes valued under $800,000. Homes valued at under $700,000 attract no duty. First home buyers purchasing a new build on or after May 1, 2025, may be able to claim a full concession. A first home owners grant of up to $30,000 is available for new homes for contracts signed on or after 20 November 2023. No stamp duty on established homes valued up to $600,000, previously $500,000. A concessional rate applies to homes that are valued up to $800,000. A first home buyers grant of $10,000 is available for new homes. First home buyers purchasing an existing build are no longer eligible for stamp duty exemptions. Tasmania ended its scheme on June 30 this year. First home buyers grants of $20,000 are available for new builds between July 1 this year and June 30 next year. First home buyers purchasing a home from July this year are exempt from paying stamp duty on established and new builds as well as vacant residential land. There is no income threshold. First home buyers grants are not available for applicants from July 2019. The grant has been replaced by the new Home Buyer Concession Scheme. Established builds are not eligible for stamp duty exemptions in the NT. However, the HomeGrown Territory Grant of $10,000 is available for first home buyers purchasing an established home. First home buyers who build or buy a new home or purchase off-the-plan are entitled to $50,000 until September 2027.

title: Housing developer walks away from 1,900-home SA project - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: Renewal SA says AVID Property Group has ended its involvement with a 1,900-home project in Adelaide's north. The development is now in the hands of the SA government, which says other developers have expressed interest in the project. What's next? Housing Minister Michael Brown says several hundred outstanding contracts will be honoured, and the government is now looking for a new commercial partner. "Hundreds" of homebuyers will not be left in limbo despite a major developer saying it is walking away from a new estate in Adelaide's north, the state's housing minister has insisted. The Eyre development near Penfield, between Edinburgh and Andrews Farm, was announced in 2010, and includes plans for 1,900 homes on a 120-hectare site. SA government agency Renewal SA said it had entered an agreement with developer AVJennings — since bought by AVID Property Group — to build the homes, and that "about 750" had been completed, along with sporting fields and a shopping centre. But it said that AVID had made the decision to "conclude its activities" in the South Australian market, leaving the remainder of the project back in the hands of the SA government. Acting Housing Minister Michael Brown said the state government would seek to partner with another developer to deliver the project, and that outstanding contracts would be honoured. "There's a few hundred contracts," he said. "AVJennings are absolutely adamant that they will be delivered … so those who have signed deals with AVJennings need not be concerned." SA Premier Peter Malinauskas later said the decision to part ways was "mutually agreed" and that the developer was "not delivering the number of houses at the pace that [the government] would desire". "We don't want to see developers sitting on economic and developable pieces of land, we're investing in the infrastructure but they're not delivering the housing hence the outcome we got here today," he said. He said "a couple of significant developers" have expressed interest since this morning. Mr Brown described AVID's move as "a commercial decision". In a statement, AVID said it had "agreed to transition the developer role at the Eyre community" to Renewal SA. "The decision … is a strategic business decision reflecting AVID's focus on the Australian eastern seaboard," it said. "While Renewal SA assumes responsibility for the future direction of the community, AVID remain committed to delivering in-progress and planned stages and amenities, including a park, streetscapes and blocks. "If you hold a contract for a lot in Stage 17 or 18, your contract remains on foot and AVID remains your point of contact for all settlement-related matters." Master Builders Association CEO Will Frogley told 891 ABC Adelaide it was "definitely disappointing" that the company had opted against further involvement in the project. "The main thing that Master Builders would really like to see is stability in the market — there's a lot of turbulence at the moment," he said. "Last year we built a record number of homes, so it is quite disappointing to see a brand that size, a national developer, moving away from South Australia." Renewal SA said the project would "remain on track" and that the "transition would not affect existing purchasers". It said AVID had committed to finishing "outstanding work on current stages, including landscaping and delivery of a reserve, while also working with existing buyers to finalise upcoming settlements required design approvals and ensure that all commitments to existing buyers are maintained". It said that work was expected to be completed by mid-2027. "Eyre is a very significant development — there's already been a lot of interest from other developers over the years," Mr Brown said. "We are extremely confident we'll find a major development partner going forward." Housing options on defence sites Meanwhile, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was in Adelaide on Tuesday morning for talks on the future of the Hampstead Barracks, which was identified as a possible future housing development site following the announcement of defence site sales earlier this year. Mr Malinauskas has previously indicated interest in the residential potential of the site. The federal government today said it was seeking to advance negotiations, "with a view to divesting the site" to the state government. It said the site "could support about 400 homes" including apartments and townhouses "around a large public park".

"There's a few hundred contracts," he said. "AVJennings are absolutely adamant that they will be delivered ... so those who have signed deals with AVJennings need not be concerned."
