VICTORIAN GOVERNMENT The main issue that Premier Ben Carroll has to deal with is not the legacy of alleged corruption of ‘the Big Build’, nor the spectre of One Nation and a weakened Liberal party coalition. It is not even the unions such as the teachers and CFMEU, nor is it the budget blowout. It is time. That is his enemy. An election is just months away, and he has to convince Victorians that the ship can be righted and that it can head in a different direction. Imagine if the SRL had a different push. Imagine the priority became the western end and the airport rail. Imagine if money was actually spent on infrastructure in the western suburbs where it was desperately needed. Imagine if Warragul got the hospital it was promised over 30 years ago. Imagine if public housing and school upgrades were deemed essential and were funded. Let’s hope Ben Carroll has some imagination and will deliver on any promises he makes, unlike previous premiers. Labor deserves a kick in the pants. Does Victoria deserve a bickering Liberal party and a right wing One Nation coalition instead? That is the choice at the moment. Only time, Carroll’s enemy, will tell. Greg Tuck, Warragul The airport rail that got away Victorians recall with regret the Allan government’s announcement postponing the Airport Rail project. It was in the same 2024 budget that affirmed a $26 billion price tag for the North East Link, after its $10 billion blowout was revealed in December 2023. It doesn’t take much imagination to conclude the one followed directly from the other. Had someone asked the Parliamentary Budget Office how much could be saved by cancelling the North East Link and downing tools right then, I’m sure they’d have dutifully tallied the billions in hypothetical, avoided construction and operating costs over subsequent decades. It would not have un-bulldozed 20,000 trees or restored the open wounds sliced through the Yarra and Koonung valleys - but maybe we’d have got airport rail on its original timetable. When it comes to stopping fiscal and environmental loss from big projects, there really only is one right time, and that’s at the original decision to proceed or not. For these decisions to serve the public interest it’s necessary that they tick all the ‘process’ boxes but as we’ve seen, not sufficiently enough. There must be a transparent assessment of their merits, including in comparison to good-faith alternatives. Tony Morton, president, Public Transport Users Association Not too late to provide statewide tree measures I read with interest the article, “I cried when the council cut down the tree by my house”, 30/7. Trees, whether they are located on public or private land are valuable assets and play a vital role in cooling our cities in a warming climate. In ‘Plan for Victoria’, the state’s blueprint on how Victoria will grow over time, the state government has set a target of 30 per cent tree canopy cover in urban areas. That isn’t an arbitrary number; it’s widely accepted nationally and internationally as the minimum amount of cover necessary for human health and wellbeing. In September 2025, the state government introduced statewide provisions over the protection of trees. Whilst welcome, it was disappointing that in July this year the state government removed a long-standing Significant Landscape Overlay - Schedule 9 (SLO9) in the City of Whitehorse which was a proven, readily enforceable local protection of trees on private land. From a legal perspective there is no reason why both statewide and local provisions cannot co-exist and complement one another. Whitehorse Council is confident that SLO9 will not undermine housing supply targets. I urge the state government to reintroduce SLO9 in the Whitehorse Planning Scheme. Yvonne Bowyer, Surrey Hills THE FORUM Carroll’s conversion As our new premier moves with lightning speed to disassociate himself from his two predecessors by promising a government of integrity, fiscal prudence and a constructive relationship with business, some of us remain to be convinced, If he had such strong beliefs and convictions, one could ask why did he continue to serve as both a senior minister and deputy premier committed to advocating the policies implemented by those from whom he now distances himself. A politician of true conviction would have resigned from cabinet and retreated to the backbench. The cynic would suggest the imminent election, with the prospect of being consigned to opposition irrelevance without the rewards of office, are responsible for Carroll’s “road to Damascus” conversion. Bob Hawke said any politician who underestimates the intelligence and common sense of Australian voters is a fool: we await November for confirmation or contradiction of that statement. William Vickers, Melbourne Tim Wilson’s past I was interested to read Deborah Snow’s profile of my local member, Tim Wilson “Second Coming”, Good Weekend, 1/8. I was unsurprised to read that “his superpower is shamelessness”; though the most shameless episode in our member’s life went unreported. During his years at the Institute of Public Affairs, Wilson several times in writing criticised and ridiculed the Human Rights Commission and the then Human Rights Commissioner. However, when the Abbott government came to power and George Brandis offered him the position of Human Rights Commissioner, he took it straightaway. Not just that, but he spent a couple of years gallivanting around Australia and elsewhere at enormous cost. At the time, many people simply couldn’t believe he had taken the HRC job and thought it was a joke. Unfortunately, it wasn’t. Tony Adami, Caulfield South White Australia’s end Apropos George Brandis’ column ″Tony Abbott recalls a whiter Australia than I do, Menzies rejected his version, as do many Liberals″ (3/8), I recall at the start of the 1961 election, Melbourne University students decided to put repeal of the White Australia policy on the agenda. As usual, prime minister Bob Menzies was to give his policy speech at Kew Town Hall. The students decided to attend the meeting to raise the issue. Some of us in the Eureka Youth League, heard about this so we joined in, and dressed well as Young Liberals, to not arouse suspicion, and many of us occupied the back of the hall. When Menzies started we all began chanting about repeal of the White Australia Policy and Menzies was drowned out. After that, he said he would never again give his policy speech in a public hall. I acknowledge the part played by Menzies, Holt, followed by Malcolm Fraser, as important, but those students finally got the disgraceful policy onto the agenda in a big way, with wide media coverage, as this was the beginning of the end. Max Ogden, Fitzroy North Albanese’s timidity Anthony Albanese’s gambling reforms demonstrate a timidity in leadership. While arguing that Labor’s proposed reforms balance the need to protect children from gambling ads while preserving adults’ freedom to bet, it actually smacks of dancing to the tune of vested interests. Australia is caught up in a pernicious web of gambling, and governments of all persuasions have become partners in the social harm gambling causes by its reliance on gambling tax revenues. Gambling is a regressive form of taxation. The current level of gambling undermines the country’s social fabric. It redirects “wealth” from broad-based society into the hands of a few who continue to manipulate all levels of society and government. It’s not about preserving an adults’ freedom to bet. You do not need advertising to be able to bet, and you certainly don’t need gambling advertising blatantly recruiting children for its future market. All 31 recommendations of the Murphy inquiry should be accepted. David Conolly, Brighton Two state impasse Your correspondent (Letters, 3/8) is right, Netanyahu doesn’t want a two-state solution, but not for the reasons your correspondent thinks. On multiple occasions, Israel has offered the Palestinians generous offers of statehood – and every time this was rejected for one simple reason. Hamas, indeed many Palestinians, do not recognise Israel’s right to exist, in fact, the terrorist group’s constitution stipulates this. Even the more moderate Palestinian Authority rewards terrorism via their Martyrs Fund. Israel is fighting an existential threat from Hamas, Iran and Hezbollah, while Egypt and Jordan decided long ago they preferred peace rather than war. Julie Krousoratis, Bulleen Pump price ride With the fuel excise now fully restored, the fuel stations have been warned by the treasurer (3/8) that the ACCC will monitor pump prices for any unwarranted increases. What has the ACCC actually done to ensure “fair” fuel prices over the years? I would suggest very little because over the past 30 years, I can recall prices increasing astronomically just before every school holiday, every long weekend, each Easter and Christmas and, way back in 2000, rising steeply just before the Sydney Olympics. So what has changed, that will now see the ACCC bring the fuel industry to account? Phil Mackenzie, Eaglemont Expert urgent care The front page headline in the Sunday Age (″Doctors pan urgent care clinics″, 2/8) almost had me choking on my cornflakes. I had been bitten by a dog the night before and had been persuaded by my family to get some antibiotic cover. As it was Saturday night, and my wounds weren’t severe, a first-time visit to a nearby urgent care clinic seemed a sensible idea. There, after having my medical history recorded and checked against the government record, I was triaged by a nurse, then seen by the doctor, given a tetanus injection, the script for an antibiotic and even the address of the nearest late-night pharmacy. So that they didn’t miss out on anything, I was also advised to see my GP for a check-up in a few days. I was out the door in 95 minutes. When I had arrived, there had been nine people in the waiting area. When I left, there was a new group. For the GPs’ organisation to say that urgent care clinics are ″doing absolutely nothing″ to ease the pressure on hospital emergency departments, can only be described as ridiculous, or in self-interest. Jeffrey Newman, Ivanhoe In your dreams Two letters (3/8) from dreamers for flying cars. Perhaps they should do a small course in energy used to get from A to B compared with a mass transit system. And, while modern cars are quite efficient at reducing passenger trauma in a collision, it’s hard to imagine a system that protects the flyers from a fall from the heights needed to get the necessary travel corridor flow. Laurie Comerford, Chelsea Fires made worse I’m tired of people blaming arson, lack of back burning and other marginal factors for bushfires clearly driven by an escalating climate crisis (Letters, “Europe on fire”, 3/8). These arguments come straight from the fossil fuel company playbook to delay action. Researchers at World Weather Attribution found that climate change made the recent hot, dry, windy conditions in Spain around 20 times more likely. They also concluded that the recent extreme European heatwave simply would not have occurred without human-driven warming. That heatwave killed 20,000 people. The blame sits squarely with the coal, oil and gas companies and the governments who enable the continuation of the damaging pollution they cause. Shame on them. Amy Hiller, Kew Fires harder to stop Whilst your correspondent is correct that human activity started most of Europe’s recent wildfires, it should be noted that Australia’s 2019-2020 Black Summer forest fires, whose scale was unprecedented both in an Australian and global context, were primarily caused by dry lightning. The reality is that regardless of their cause, once started wildfires are now likely to be harder to extinguish due to ongoing climate change. Thus, particularly in the extratropics, there have been dramatic increases over recent decades in the area burned by wildfires, in their intensity, and in the length of the fire season. Geoff Feren, St Kilda East Abbott’s exclamation When will Tony Abbott do the right thing and publicly admit that he was wrong to denounce climate change as ″absolute crap″ in 2009? Shame on him and the party that appointed him its chairman. Juliet Flesch, Kew Keep it beautiful Living in rural Victoria, I watch in horror as the litter piles up along roadsides. Having grown up in the 1970s I recall the Keep Australia Beautiful campaign, which made me believe that change is possible. I wonder why there appears to be no effort towards managing this current, calamitous situation that I realise is complex, but history has proven can be rectified. Please can we have immediate action? Sharyn Cook, Wimmera AND ANOTHER THING Real estate ″Property price slump deepens: Melbourne remains the weakest market in the nation″ (3/8). Well, I’m no economist, but surely that can be rephrased as: ″Housing becomes more affordable in Victoria″? Caroline Williamson, Brunswick Am I the only reader sick of seeing articles about the lives of Antony Catalano and Luke Sayers? Ann Maginness, Beaumaris Furthermore I don’t trust any Trump-declared Gaza deal. I don’t trust Hamas’ promise to completely disarm. I do trust the likelihood of Israeli PM Netanyahu breaking the deal on some imagined or concocted provocation, however flimsy. Kevin Burke, Sandringham Using AI and a bit of luck, the SRL could do a left turn out to Tullamarine airport – a loop so near and surely it’s not too late ? Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove If poorer families can’t allow members to go to uni, perhaps those with excess money made from property could help out? Bruce Dudon, Woodend I’ve just seen Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey. Still a bit unsure. Were they from Los Angeles or New York? Philip Henseleit, Glenlee The best consequence of an Australian republic? No more shrill demands for ″royal” commissions! Peter Bennett, Clifton Hill Gina Rinehart is a flesh and blood person, not a punching bag. Shame on the ABC TV for the comments aired on Race Around The World, which were outrageous, hurtful, demeaning and frankly, disgusting. Sally Dobson, South Melbourne Re youth crime: perhaps it’s time to take a leaf out of the US justice book and lock up irresponsible parents. George Stockman, Bendigo Finally Growing up in Ashburton in the 70s, my family was fortunate enough to be under the care of a new, young dentist, Lesley Aisen. And today (Letters, 3/8) my suspicions were confirmed – he is the regular contributor to The Age. I am now basking in some reflected glory! title: The pay rise buyers needed to keep up in property market - theage.com.au
raw_text: Despite a decline in home values, households who have been searching for a house to buy this year will still need a pay rise just to keep up. In just six months, a household would have to find thousands of dollars of additional earnings to qualify for a loan to purchase a typical house due to rising mortgage costs, even though that house is now cheaper, new Cotality research shows. In Melbourne, someone trying to buy the median house in January would have needed a household income of $103,877. But by July, they would have needed a raise of $1786, to an income of $105,663, to afford the median house valued at $936,528. In Sydney, a household would now need an income of $172,543, up from $170,166 in January, to service a mortgage on the median house, valued at $1,529,308. The data, which is based on median home values as at July, assumes households with a 20 per cent deposit borrowed at market interest rates of 5.5 per cent in January and 6.25 per cent in May, signing up for a 30-year-loan. Other household expenses are assumed to be 30 per cent of the household income. It comes as the RBA held the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent on Tuesday, saying that housing prices are falling in some capital cities and new housing loans are declining noticeably. title: Four homes in two weeks: Labor unveils townhouse fast-track plan - theage.com.au
raw_text: Victorian landowners who want to build four homes on a single block will be able to get approval within just two weeks. Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny announced the change on Wednesday, and said fast-tracking to construction of townhouses and units would bypass council processes, complex paperwork and lengthy approvals to boost housing supply in Victoria. Labor has also once again opened the door to reviewing stamp duty, the tax paid on the purchase of homes, which economists have long argued is highly inefficient. The party’s new platform has vowed to consider its effectiveness. Kilkenny’s planning overhaul will mean applications to build up to four homes on one block that meet building codes will from next month be approved within 10 business days. The existing process can take more than two months. The government last year implemented a 10-business-day approval process for landowners subdividing a property in half, which it said had prompted a 50 per cent increase in applications for townhouses and low-rise developments. “It’s a small step, but it’s going to make a difference,” Kilkenny said of the latest move. “That means four homes that comply with the townhouse code will be approved in 10 days. Council will not be able to object to the planning application.” Kilkenny made the announcement at a housing policy debate hosted by the Australian Property Developers Association on Wednesday. Opposition housing spokesperson David Southwick, One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering and Family First’s Alex Van Der End were also present at the debate, moderated by former ABC journalist Michael Rowland. Van Der End replaced Greens housing spokesperson Gabrielle de Vietri, who was absent attending to a family medical situation, the audience was told. Southwick and Pickering received a generally warm reception from the crowd of property developers compared with Kilkenny, who has served as planning minister for nearly four years. In 2023, the state government pledged to build 800,000 homes over the next decade, including through higher density activity centres around transport hubs in established suburbs. Kilkenny defended Labor’s record, despite only about 50,000 homes being built annually since then, below its 80,000 target. “Every state in Australia and nations around the world are struggling with this issue of a housing challenge,” she said. Housing was a key feature in the Labor Party’s new policy platform, which noted the party would work to “support fast approvals for planning applications, building on reforms already made”. The platform also stated Victorian Labor would work to “consider the effectiveness of stamp duty”, a tax paid to the government on property sales that is a major source of revenue. It is due to bring in $10 billion this financial year, according to budget forecasts. Labor has abolished stamp duty for homes under $600,000, and it is applied at lower rates for properties up to $750,000. While the policy platform included a foreword from Premier Ben Carroll, it was created by the Labor Party in consultation with stakeholders and does not necessarily represent future government policy. Property industry figures argue government red tape and taxes have restricted their ability to deliver housing for Victorians. Kilkenny acknowledged there were challenges facing the sector, but pointed to construction material costs and also “events that are happening elsewhere in the world”. “I will talk up Victoria because I know that Victoria is the fastest-growing economy over the past 10 years,” Kilkenny said during the debate. “One in three first home buyers in Australia are from Victoria. We have the most affordable homes for first home buyers. We have the most affordable rent here in Victoria.” The Coalition, if elected, will abolish stamp duty for homes up to $1 million and focus on lowering property taxes, boosting supply in outer-urban greenfields and expanding high-density housing in the inner city. Southwick said the Coalition would offer certainty and hope to property developers, guaranteeing that it would not impose new or increased taxes on the industry should it form government after November’s state election. Southwick said the government’s plan to build high-density housing around activity centres was “trying to redirect people” to established suburbs, rather than letting demand guide supply. “If people want to live in an apartment in inner Melbourne, then great. If someone wants to live in high rise, low rise, great,” he said. “I think it’s important for the market to dictate that.” He also said property developers should be consulted more often. “We need to build homes alongside the people in the room today,” Southwick said. Pickering also said One Nation would look at rolling back all property taxes and red tape needed to be cut. “We’re seeing red, blue, black and green tape become an impediment to all projects across the state,” he said. Pickering said a One Nation government would impose a “two-out-one-in policy” on red tape to reduce regulation. He said businesses should receive a guarantee from the government that regulatory goalposts would not shift in the time between approvals and delivery. Pickering did not go into details over One Nation’s housing policy. Asked if the party had modelled the impact of cutting all property taxes, he said it lacked access to resources the major parties had. title: The suburbs where house sellers want up to $1.75m more than buyer budgets - theage.com.au
raw_text: Australian property buyers are underestimating the cost of properties in coveted areas by up to $1.75 million, new data shows, even as prices drop in the current downturn. Analysis comparing Domain search data to median prices across capital cities from August last year through to the end of July shows buyers are searching at lower price points than sellers are asking for their homes in the same area. The disconnect tended to be widest in inner suburbs, Domain’s Matching Demand Report, released on Thursday, showed. Domain chief residential economist Dr Nicola Powell said she thought there was probably an element of aspiration in searches for sought-after areas, especially in a moment where prices were falling. “You don’t know what you can afford in an area until you actually start doing that research and understanding the market dynamics,” she said. She thought with house prices falling most in prestige areas in Sydney and Melbourne, upsizers were probably looking to see how far their money might go, and finding there was still a reasonable gap between expectations and reality. “This is where you get that nudging effect and being brought back to reality,” she said. “[Buyers] start to look at other property types, and that’s where townhouses and units and apartments really do have a much greater balance between seller and buyer pricing.” House buyers in Sydney’s Eastern Suburbs - North region had the biggest gap between their median search price ($3.5 million) and the actual suburb median of $5.25 million. In Melbourne, house buyers in Bayside, Boroondara and Stonnington were all looking for homes about $1 million below what sellers were asking. Buyers in Perth’s prestigious Cottesloe - Claremont region had a $1.6 million gap between their budgets and sellers’ hopes. Median searches in Brisbane’s Inner Region were $1.2 million under the area’s $2.5 million median listing price. Sydney buyer’s agent Michelle May said houses in prestigious regions – particularly in Sydney – having the largest gap in search and listing prices wasn’t surprising given many Australians browsed real estate listings with no plan to buy. “Who doesn’t love a little bit of property porn, right?” she said. But she thought it also reflected a common experience of dealing with first home buyers, many of whom underestimated the real price of a coveted area, noting the same could be true for sellers in the current market. “I think a lot of vendors overestimate their own property’s value,” she said. “It’s always better than their neighbours’, right? It’s just a natural instinct.” Melbourne buyer’s agent and managing director at Cohen Handler, Nicole Jacobs, said she would have expected people to be searching above the suburb median, rather than below, anticipating discounts on top-tier properties in a falling market. “That shows me that people have decided to be conservative in their budgets and what they’re looking for,” she said, given cost-of-living pressures and potential future rate hikes. “[They’re] hoping that the market has pulled back enough for them to be able to find what they want in that lower bracket.” Across the country, houses in inner ring areas within 10km of the CBD were more likely to see a gap between buyers’ expectations and the listed prices of the homes they were searching for, with Melbourne seeing the second-biggest gap – a $440,000 shortfall from the $1.54 million median listing – after the much tighter Canberra market. Powell said that Melbourne has a large disparity between house prices in coveted inner-ring suburbs and its more approachable outer rings, which was reflected in the bigger gaps. “When you compare it to a market like Sydney, where affordability pressure is really evident across the entire city… Melbourne really is the only [city] that has that strong disconnect,” she said. She thought Melburnians might be waiting to see when and how far “the knife will fall” on houses in prestige areas that have already seen prices tumble up to 20 per cent in the past year. The gap between buyers’ expectations and listed prices for townhouses and units is significantly less across the board, and in most cities there was a greater proportion of regions where searches were either on par with or above the median listing price. PRD chief economist Dr Diaswati Mardiasmo said large gaps between searches and listing prices in the top end of the market reveal how buyers whittle down their preferences as they make the hard decision about what they can actually afford to buy. “[It’s] what I call the sweet spot between want and affordability,” she said, which was driving the gap between buyer and seller prices.

title: Bipartisan housing bill becomes law despite Trump’s refusal to sign it | Donald Trump - The Guardian
raw_text: A major housing bill has automatically become law without Donald Trump’s signature, after the president said he would refuse to sign the legislation because Congress has not approved new restrictions on voting nationwide. The measure, known as the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, is the biggest change to federal policy for buyers, renters and homebuilders in decades, and Congress approved it with large margins last month after lengthy negotiations between Democrats and Republicans. But Trump tied the bill to the Save America Act, which would impose a host of new restrictions on voters and state election officials nationwide ahead of November’s midterm elections, in which Republicans will be defending their majorities in the Senate and the House of Representatives. A version of the Save America Act passed the House in February, but it is opposed by Senate Democrats and lacks the votes in that chamber to overcome the filibuster. As the clocked ticked past the midnight deadline for Trump’s signature on Saturday, Elizabeth Warren, the Democratic Senator for Massachusetts, said: “Trump refused to sign it, but he couldn’t stop it. This law is groundbreaking. It will build more housing, bring down costs, and for the first time, stop private equity from buying up homes.” Last month, Trump canceled a signing ceremony for the housing bill, denying his Republican allies an opportunity to publicly highlight their efforts to address housing affordability, which surveys indicate is a top concern among voters. The president later called the measure “a big yawn” and “so unimportant” compared with the Save America Act. On 29 June, the House speaker, Mike Johnson, sent the housing bill to his desk, triggering the 10-day countdown after which it became law without his signature. In a Friday-morning post on Truth Social, Trump wrote: “I will not sign the Housing Bill, which has been fully approved by Congress and sent to the White House, in PROTEST over the fact that the United States Senate is not capable of passing THE SAVE AMERICA ACT.” The president gave no indication he would veto the housing bill, and the White House declined further comment. Democrats pilloried Trump for not signing the measure, with the House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, writing on X: “Republicans would rather make it harder to vote than easier to afford a home.” The Senate’s top Democrat, Chuck Schumer, said: “His priorities couldn’t be clearer: higher costs for families and more power for himself.” Trump’s focus on the Save America Act has compounded concerns about how his administration is preparing for the midterms in November. On Thursday, the president fired the last three commissioners on an independent federal body that assists election administration nationwide.

title: NSW should compensate elderly woman whose public housing was inundated with sewage, ombudsman finds - The Guardian
raw_text: An elderly public housing tenant whose home was damaged by sewage overflows will be fully compensated by the New South Wales government after it disposed of her personal belongings without her consent and failed to properly support her insurance claim. The NSW Ombudsman on Friday published a summary of the report after an investigation in which it found Homes NSW acted unreasonably in how it handled the tenant’s contaminated belongings and “failed to provide full and accurate information to the insurer”. The woman, whose name and suburb were not made public, had lived in the unit for more than 15 years. She reported three successive sewage overflows within three months, which saw raw sewage enter the property. After the third incident she was relocated, but her belongings remained in the contaminated unit for two months before being boxed up and moved to a vacant property. The furniture, household items, and family heirlooms were not cleaned nor returned to her, despite Homes NSW telling her “she would be actively involved in the decision to keep or dispose of any items”. She was later told “she would be adequately compensated” through an insurance claim, according to the report. When the claim was lodged, the insurer denied liability and offered a small “goodwill” payment. The report found Homes NSW’s failure to provide the insurer with “full and accurate information” which contributed to the rejection of the claim. The ombudsman’s recommendations included an apology and full compensation “in accordance with her itemised compensation claim”. It also recommended an additional payment for “the distress and suffering she experienced while trying to resolve her claim over more than five years”. Homes NSW has accepted all of the recommendations and will implement them by next month, according to the report. title: Unions unveil plans to extend standard lease agreements and increase public housing amid crisis - 7NEWS
raw_text: Millions of Australian renters could be offered leases of at least two years under a union push to provide greater security amid the housing crisis. The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) will put the proposal to the federal government on Wednesday, calling for a new national standard requiring landlords to offer tenants at least two years of housing security. WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Push for two-year rental leases to ease housing crisis Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today The plan would also introduce stronger protections against unfair evictions and rent gouging. Renters would remain free to choose a shorter agreement. Greater security was “really important” for working Australians struggling with rising housing costs, ACTU President Michele O’Neil told Sunrise on Wednesday. “What you need is housing that you can rely on. We’ve got a problem both with affordability as well as security, and a whole lot of workers find housing really stressful and not affordable,” she said. “What we see when leases end is that’s often a time when rents go up, and people having to move constantly makes it really hard to find accommodation near where you work. “Workers need to live close to work. Otherwise, all the money they are earning is getting taken up either in rents or mortgages or in paying for the commute to get to work.” Rents have risen by about 23 per cent over the past five years, while a report released by Anglicare Sydney last year found just 1 per cent of rentals nationwide were affordable for essential workers earning the minimum wage. The proposal comes as “mum-and-dad” property investors face their own financial pressures, with elevated interest rates adding to rising costs. However, O’Neil said the union’s proposed changes were aimed at professional landlords with multiple investment properties rather than people who owned one or two. “What we have seen is changes in the way that the tax system works, which are actually going to benefit people who really want to have housing as a home,” O’Neil said. “Our rental market is dominated by professional landlords. They’re the people who have been making money, and we need to put some tighter controls in so that there’s support for security and to stop rent gouging.” Push for major public housing boost The ACTU is also calling for public housing to account for one in every 10 new homes built, alongside a goal of increasing it to at least 6 per cent of Australia’s total housing stock. The proposed construction rate would represent a fivefold increase from the current level of about one in 50 new homes. “We want to see one in 10 new houses being built being public housing. That means a massive effort from the federal government and the state governments,” O’Neil said. “Having housing in the regions and communities where we need our nurses, teachers and aged care workers to be able to live is a really critical thing that we need to do to support workers.” The proposals follow union calls to increase access to home ownership and its support for capital gains tax and negative gearing changes announced in the federal budget. title: 'Fibro dog box' social house gets so hot the TV breaks down - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: A lack of thermal standards in NSW social housing is exposing tenants to extreme heat risks, a new study has found. Tenants in Greater Sydney had indoor temperatures of 29 degrees Celsius for 70 days during one summer. What's next? While thousands of social homes have had thermal safety improved, the study's authors say standards need to be lifted throughout NSW. It gets so hot in Mark Hartley's social housing home in summer in Sydney's west that his TV breaks down. Mr Hartley lives in what he describes as a "fibro dog box" in South Windsor with no insulation, air-conditioning or cross-breeze. "The sound goes, the picture goes. And it's basically all from heat," Mr Hartley said. In one recent summer, the front room reached an indoor temperature of 42 degrees Celsius and stayed above 35C for 11 hours. He says there is no cool part of the house, so when it gets too hot he drives to the banks of the Hawkesbury River to cool off. "It's detrimental to my health, to think that I have to leave my home during the day when the sun's out," Mr Hartley said. "What world do we live in where you can't put a ceiling fan in to keep someone cool? "It's an 80-year-old home that's very well built, but not built for … conditions of Australia." Cooling costs bite Mr Hartley would like to make his place cooler but the home was made using asbestos, so he says he can't get a hole drilled without a hazmat suit. He tried using an air-conditioner but his electricity bill soared to $500 a quarter, chewing up a significant chunk of his Centrelink benefit. "Actually affording the electricity to keep cool and, and then keep warm in winter is, is off the chart," Mr Hartley said. It's a similar story for Lynne Dunn from Richmond in Sydney's Hawkesbury region, who is also in an uninsulated one-bedroom fibro home. The age pensioner says she spends most of the summer with the fan on, the curtains drawn and the door closed. She says wearing the $70 a fortnight to run air-conditioning and heating in winter is worth it. "I'm not going to be hot or cold. I'd rather not eat than that," Ms Dunn said. Study finds low standards leading to extensive indoor hot spells A new study highlights the low thermal safety standards of social housing in NSW, and the extreme heat currently being experienced. The study led by researchers from Western Sydney University found indoor temperatures in social housing across the city reached 29C for 70 days during summer. Using loggers inside and just outside homes across Greater Sydney, it found tenants of social housing experienced indoor temperatures above 35C for up to 32 days in one summer. Professor of urban management and planning Sebastian Pfautsch said social housing was often built without thermal safety in mind, whether they were apartments or free-standing homes. "This is mostly the case, because of the combination of single glazing, lots of window space with single glazing — so not very well insulated homes — and the lack of income," Professor Pfautsch said. "Even if you have air-conditioning, you can't afford to switch it on because you can't afford the electricity bill." Professor Pfautsch said health risks associated with heat exposure increase once temperatures rise above 29C. The study published in Urban Climate suggests social housing tenants in Western Sydney will experience up to 148 days of indoor temperatures above 29C by 2060. Professor Pfautsch said it was problematic that there were no standards for thermal safety in NSW social housing, given the homes built today will likely swelter through more frequent extreme heat with the warming climate. "We need to realise that living thermally safe is a basic human right," Professor Pfautsch said. "So what we really need to look at is how do we build the next generation of affordable and social housing in a way so that people are thermally safe? "In a warming future, we can't do that by putting single glazing in or aluminium frames or very, very little insulation." Higher standards in new builds under construction codes A spokesperson for Homes NSW said there was no standalone thermal safety standard for social housing in NSW, but new construction had to meet the National Construction Code and the NSW Sustainable Buildings SEPP which brought in thermal safety standard in 2004 was last updated in late 2023. Some of these standards require fans in all living areas and bedrooms and new homes with air-conditioning use solar cells to offset power bills. "As part of the Social Housing Energy Performance Initiative (SHEPI), Homes NSW has upgraded the energy efficiency at more than 11,000 social housing properties since 2024, improving our tenants' thermal comfort and helping to reduce energy bills," the spokesperson said. NSW Housing Minister Rose Jackson said not all social housing properties could be effectively retrofitted for thermal comfort. "That's one of the key reasons why we are replacing aging social housing with modern, well-designed and energy efficient homes through renewal projects like at Waterloo Estate and Telopea," Ms Jackson said. "Many of our public housing tenants are elderly or vulnerable so we take managing heat stress very seriously." Aging homes need government investment, provider says A spokesperson for social housing manager Link Wentworth said many older properties, often built before current building standards, required significant investment to improve thermal comfort and energy efficiency. "As a community housing provider, our rental income is intentionally low to ensure housing remains affordable, meaning major upgrade programs often require additional government investment," the spokesperson said. "Continued investment in aging social housing stock will help accelerate these improvements and support residents to better cope with extreme weather." Link Wentworth's spokesperson said they had completed $1.3 million of energy upgrades funded through a NSW government grant in 2025. The study comes after the Bureau of Meteorology declared an El Nino weather event, which often leads to dry and warm weather on Australia's east coast.

title: Investors 'all but gone' from Melbourne property market after budget - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: Real estate experts say Melbourne's lowest auction clearance rate in five years shows investors' trust in bricks and mortar has been rattled by changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. Buyer advocate Cate Bakos says investors have "all but left the market", but the Real Estate Institute of Victoria says the data needs to be viewed in context. Newer results, from Saturday's auctions, showed a slight improvement on the previous weekend's data. Yuki He bought her first investment property in Melbourne two years ago. She said she was confident she had made the right financial decision to invest in real estate. But then the federal government unveiled its May budget. "It directly hit my investment portfolio," she said. The government announced that from July 1 next year, negative gearing would be abolished for existing residential properties purchased after budget night, and a 50 per cent discount on the capital gains tax owed on any profit made from selling an investment property would instead be based on inflation from July 2027. Ms He said she was relieved to be spared the changes to negative gearing, and she supported initiatives to make housing more affordable for others. "I wouldn't say I am a fan of Labor but I do appreciate their courage to take this step because hopefully this is doing the job it's supposed to," she said. But she said with the change to capital gains and Melbourne's property prices now falling, she had some difficult decisions to make. "I'm losing money on the interest I pay every month, so what's the point of this investment?" she said. Changes reflected in low auction clearance rate Last weekend, Melbourne recorded its worst auction clearance rate in five years, with just 50.2 per cent of properties going under the hammer achieving a sale. While Melbourne's rate was the second best of the capital cities, according to property research firm Cotality, the result was on par with when the city was in the midst of 2021 COVID lockdowns. Data from Saturday's auctions showed a slight improvement, up to 54.6 per cent, which was the best result of all capital cities. Real Estate Institute of Victoria (REIV) CEO Toby Balasz said the clearance rate acted as a barometer for how buyers, sellers and investors were feeling about the market. "There has been some pretty troubling data released in terms of the clearance rates," he said. "We want to see them obviously much higher than what they are at the moment and that would suggest that there's probably a lack of confidence in the market." Buyer's advocate Cate Bakos said the clearance rate had been falling in early 2026 because of consecutive interest rate rises and cost of living pressures. "But we saw a dramatic change after the 12th of May and that was entirely down to the budget announcements," Ms Bakos said. "Investors in established locations are pretty much all but gone." Ms Bakos said the exodus had caused a ripple effect through to owner-occupiers, causing them to hold off on purchasing. "People are fearful," she said. "It's very hard to feel like you can enact a contrarian kind of response to a shock wave like this because most people will be saying to themselves, 'Is now the best time that I could get in or should I wait a little bit longer and see if prices fall any further?'" Ms Bakos said sellers were nervous about the possibility of a further deterioration in the market. "We've seen a lot of vendors withdrawing their properties from sale, both private sale and auction," she said. She said the same situation was playing out in regional Victoria, but auctions were rarer in that market, and that while other states were also seeing low clearance rates, Melbourne was being hit particularly hard because of the Victorian government's changes to laws requiring reserve prices to be published a week before an auction. Ms Bakos said investors were not only pulling out of purchasing, but were getting appraisals done on their existing properties and engaging agents to sell, which could have impacts for renters. "We're not building enough new property," she said. "Even when those renters are looking at other options, it's going to be smaller-scale dwellings such as apartments in the city-type areas or houses in the fringe areas, and that's not viable for a lot of families," she said. Financial adviser Alex Jamieson said he was already seeing that play out among his clients. "The majority of the conversations that we're having with clients at the moment are really around exiting their investment properties," Mr Jamieson said. "Those conversations, to be honest, were already starting to be had before the federal budget. "If anything, the federal budget changes accelerated some of those types of inquiries and conversations." However, he said he was still shocked to see last weekend's auction results. "It always takes your breath away when you see a figure of those types of clearance rates," Mr Jamieson said. He believed investors should not be too hasty about selling up and moving into stocks and trading funds. "The simplicity of the share market does attract people in that there aren't the headaches with being a landlord and all of the things that go with it," he said. "[But] for some people investing in shares, the volatility and the keeping awake at night can really be a concern. "There's not enough housing stock and that still needs to be addressed, so once some of those things normalise, our view is let's reassess it in 12 to 18 months time, which coincides quite neatly with the new capital gains tax regime." The federal government said the drop in clearance rates earlier this year showed the changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax were not to blame. "Our reforms are about delivering more affordable options, helping first homebuyers into homes and helping young Australians get ahead," Treasurer Jim Chalmers said. "A range of factors impact house prices and we know that because clearance rates were moderating well before the budget." The REIV's Toby Balazs said it was important to remember that the market always slowed in Melbourne in winter and there was nothing yet to suggest that the wavering confidence would continue into the busier spring selling season. "The fact that there is less properties on the market at this time of year is not abnormal," he said. "We have been asking the government to provide an environment whereby people from both the property investment and owner-occupier point of view are wanting to transact and wanting to make property decisions that encourage activity, as opposed to people not feeling confident to be able to go ahead and make that property purchase." In a statement, the Victorian government said it was introducing new laws to put "power back in the hands" of people buying a home. "This reform is currently before parliament and is not yet law, so it's wrong to say it’s contributing to low auction clearance rates," the spokesperson said. Subject to the bill passing parliament, the laws would come into effect on October 1 this year. Loading...

title: Locals worried remote Gove Peninsular town won't survive housing crisis - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: Nhulunbuy residents and a senior Northern Territory government official have accused an economic development group, based in the remote mining town, of not doing enough to support small business. title: 'It's insane': NT government divides opinion with plan to reduce block sizes - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The Northern Territory government has prepared a legislative amendment to reduce the minimum block size in low-density suburbs from 800 to 450 square metres. Residents say they are concerned for the liveability of local suburbs, while industry and advocacy groups have voiced conditional support for the proposal. What's next? The government will open its amendment to public feedback on Friday. The Northern Territory government has divided public opinion with a proposal to reduce block sizes in suburban areas, paving the way for more homes on smaller plots of land. The proposal will see the minimum block size in low-density residential zones such as Darwin's northern suburbs reduced from 800 to 450 square metres. NT Lands, Planning and Environment Minister Josh Burgoyne this week confirmed an amendment to the Planning Act had been prepared based on the proposal. "Exploring housing diversity, including smaller homes on smaller lots, will help boost housing supply and improve affordability," Mr Burgoyne said. Deputy Opposition Leader Ed Smelt has pushed back on the approach, saying relying on the "ad hoc" decisions of home owners would fail to make a dent in housing supply. "This government doesn't have a plan for affordability or growing our housing stock," Mr Smelt said. "You need to look at activity centres, at transport corridors, at where growth and development is occurring, not going out to our low-density communities and trying to subdivide them." Data from the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council indicated the NT was lagging behind other states and territories in meeting its obligations under the National Housing Accord, with a growing number of housing approvals and a diminishing number of completions over the past year. Locals fear for liveability of suburbs Top End residents have been quick to voice their concerns about the proposal, with many contacting ABC Radio Darwin this week to say they fear the changes could negatively impact the liveability of NT suburbs. "I think it's insane," one caller said. "If you want to live on a minuscule 450 square metre block, they're all out there already in the new suburbs, so why destroy those beautiful old suburbs with their beautiful gardens?" Another caller said: "We live outside; when we have friends over, we entertain outside because we get that beautiful breeze through the garden — if we just build wall-to-wall houses, Darwin won't be that beautiful, tropical, liveable city anymore." Mr Smelt, whose electoral division of Nightcliff is mostly zoned as low-density residential, said he had fielded similar concerns from his constituents. "They love the larger blocks, the trees, the sea breeze, having space around them, that's why people choose to live here," he said. A discussion paper published by the NT Planning Commission indicated that under the changes, home owners could build an additional dwelling on their block, demolish their home and build two new dwellings, or subdivide their house, so long as the new property adhered to the 450 square metre rule. In response to the concerns, Mr Burgoyne emphasised that subdivision was entirely optional. "Our government is creating new opportunities for Territorians who want to subdivide their land — no-one will be forced to subdivide their block," he said. Darwin-based infrastructure planner Graeme Finch said while the plan had its benefits, there was a string of logistical challenges to consider in addition to local concerns about aesthetics and livability. "I think we do need some densification in the older suburbs where we have commercial centres, but we need to do it in a managed way where we don't overload the existing infrastructure in terms of traffic volumes, power, water, and sewer," Mr Finch said. Stakeholder organisations give conditional support Industry bodies and advocacy groups have said the proposal was mostly positive. "It's a great opportunity for small developers and families to develop and sell their blocks and provide much-needed work for our industry," Master Builders NT president Jim Eadie said. He noted, however, it would take time for change to occur, and that there was a risk that electricity and water costs could deter some home owners from taking advantage of the changes. "There's infrastructure costs that might be applicable with duplicating the blocks, because you're going to double the sewer, the power, and the water supply to each block," he said. "The Power [and] Water authority and the NT government could provide some supports to incentivise those developments." Chief executive of housing and homelessness body NT Shelter, Annie Taylor, said the social services sector supported the changes if they resulted in more affordable housing. "We need to recognise that we don't just want to reinforce private market dynamics, which are not working for a lot of Territorians, particularly our key workers," Ms Taylor said. Ms Taylor suggested the NT government should also adopt mechanisms such as mandatory inclusion zoning, which would see social and affordable housing developed alongside new builds. "It's all well and good to build more housing, but it needs to be affordable for the people who live in it, otherwise our essential workforce will leave the NT," she said. The proposal will be open for public exhibition for 28 days beginning on Friday, July 24, during which time Territorians will be able to give their feedback on the proposal.

title: Inner Melbourne council walks away from plan for key worker housing - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: The City of Yarra has halted plans to build at least 50 affordable rental apartments for workers in Abbotsford. Councillors unanimously voted to stop work on the project at a council meeting on Tuesday night, saying market conditions weren't right. The Urban Development Institute of Australia says there is a growing feasibility gap in Victoria for affordable and social housing projects. An inner Melbourne council has halted plans to build new affordable housing for local workers priced out of the private market due to a lack of available funding for the project. The Yarra City Council project had already completed an initial expression of interest campaign for the building, which would transform a Collingwood car park into at least 50 discounted rental apartments. However, councillors unanimously voted to stop work on the project on Tuesday night after a panel reviewing the proposals identified "significant funding and delivery constraints". Councillor Evangeline Aston said they were "disappointed", but that council was always "very clear" it would not use ratepayers' money to fund the project. "We were … [not going] to get into a field that we have no obligation to be in and to sign us up to ongoing operating and maintenance expenses," Councillor Aston said. "The market reality determines the situation here and the reality is that the money is just not there." Limited funding options Tenants in the eight-storey building would have had their rent capped at 75 per cent of the local rate, but had to be working in the municipality to be eligible. To realise the project, the council had resolved to lease a 2000-square-metre parcel of land behind the St Philip's Anglican Church to a delivery partner, but no further funding was guaranteed from the council itself. Council staff reviewing proposals from potential delivery partners found the project could not be delivered under the proposed model. "There is currently limited funding available within the sector and no clear state or federal government mechanism that enables local government to effectively deliver an affordable housing project of this type without significant external funding," they wrote. The smaller scale of the project meant it fell short of eligibility for the Housing Australia Future Fund, councillors said. At the meeting, Councillor Kenneth Gomez said the federal government should have worked with them to make the project happen. "Frankly, I'm disappointed in the federal government," he said. "We went to them with outstretched hands saying, 'Let's do affordable housing in Yarra', but it seems the rules around sizing worked against us." Councillor Aston said council would continue to support social and affordable housing, and would reconsider the project if market conditions changed in future. "We will continue to advocate for funding, and if the conditions change," she said. "We've done all the work, got all the preparation, we can pick this up and hit the ground running again to try and make the most of those conditions." Nick Staikos, Victoria's housing minister, said his government was not relying on local councils to build social and affordable housing. "Not that I've had this discussion with the City of Yarra, but I'd encourage them to partner with a community housing organisation and consider submitting an application to our Social Housing Growth Fund," he said on Thursday morning. Community Housing Industry Association Victoria said of 13 Victorian council-led affordable housing projects over the past 20 years, all of them required state or federal funding to get off the ground. "Councils are on the front line of the housing crisis in their communities and they're doing the heavy lifting to find solutions, but they can't do it alone," CEO Sarah Toohey said. "Whether providing land, opening housing trusts, or facilitating planning agreements, no council-led housing project has been delivered without a funding contribution from the government, and projects often involve multiple funding partners." She said it was critical the state government committed to an annual funding pipeline so councils could deliver the social housing. She urged the City of Yarra not to abandon the project. The proposal marked a second bid to redevelop the Collingwood Town Hall precinct off Hoddle Street after a larger proposal with a mix of housing types was voted down by a previous council in 2021. It came in the midst of a significant uptick of approvals for affordable housing projects, partly driven by schemes that offer incentives for developments with below-market housing. However, the model has attracted criticism, including for income requirements that can lock prospective tenants out of the scheme. By contrast, the City of Yarra — which has been critical of some developments fast-tracked under the state government's affordable housing scheme — proposed setting higher income limits, a move that would have broadened eligibility for the Collingwood building. Project documents said market housing would only be considered if the project was unfeasible without it. Locals consulted on the project were split on whether council land should be sold or leased, but those who were supportive said housing affordability was a key issue. Others believed council assets should not be leased or sold. The council said it would reconsider the proposal if funding or market conditions changed. Growing feasibility gap The Urban Development Institute of Australia is a non-profit advocacy and research body for developers. CEO Linda Allison said there was a growing feasibility gap in Victoria for such projects. She said developers were struggling to get loans because of global economic and supply chain uncertainty and the higher costs of finance and taxes. She said new apartment completions were at a 15-year low, pushing Victoria further behind on its housing targets. "If at-market housing isn't feasible, affordable housing is even more challenged," she said. "The next Victorian government must remove these roadblocks and make the delivery of homes easier, more affordable, and more certain." A state government spokesperson said the Collingwood Town Hall Affordable Housing Project was a matter for the City of Yarra. They said the government had invested $8 billion in social and affordable housing which was delivering more than 16,000 homes across Victoria. "We also recently changed rent settings in the Homes Victoria Affordable Housing Rental Scheme to make it more accessible for Victorian families." Loading...

title: Homelessness a visible crisis on Canberra's streets - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: It is often dubbed an invisible crisis, but in one of Australia's most affluent and progressive cities, evidence of homelessness is becoming harder to ignore. "People don't want to look at it, because it's gritty and it's hard and it's hard to fix," Havelock Housing chief executive Kylie Maiden said. "But you only have to walk through Garema Place to see that it's not invisible — there are a lot of people sleeping rough in this city in very cold, cold winters." Across Canberra, homelessness services are reporting an increase in demand tied to the cost of living. Vinnies Night Patrol hits the road 364 nights a year, with volunteers in vans supplying food, hot drinks, toiletries, warm clothes and bedding to those in need. Last financial year, the service provided more than 19,000 instances of support in Canberra and Queanbeyan — a 38 per cent jump on the previous year. The van's busiest stop is in Civic. "It can get up to maybe 50 or 60 people here, and we just end up giving out black coffee because we run out of milk," volunteer team leader Angus Hutchinson said. The number of material items Night Patrol provides to keep people warm and comfortable overnight has also increased by 58 per cent in one year. "People say that I'm only two pay cheques removed from coming out here," Mr Hutchinson said. "I think everyone's feeling that lately." Some of those who use the service are sleeping rough in tents in public parks, or in sleeping bags next to concrete buildings. Others, like Victor, have a home in public housing, but are struggling to afford the essentials. "I come out to get some food to supplement my diet. "You might shorten the [public housing] waitlist, but the waitlist will just keep growing."

title: Young Australians' home ownership rate at an 80-year low, report shows - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: In short: Generational inequality is pushing more young Australians out of the housing market, Anglicare's new Falling Behind report shows. The report found home ownership among 25-34 year olds has fallen to an 80-year low. Anglicare Australia executive director Kasy Chambers has welcomed efforts to remove tax breaks for investment property and called for a shake-up to the Youth Allowance payment. More young people are abandoning hopes of home ownership amid increasing generational inequality, according to a new report. Anglicare's Falling Behind report, released on Tuesday, found home ownership among 25-34 year olds has fallen to an 80-year low — highlighting intergenerational inequality from tax settings that favoured housing investment. Young Australians are facing a future where working hard does not guarantee security, Anglicare Australia executive director Kasy Chambers said after the report's release. "The economic foundations underneath them have shifted," she said. Ms Chambers said there was a perfect storm that led to inequality between the generations. "What we can see is that we've got young people coming into a workforce that is more insecure, we can see that we've got increased costs," she said. "People are studying longer. We know that it takes much longer to save a deposit for a house in terms of the annual average income versus the deposit." Investment tax breaks fuelling the generational divide Anglicare's report found older Australians "appear insulated" from today's economic pressures, having earned wages during a stable period in the job market and amassed wealth from investments which are taxed less severely than wages. The report found that while older Australians' wealth has significantly increased over time, their share of income tax has not. It said young people are "absorbing the impact" with lower wages proportional to house prices and cost of living — affording less opportunity to amass wealth. The Albanese government this year introduced tax changes on investments including shares, investment properties and the sale of businesses. Treasurer Jim Chalmers unveiled the sweeping changes in the May budget, describing them as the "most important and ambitious" reforms in decades, which would make the system "fairer and stronger for workers, businesses, first home buyers and future generations". Ms Chambers welcomed the federal government's efforts to remove tax breaks for investment income, but said more measures were needed from the federal government to even the playing field. "We need to look at taxing wealth the same way as income, because otherwise, what we're seeing is that the wealth gets concentrated," she told reporters in Canberra. "Once it gets concentrated, it's very difficult to share that again ... one dollar is one dollar in taxation terms." Low welfare payments prevent youth from catching up The Anglicare head also called for a shake-up to the Youth Allowance payment, citing the report's findings that young Australians are eligible for less support from Centrelink despite facing the same costs as older people. The maximum payment amount for a single person with no children on Youth Allowance is $677.20 a fortnight. The rate is below the poverty line, JobSeeker and the aged pension, which Ms Chambers said is contributing to generational inequality. "We have a social security system that literally says a young person needs less money to live on simply because of their age," Ms Chambers said. "Rent isn't cheaper when you're 23. Groceries aren't cheaper. Electricity isn't cheaper. Yet young people are expected to survive on the lowest payment in the system. "Poverty should not be a rite of passage." The report also highlighted that a single person on JobSeeker falls behind by $251 a week after paying for rent, food and transport — while a single parent on parenting payment falls behind by $174 a week and a couple with two children on JobSeeker falls behind by $428 a week. It found nearly half of all low-income renters aged under 35 are experiencing rental stress, and not a single rental property across the country was affordable for a single person on the support payment. ABC/Wires
