title: What will the inflation data mean for rates? - ABC listen - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
raw_text: Fresh data out today shows prices are rising slower than they were earlier in the year, but still well above the Reserve Banks target. So does that mean the Reserve Bank might be forced to hike rates even further? And Canada has loaded its tariff cannon to aim at its southern neighbour… will it light the fuse? Carrington Clarke and Diana Mousina, Deputy Chief Economist at AMP break it all down on ABC Business Daily. Got a burning business question? We'd love to hear your questions! If there’s business and economic news that has you stumped or you'd like further insight into, we're here to help. Send a short voice recording to Carrington and the team at abcbusinessdaily@abc.net.au and we'll attempt to answer it. Credits Image Details This content was transcribed automatically and may contain errors. Read more on how the ABC is automatically creating audio transcripts. Speaker 1: ABC Listen. Podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Speaker 2: Hi, it's Sam Hawley from ABC News Daily. The podcast that brings you one big story affecting your world each weekday in just 15 minutes. These glasses are always on. They have microphones, they have cameras and they basically become face-mounted data vacuums. Join me for ABC News Daily. Find us on ABC Listen. Speaker 1: Fresh data out today shows prices are rising slower than they were earlier in the year, but the rate didn't fall as much as expected and it's still well above the Reserve Bank's target. Does that mean the bank might be forced to hike rates even further? Meanwhile, Canada has loaded its tariff cannon to aim at its southern neighbour. Will it light the fuse? Welcome to ABC Business Daily. I'm Carrington Clarke. And today I'm joined by a very special guest. Speaker 3: Diana Mousina from AMP. Speaker 1: Thank you so much, Diana, for joining us. I've been wanting to get you on the show. It's great to be able to do it on Inflation Day. You haven't had a huge amount of time to process all the data. So thank you for joining us so quickly after it, but we wanted to get this episode out as quick as possible. So, I mean, the headline is that we've seen inflation fall from 3.8% down to 3.5%. That's above what most economists were estimating the numbers would be. The trimmed mean, which people often talk about being the Reserve Bank's preferred measure because it strips out some of those volatile elements, is sitting at 3.6%. I just want to go for kind of top-level analysis. Is this evidence that the three interest rate rises we've already seen haven't been enough? And will the Reserve Bank be forced to hike even further, do you think? Speaker 3: I think it suggests that we probably need another rate hike. The increase in the trimmed mean definitely concerns me. And some of the components also look a little bit too high, particularly in things like dwelling construction costs. We know that that's been a problem for the past six months. But the broader issue is really that in the past 12 months, we've seen this continued increase in the trimmed mean, which is basically the underlying rate of inflation. And I just think it's way above the RBA's comfort level. And we've actually now revised up our estimate for the September quarter inflation figures. And that's now looking like it's going to be above the RBA's own forecast. So it's going to be a problem for them. I think it will be hard at upcoming meetings, especially after we get the quarterly inflation data, for the RBA to argue that they're still on track with their inflation forecast. Speaker 1: And do you think it's likely then that we will see a hike at the next meeting, which is at the end of September? So we will have more inflation data just before that meeting, is that right?Or do you think it's more likely it'll happen in November? Speaker 3: We get another monthly before the next meeting, but our base case has been that we get another rate hike in November, and that will follow the usual quarterly inflation data. And we know that there's still some issues with the monthly trimmed mean. That's why the RBA prefers to look at the quarterly, which they have a really long time series for. You know, maybe there are just funny things that are going on with the monthly numbers, which can move up and down. So I think that they would probably prefer to wait for the quarterly. Also because that would give them more time to assess what's going on in the labour market and to see if there is actually any more movement on impacts of prior rate increases. Plus, they probably want to see what's happening to property prices, if they're falling even more, or the big falls have started to moderate. I mean, that's what the daily data suggests. But I think they probably just want to buy themselves a bit more time rather than really trying to put a massive handbrake on the economy right now. Speaker 1: What did you make of the minutes that we had out yesterday from the last Reserve Bank meeting? It was a unanimous decision to keep it on hold, but there does seem to be some disagreement within the members who get to vote about whether or not, or how quickly they might need to raise rates even further. Did you, should we read, how much should we read into those minutes? And do you think that did potentially raise the chance of there being a rate hike, either in September or November? Speaker 3: Yeah, you know, sometimes when you read these different bits and pieces from the Reserve Bank and you listen to the speech, sometimes the tone can sound so different. So, for example, the post-meeting statement from the August meeting, and then the forecast sheet that went with it, the Statement of Monetary Policy, followed by the Reserve Bank Governor's testimony. I mean, she sounded quite hawkish in that testimony, which you were at as well, and you would have seen that. So, I don't think I, you know, I didn't really try to read too much into the minutes. I don't think it really gave me anything new. I sort of take my lead as to the latest speech that the Governor or the Deputy Governor or the Chief Economist of the RBA has made as my sort of guiding star as to how they're thinking about things. I also think that they try to moderate market pricing and market expectations. Speaker 1: Let's break down some of the numbers in this inflation data. Now, you did point out that one of the things that has been forcing up inflation in Australia has been housing, which has then broken down into different categories. You spoke about construction costs. I mean, new dwelling prices rising 5.7% over the last 12 months. That's a pretty fast clip. Then we also have rental prices rising at 3.6% in the 12 months to the most recent data. Now, those are pretty big numbers. I mean, the most recent kind of advertised rents show even much higher rates of asking rents for people trying to get a new property. But is there any evidence that this is starting to moderate and how worried are you about what we're seeing in housing? Speaker 3: There's not really much evidence that it's noticeably moderating, I guess. It's not as high as it was the back end of last year, which is when the RBA really got concerned about it, but it's still elevated, basically. It looks like rental growth is going to grow at 3.5% or so in the next 12 months, which is still pretty elevated. The vacancy rates are still ultra low across most capital cities, sub 1%, basically, which indicates that rental price inflation is still going to be pretty high. We have a supply issue, basically, where we're just not building enough homes to keep up with demand for them. And we can see those numbers coming through every single month when we see the building approvals data. I mean, obviously, building approval is not the same thing as a completed dwelling, but it's a really good sign as to how many completions we're going to get. And we just don't have enough completions that are going on. Speaker 1: And that's just because of high immigration, high population growth? Is that what's leading to this mismatch? It's a factor Speaker 3: of demand running above supply, basically. And there are many components of that. Demand is driven mostly by immigration growth because the natural increase that we get from more babies being born, they usually just get put into an existing household. But I think it's more... You know, it's easy to say, oh, like, let's just blame high migration. But I think it's more of a problem that supply is just not high enough. Or, you know, we're just not calibrating demand and supply levels properly. If we really wanted to make them match better, we need to reduce demand and increase supply. And we just haven't done that. But the inflation figures, it's not just the housing story that's an issue. We can see high price growth for even things like the discretionary side. So accessories and clothing services. I mean, this is all still linked to consumer spending. Garments for women were elevated in the month of July. Speaker 1: And that seems surprising, right? That seems... When people talk about people under financial pressure, that people do seem to be still out there spending money on things that we consider to be discretionary, things that they don't necessarily need to buy. Speaker 3: What people do, not what they say. And they've been saying that they feel like things are really hard, you know, for a really long time, basically since the pandemic. And yes, of course, there are pockets where people are very much struggling. But on average, which is what we have to look at when we're looking at economic statistics, on average, consumer spending is still holding up quite well. And that's exactly why we've had these interest rate increases this year, because there's still this ongoing spending, which is fueling inflation. Food inflation was also high in July, which is not necessarily a sign of increased demand. It could just be some supply issues. And global food prices, on average, have seen some upside in the past few months. But even in other areas, parts of services, so education, medical, hospital services, not so much discretionary parts of the market, but still areas that we can see high price growth. And even in things like audiovisual computing, media and services, basically our subscription fees. So people are still spending on services as well as goods. Speaker 1: One of the big, most volatile movements of elements this year has obviously been what's happening in energy prices, particularly in fuel prices, I should say. It's been kind of messy data for the Reserve Bank to look at, because we've had government changes to the fuel excise that have moved in different directions at different points. How messy is that when you look through the data? And has that impacted the overall inflationary rate? And obviously then the question of that pass-through to some of the things that fuel is an input cost for, like food and other parts of the economy as well. Speaker 3: Yeah, I think that the biggest outright indirect impacts that we can see is probably in food, although food inflation has been high now for a number of months really, and it never really slowed significantly post pandemic. We kept on seeming to have these supply challenges through different parts, and there's an egg shortage because the bird flu disease, or there's a coffee bean shortage or a cocoa bean shortage. So sort of all these ongoing supply challenges around the world, and of course, all these wars happening in many parts of the world, which increases transport costs and also reduces the supply of these goods. But I would say that there's some indirect impact there on prices for food and also in eating out. I forgot to mention that as well, eating out inflation was still incredibly high. It is difficult for the RBA to be able to, I suppose, forecast how the conflict is going to impact their inflation numbers, because all they can really go by is the forward market pricing for oil. And that's just what they've had to use when they're doing their forecast. So it does mean that there's more errors in the headline inflation figures, but then you sort of get an offset from that by the underlying or the trim mean inflation data, which is meant to look through a lot of the big up and downs, which oil would be one of those. Speaker 1: I wanna use the line you've just given me, that look at what people do, not what they say, and bring that to the question of war in the oil market. We had news overnight about Iran and Oman potentially coming to some sort of agreement where they will start to take control of, which together collectively take control of how ships start to move through the Strait of Hormuz. We saw a 6% reduction in the price of Brent crude, the international benchmark on expectations that perhaps we might start to see a normalization of sorts of the flow of energy. As an economist who's keeping an eye on this stuff, how closely are you paying attention to these type of reports in order to change your forecasts? Or do you actually have to wait to see ships moving through that Strait before you start to think, oh, we're actually gonna see a noticeable reduction in the price of oil, for example, that is worthy of changing our forecasting for? Speaker 3: Yeah, I have to say it's an incredibly difficult period to be doing forecasts. I think the oil price actually gives you a really good guide because it's meant to take all of that stuff into account. The issue with looking at the daily data coming out of Hormuz, or even through some of the other pipeline channels that we have through Saudi Arabia, and we've seen an increase in that offsetting Hormuz, is that that doesn't really capture necessarily completely oil inventories around the world and oil supply. So we also have to try and track that through some international agencies that are much closer to this than we are in oil experts. So we look at that to look at oil inventory rather than just looking through shipping, because initially there was a lot of concern that we wouldn't be able to last, that the global economy wouldn't even last a month with the shipping closures. And it's been more than six months and the oil prices are back at $80 a barrel. So we need to look at inventories as well. The other difficulty at the moment is that according to unofficial data, the shipping from Hormuz is actually back to not completely normal, but 50, 60% of normal levels because a lot of the ships are apparently turning off their transmitters and are going through these sort of back channels or the US back route rather than the Iran and Oman route. So they're sort of getting through on the sly, but it's not coming up in the official numbers. And that's why oil prices have fallen. So it's actually really hard to know what is going on there. I know that some analysts have actually been sent there like at Cetrine to see how many ships are passing through. But I think the best we can do is look at the current oil price, which I think reflects that. And then also look at the forward oil price to see what traders are forecasting. That's the best guide that we can use for our forecasts. Speaker 1: Yeah, I don't know how I'd feel if my boss sent me over as an oil analyst to watch what's going on the Strait of Hormuz. I don't know if it's a sign that you're in favour or out of favour. Yep. The other news we were watching, we have been watching over the last few days, is what's going on between North American giants, the United States and Canada. I mean, this has been a kind of through line for Donald Trump in his first administration, but it's really heated up in his second. Taking the boot to Canada and its economy, he keeps claiming that Canada has been ripping off America for decades. He seems to think that if you've got to, if you're buying more of a country's goods and you're selling to it, that somehow you're being dotted and you're losing that money. He uses a $60 billion figure that he says America is losing to Canada. I mean, the range of tariffs that are now in place on Canada are quite extraordinary. And Canada has now returned fire or outlined how it will return fire, including going after critical parts of the economy like aluminium and steel, but also hitting some kind of politically sensitive items like fish products, which seems pretty targeted towards the main Senate election that's coming up, which will be crucial for control of the Senate, maybe do some damage to the Republican candidate there, but a range of other products, which interestingly often mirror the products that America has put a tariff on coming from Canada. It's the same going the other direction because these two economies are so interconnected that actually they're buying and selling similar items to each other. What do you make of it, first of all? How big an impact will it have to kind of the global economy? And is there a lesson for Australia, do you think, and how this is playing out for Canada? Has Australia done the right thing maybe by trying to keep a low profile? Well, Speaker 3: we have less to lose because we don't do as much trade with the US as Canada does. It's one of their main trading partners. I sort of think that this won't end up being as bad as it's reported to be because this is the ongoing story with tariffs. Speaker 1: You think it's a taco moment, a Trump always chickens out moment? Speaker 3: Yeah, but like the US threatens some rate and then it goes back to a certain point and then it's something a bit lower because of taco, because prices actually go up for consumers. But more importantly, between the US and Canada, about 80% of goods that move between the two countries are under the USMCA free trade agreement. And apparently, even if a lot of goods weren't actually incorporated into USMCA, companies have tried to register themselves to become aligned to be able to use that free trade route. So I wonder if that's actually going to become more of a thing. And so at the moment, based on these new tariffs, that's going to impact about 80% of Canadian goods exports. I mean, we're not talking, it's still a decent amount for sure, but is it going to spell a big downturn in growth for Canada? I'm not sure, and I don't think so. I think what we can safely say though is that inflation is going to stay elevated both in Canada and the US because of this. I mean, Canada has less of an inflation problem now because it's gone through a bit of a growth downturn, but you'd have to think that this is going to be inflationary for their country because they're biting back with their own tariffs. I just think at the end of the day, these tariff rates are not going to be as high as what they are initially set out to be. title: How close Australia is to hitting key target - News.com.au
raw_text: Surge in building approvals fails to close Australia’s growing housing shortage Australia has approved enough homes to outpace population growth, but experts warn the nation remains well short of its ambitious target. Australia has approved enough homes to match its growing population, but more work needs to be done to reach its ambitious National Housing Accord (NHA) target. Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows building approvals soared in the month of June, largely due a spike in apartments. Private sector dwelling excluding houses soared 17.8 per cent in June, although this followed an 11 per cent fall in May. At the same time, private sector house approvals increased by 0.4 per cent to remain above 10,000 houses approved for each of the last six months. Overall building approvals reached their highest levels since August 2021. AMP economist My Bui said building approvals had caught up with population growth. “Despite some softness in 1Q26, recent strength meant almost 205,000 dwellings were approved over the last financial year, up from 189k in 2024-25,” she said. “This is above the roughly 190k dwellings needed to house population growth.” Even though Australia is building more houses it is still well behind its NHA targets. As part of Labor’s response to rising housing costs, the government announced an NHA, a banding together of all levels of governments to build 1.2 million new homes over five years until June 2029. This equates to 240,000 new homes every year. Despite approvals lifting since mid‑2024, on a per capita basis the picture is softer. Only nine dwellings were approved per 1000 people in the 2025‑26 financial year. This is substantially lower than 12 approved per 1000 residents in early 2015 and only a marginal improvement from the eight per 1000 residents in June last year. Ms Bui said the boost in housing approvals wasn’t enough to make up for previous years’ shortcomings. “It is not a particularly large number, given Australia underbuilt relative to population growth between 2022 and 2024,” she said. “And because completions lag approvals due to project abandons and long construction times, it is unlikely we are making much progress in closing the accumulated housing shortage.” Commonwealth Bank associate economist Lucinda Jerogin said cost pressures would weigh on the sector going forward. “Looking ahead, higher interest rates remain a constraint on construction activity, while supply‑chain disruptions associated with the Middle East conflict and broader capacity constraints in the sector pose upside risks to construction costs,” she said. “Although pass-through has been limited to date, the recent escalation in hostilities increases the risk of renewed cost pressure.” Housing Industry Association chief economist Tim Reardon said there was a long lag between changes in market conditions and building approvals. “The impact of rising interest rates, global conflict and tax increases are unlikely to be observed in approvals data until late this year,” Mr Reardon said. More Coverage “While leading indicators of confidence have deteriorated since the budget, and investors are expected to withdraw from the new home building market, this won’t impact approvals for some months yet.” Mr Reardon said more needed to be done to help increase the supply of housing. “Nonetheless, with housing affordability at its worst levels in over 30 years, it is more important than ever that policymakers support housing investment and development by reducing the costs of home building, not increasing them,” he said.

title: Sydney suburbs defying downturn revealed - News.com.au
raw_text: Sydney suburbs defying price downturn revealed While most of Sydney’s property market falls, a handful of suburbs are holding strong or even recording growth. Sydney’s slim pockets of property price growth are now overwhelmingly concentrated in the city’s most affordable outer suburbs, where first-home buyers, newly arrived migrant families and a shrinking pool of investors are competing for homes. PropTrack data reveals median house values increased in just 28 suburbs across Greater Sydney over the past three months, while unit values increased in 72 suburbs, or about 20 per cent of the suburbs with available unit data. MORE: Sydney suburbs with biggest price falls revealed Unit values flatlined in about 11 per cent of the market and fell in 69 per cent of suburbs. Most growth areas were more affordable suburbs still attracting demand from households priced out of the rest of the market. Some suburbs with the greatest quarterly growth included Berkeley Vale (14 per cent), Kincumber (11 per cent) and Thornleigh (8 per cent). B.Invested director and buyer’s agent Nathan Birch said recent tax reforms had split the market, with prices falling across most areas, especially for luxury homes, while continuing to rise in a handful of cheaper suburbs. MORE: ‘Cooked’: Landlords not allowed to rent homes These lower priced suburbs were mostly on the edges of Western Sydney and were continuing to grow because they attracted stiff competition from three major groups, Mr Birch said. One was overseas migrants seeking out homes after getting permanent residency, the other was first-home buyers accessing the government’s 5 per cent deposit scheme, and the remaining demand was from the few investors still actively searching for homes, who were attracted to the higher rental yields available in cheaper areas. “The government reforms have pancaked everyone into the bottom of the market and that’s meant prices for the cheapest properties are rising,” Mr Birch said. title: Radical plan could change renting forever - News.com.au
raw_text: Sydney rent cap: Greens propose new rent control legislation to freeze soaring costs A new push is underway that could fundamentally change the rules of renting in Australia’s dearest city, and not everyone will be pleased. The NSW Greens have pledged to cap rents, with the party arguing soaring housing costs in one of the world’s most expensive cities have left many households choosing between paying the landlord and paying for essentials. The NSW Greens have launched a campaign to introduce rent controls, with Newtown MP Jenny Leong saying the party will aim to introduce the legislation to parliament later this year. The proposal comes as fresh figures show Sydney’s rental market continues to spiral, with house rents in some suburbs surging by more than 40 per cent over the past year. “We want to cap rents,” Ms Leong told news.com.au. “We know that for many households, their rent is by far the biggest chunk out of their weekly budget, yet governments have refused to do anything to regulate it.” Ms Leong said options being canvassed include limiting rent increases to inflation, restricting increases to once a year or preventing increases during fixed-term leases. The party has previously pushed to tie rent increases to the Consumer Price Index and unsuccessfully attempted to freeze rents during the housing crisis. “We’ve given notice of a rent control bill with the intention of starting a conversation,” she said. “We’re asking renters what would actually reduce the financial pressure they’re under.” The consultation is expected to run over the coming months before legislation is introduced around the September or October parliamentary sittings. The push comes against the backdrop of one of Australia’s tightest rental markets. According to Domain’s latest Rent Report, Sydney’s median asking house rent has climbed to a record $850 a week. Some suburbs have experienced even sharper increases. Abbotsford recorded the biggest annual jump for houses, with asking rents soaring 41.3 per cent to a median $1300 a week. Milperra followed with a 29.4 per cent increase, while Monterey rose 28.9 per cent. Forest Lodge, neighbouring Ms Leong’s electorate, saw house rents jump almost 22 per cent over the year. Unit renters have fared little better, with suburbs including Concord West, Enmore and Millers Point recording double-digit increases. For many tenants, Ms Leong said the financial burden was only part of the problem. “There is an underlying stress that exists for every renter in New South Wales when they know they could get an email tomorrow saying their rent is going up by $100 a week,” she said. “People are deciding they’ll just wear the increase because they don’t want to go through the stress of moving again. “They’re sacrificing things like medicine and other essentials to keep a roof over their head.” The proposal has received backing from the Tenants’ Union of NSW, which says requests for help over rent increases have exploded since the pandemic. Policy and Advocacy Manager at the union Eloise Parrab said calls about rent increases had risen from around 700 a year before Covid to about 2500 annually. “Renters are in a really tough situation facing rapid rent rises,” Ms Parrab said. “Unlike other essential services, there are few hardship protections built in. “We do need to consider how we can implement rental price regulation in NSW and Australia to prevent these harmfully fast increases.” She said more renters were falling into housing stress as escalating rents consumed larger shares of household incomes. “Too many are spending too much on rent, with little left over to cover basic necessities,” she said. The pressure is reflected in countless stories being shared by renters online. One NSW renter said their weekly rent had climbed from $500 in 2019 to $750 today. “My weekly wages have not increased $250 in six years,” they wrote. The Greens argue rent regulation is already used elsewhere. “The ACT has a form of rent control,” Ms Leong said. “There are other countries around the world that regulate rents, and we want Sydney to stop being known as one of the most expensive cities in the world to rent in.” She downplayed suggestions the proposal had been inspired by New York mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani’s housing platform, saying the Greens had been advocating rent controls in NSW for almost a decade. “We’ve been fighting for housing justice in Sydney for a very long time,” she said. “We need to create a city for everyone. “The way we do that is by getting rents under control.” More Coverage The party has previously attempted to amend NSW tenancy laws to cap rent increases and also unsuccessfully pushed for a statewide rent freeze. Those Greens attempts were voted down by both Labor and the Coalition. But with Sydney’s rental crisis showing few signs of easing, the debate over whether governments should step in to regulate rents appears set to return to the centre of NSW politics later this year.

title: ‘Thought it was mould’: Silent rental horror making kids sick - News.com.au
raw_text: ‘Thought it was mould’: Silent rental horror making kids sick Tens of thousands of Aussie families could be unknowingly living in toxic homes - and legally, nobody has to tell them before they sign the lease. Families could be unknowingly moving into Queensland rental homes contaminated with methamphetamine residue because there is no legal requirement for landlords to disclose a property’s history to prospective tenants. That’s the warning from Queensland meth decontamination specialist Steve Annells, who says he is called to about two contaminated homes every week and believes many more are slipping through the cracks. Mr Annells, who has specialised in meth decontamination since 2018, said almost every contaminated property he entered had one heartbreaking thing in common. “Ninety-eight per cent have children’s clothes or toys,” he said. “The hardest jobs are when there are kids living there. They’re the vulnerable ones.” One family contacted Mr Annells believing mould was making their son sick. Instead, testing revealed meth contamination throughout the home. “Their 10-year-old had sores over his whole body. His skin looked raw,” he said. “I asked if I could photograph it because people need to understand what this can do.” Mr Annells said meth residue could remain inside a home for up to a decade and that an ordinary bond clean would not remove it. “People think a coat of paint or a bond clean will fix it, but it won’t,” he said. “It has to be chemically neutralised and tested properly.” He said professional remediation typically took about three days and could cost between $10,000 and $30,000, depending on the level of contamination. RELATED: Meth contamination: a hidden hazard that could cost your home As awareness grows, Mr Annells said demand for his services had steadily increased, with properties across southeast Queensland and regional centres including Longreach requiring treatment. He said homes in suburbs including Yarrabilba, Hope Island, Sanctuary Cove, Marsden, Woodridge, Deception Bay and Mitchelton had required decontamination, with four Yarrabilba properties recently referred to him after tenants had already moved in. Mr Annells believes Queensland should follow New Zealand by introducing mandatory testing and a register of contaminated properties. “A watchlist would stop people unknowingly moving into these houses,” he said. “At the moment, if someone chooses to ignore the problem and rent it out anyway, the next family may never know.” Brisbane woman Connie Cicchini claims meth contamination has had a dire impact on her life since she discovered tenants had been smoking meth in her retirement nest egg investment property. Ms Cicchini believed that all she needed to do was get her Zillmere property cleaned, but the contamination kept returning.Ms Cicchini had been letting the property while living with and caring for her ailing father. After his death in February 2023, she had intended to move into the investment property, only to find the methamphetamine contamination had recurred. She could not in good conscience re-let the property and after the third cleaning attempt organised by her insurer NRMA found the contamination had recurred — after a three-year dispute that was eventually decided by the Australian Financial Complaints Authority — the insurer during the dispute resolution process eventually agreed to pay the property’s full insured value. An RTA spokesperson said while Queensland’s Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act did not specifically deal with drug contamination, property owners were responsible for ensuring rental properties were fit to live in, kept in good repair and complied with health and safety standards throughout a tenancy. “The RTA understands the serious nature of alleged drug contamination in a rental property, and the concerns it may raise for all parties about the safety of a tenant’s home and a property owner’s investment,” the spokesperson said. The RTA also confirmed it does not maintain a register or watchlist of meth-contaminated properties and said the Queensland Government was not considering changes to rental laws at this time. Real Estate Institute of Queensland chief executive Antonia Mercorella said there were no laws in Queensland specifically requiring the disclosure of crimes or events that had occurred at a property when it was sold or rented. She said landlords were nevertheless required to ensure rental properties were fit to live in, in good repair and complied with Queensland’s minimum housing standards. “Appropriate remediation works may be deemed necessary,” Ms Mercorella said. title: Sydney, Melbourne in ‘sharpest’ fall on record - News.com.au
raw_text: NAB declares Sydney, Melbourne housing downturn ‘only a third of the way through’ Bank economists warn the pain gripping Sydney and Melbourne property markets is far from over, and it’s about to get worse. Experts at a leading Australian bank have made a grim prediction on the state of the housing downturn in Sydney and Melbourne, declaring it is only a third of the way through. NAB chief economist Sally Auld told an audience at a summit on Monday the “adjustment” to values in the nation’s two biggest cities would “probably take the better part of a year”. “We think we’re about a third of the way through that, both time-wise and also prices,” she said at the event in Melbourne. “We think if you were to take an average dwelling price across the capital cities, it’ll fall about 7 per cent from peak to trough. “Some cities will do a little bit worse, so Sydney and Melbourne will see bigger declines. Other capital cities like Adelaide, Perth and Brisbane, price growth will cool, but they will be relatively better off.” The decline in property prices began to gather pace in February when the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) made its first of three rate hike calls in 2026 amid stubborn inflation. At the time, house prices and buyer activity had been “continuing to pick up”, the RBA’s monetary policy board noted, as Sydney hit a record median peak of $1.76 million. Then the war in Iran, starting at the end of February, added a new level of economic uncertainty which was credited with smashing consumer confidence. Reforms to capital gains tax and negative gearing concessions in the May budget, which were already impacting the market due to widespread media leaks, further evaporated demand from property investors. NAB this month revised its forecasts for 2026 to a position where it saw declines across all capital cities each month to the back half of the year. It has Sydney and Melbourne falling 9 per cent for the calendar year and the combined capital rate at -5 per cent, slashing growth in Brisbane 4 per cent), Perth (8 per cent) and Adelaide (2 per cent). “We expect prices to level out in early 2027 before beginning to grow modestly in H2 2027 as lower rates begin to provide support and sentiment in the market improves,” its August housing monitor report states. Fellow big four bank ANZ this month laid out an even starker future for the national market, forecasting a 10.6 per cent drop across the combined capital cities over the next 18 months. Primara Research has found that would wipe $1.3 trillion from Australia’s total wealth, with about 57 per cent of all household wealth tied up in property. The total value of all dwellings in the country was put at $12.772.6 trillion by the Australian Bureau of Statistics as of the March quarter. title: Age it’s ‘too old’ to live with parents - News.com.au
raw_text: Half of Gen Z Australians still living at home with parents, HILDA survey finds Stagnating wages and soaring housing costs have turned moving out into a luxury, with half of all young Aussies now living at home with their parents. Half of all young Aussie adults are still living at home with their parents as stagnating wages and ballooning housing costs put the brakes on plans to move out. The latest Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey found 50 per cent of Aussies aged 18 to 29 were now living with their parents, up from 39 per cent in 2001 and 47 per cent in 2012. Want more finance news? Download our new app for even more coverage The Melbourne Institute data is one of the nation’s most important social studies and has annually tracked the lives of more than 17,000 people living in 9000 households since 2001. The latest data was collected in 2024. The biggest change was for those aged 18 to 21, with the number living at home spiking from 69 per cent in 2001 to 85 per cent in 2024. For those in the 22 to 25 age bracket, the number rose from 35 to 48 per cent, while for those between 26 and 29, it went from 17 to 22 per cent. Men were more likely to live with their parents than women, with 55 per cent of younger males living at home compared to 45 per cent of women. Age it’s ‘too old’ to live with parents So how old is “too old” to still be living at home with your parents? Finder surveyed 1010 Aussies in May and found the average person thought 31 was “too old” to still be living at home. Gen Z and Baby Boomers were the least tolerant of the generations, with both age groups putting the cut-off age lower at 30. Millennials and Gen X, on the other hand, thought age 32 was still acceptable to live at home. Finder personal finance expert Sarah Megginson told news.com.au there was still a negative perception and “taboo” around living at home in Australia, despite current cost of living pressures. “There’s a bit of shame attached to it. But in other cultures, multi-generational living is very normal and very accepted, and it’s not a sign that you have failed or that things are not going well for you in the same way,” she said. “It’s got a stigma in Australia.” But Ms Megginson said there had already been a major shift around when it was acceptable to live at home, with all generations surveyed agreeing the cut off was aged 30 and over. “It’s pretty much accepted now that to be living at home in your 20s is completely normal. That is such a generational shift,” she said. “When I think about my mum, who is a Baby Boomer, by the age of 21, she was married, moved out and had three children. You could not get more opposite now.” Ms Megginson said many Baby Boomer parents and grandparents were now seeing the struggles of young Aussies first-hand within their own families. “I think they’re seeing that it’s not the same and that it’s difficult to buy a home and to hit all those same milestones that they did at a younger age,” she said. Housing stress hits high Housing costs have been rising sharply since 2021, with the HILDA report finding 36 per cent of renters and 30 per cent of mortgage holders were now spending more than 30 per cent of their disposable income on housing. HILDA report co-author Professor Roger Wilkins said researchers had seen “big jumps” in the number of people facing housing stress. “In 2024, it affected 23 per cent of private renters across the country, and that number is very similar for those in social housing,” he said. “We’ve seen much smaller shifts for owners with a mortgage, but with 9.6 per cent experiencing housing stress in 2024, it’s the highest proportion it’s been since 2017.” For young Aussie mortgage holders, the number in housing stress has remained relatively stable over the last two decades, ranging from 8.6 per cent in 2001 to 9.9 per cent in 2024 for those in the capitals. That’s despite substantial cost increases, which the report said suggested mortgage entry was now “increasingly restricted to those with higher earnings, substantial savings or access to family wealth”. The picture is “more concerning” for young Aussie renters, with 39.5 per cent spending more than 30 per cent of their income on rent, up from 25.8 per cent in 2001. About 25.3 per cent are in housing stress, up from 17.6 per cent. While employment rates have hit new highs, Prof Wilkins said wages were not keeping up with rising costs. “Our earnings are not rising enough to keep up with the big increases in housing costs and other non-discretionary spending, so the average person is likely to be under more financial pressure,” Prof Wilkins said. The report noted the findings reflected broader patterns of declining homeownership and rising intergenerational wealth inequality in Australia. “Each successive cohort of young adults who leave the parental home faces greater affordability pressures than the one before, and more young adults remain in the parental home for longer,” it said. “Yet remaining in the parental home may come with its own costs, raising the question of whether young adults who leave end up in housing that better meets their needs despite the affordability challenges they face.” Ms Megginson also doesn’t see the trend slowing down anytime soon. “Especially with rents at historical highs … renting in many areas now is just as expensive as having a mortgage,” she said. “It’s so unaffordable that we can see people are going to delay that rent step further and further.” She recommended young Aussies have a time frame and a plan in place, and have open conversations with their parents so everyone is on the same page.

title: ‘Silver lining in plunging house prices - News.com.au
raw_text: Falling house prices could spare mortgage holders from aggressive RBA rate hikes The biggest fall in household wealth in Australian history could be the unlikely shield saving mortgage holders from relentless interest rate pain. Mortgage holders are tipped to be hit by rising interest rates next week, but the sharpest fall in wealth in Australian history may spare them from further interest rate pain. This is due to the “wealth effect” – when prices go up, people feel richer and are more likely to spend. The same applies in reverse – when prices of assets such as housing falls, people feel poorer and spend less money, which takes pressure off inflation. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said the plunge in house prices was doing some of the RBA’s work for it, taking the pressure off further rate hikes. ”Falling house prices is part of the transmission mechanism. So yes, it makes the RBA’s job easier, but it’s by design – that’s the way monetary policy works,” Mr Oliver said. ”It depresses house prices, people feel poorer, and they spend less.” Markets have almost completely priced in a rate hike on September 29 while putting about a 45 per cent chance of a second rate hike in December. There is also a 17 per cent chance of a third rate hike by May 2027. REA Group figures show the housing market has now entered its fifth straight month of decline, down 0.2 per cent in August. National house prices have now dropped 2.7 per cent from peak to trough since March, although they are still up 1.8 per cent over the last year. Experts predict the falls will be more than 10 per cent. Crunching the numbers, Mr Oliver said the RBA’s own analysis showed just how big a drag falling prices could have on spending. ”Each 10 per cent fall in house prices knocks about 0.8 per cent off consumer spending after six months and over a year or more knocks about 1.6 per cent off consumer spending,” he said. ”If it is a 10 per cent fall, then you’re knocking about 1.5 per cent off consumer spending. “Consumer spending normally grows about 2 per cent, but you’ve got a drag coming from the wealth effect and it only grows 0.5 per cent.” Dwarf any other fall in history Modelling from Primara Research using ABS and ANZ data found household wealth is set to be smashed. Based on the modelling, falling property prices will strip $1.3 trillion from household wealth. Currently, national prices sit 3.6 per cent below their March 2026 peak, with ANZ forecasting a national peak-to-trough drop of 10.6 per cent in property prices, with Sydney facing the steepest decline of 14.5 per cent. The fall in value is expected to be 1.89 times bigger than the global financial crisis (GFC) and 2.14 times bigger than the falls when interest rates jumped in 2022. Although, as a share of household wealth, it would be smaller than the GFC, as household wealth has tripled from $6 trillion to $19.2 trillion since then. Primara Research head of research and data Peter Drennan said the size of the shock was unthinkable before 2008. “But property values have roughly tripled since then, so even a smaller percentage fall now adds up to a bigger dollar loss than the GFC ever did,” Mr Drennan said. Not part of our agenda In a grim update for property owners, RBA governor Michele Bullock explicitly ruled out making any interest rate decision that could help or hurt the housing market. “One point to make upfront here, we don’t target housing prices,” she said. “We do observe closely what’s going on in the housing market because it is one area that monetary policy has an impact.” While taking part of the blame for the housing market’s fastest fall in four decades, Ms Bullock said negative gearing and capital gains reforms also stopped investor activity. “You can see very directly the impact of the tax changes because you can see housing approvals for investors have just dropped,” she said. “They’ve dropped for everyone, but they’ve really dropped a long way for investors. More Coverage “It has changed the dynamic for investors whether it’s worth them investing in housing or not.” However, Ms Bullock said house prices had surged since the beginning of Covid and were now coming down from “a very high base”. “At the moment, if you look at how it’s correcting relative to other corrections, and the downturn is sort of in the lower range of downturns in the past, but it’s certainly not out of the ballpark of the sorts of downturns we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

title: Low-income Australians should accept substandard homes, Liberal frontbencher says - SBS
raw_text: in brief - Liberals are this week pushing for a reduced housing code, which could streamline construction at the cost of quality. - Opposition housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg conceded that the proposal would come with "trade-offs". The Coalition's plan to boost housing stock will involve "trade-offs", a Liberal frontbencher has said, after suggesting low-income households should accept living in substandard homes. Opposition housing and homelessness spokesperson Andrew Bragg announced on Wednesday that the Opposition would reduce the national housing code from 2,000 pages to 80 if elected. When asked by ABC Radio National on Thursday morning whether his policy means low-income earners should just accept living in substandard housing, he replied: "Yes, definitely." He went on to say that building more homes under a streamlined code would come with "trade-offs". "It's more important to have a house than to not have a house. And so, given the affordability crisis we have in the housing system, we need to just build more houses," he told the ABC. News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Bragg's comments follow remarks made by his Liberal colleague and treasury spokesman Tim Wilson, who suggested in some cases people could put "a jumper on in winter rather than spending huge amounts of money" on improving housing quality. He told ABC RN on Wednesday there should not be a one-size-fits-all policy — such as mandated energy efficiency — for construction. "There are some places in the country where you will get cold spells or hot spells for a very small amount of the year, whereas for the rest of the year, it's not necessary," he said. "We have a risk that Australians can't afford to rent or to buy their own home by the government's own budget design. We need housing stock that meets different needs in different environmental conditions. Queensland is not the same as Tasmania or Victoria. Western Australia is different again." Proposal does 'nothing to fix' housing crisis, advocate says Affordable housing advocates told SBS News that stripping back construction regulations is a way for developers to profit from "unliveable" homes. "Too many renters are already living in homes that are freezing in winter, stifling in summer, riddled with mould and damp, and expensive to heat and cool," Everybody's Home spokesperson Maiy Azize said in a statement. "Older people and people with disability already struggle to find homes they can safely and comfortably live in." Azize added that the government should focus on social housing that is "built to last". "We have a housing crisis because people cannot afford a home. Building more poor-quality homes does nothing to fix that crisis. It simply gives developers another way to profit from it," Azize said. Australian Council of Social Services CEO Dr Cassandra Goldie agreed, adding that construction of social housing should "drastically scale up". She described Bragg's comments as shocking. "The changes to the building code proposed by Senator Bragg would simply remove costs from the builder and move them onto the household - locking them into higher power bills for decades, deepening inequality, risking lives, leaving future generations with homes that are expensive to run," she told SBS News. title: When should you be able to access your super? Battle lines are being drawn - SBS
raw_text: in brief - Labor says it will defend Australia's superannuation scheme after criticism from the Coalition and One Nation. - Liberal senator Andrew Bragg said the scheme was "illiberal", while One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said it was "broken". Political battle lines are being drawn over superannuation, with Labor vowing to defend the retirement savings system as the Liberal Party and One Nation attack it as a failure. On Monday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers signalled super could become a political issue at the next federal election. "The stakes are high at the next election for a whole range of reasons, and one of them now is the future of Australia's world-leading compulsory superannuation system," Chalmers told reporters as he arrived at Parliament House. "The Liberals, the Nationals, and One Nation would end compulsory superannuation as we know it. Their policy and their ideology on super would absolutely decimate the economic security and retirement incomes of millions of Australian workers. "They share a dangerous and divisive anti-worker, anti-super ideology, and if this plays out after the next election, Australian workers will be much worse off." News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. However a senior Liberal senator later sought to dispute that was the party's ambition. The stoush began last week when Liberal senator Andrew Bragg declared superannuation an "illiberal experiment". "It’s one of the biggest public policy failures since federation, in the sense that it hasn’t helped the budget, and it has not really helped many people get off the pension," he told ABC radio on Thursday. "What it has done is it has created a huge viper's nest for banks and financiers and unions to pilfer, which is why what you saw at the Labor Party conference was now you're going to have super for under 18s." The Association of Superannuation Funds Australia (ASFA) refuted Bragg's comments, pointing out Australia's age pension expenditure had decreased since the scheme was introduced in 1992. "Super has meant that even as our population ages, the government's Age Pension bill is going down instead of up. OECD projections have Australia at the lowest public pension spending in the OECD by the mid-2030s," ASFA CEO Mary Delahunty said. "Super has also meant that reliance on the Age Pension has fallen, with 12 per cent fewer over-65s receiving a part or full Age Pension today than in 2012. This will keep falling as we see the effects of higher super guarantees coming in. "A lower reliance on the Age Pension is a massive public policy success." Under the current system, all Australian employers are required to pay a minimum 12 per cent of an employee's salary into a nominated super fund, which cannot be accessed until a person is 60. Chalmers 'making things up': Hume Deputy Opposition leader Jane Hume said the Liberals would not make any changes to compulsory super, saying the treasurer was "simply making things up". "I think the treasurer has taken a leaf out of the Mad Men Don Draper book; if you don’t like what they’re saying about you, change the conversation. Can I make it very clear: the super guarantee is here to stay," she told reporters in Canberra. Hume said the Coalition would consider adopting an early super access policy, telling News24 economic security in retirement hinged on home ownership, rather than a person's superannuation balance. The Coalition has taken a "super for housing" policy to the last two elections, which would allow first-home buyers to withdraw up to $50,000 to buy a property. On Sunday, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson waded into the debate, labelling Australia's superannuation scheme "broken" and suggesting financially struggling Australians should be able to access super early. "A lot of Australians are doing it tough now and struggling to pay off their mortgages," she told News24 on Sunday, adding the policy proposal was yet to be finalised. "In some ways, I feel that you should give them their money now, and let them help them with the cost of living." Hanson's deputy, Barnaby Joyce, backed those calls, telling Seven that the current rules only allowed early access in extremely limited circumstances, such as medical treatment. "I think one of the hardships people have is if they can't feed themselves. And another hardship is if they don't have a house and they're put out on the street and they're living in a car," he said on Monday. "Surely it's their money and we should give a little more respect about what they can do with their own money." Labor's assistant minister for housing, Julian Hill, said accessing super early to pay for housing deserves "a gold medal for the stupidest policy". title: Real estate agent’s viral posts show our property market angst - SMH.com.au
raw_text: An inner west Sydney real estate auctioneer with an influencer side-hustle, Tom Panos is someone few would have heard of. But he has become an overnight celebrity and viral sensation after his weekend property post hit the current property zeitgeist bullseye. His weekend post reflected, in equal parts, a sense of panic and desperation for property sellers and caution and disinterest from buyers. Both opportunistic sellers and bargain hunting buyers are populating the sidelines. Panos’ description of the results of last weekend’s auctions he conducted makes for sensational listening – none sold and not even one offer on any of the properties. “I didn’t have a single person register to bid. Do you understand? Not one registration. Not one person even said to themselves, ‘You know what? There’s a few bargains out there. I might go in and just see what’s actually happening’,” the auctioneer said in a video on social media platform X. Panos’ colourful reflections on the market, which he puts on social media sites including X, no doubt help to raise his public profile. However, it is also a sign of the growing property market angst that his posts have gone viral online, while also being picked up on morning television and in other traditional media. It had been the worst he had experienced in 30 years, Panos said. From his position at the coalface of Sydney real estate, Panos reckons some particularly prestige markets in Sydney have already fallen by 20 per cent, while the middle valuation markets are off 10 per cent. He reckons the only category in which prices are rising is at the lower end, where first home buyers are operating. The initial auction clearance rate across the country last week does not necessarily reflect Panos’ experience. At first blush a little more than half of the properties that went under the hammer were sold – although this figure is likely to be revised down. But it’s been 12 weeks now that clearance rates have been well below averages and the negative effect on prices is becoming clearer with each monthly pricing result. Those optimists who subscribe to a short-lived or gentle correction in pricing are looking increasingly isolated. And there is a growing chorus of property experts predicting a rush of fresh housing stock will hit the market in spring and further depress prices. Last week the Australian Property Institute declared its finding that the government’s proposed changes to negative gearing was acting as the largest weight on house prices, even greater than this year’s interest rate rises. And while one shouldn’t subscribe to the school of property price armageddon, it is fair to assume that another interest rate hike of 0.25 percentage points would seal the deal for a decline in national house prices for 2026 that could run into 2027. The good news is that interest rate markets are punting that the Reserve Bank is unlikely to increase rates next month, but the bad news is that markets predict one more rise in interest rates before the end of the year. We will have a clearer picture on how the RBA may be assessing the economic landscape after the June quarterly inflation number is delivered on Wednesday. Inflation is feeding into overall consumer caution as are the twists and turns of President Donald Trump’s Middle Eastern war and its impact on petrol prices. These are not the ingredients for robust economic growth or a vibrant retail sector. Myer’s chief executive this week warned that a sales slump in June and July (that followed a strong May) had already resulted in more promotional activity than had been planned. For the full year to July Myer was expecting sales to limp 0.3 per cent higher. ANZ-Roy Morgan’s measure of Australian consumer confidence fell 4.4 points to 71.2 points last week, which is its lowest since June. This evidence is all pointing in the same direction. And one would have to agree with Panos – that now is not the time to be selling a home. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. title: ‘The worst we have ever seen’: Mayor leads Katoomba housing plan backlash - SMH.com.au
raw_text: A fight between Katoomba residents, the council and a developer over a piece of unused land has been slowly intensifying for more than a year. The issue? Nine proposed buildings up to five storeys on a site located along the aptly named Narrow Neck Road. The state significant development application, which falls under the Housing Delivery Authority pathway, has racked up 738 submissions objecting to the plan, many frustrated Facebook posts from the Blue Mountains City Council mayor and near silence from developer, VDM Prime. Under the proposal, seven residential buildings with 218 dwellings would be built, along with one mixed-use and one restaurant building, which would also feature an education facility. The 1.6 hectare site is located within the Katoomba Golf Course Housing Precinct and would neighbour Yarrabee Katoomba, a recently completed development that features 24 three-bedroom duplex residences. Chief among the concerns from those opposed to the $92 million development include the scale of the project and the potential bushfire risk. “The site is located in a high bushfire-risk area with limited evacuation capacity via Narrow Neck Road,” a submission from Nastia Gladushchenko read. “Increasing residential density at this location creates unacceptable life-safety risk for both existing and future residents during emergency events.” Since May 2025, the council has been encouraging residents to provide feedback on the proposal, putting out three separate media releases and providing a 95-page submission objecting to the development. Blue Mountains Mayor Mark Greenhill has also voiced his opposition to the development, which he labelled in a Facebook post as “the worst we have ever seen”. Greenhill has now called on NSW Minister for Planning Paul Scully to request the independent planning commission to start a public hearing into the proposal following the backlash from the community. “I find it impossible to believe that any reasonable authority would approve this in this location. Personally, I would be shocked if it was finally approved,” he told the Herald. But VDM Prime disagrees: the development application for the project said the site is not on bushfire-prone land and would provide broader housing choice in a high amenity mixed-use environment. Little is known about private developer VDM Prime and its director, Ukranian born Yuri Rudi. An ASIC report on the company revealed that as of April, the Narrow Neck Road site has been listed as its principal place of business. The environmental impact statement for the development said that leaving the site as it currently is would result in the land remaining vacant and underutilised, and would represent a “missed opportunity”. “Adopting the ‘do nothing’ approach would prevent the site from realising its potential to deliver a mixed-use development with inclusion of affordable housing,” it said. VDM Prime was contacted for comment.

title: The tree-change town where house prices have plunged $133,000 - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Home buyers could expect a six-figure discount on a typical property in the charming regional Victorian town of Daylesford, or as much as $400,000 on some top-end homes, as the wider market weakens. Many other parts of the state are pricier than a year ago as investors and first home buyers flock to more affordable options - but those who might have looked for a weekender in Daylesford are pulling back. Buyers are now arriving from NSW, Queensland and SA as the town offers both high amenity and better value. The median house price in Daylesford has fallen by $133,000 since it peaked at $925,000 in the March quarter of 2023, Domain data shows. The typical house there now costs $792,000, a drop of almost 14 per cent from the peak three years ago. Separate figures show it had the third-weakest growth in house prices in regional Victoria over the past five years. Some high-profile Daylesford homes have had hefty price cuts. The town hosted last year’s season of reality renovation TV show The Block, in which contestants transform a house, sell it at auction and pocket any premium over the reserve. The Block airs on Nine, owner of this masthead. Two of the homes failed to sell at auction in October, when they had price guides of $3 million to $3.3 million. Hannah Thetford and Candice Wood’s house at 4 Cedar Lane now has a price guide of $2.59 million. Emma Shanahan and Ben Cox’s home at 5 Cedar Lane now has a price guide of $2.6 million. It had attracted competitive bidding at auction up to $2.97 million, when a vendor bid of $3.1 million was placed and the home passed in. McQueen Real Estate director Kim McQueen – who represented a Block home that sold under the hammer and is not involved in the remaining listings – said the town had a high volume of investor buyers and had been affected by changes to property taxes. The Victorian government increased land tax on secondary properties, and recently the federal government introduced changes to the tax treatment of negative gearing and capital gains. Buyers in the past may have used a home as a weekender and let it out as a holiday home at other times, but that had changed, McQueen said. “It is certainly tougher. Things are on the market for a lot longer than they were a few years ago, but they do sell,” she said. “It is a buyer’s market.” Prices have fallen, McQueen added, but standout homes still achieve exceptional results. Belle Property Daylesford director Will Walton noted tax changes, plus rising interest rates that reduced borrowing capacity, the cost of living and the broader economy as reasons for the downturn. He thought that that created opportunities for young families, first home buyers and pre-retirees. Walton was now seeing buyers from Melbourne – as well as NSW, Queensland and South Australia – drawn to the temperate climate, good value, welcoming community and top hospitality options. “Several buyers have said the cost of living has made relocating and selling a metro property, then purchasing a potentially larger premium home in Daylesford, an economic relief option,” he said, adding they see it as like an inner suburb without the expense. Walton has the listing for 4 Cedar Lane and said it had received a lot more steady interest since the price adjustment, in line with the rest of the market. Ray White Sunbury director Aaron Hill is handling the sale of 5 Cedar Lane and, while declining to comment on the property, spoke broadly about the area. “It is a tough market out there in Daylesford and things are taking a lot longer to sell,” Hill said. Another of the homes from The Block that did sell at auction in October is already up for sale again, also discounted. Sonny and Alicia Aplin’s house at 2 Cedar Lane sold for $3.06 million. It is now on offer for $2.9 million to $3 million through BigginScott Daylesford’s Tom Shaw and Teagan Monaghan. Monaghan said some extra assets and prizes were included in the home’s Block auction that did not form part of the current sale, so the two prices are not a like-for-like comparison. “The property’s premium price point also means it appeals to a much smaller buyer pool,” she said. Monaghan said the broader Daylesford market had stabilised compared to the rapid growth during and after lockdown years. “While quality homes continue to attract strong interest, we have seen a modest softening in pricing over the past 12 months as buyers become more value-conscious and vendors adjust to current market conditions,” she said. “Well-presented homes that are priced in line with current market conditions continue to perform strongly, while properties that are overpriced are generally taking longer to sell.”

Separate figures show it had the third-weakest growth in house prices in regional Victoria over the past five years. Some high-profile Daylesford homes have had hefty price cuts. The town hosted last year’s season of reality renovation TV show The Block, in which contestants transform a house, sell it at auction and pocket any premium over the reserve. The Block airs on Nine, owner of this masthead. Two of the homes failed to sell at auction in October, when they had price guides of $3 million to $3.3 million. Hannah Thetford and Candice Wood’s house at 4 Cedar Lane now has a price guide of $2.59 million. Emma Shanahan and Ben Cox’s home at 5 Cedar Lane now has a price guide of $2.6 million. It had attracted competitive bidding at auction up to $2.97 million, when a vendor bid of $3.1 million was placed and the home passed in. McQueen Real Estate director Kim McQueen – who represented a Block home that sold under the hammer and is not involved in the remaining listings – said the town had a high volume of investor buyers and had been affected by changes to property taxes. The Victorian government increased land tax on secondary properties, and recently the federal government introduced changes to the tax treatment of negative gearing and capital gains. Buyers in the past may have used a home as a weekender and let it out as a holiday home at other times, but that had changed, McQueen said. “It is certainly tougher. Things are on the market for a lot longer than they were a few years ago, but they do sell,” she said. “It is a buyer’s market.” Prices have fallen, McQueen added, but standout homes still achieve exceptional results. Belle Property Daylesford director Will Walton noted tax changes, plus rising interest rates that reduced borrowing capacity, the cost of living and the broader economy as reasons for the downturn. He thought that that created opportunities for young families, first home buyers and pre-retirees. Walton was now seeing buyers from Melbourne – as well as NSW, Queensland and South Australia – drawn to the temperate climate, good value, welcoming community and top hospitality options. “Several buyers have said the cost of living has made relocating and selling a metro property, then purchasing a potentially larger premium home in Daylesford, an economic relief option,” he said, adding they see it as like an inner suburb without the expense. Walton has the listing for 4 Cedar Lane and said it had received a lot more steady interest since the price adjustment, in line with the rest of the market. Ray White Sunbury director Aaron Hill is handling the sale of 5 Cedar Lane and, while declining to comment on the property, spoke broadly about the area. “It is a tough market out there in Daylesford and things are taking a lot longer to sell,” Hill said. Another of the homes from The Block that did sell at auction in October is already up for sale again, also discounted. Sonny and Alicia Aplin’s house at 2 Cedar Lane sold for $3.06 million. It is now on offer for $2.9 million to $3 million through BigginScott Daylesford’s Tom Shaw and Teagan Monaghan. Monaghan said some extra assets and prizes were included in the home’s Block auction that did not form part of the current sale, so the two prices are not a like-for-like comparison. “The property’s premium price point also means it appeals to a much smaller buyer pool,” she said. Monaghan said the broader Daylesford market had stabilised compared to the rapid growth during and after lockdown years. “While quality homes continue to attract strong interest, we have seen a modest softening in pricing over the past 12 months as buyers become more value-conscious and vendors adjust to current market conditions,” she said. “Well-presented homes that are priced in line with current market conditions continue to perform strongly, while properties that are overpriced are generally taking longer to sell.”

title: Why property investors may be buying in the wrong suburbs - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Property investors who bought units in investor-heavy suburbs made a smaller capital gain over the past 16 years than buyers who purchased in areas with more owner-occupiers. Every $100 invested in the unit market in a suburb with a high proportion of owner-occupiers in 2010 would have risen in value to $199 by this year, new research from Cotality found. But that same $100 invested in a suburb with a high proportion of investor-owners would have risen only to $165 over the same time period. The research comes as changes to the tax treatment of property investment announced in the recent federal budget prompt some investors to reconsider their plans. Cotality measured about 3000 suburbs over 16 years and grouped them into four cohorts depending on the proportion of owner-occupiers compared to investor owners in the suburb. The research found that suburbs with a higher share of owner-occupiers generally recorded stronger capital growth over the long term, and the outcome was most pronounced in the unit market. Investor-heavy areas can be more sensitive to changes in sentiment, lending conditions and supply, the researchers said, and developers target investor-heavy suburbs to deliver new apartment towers. Cotality research director Tim Lawless said the apartment sector can have more fluctuations in supply as one new apartment development could add an extra 100 dwellings or more to a suburb. “There probably is an element of a herd mentality – going with the flow and buying where other investors have already purchased,” he said. Investors buying for financial returns react more strongly to price signals than owner-occupiers, while investor purchases tend to pick up when dwelling values rise in a suburb, the report said. But owner-occupiers tend to buy for lifestyle reasons and may be more likely to renovate their home and hold for longer. Owner-occupiers also tend to buy in areas with features such as sought-after public schools or near public transport. Lawless suggested investors chasing capital growth should put themselves into the mindset of an owner-occupier, and look for factors such as liveability, amenity and public transport, which can drive stronger rates of capital growth. But he noted the ratio of owner-occupation was only one of the factors investors should consider – a correlation between owner-occupation and capital growth was not necessarily causation. “Capital gain has always been the main game for investors, especially in markets like Australian housing where yields tend to be extraordinarily low,” he said. “That is going to be changing over time, especially if negative gearing reforms are here to stay – it does imply investors will probably become more cognisant of opportunities for cashflow or the yield of the suburb.” PRD chief economist Dr Diaswati Mardiasmo said buyers may find it more competitive to purchase a unit in owner-occupied areas, bidding against families willing to pay to stay in their preferred suburb. Investors, meanwhile, tend to chase the lowest possible price to support rental returns, even if that means considering a different suburb. She said investor-heavy areas may have recorded comparatively weaker price growth because of the types of units in the area. “When it comes to suburbs with a lot of investors, there’s normally a lot of units in that area to start with, and a lot of the time the units are your standard two-bedroom, two-bathroom unit,” she said. “In owner-occupier suburbs there’s usually a lesser amount of units to start with and the units that are there are not like your tower blocks … usually gentle density units, four storeys, five storeys, where there’s only 15, 20 units in that block.” The research looked at capital gains from 2010 until this year, and did not forecast the future growth prospects for the unit market. The May federal budget’s changes to the tax treatment of capital gains and negatively geared properties may make some investor-heavy markets less attractive, including where buyers have relied on tax benefits or strong future growth assumptions, Cotality said. The report said unit suburbs with a high share of investor-owners face the most concentrated risk and are more sensitive to any pullback in investor activity. Different levels of government have also been trying to improve housing affordability by delivering more supply, including apartments close to public transport. Lawless said supply typically ran counter to the opportunity for capital gains. Any pick-up in housing supply would be “great news” for housing affordability, “but it does imply less upward pressure on housing prices”, he said. “You’d have to expect there’s going to be less capital growth in the market because there’s a better balance between those forces.”
