title: ‘Do a few big things well’: people share what they want from Andy Burnham - The Guardian
raw_text: With Andy Burnham having entered Downing Street, we asked people to tell us what they wanted from the new prime minister and government. About 400 people from around the UK responded to an online callout asking about the values and issues they care about. The words that came up most when people outlined how they wanted Burnham to govern were honesty, integrity and courage, and the biggest issues were the climate crisis, the cost of living and health and social care. Here are some of the responses. Values in government Issues and policies - Climate crisis “I would like someone who listens to the public and not to the ultra-wealthy and lobbyists. I want a robust action plan to tackle the climate crisis and to ensure Britain is prepared to deal with the effects of climate change including improving infrastructure, investing in agriculture and renewable energy. “I want someone who will stand up to the fossil fuel lobby and not crumble under the pressure, we need net zero and we need it now.” Samantha, 35, works in media, Oxfordshire Climate activists demonstrate over concerns Burnham may overturn plans not to exploit the Rosebank oil and gasfield in the North Sea. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Shutterstock “I would like to see the next PM address climate and nature harm. We also need to put in place urgent adaptation measures against extreme weather, including in schools and hospitals.” Annie, 72, Devon “Burnham needs to get to grips with the environment. Renationalise the water companies. Our rivers and seas are polluted while the private companies pay dividends and massive salaries to CEOs who destroy our environment. “Likewise, fully renationalise our other utilities and speed up the transition to a green energy economy.” Robert, 62, retired, Kent - Cost of living and inequality “We can’t have a society in 2026 that is so unequal that you’ve got people who can afford to have a financial adviser to pay whatever tax their moral compass points to, but then you have people like one elderly woman who died of severe hypothermia because she was terrified of putting on the heating and of high energy bills. Hopefully, Burnham will have that at the forefront of his mind.” Su, 65, retired, Suffolk “I would like to see genuine structural changes to make a difference to people living in poverty, especially children. I don’t want just more tinkering around the edges. I want there to be proper investment in our public services and housing.” Louise, 49, stay-at-home mother, Stockport “I would like to see Burnham work in the interests of the British people, people from all communities. His first action must be to deal with the ongoing and everlasting cost of living crisis and cost of energy crisis.” Laurie, public sector worker, West Midlands The continued cost of living crisis in the UK is almost unavoidable in any political discussion. Photograph: TM O Pictures/Alamy “Three years is not much time to make many significant changes. What people will need to measure is a reversal in their standard of living – energy and food costs would be a start. “If ordinary people do not feel it in their wallets then Burnham will be unlikely to gain a majority in the next election. Reducing inequality is the right way to go.” Douglas, 66, retired teacher, Aberdeenshire - Health and social care “The number of people I talk to on a daily basis who want an absolutely tip-top NHS, but when you mention putting up taxes to pay for it, people aren’t willing to pay for it. “I think we need to be honest with ourselves about what we expect from our public services with the resources we’ve got. A conversation could be had around what we can afford as a country, and what we are prepared to do without?” Su, 65, retired, Suffolk “I want to see deliverables. On adult social care: we’ve been talking about this for years, but have done nothing. Care workers should be regarded as professionals (and paid as such), and it should be possible to register for an NHS dentist.” John, 60, statistician, London “My partner is on Pip [personal independence payment] and I’ve had friends who have been on Pip their entire lives, but it becomes an exercise in point-scoring. It feels very impersonal, very dehumanising. “What I would want from a new government is more care, to move away from having private firms doing assessments and to take into account the context of people’s situations.” Jakob, 25, works in higher education, Leeds People who responded to the callout also wanted Burnham to focus on housing, international affairs – including closer ties to the EU – defence, work and education for young people and electoral reform. - Housing “We have measured success by the number of houses built, but I think we should measure success by the quality of lives these homes create. Local authorities are used to having skills and teams that deliver housing at scale. Many have lost that expertise in infrastructure and I think that needs to be put right.” Stuart, 63, motor industry worker, Staffordshire - International affairs “The next PM needs to be taking a firmer approach towards the USA and Israel, in the style of the Spanish PM. We have the economic and diplomatic leverage in terms of sanctions, trade and travel bans to put a spotlight on Israel’s actions in Gaza and the American administration’s decimation of international aid and domestic green energy.” Trudi, 52, charity worker, London Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has been notably outspoken about the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. Photograph: Necati Savaş/EPA “He [Burnham] is right to say Gaza is a scar on our collective conscience and I would like to see something concrete done about it.” John, 47, editor and publisher, Lancaster - Defence “Labour must not be afraid to increase income tax in order to afford their capital programmes and the necessary increase in defence spending. Also, Labour must end the scourge of offshoring unless it is necessarily a part of Nato and EU coordinated programmes.” Steven, 66, retired civil servant, Blackpool “Fund an increase in defence spending through a wealth tax rather than making cuts that will affect vulnerable groups.” Michelle, Gateshead - Closer ties to EU “Repair Britain’s economy by fixing our relationship with the EU and undoing as much of the harm of Brexit as possible.” Ruby, 25, student, London - Education and work for young people “I feel that we are producing a generation of children who do not enjoy learning. I also think that hot-housing and spoon-feeding to achieve results is not equipping young adults with the skills they need to survive in the world of work (if they can get it). “The rise of AI in the workplace is contributing to the unemployment figures and that is an issue that will only get worse. This is a problem that is going to need a lot of thought and possibly radical action.” Christine, 71, former primary school teacher, Birmingham - Electoral reform “Electoral reform including abolition of the House of Lords could be the start of doing things differently, together with tackling political donations, the lobbying industry and the ‘revolving doors’ culture of MPs and civil servants.” Jeremy, retired, Bath Other issues that were discussed included education reform, with people wanting schools to be more inclusive and less target-driven. Immigration was also something people spoke about. They wanted a fairer, more compassionate and economically pragmatic approach.

title: Tice should apologise to firefighters for ‘enjoy it’ remark on extreme heat, says Labour | Richard Tice - The Guardian
raw_text: Richard Tice should apologise to firefighters for his comments this week urging British people to “enjoy” this summer’s extreme heat, according to the Labour party chair. Bridget Phillipson has called on Reform’s deputy leader to say sorry to those who, over the last few weeks, have battled wildfires across the country that have forced evacuations and destroyed homes. Her comments underline Labour’s confidence that voters have been alienated by Reform’s increasingly strident attacks on net zero policy, even as the prime minister comes under pressure for saying relatively little on the issue. Tice told a press conference this week: “When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it. And if it means that English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic. That means we can take on the French – fantastic. “Let’s celebrate some of these things rather than just be sort of doom and gloom about it.” Phillipson told the Guardian on Wednesday: “I think he owes an apology to the firefighters who were battling in extreme conditions, putting themselves and their lives at risk in order to protect people’s homes and deal with these extraordinary fires that we’ve seen. He should apologise to them. “It’s not funny to crack jokes about sparkling wine at a point at which our brave firefighters are out there kind of battling the real-world impact of what we’re seeing from climate change.” Reform did not respond to a request to comment. Labour has sought to highlight Tice’s comments in recent days, including by releasing a video putting his words next to footage of homes destroyed in the Stourbridge wildfire. He made the remarks as part of a broader attack on net zero policies, which have also been a target of the Conservative party in recent days, despite the increasing frequency of extreme heat events. Claire Coutinho, the shadow energy secretary, gave a speech on Wednesday criticising the government’s push to achieve net zero carbon emissions by 2050. She said the UK “should focus all our attention on making electricity cheap, and then let consumer choice be king”. Andy Burnham has been criticised by climate campaigners for saying little about the climate crisis. The prime minister held a Cobra meeting last week to discuss the impact of the heatwave and drought, but failed to mention climate breakdown, focusing instead on disposable barbecues. Later, on a visit to Stourbridge, he said: “We have to face up to the changing climate … there’s no point denying where we are. We need to face up to it. We need more clean energy.” Ministers are expected to announce in the coming weeks whether they will approve two new giant oil and gas fields in the North Sea. Phillipson defended Burnham’s record on the climate crisis. “I don’t think it’s fair to say he hasn’t spoken about it,” she said. “And he’s seen it first-hand on his visit to the West Midlands – the real impact of what this means in terms of people’s lives, their communities, their homes, the devastation that’s been caused.”

title: No special carve-out for states using fossil fuel to power datacentres, Chris Bowen insists, despite new conditions - The Guardian
raw_text: Chris Bowen insists federal Labor’s new national laws on datacentre power supply will not include carve-outs for Queensland and the Northern Territory, with states that are eager to use coal and gas required to make their case to the national regulator. The energy minister told Guardian Australia on Friday the only concession agreed at Wednesday’s meeting of national cabinet was that existing coal and gas supply could be used on the condition it could be shown to be cheaper than renewables. Anthony Albanese had gone into the meeting clear that new national rules, expected to be debated in federal parliament next year, would mandate the use of renewable energy, and ensure datacentres did not push up prices for homes and businesses. The prime minister said new developments would be required to make a positive contribution to the country’s energy transition. After the meeting, NT’s chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, and the Queensland premier, David Crisafulli, both claimed wins. Finocchiaro said gas from the massive Beetaloo basin project would now be available for datacentre power, while Crisafulli said his government could control the energy mix due to state-owned systems. But on Friday, Bowen said there would be no carve-out for any state or territory. “The Commonwealth, as we always said we would, will be legislating nationally consistent commonwealth legislated datacentre standards, which will require in every state and territory 100% renewables, backed by firming,” Bowen said. “That was the case, is the case, will continue to be the case. “The only change or concession made is that where a state-owned government instrumentality feels they can provide the energy cheaper than renewables. They can apply for exemption, but the Commonwealth will decide whether to grant that or not.” The Australian Energy Regulator will be required to consider every application, with state or territory governments obliged to prove a non-renewables option is cheaper. Bowen called that “a very hard thing to do”. “Any suggestions of a wholesale carve-out for Queensland and Northern Territory is not accurate,” he said. After the talks in Sydney, Albanese described the decisions taken as allowing flexibility for governments with state-owned power systems. A communique signed by the leaders indicated further consultation, with the federal government continuing work on “consistent mandatory standards” for energy, water and land use. The meeting followed the latest forecast from the Australian Energy Market Operator showing datacentre power use is projected to increase seven-fold over the next decade. Bowen told the National Press Club earlier this month that the federal government would override state governments that oppose new national rules on datacentres, using powers in Australia’s constitution. Separately on Friday, Bowen released the latest quarterly data on Australia’s carbon emissions, showing a 1.6% fall in the year to March 2026, led by solar, wind and batteries that have replaced coal and gas generation. The fall reflects a 5.6m tonne cut in electricity emissions, as well as a 300% increase in battery power discharge. Bowen said there was more work to do in transport and still “a long way to go” in the overall transition. So far, emissions are down 25% on the June 2005 baseline, as Labor works to achieve a 43% reduction by 2030. The government’s longer-term emissions reduction target is a 62%-to-70% cut by 2035.

title: Health, wealth and housing: here’s what forecasters think Australia will look like in 2066 - The Guardian
raw_text: - 1. How wealthy will we be? The intergenerational report says household wealth will continue to rise into the 2060s, but younger people will experience “smaller gains” compared with previous generations. Wages and living standards are expected to grow “sustainably”, driven by productivity growth. But several economists have said the government’s long-term productivity forecast of 1.2% growth is a stretch, and lower productivity will affect overall wealth. Households will have more super and rely less on the aged pension in retirement. The report’s medium-term expectation, ie within the next 10 or so years, shows the median superannuation balance will increase for 65 to 69-year-olds from $204,000 in 2024 to $450,000, not adjusted for inflation. The government projects superannuation drawdowns to rise to almost 6% of GDP by 2066, while spending on the aged pension will fall from 2.3% to 1.8% of GDP. But an ageing population and a reliance on income tax will put more pressure on working-age Australians. The current inability of younger generations to crack into the housing market will have longer term impacts, which the government says it hopes to turn around through its tax changes. - 2. Will there still be a housing crisis? Home ownership is a key theme of the report and, while it does not predict the 2060s home ownership rate, it provides sober insight into today’s housing crisis. Had home ownership rates remained at 1981 levels, an additional 250,000 people aged 25 to 34 would now own their own home, with or without a mortgage, according to the report. Declining housing affordability has deepened intergenerational inequality, it notes, with tax concessions – such as negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount – contributing to the problem. Treasury estimates 80% to 90% of investor housing lending had gone towards buying existing housing stock rather than new dwellings since 2019. - 3. There will be more people dying than being born For the first time, deaths are projected to outnumber births by the 2060s, with the number of people aged over 85 tripling, and life expectancy increasing due to better healthcare and lifestyles. Life expectancies will increase to 89.5 years for women and 86.1 for men. The birthrate is expected to decline considerably from 1.44 babies per female to 1.34 by 2066. The report estimates the population to be 39.3 million, 1.8 million people fewer than projected in the 2023 report. The report expects more women and older people to be working but the ageing population will reduce the overall share of people in the workforce and the number of taxpayers, putting pressure on future budgets. Despite this, Australia is well placed, the report says: “The working-age population is projected to continue growing, supported by ongoing migration, while many Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries are projected to experience declines”. The changes will also require a drastic increase in health spending, with health expenditure expected to rise from 4% of GDP in 2026 to 6.2% in 2066. One-third of the projected increase is linked to ageing. - 4. AI will create productivity gains The economic and social implications of artificial intelligence are “profound” and will have a greater impact than any other technological boom, the report says. However, its ultimate impact depend on how it develops and how broadly it is adopted. There are also concerns AI will fuel misinformation and cybersecurity risks. “The challenge for Australia is to harness and share these benefits widely whilst mitigating its potential to generate societal harms such as misinformation, scams and malicious cyber operations,” the report says. There’s no evidence yet of AI taking future jobs, but that it will increase productivity by making some tasks automated. Australia will be in a good position to “capture value” from AI, due to Australia’s location, land, and energy and water resources. - 5. Effects of climate crisis ‘uncertain’ Australia is well placed to meet the global energy transition, with vast renewables resources, but the broader effects of climate change 40 years from now are “highly uncertain”. Australia’s uptake of rooftop solar and batteries is the highest rate in the world and expected to increase, with the cost of solar photovoltaic (PV) modules and battery energy storage systems falling by 80% since 2015. But the report says global heating will have the greatest impact on major cities with lower elevation, while hotter temperatures could reduce productivity of workers, affect agricultural crop yields and damage tourism. It warns the increasing severity and changing frequency of climate-related events “will require stronger risk management approaches” from the government. By 2066, Treasury modelling shows heat stress could reduce crop yields by 3.6% under a 3C+ scenario, or 1.2% under the Paris-aligned scenario.

title: The climate fight has one great ally. You just can’t look at it directly | Bill McKibben - The Guardian
raw_text: As climate experts from around the world gather in New York for their annual week of talking through the world’s deepest dilemma, the vibes are mostly bad. Though 2026 seems likely to set a new global temperature record (and 2027, as El Niño gathers steam, is almost certain to break it), and though the planet has careened from one climate disaster to another (European heatwaves that killed tens of thousands, a Nepali flood that wiped out entire communities), and though scientists warn that we’re reaching precisely the global tipping points they’ve long feared (the new research on the faltering great currents of the Atlantic should send a literal chill up your spine), there’s a distinct lack of political momentum. The host superpower is attacking country after country in search of oily “energy dominance”; even the noblest of its opponents (Canada’s Mark Carney, hope of democratic rebirth in the Americas) is busy building new oil and gas pipelines in the hopes it can bolster his besieged economy. Britain, which finally purged coal power from its energy system last year, now seems poised to start new drilling in the North Sea. If there’s an apocalyptic fear that can still rouse politicians to action, it seems to be AI agents breaking through firewalls, not European nations facing firestorms. But there is one solitary (and very literal) ray of sunshine amidst this gloom: the steady rise of solar, wind and batteries. That clean energy trinity has broken out of its Chinese base and over the last few years expanded quickly across the planet – from Karachi to California to Cuba, solar panels are going up faster than any energy source has ever grown. It’s even begun to demonstrate that it can drive emissions down: China seems to have started on its downward slope years before most thought it could, and California has cut the use of gas to produce electricity in half in the world’s fourth-largest economy. None of it is happening fast enough to catch up with the physics of global warming, though – which is precisely why civil society will now try to double down on this one bright spot, and push for a rapid acceleration of clean energy; this transition is going fast, but it needs to go much faster. And it can – China and India are using barely half their solar panel factory capacity, and too many countries are hedging their bets, using clean energy as additional power instead of replacing fossil fuels. That’s why a group of leading advocates will deliver a letter to the UN this week, urging faster action. The letter offers a clear goal for the entire world to rally around: clean energy access for everyone, everywhere by 2030. And a way to get there: raising funds to bring clean energy to the poorest corners of the world and organizing in our communities, including for a global Sun Day of action next year to kick off what could be the great uniting project of our time. The signatories range from the most popular active politician in the US (that would be Bernie Sanders) to the most morally grounded spokesperson of the global south (Yeb Saño of the Philippines, say, whose witness after devastating hurricanes helped produce the Paris accords). It comes from great diplomats such as Laurence Tubiana (who helped midwife those Paris agreements) and celebrities and activists such as Jane Fonda. There are leaders from the world of clean energy (Danny Kennedy, for instance, the secretary of the Global Solar Council), and stalwarts from the continents most damaged by rising temperatures (South Africa’s Kumi Naidoo, president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative). Clean energy entrepreneurs, such as Muhammad Mustafa Amjad of Renewables First in Pakistan, but also the world’s most famous rock climber, Alex Honnold, who runs his own solar non-profit. As they write: The path forward is difficult, but the way is clear. We want solar for everyone, everywhere, before the decade is out. We know that standing up to the powerful can be scary. But if there is one thing that unites us, it is that we live beneath the same sun. That unity is our strength, and we must use it to act now. The letter will be accompanied by the unveiling of a giant mural near the celebrated High Line in New York City. The message is simple, but its three words convey the solution to so many of the interlocking crises we now face: clean energy now. By the time advocates gather for next year’s New York Climate Week, the landscape may be very different. The physical landscape (there is, I fear, no doubt that El Niño will change the literal map of the world), and the political landscape. If a resurgent movement demands action, we finally have the tools to make that demand matter – a working planet that runs mostly on sun and wind is in tantalizing reach. At the last possible moment, with backs to the wall, we still have our face to the sun. - Bill McKibben is the Schumann distinguished scholar at Middlebury College. He is the founder of Third Act, organizing people over 60 for progressive change

title: Trump’s love of fossil fuels is about more than money | Moira Donegan - The Guardian
raw_text: You can impress a certain kind of person at a party by reciting the fact that there are more yoga instructors in the US than there are coalminers. In fact, the disparity is greater than this catchy phrasing suggests: there are actually more yoga instructors in the US than there are people employed in the entirety of the coalmining industry, miners and otherwise. It’s not even especially close: about 38,000 people in the US work in coal, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, compared to about 100,000 yoga instructors who are registered with the Yoga Alliance, an industry group. If you looked only at the numbers, you might think a politician would be incentivized to talk about the interests of the yoga industry, about the dignity that yoga jobs give to American families, or about the need to foster growth in the yoga industry, more than they talk about these things for coal; after all, yoga, not coal, is putting food on the table in more American households. But no politician would ever talk about the interests of yoga teachers, or wax poetic about their role in the American dream, the way they do with coal miners; if they did, they’d be laughed out of the room. And we all know why: yoga is thought of as decadent, cosmopolitan and feminine, while coal mining is imagined as hardscrabble, honorable and masculine. This was at the forefront of my mind this past weekend when the EPA announced that it would lift limits on carbon emissions from coal- and gas-burning power plants, a reversal of Biden and Obama era climate policies. It’s just the latest in a long line of energy industry deregulation efforts by the Trump administration, which has also loosened or removed limits on carbon emissions from vehicles and household appliances; in 2022, the Republican-dominated supreme court ruled, in a six to three decision along party lines, that the EPA lacks the independent authority to regulate carbon at all. Some of the motivations for the Trump administration’s pro-carbon, anti-green policy postures have to do with cold, hard cash. Fossil fuel companies have given a staggering amount to Trump over the past several years, with energy companies donating at least $75m to his campaign, in addition to large personal donations from executives. They’ve kept the money flowing since. Oil and gas companies donated nearly $12m to Trump’s 2025 inauguration fund, and have continued making large contributions to Trump affiliated Pacs. At least $25m has come just from one oil firm, Energy Transfer Partners, and its CEO. The industry and its major power brokers may see these contributions as a way to purchase a favorable regulatory environment; when he solicited contributions from the energy industry during his 2024 campaign, Trump characterized their donations as part of a “deal”. But part of Trump’s love of fossil fuels – and his accompanying hostility to climate change mitigation, green initiatives, and nature conservation – might be less transactional than libidinal. Because to him, part of the appeal of climate-destroying, future-inhibiting, polluting energy industries is not merely that their executives are writing him checks. It’s that he sees these industries, and these forms of energy consumption, as more manly. This is the theory put forth by the Virginia Tech professor Cara Daggett, whose 2018 paper “Petro-Masculinity: Fossil Fuels and Authoritarian Desire” has become something of a cipher for political observers, eager to understand the Trump administration’s commitment to dirty energy even at the cost of the country’s competitive advantage (China, for instance, has surpassed the US in solar panel production at an alarming rate). For Daggett, much of the American right’s energy policy posture is not explainable by recourse to strictly material measures: it requires a psychological explanation. To them, she argues, oil, gas and the lifestyle markers and forms of consumption that they enable – think cowboy hats, broad asphalt highways, and big trucks parked before a field of swinging pumpjacks – represent an ideal of American manliness and dominance whose symbolic power has become a meaningful obstacle to a US energy transition. In other words, the Trump administration isn’t just committed to doubling down on America’s reliance on oil and gas because those are the industries that enrich their donors and friends. They’re also committed to fossil fuels because they see them as manly, and understand green energy, by contrast, as effeminate. If this sounds too stupid to be plausible, remember that this is Donald Trump we’re talking about. His policy decisions are not the result of a complex weighing of benefits and liabilities, or a sober assessment of competing interests: they are decisions based on gut feelings and often motivated by obscure resentments. Trying to articulate ideological coherence in the man is a bit of a fool’s errand: he has no discrete ideological worldview and seems to operate largely on impulse and id. But if Trump has no ideology, he most certainly has a psyche. If there is a single throughline in Trump’s actions and priorities, it is his reverence for the most brutish and regressive form of masculinity: his admiration for those who dominate and humiliate their rivals, his desire to punish those he sees as weak, his contempt for responsibility, his ostentatious recklessness towards the wellbeing of others or the prospects for the future. It might sound childish, but that’s by design; Trump, after all, is the man who sat in the cab of a semitruck on the White House lawn, blowing the horn like a sugared-up kindergartener. Responsibility is for grown-ups, which, in his mind, means it is for wimps. - Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

title: Solar panels going to landfill while Labor’s $25m recycling scheme on hold - The Guardian
raw_text: Recycling operators have expressed growing alarm about delays to a solar panel recycling scheme promised by the Albanese government with fears some could go bust while they wait. The $25m pilot scheme was announced in January to help develop a local industry for the recycling of panels and the recovery of valuable materials such as copper and aluminium. A process to appoint an entity to run the pilot was suspended in May after an undisclosed complaint, first reported by Renew Economy. The scheme had been due to commence mid-year. Four months on, eight solar recycling companies have written to several ministers to urge the government to lift the suspension. Their concerns follow the government’s recent decision to shelve plans for mandatory national packaging standards. The companies said the prolonged delay threatened the financial viability of operators in the emerging solar recycling industry and hindered Australia’s ability to recover “high-purity critical materials”. They wrote “every month of delay exacerbates the volume of solar waste entering landfills, damaging public trust in renewable energy infrastructure”. James Petesic, one of the letter’s signatories, is the co-founder of solar panel recycler PV Industries, which has facilities in Sydney and Melbourne. He said there had been little communication or clarity about the pilot’s future since the federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water suspended the procurement process in May. “The more time goes on, the more panels are coming off roofs,” he said. “And … the more we risk losing recycling capacity because more businesses will go into administration.” Petesic said the ongoing delay was affecting investor certainty in the industry. The letter urges the government to use a public interest provision in procurement laws to lift the suspension, so that the pilot can still progress while the complaint is investigated. Petesic said one of the biggest issues for the nascent industry was supply of solar panels. About one in three Australians have rooftop solar but most rooftop panels are not recycled at the end of their life. Recyclers have struggled to secure enough panels, with many ending up in landfill or waste stockpiles. Victoria is the only state with an outright ban on solar panels going to rubbish dumps, though some landfill sites in other jurisdictions also refuse to accept them. Petesic said as households installed home batteries, many were choosing to upgrade their solar panels at the same time, increasing the volume of panels that were becoming waste. He said the goals of the pilot scheme were to support transport of panels to recyclers, guarantee supply of panels for recycling and help the solar recycling industry to grow. The pilot was also intended to inform development of a mandatory national solar panel recycling scheme. The chief executive of the Australian Council of Recycling, Suzanne Toumbourou, said the delay would have “knock-on effects” for people who had invested in solar recycling. “There has been absolutely no clarity about the nature of the complaint that has held this process up indefinitely, which means the sector has no concept of what the way forward looks like,” she said. “Investment confidence has already been shaken by the delay itself but the indefinite nature of it amplifies that.” A department spokesperson said the government “remains committed to the policy objectives of the national solar panel recycling pilot”. They said the appointment process remained suspended in accordance with the government’s procurement rules. Gayle Sloan, the CEO of the Waste Management and Resource Recovery Association, said instead of the pilot scheme the government should introduce national regulations that made producers of solar panels responsible for what happened to them – whether that was repair, reuse or recycling. “We don’t need more trials. We need regulation that places the responsibility squarely on producers,” she said.

title: Coal mine extensions and data centres hindering NSW net zero targets - abc.net.au
raw_text: In short: The Net Zero Commission has released its annual report, which concluded NSW is unlikely to meet legislated 2030 and 2035 emission reduction targets. It has pointed to coal mining expansions currently before the state's planning authorities, and the possibility of new data centres being built, as snags to reducing carbon and methane. What's next? The NSW Energy and Climate Change Minister says the government will seriously consider the recommendations made by the commission. Coal mine expansions and a surge in new data centres risk pushing New South Wales further from its emissions reduction targets, which the state's independent climate watchdog says it is already on course to miss. The NSW Net Zero Commission (NZC) annual progress report found the state is falling increasingly further behind on reducing emissions. According to government projections, NSW will fall between 10 and 20 million tonnes short of its 2030 emissions target, up from an estimated 7 million tonnes the year prior. It comes as 20 applications to extend coal mines sit in the planning system, including the proposal to extend Hunter Valley Operations currently before the Independent Planning Commission (IPC). Meanwhile, the NZC cited Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) forecasts that data centres will add eight terawatt hours to annual NSW electricity demand by 2035, equal to 13 per cent of current demand. The commission called for these projects to "be cumulatively assessed against the legislated targets and required to implement mitigation measures". It found the "pace of decarbonisation must urgently increase" if the state is to meet its targets. "Accelerating the transition of the electricity sector is critical, both to replace coal-fired power generation and to enable the wider electrification of transport, buildings and industry," NZC chair Nick Rowley wrote. "Many low-emissions technologies are available today and their uptake must be accelerated across the economy." Data centre oversight The NZC report zeroed in on the data centre pipeline as a growing consumer of electricity and potential source of emissions. "Data centres are a new and fast-growing source of electricity demand that could have ramifications for the electricity sector's transition," the Commission said. NSW Greens climate change spokesperson Sue Higginson said data centres were being rolled out without appropriate legislation. "These data centres are energy and water insatiable beasts," she said. "They are not going to assist us in meeting our emissions reduction targets." The NZC said policy setting could be introduced so that data centres can operate in a way that aligns with the state's emissions goals This included four principles to guide planning approvals. 1. Data centres should fund new renewable energy generation commensurate with their demand, ensuring genuine additionality. 2. Data centres should actively contribute to grid reliability by limiting energy consumption during peak periods and offering demand response capacity during system stress events. 3. Data centres should meet world-leading standards for energy and water efficiency, with ongoing public reporting to ensure compliance. 4. The most suitable location for data centres should be determined, with regional locations actively considered where workloads are not genuinely latency-sensitive. Coal projects 'inconsistent' with targets In the state's Hunter region, the IPC is examining whether to permit a major extension of the Hunter Valley Operations to extend the life of its coal project to 2045. The report noted it was one of 20 expansions or extensions currently in the planning system. The commission referred to its Coal Mining Emissions Spotlight Report, which found continued extensions and expansions to coal mining in NSW are inconsistent with the state's targets. "Continued approval of coal mining extensions and expansions is a barrier to resources sector decarbonisation and achievement of legislated targets," the commission stated. "All emissions associated with these projects make achieving the emissions reduction targets harder." Renewable rollout lagging Despite broad policy support for renewables, the commission found the renewable rollout was running "behind schedule". NSW is aiming to add 12 gigawatts of renewable generation by 2030. The report stated to reach that target, the state would need to nearly double the amount of renewable generation commissioned each year. The NZC made several other recommendations to help the state reach its targets. The report identified reducing methane, largely in the agriculture, coal and waste sectors, will have a significant impact as the gas has contributed to 30 per cent of the state's emissions. Minister for Climate Change and Energy Penny Sharpe said the government recognised it had more work to do. "That is why we are accelerating the amount of renewable energy in the grid, decarbonising our transport and manufacturing sectors, and developing a new climate strategy this year to drive further action," she said in a statement. "We welcome the Commission's independent advice and will carefully consider its findings and recommendations."

title: PM's data centre plan may hit roadblock as energy debate heats up - abc.net.au
raw_text: New AI data centres in Australia will be required to deliver "at least as much energy" into the grid as they take out under mandatory rules under the government's blueprint for AI regulation. And as the race to attract the power-hungry warehouses accelerates, political debate about how to generate the energy to feed them is intensifying. There are about 160 operational data centres across the nation, but that number is expected to balloon to accommodate the rise of AI. During a major speech on AI earlier this month, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the government wanted the next generation of data centres to build "new renewable generation and firming" to strengthen the nation's energy resilience. The government is pursuing batteries, pumped hydro, and gas as firming energy technology, which is used to stabilise the grid when renewables such as solar and wind are unavailable. But the Coalition says a moratorium on nuclear power is deterring investment in Australia. Under the government's proposed mandatory standards, new data centres will be required to underwrite new power supply, minimise water use, and maximise energy efficiency. It is understood the government will use a yet-to-be-determined energy threshold to decide which future data centres are captured by the mandatory standards. The plan has already hit a snag, with Queensland and the Northern Territory signalling yesterday they will not back national standards requiring facilities pursue renewable power. 'Not all data centres are created equal' Data centres that support AI technology typically have greater energy and space requirements than traditional data centres used to store and process information, and according to recent analysis from McKinsey and Company, will account for 70 per cent of data centre demand from 2025–2030. The prospect of large-scale facilities cropping up in Australia's cities and regional areas has sparked community concern, especially around higher power prices and potentially harmful impacts on the environment. But the government says an influx of data centre applications means Australia can be selective. Assistant Minister for Technology Andrew Charlton said the government was receiving more applications than Australia could build, creating an opportunity to prioritise projects. "Not all data centres are created equal," Mr Charlton told the ABC. "Better data centres are the ones that bring their own clean energy, that use water responsibly, that contribute positively to their community. "Worse data centres are the ones that plug into our grid, drink our water and push up bills." The proposed rules for large data centres will build on a set of non-binding "expectations" released by the government earlier this year. The expectations state that facilities should "not place upward pressure on energy prices", make a "positive contribution" to the nation's energy transition, and work in coordination with energy regulators and suppliers. The CEO of Data Centres Australia, Belinda Dennett, said operational data centres in Australia were already offsetting 70 per cent of their energy use with renewable energy projects, but there was still a reliance on diesel for back-up power. "Data centre operators and their customers currently underwrite new, renewable energy generation and firming, and pay their way on energy and water infrastructure," Ms Dennett said. "Diesel generators are installed as back-up power generation because critical infrastructure requires 24/7 availability." In a recent submission to a NSW parliamentary inquiry into data centres, the National Health and Medical Research Council's Centre for Safe Air stated diesel emissions included several harmful pollutants that could have negative health impacts, and that back-up diesel generators were "one of Australia's most significant unregulated sources of harmful air pollution." According to Data Centres Australia, diesel generators are used for a limited number of hours per year for "periodic maintenance testing", and actual emergency use is rare and brief. The organisation describes emissions from data centre generators as negligible. Qld, NT oppose plan for national rules Energy ministers met virtually on Tuesday to discuss data centre energy use as part of the Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council. QLD and the NT both knocked back several elements of the government's framework for AI, including the plan to legislate national standards for large-scale data centres to ensure facilities underwrite new renewable power supply. "Queensland will always support proposals that deliver affordable, reliable and sustainable power, however, we will not support underdeveloped ideas that hand increased power to Canberra at the expense of Queenslanders," Queensland Energy Minister David Janetzki said. NT Energy Minister Gerard Maley said the Territory was committed to "ensuring that costs associated with data centre electricity demand are not transferred to consumers". "While we will continue to engage in national discussions, any reforms must recognise the Territory's unique electricity system and investment environment, rather than impose a one-size-fits-all approach." The council, not requiring unanimity from all ministers, agreed to progress action to ensure what was described as "a significant pipeline of data centre developments" are beneficial to the nation's energy grids, and prevent additional costs on households. The opposition from the Qld and NT sets the stage for a potentially fiery meeting of National Cabinet in August, where the prime minister will seek agreement on the national standards from state and territory leaders. Coalition MPs push for nuclear-powered data centres Shadow Energy and Emissions Reduction Minister Dan Tehan has argued the government's proposed standards for data centres are too restrictive. "The problem is that the government has said that pretty much it's wind and solar as the only two forms of renewable energy that data centres can use," Mr Tehan told the ABC. Ahead of releasing the Coalition's revitalised energy policy, Mr Tehan has said that all options should be on the table to power future data centres, including nuclear energy. "When [companies] look to invest in Australia, they are deterred by our moratorium preventing them from powering their centres through nuclear," Mr Tehan said in a statement. Mr Tehan said that US companies such as Google and Amazon were investing in "their own zero emissions nuclear power to power data centres". According to the International Energy Agency [IEA], nuclear energy plays a supporting part in powering the world's biggest data centre markets: the United States and China. The autonomous intergovernmental organisation expects nuclear power's role to grow from 2030, when it is expected that more small modular reactors [SMRs] come online. Google, for example, signed a landmark deal in 2024 with Kairos Power to buy energy from several SMRs to help support the tech giant's AI infrastructure. The first of the reactors is expected to come online by 2030. Nationals Deputy Leader Darren Chester, whose electorate of Gippsland in Victoria is experiencing significant data centre investment, said he believed that it was "inevitable" that Australian-based facilities would be powered by nuclear energy to some degree in the future. Mr Chester said "large-scale" nuclear reactors were "proven technology", but he would be open to other options in the years to come, such as SMRs. "Removing the moratorium on nuclear [energy] is a sensible thing to do," Mr Chester said. Shadow Infrastructure and Sovereign Capability Minister, Andrew Hastie, said it was not feasible for AI data centres to be powered solely off renewables. "There needs to be a mix of base load power, and nuclear should be part of that mix," Mr Hastie said in a statement. The Coalition's nuclear energy aspirations for Australia suffered a significant blow in its election drubbing in 2025. An internal review found the opposition's election campaign was perceived as "incoherent," and acknowledged the Coalition's plan for nuclear was among policies widely criticised as "politically mistimed or alienating". At the core of the policy was a plan to build seven nuclear power sites, but the party did not specify whether large-scale reactors, small modular reactors [SMRs], or a combination of both, would be used. National science agency CSIRO and the Australian Energy Market Operator [AEMO]'s latest GenCost report showed introducing nuclear power to Australia would attract significant up-front costs. "New large-scale nuclear costs are significantly lower than nuclear SMR, but both represent moderate-to high-cost sources of electricity generation," the report stated. Nuclear power generation has been banned in Australia under federal laws since the late 1990s. States and territories also have legislation prohibiting nuclear energy production, with some jurisdictions also restricting certain nuclear-energy-related activities, such as uranium mining. Labor is emphatically opposed to lifting the moratorium on nuclear energy in Australia. Energy Minister Chris Bowen recently told Sky: "Nuclear is not an answer for Australia any time." Instead, the government is focusing on transitioning to renewable energy, specifically solar and wind energy backed up by hydro storage and gas, with a goal of having 82 per cent of electricity generated by renewables by 2030. Experts weigh in on how to power Australia's data centres Tony Irwin, a nuclear energy advocate and ANU honorary associate professor who spent three years building nuclear reactors in the UK, believes nuclear energy should be used to help power data centres. "Solar and wind obviously can play a part in it. But nuclear should also be playing a part because, as I say, it's reliable, it's low emissions," he said. Mr Irwin believes large-scale reactors could be used, but SMRs and what are known as "micro-reactors" could be less costly. Operational SMRs are only found in Russia and China, according to Energy Strategy Reviews. Micro-reactors are still in development. The prime minister said in his speech that both Australia's land and sunshine were among reasons the world was "queuing up to invest" in the nation. "Think about what we have … the space to build. The sunlight to power affordable, renewable, reliable energy," he said. "Truly, there is nowhere else you'd rather be than Australia." Tony Wood, a senior fellow at Grattan Institute's Energy and Climate Change Program, welcomed the government's new rules but questioned how data centre operators would be forced to supply their own renewable energy. "We are going to get on top of this. That's what this is about, and I fully support that," he said. "I've not seen anything that really expands on how such a requirement would be implemented." Mr Wood said the opposition's push for nuclear power for data centres was a "political sideshow". "The only reason, and it's a possibility, that nuclear may come back on the agenda for Australia is if what we're doing now turns out to be far too expensive and far too difficult, that is backing up wind and solar with gas, for example," Mr Wood said. He described the government's plan for Australia's energy transition as "plan A". "I think we've got a very strong plan A and we should stick with it in Australia," he said. "And just because someone else does it [nuclear energy] doesn't mean we should fire." But Edward Obbard, an associate professor in nuclear engineering at UNSW Sydney, said he found it "strange" that power sources were aligned with different political parties and values in Australia. "I think nuclear technology needs to be assessed like-for-like with other technologies and applied where it's useful," Dr Obbard said. "But no-one's really doing that assessment properly now because you just look at Australia and say, 'Oh yeah, it's illegal, never mind', and just sort of move on. "We're not actually considering how all these technologies could be applied and how they could work together." Greens urge pause as AI race accelerates Beyond the obvious, at least initial, financial benefits, the Labor government also sees attracting AI data centres as a key to building sovereign capability. "Not just adopting or accommodating AI. Designing it, making it, building the capability right here … building our sovereignty — and our economic resilience as a result," Mr Albanese said. As the prime minister urged haste on AI, the Greens have called for a moratorium on data centre approvals until mandatory standards are implemented, saying the government must take its time to get the right policy settings in place. "With more than 90 data centres already in the pipeline, we cannot allow a free-for-all in the meantime," Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said in a statement. The federal government says it will legislate the new mandatory regulations early next year.

title: Victoria is about to host Australia's first offshore wind auction. But what is it? - abc.net.au
raw_text: In long-awaited news for the offshore wind industry, the Victorian government has officially opened its offshore wind auction. Energy Minister Jaclyn Symes opened the Request for Proposal process for the state's first two gigawatts (GW) of offshore wind. This will provide enough energy to power about 1.5 million homes each year. "This auction is a giant leap towards getting Australia's first offshore wind projects built, attracting billions in investment, creating thousands of jobs and delivering the reliable power we need as coal retires," Ms Symes said. But what does this actually mean and why is this important? The auction explained Auctions might bring to mind dozens of property buyers jostling to secure a piece of property on a Saturday morning. In a similar vein, offshore wind proponents will now bid for government support to help deliver their projects. The government will assess each bidder based on their ability to deliver on power, and also on value for money. Successful bidders through the auction will win contracts through what is called the Energy Services Entry Mechanism (ESEM). The ESEM is a recommendation by the federal Energy Department to encourage new investment in the energy sector. To secure investment, renewables projects need to show they are going to make money over the course of their life span, which can be decades. But energy buyers aren't willing to sign deals that far into the future. The ESEM bridges the gap by providing long-term contracts to reassure the investors that there will be a buyer for the power it produces in the later years of its life span. But the ESEM isn't in place yet and while nearly all Australian energy ministers agreed last year in principle to introduce it, Queensland remains opposed. Why build offshore turbines in Gippsland? Gippsland was declared Australia's first offshore wind zone by the Commonwealth government in 2022. The area was chosen for its strong winds and relatively shallow waters off the coast and proximity to existing power grid infrastructure in the Latrobe Valley. There are currently nine proponents who hold feasibility licences for wind farms off the coast of Gippsland. It is unlikely all nine will bid for this first auction. The successful projects will move towards investment, construction and operation. But it will not be a fast process. The auction closes in August 2027 and contracts will be awarded in 2028. Why do we need it? A significant amount of coal-fired power is due to exit the grid in coming years, and Australia is in a race to replace it with renewables. Gippsland's Yallourn power station is scheduled to close in July 2028, and the Eraring power station in New South Wales will follow in April 2029. The latest AEMO Integrated System Plan says two-thirds of Australia's remaining coal-fired plants could be retired by 2035. It warns coal plants could close faster than forecast and some are only active during times of peak energy demand. AEMO also says by 2036, data centres will consume almost as much power from the grid in a decade as all households in New South Wales and Victoria do today. This creates the risk of an energy supply gap. Victoria has a target to produce at least 2GW of offshore wind by 2032, increasing to 4GW by 2035 and 9GW in 2040. But the Victorian auditor-general warned in December last year that the state was unlikely to reach its offshore wind target due to delays in establishing the sector. Victoria was due to hold an auction for offshore wind last year, but then-energy minister Lily D'Ambrosio announced in September 2025 that the auction would be delayed. How has the announcement been received? The final announcement of the auction means certainty for the sector. Erin Coldham is the chief development officer of Southerly Ten, the proponents behind the Star of the South offshore wind farm. The wind farm is the country's most advanced, and has just completed its public submission hearings on its environmental approvals for its state development works. Ms Coldham said the auction was welcome news. "What this auction does is it allows the government to choose those projects that can offer the best value for money and to help provide some level of comfort around the revenue so that we can build the project with confidence and ensure that it is successful," Ms Coldham said. Environmentalists have also welcomed the news. Environment Victoria senior climate and energy advisor Kat-Lucas Healey said offshore wind would play a crucial role in the state's transition to renewables. "Offshore wind is a really great part of that because it's a different wind resource than it is onshore, so it starts adding to that diversity and plugging those gaps," she said. Why should taxpayers help fund this? Naysayers might be asking why taxpayers should help pay for this. Energy Consumers Australia said the broader benefit to society would justify the cost, in a submission to the federal government about the ESEM. "When emissions policies impact the electricity sector, such as accelerating the need to replace emissions-intensive capacity and build new transmission, we think there is a very good argument that taxpayers are the right constituency to pay, since all citizens benefit," the report said. Clean Energy Council chief executive Jackie Trad said it was not unusual for a government to financially back an industry, citing the federal and New South Wales governments' recent decision to provide $2.5 billion for the Tomago Aluminium Smelter. "Having a manufacturing capacity in Australia is critical and important," she said. "I would say energy, electricity as one of the key things that powers our economy, that creates economic prosperity, that provides real momentum for jobs … particularly in the regions, that is money worth spending." What does Victoria's election mean for the auction? Grattan Institute senior energy program fellow Tony Wood said while the auction announcement was a step forward, there was still a lot that was unknown. Mr Wood said the extra cost to build offshore, along with the upcoming November election, provided significant risks to ensuring a smooth transition. Renewables look to be a key battleground at the election, with the Coalition pledging to scrap key transmission project, VNI West. "There must be a risk that they still cancel with all this and therefore the whole thing will be called off," Mr Wood said. The Victorian opposition says it will open up new gas supplies if it wins the election. Opposition energy spokesperson David Davis said the Coalition had always supported offshore wind in principle, but was critical of how the government had managed the rollout. "With respect to offshore wind, we have always seen that there could well be a significant role for offshore wind and indeed when the bill went through parliament, we did not oppose the bill," he said. "We've always said that in the case of offshore wind, it's a matter for the government to get matters in place, and it is the government of course that is delayed in its approach." Mr Davis said if the Coalition won the election, it would maintain the contract process, with some oversight.

title: Australians cut ties with servos as EV record sales continue - abc.net.au
raw_text: Australian drivers have entered "a new phase", experts say, with electric vehicles accounting for one in five new car sales for the third consecutive month. July sales data published today shows the share of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) easing slightly from the record set in June, with 23,510 vehicles sold, claiming 21.7 per cent of all new vehicle sales. It means the sales share of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) tripled year-on-year in the wake of the war in Iran and the ensuing fuel crisis. After the June record of 23.3 per cent, many were tipping a drop with the financial year ending. But with conflict in the Iran war again heating up and the return of the fuel excise, the price of petrol jumped again, and Australian drivers are looking to cut ties with the servo. "It's incredible what a year in a war will make," said Rebecca Huntley, a social researcher who recorded a significant jump in support for EVs. "If you were to have a poster of the greatest influencer when it comes to EV take-up in Australia, it'd have Donald Trump." Toyota remains the most popular brand of new cars being sold overall with more than 115,000, but Chinese EV maker BYD is on its heels, selling more than 60,000 cars in July. "What the numbers are telling us is that we are actually moving into a new phase," said Andrea Pellegrini, a lecturer and researcher at the Institute of Transport and Logistics Studies at the University of Sydney. "Now actually we are kind of going into a phase where the market is becoming more mature." The Federal Chamber of Automotive Industry (FCAI) acknowledged electric cars played a part in record sales for July, but sounded a warning that charging infrastructure needed to keep pace. "Accessible and dependable charging will be critical to maintaining consumer confidence as electric vehicles become a larger part of Australia's new-vehicle fleet, "FCAI chief executive Tony Weber said. Changing EV attitudes In years gone by, some politicians have said EVs would "end the weekend" by sidelining SUVs, once considered necessary for towing boats and caravans. But the capability of hybrids and EV options is catching up, and with the price of fuel firming above $2, and much higher for diesel, the tables have turned. "People started to go, oh my God, I might be going away on a weekend and I might not be able to get petrol," Dr Huntley said. "Suddenly, that kind of reliability factor of combustion engines started to feature in people's minds." Past concerns about range and charging limitations of EVs are also fading, according to Dr Pellegrini. "General overall concerns about the electric vehicle, kind of the ease after they purchase the vehicle," he said. "They are less concerned about the waiting time, the driving range, but also they think that it is good value for money once they start driving the vehicle." Energy independence Dr Huntley and her team have just published the second Clean Energy Solutions Index, a national research project that surveys thousands of people and ranks public support for the renewable energy transition. Overall, the index recorded a modest one-point increase in "deep support" for the energy transition to 61 out of 100. Many of the 11 clean solutions it tracks have remained either unchanged or, in the case of some infrastructure projects like onshore wind, dipped slightly. However, the stand-out in the 2026 report was support for EVs, which rose six points. "That insecurity around the technology of combustion engines has, I think, accelerated the consideration of EVs for a lot of people," Huntley says. "And when we talk to people who've made the switch, it's a bit like taking back control, having agency, feeling like if something like this happens again, which a lot of people expect that it might, it's just not going to affect me as much." For about a decade, Margaret Killen had a sticker on her old diesel car that proudly claimed her next car would be an EV. A year later, she finally made the switch. "It's been going really well, and I'm really pleased with my purchase," Mrs Killen said. It was an expensive outlay, but with solar on her home, her vehicle running costs are now much lower. "The benefits are now playing off, you know, playing out as in we've got a charger at home, we pop it on when it's low peak or sometimes we have free power hours in Tassie." More support needed for renters Buying and charging an EV is a much simpler proposition for someone who owns their own house and has rooftop solar. But more than 10 per cent of Australians live in an apartment, and more than 30 per cent are renters. It's an area Pellegrini said needed greater consideration and investment. "If you're a renter, it makes it very complicated to have a private charger installed at your property because you do not actually have a say in it," Dr Pellegrini said. "That segment of the market is actually really crucial because we know that if people live in apartment units and they want to buy an electric vehicle, currently they mostly rely on the public infrastructure system. But according to Dr Huntley, politicians and leaders sometimes underestimate the enthusiasm for new technology. "There's so much opportunity in the renewable energy revolution at the household level that can lean into Australia's love of technology, love of being able to control the things that you're doing," she said. "The biggest question is not, we don't want this; the biggest question is, is everybody going to get to share equally in this opportunity we have?"

title: Victorian offshore wind auction opens with plans to power 1.5 million homes - abc.net.au
raw_text: In short: The Victorian government has opened its offshore wind auction, calling for companies to bid to provide 2 gigawatts of power. Successful projects will receive government support and will deliver enough electricity to power 1.5 million homes. What's next? Companies will have one year to enter bids, and the government expects to award contracts in 2028. The Victorian government has opened its first offshore wind auction, inviting companies to bid to supply the first 2 gigawatts (GW) of power to the grid. The auction is expected to deliver enough electricity to power 1.5 million homes each year and create thousands of jobs. Successful applicants will receive government support to deliver their projects. Victoria is home to Australia's first declared offshore wind zone in waters off the Gippsland coast and another off the state's south west coast near Warrnambool. Bidding in the auction is now open and will close in August next year. The Victorian government said it expects to award contracts in 2028, allowing successful projects to move towards securing investment, construction and operation. The auction was planned last year, but was delayed while the state and federal governments worked on the timing. The first offshore wind is not expected to enter the grid until 2035, seven years after the closure of the Yallourn coal plant in the Latrobe Valley. Last year Yallourn provided 14.8 per cent of Victoria's power. Victorian Energy Minister Jaclyn Symes said offshore wind was an "amazing opportunity" for Victoria which would produce cheap, reliable power and deliver thousands of jobs, particularly in Gippsland. "Offshore wind is a very important component of our future way to create energy as coal retires," Ms Symes said. The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) has indicated that demand for electricity was exploding due to the growth in data centres, which it forecast would draw as much power as all homes in Victoria and New South Wales by 2036. But Ms Symes said AEMO had indicated that Victoria would not face a shortfall when Yallourn closes. The government planned to award contracts through the Electricity Services Entry Mechanism (ESEM), a scheme to drive investment in the sector. The ESEM was agreed in principle late last year by energy ministers across Australia, with the exception of Queensland, and is yet to be adopted. The government will assess bidders based on their value for money and ability to deliver benefits for local communities. Victoria has a target to produce at least 2 GW of power from offshore wind by 2032, increasing to 4 GW in 2035 and 9 GW in 2040. [Symes pic] Auction welcomed by industry Offshore wind developer Southerly Ten has welcomed the opening of the auction, saying it was "really good news" for the industry. "It's really the signal that government is looking to bring offshore wind into the market and we know that's really important as some of the coal plants start to retire over the coming decade," chief development officer Erin Coldham said. "One of the things that's really critical to make sure that offshore wind projects can proceed is to have that partnership with government through these types of contracts." Southerly Ten is the developer of the 2.2 gigawatt (GW) Star of the South, which is Australia's most advanced offshore wind project. Ms Coldham said the company would review the auction documents in anticipation of bidding. "We've been working very hard over a number of years to get all of the approvals ready, and this is really the next step for us to participate in this process, see what the government is seeking and take the project forward from there," she said. Major development but questions remain Grattan Institute energy program director Tony Wood said the beginning of the auction was an "important next step in what could be a very important process" for the grid. Mr Wood said offshore wind offered "significant benefits" to Victoria. But he also warned offshore wind faced challenges because it was more expensive to deliver than other renewables and it would be years before projects were built. "So there's a lot of things ahead yet, but it's an important next step in what could be a very important process." But offshore wind had the advantage of producing more electricity more consistently than wind energy generated onshore, he said, as well as being available when other renewables were offline. "A typical onshore wind turbine might produce, on average [power], about 30 to 40 per cent of the time. Offshore wind has the potential for producing electricity 50 per cent of the time or more," Mr Wood said. There are also benefits to basing offshore wind in Gippsland, which the government says has the one of the best offshore wind resources in the world. It is also able to connect to high-voltage power lines built in the Latrobe Valley to connect coal plants to the grid, minimising the need for new transmission lines. Mr Wood said it was also unclear how the ESEM mechanism would work. "The intention would be to provide contractual certainty … so that investors can go along and know that they'll have some risk, but they'll also be protected," he said. "So at the moment, that still seems to be quite complicated, and I'm not sure how that's going to play out."

title: Bill granting 'extraordinary powers' to speed up development passes parliament - abc.net.au
raw_text: In short: Queensland parliament passed its controversial critical minerals bill on Wednesday night, which grants the executive branch of government significant powers to expedite what it deems "strategic" projects. The government says the bill will attract investment, while critics say stronger land acquisition powers do not have enough safeguards. What's next? Peak industry bodies and conservation groups are waiting to see which project will be first to be fast-tracked by the state government under the new legislation. A controversial bill granting the Queensland government significantly expanded compulsory acquisition powers has passed state parliament. The new law allows for projects to be declared "state strategic" by the government, meaning projects can be streamlined through a suite of new powers granted to the coordinator-general. The State Development and Public Works Organisation (Critical Minerals) and Other Legislation Amendment Bill (2026) is touted by the government as essential for the state to capitalise on the critical-minerals boom. Critics of the bill, which passed through parliament on Wednesday night, said it put too much power in the hands of the planning minister and eroded fundamental legal safeguards. Significantly, the bill allows for the government to acquire land for private projects for the first time. The bill also weakens appeal rights and allows for other legislation to be edited through new "modification orders". The Crisafulli government said the powers would not automatically allow a project's approval or remove existing environmental, planning, resources, or other approval requirements. Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the bill was aimed at securing investment in critical minerals. "This legislation gives us the tools to attract investment, create jobs and build new industries," he said. "There's billions of dollars on the table." Critical minerals are materials the state government describes as being crucial for modern economies and are at risk of supply chain disruption. Deposits in Queensland include vanadium and cobalt for batteries, and copper for electrical, renewable and digital infrastructure. Late amendments Queensland's agriculture industry was a vocal critic of the bill, airing concerns that prime agricultural land would be taken for mining, renewable energy and tourism projects. The day the bill passed, amendments were added that excluded renewable energy projects and data centres from being declared state strategic. Amendments were also made to ensure a Regional Interests Development Approval (RIDA) was still required. A RIDA is a separate legislation used to protect areas of special economic interest, including agricultural land. AgForce Queensland president Shane McCarthy said he negotiated with the government right up until the last minute. "They have taken on some of our recommendations … we would have preferred it to go a little bit further, but you never get [all of what you] asked for," he said. "It's great to see a government that actually listens and takes on board what their regional constituents are saying." Queensland Farmers Federation CEO Kylie Porter said she believed the legislation was aimed at achieving balance. "Legislation is one piece, but we also now need to make sure that our proponents of critical minerals are really acting in a way that's very appropriate for the interests of our agriculture community," she said. 'No meaningful safeguards' Environmental Defenders Office Queensland managing lawyer Andrew Kwan said the late amendments failed to address the bill's central flaws. "These amendments add no meaningful safeguards, tighter eligibility criteria or greater transparency and accountability around the use of these extraordinary powers," Mr Kwan said. "In the face of climate change and continued environmental decline in Queensland, major projects must face robust assessment and public scrutiny, not unjustified fast-tracking or weakened legal protections." Critics said that while critical minerals were important, nothing in the bill restricted the powers to govern just critical-mineral projects. In July, Mr Bleijie used the $140 million Whitsunday Skyway cable-car project between Airlie Beach and Conway National Park as an example of a project that could be expedited under the law. Pascale Whyte lives near the proposed cable-car base station site and is disappointed the law has passed. "What this bill does is flip the basic Queensland principle of a fair go on its head," she said. "It gives a commercial tourism project, complete with a luge track, the same fast-track powers as a critical mine, and it strips away the safeguards that let everyday residents be heard. "That's not streamlining, that's overriding our community's rights." The Skyway project has not been declared a state strategic project. Conservation groups protested across the state last week, calling the new legislation an overreach that put the environment and land rights at risk.

title: Will AI data centre rules be imposed on the states? - abc.net.au
raw_text: The federal government is intending to push ahead with new national energy and water rules for AI data centres. And despite opposition from some states and territories, it seems the government's willing to go over their heads and force the changes. Image Details This content was transcribed automatically and may contain errors. Read more on how the ABC is automatically creating audio transcripts . Speaker 1: The federal government hopes to settle new energy and water rules for massive AI data centres at a national cabinet meeting this week. But not everyone's a fan of the proposed standards, which could force the government to create laws to override the centres. So what's the government proposing? And why is it an issue for some? In cities and regional areas across the country, the AI boom's driving the construction of scores of large-scale data centres. Right now there's over 160 of them, but that number's expected to balloon. Thing is, they need a huge amount of energy to operate. It's estimated that the centres currently use 2% of Australia's energy. That's estimated to be around 6% by 2030, and possibly as high as 13% by 2040. As part of a big speech he did on AI back in July, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he wanted new data centres to deliver at least as much energy into the grid as they take out.
