title: SA's statewide blackout was 10 years ago — but electricity debate is still live - abc.net.au
raw_text: Blackouts come in different forms — there are those that affect memory, and those that affect electricity. But no mental blank has impaired the vividness of Tom Koutsantonis's recollection of the time when, on a tempestuous spring afternoon 10 years ago, power was cut to the whole of South Australia. Reflecting on the precise moment when the statewide blackout began, the Labor MP smiled wryly at the irony of the circumstances in which he found himself at the time. "I was actually in the parliament on my feet moving legislation relating to the National Electricity Market (NEM)," he said recently. About 4pm on September 28, 2016, electricity supply to more than 850,000 properties and approximately 1.7 million residents was disrupted, leaving South Australia in darkness. Mr Koutsantonis was then the state's minister for energy — a portfolio which, despite changes of government in the intervening years, he holds again today. His first inkling that something was wrong was prompted by an apparent malfunction at the entrance to the parliamentary chamber. "I heard the magnets in the parliament [doors] release and all the doors suddenly open or close, depending on their position," he said. Suspecting there had been "some sort of brownout", he was then told by an advisor that what had occurred was far worse than that. In the same moment that Mr Koutsantonis heard parliament's doors start to glitch, energy industry analyst Danny Price was on his computer monitoring the situation closely. "I just saw demand drop off a cliff, so I knew straightaway it was a blackout," he said. "I wasn't surprised — I was watching the weather in South Australia for a day or two beforehand. You could see a very big storm was brewing." While supply was slowly restored over the coming hours, some parts of the state were without power for more than two days. An early estimate of the economic impact concluded that the blackout cost businesses more than $360 million — but money wasn't everything. At Flinders Medical Centre, there were distressing consequences for prospective parents when dozens of embryos were lost at a private fertility clinic because mains supply was cut. Twisted transmission towers At different times, energy policy, renewables and extreme weather have each been lambasted as the prime culprit for the statewide blackout. In a 2017 report, the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) concluded that overly sensitive protection mechanisms in some of the state's wind farms were to blame. "Activation of this protection feature resulted in a significant sustained power reduction for these wind farms," the report stated. AEMO found that the sudden dip in output triggered a power surge along the Heywood Interconnector from Victoria, which in turn caused the system to trip and SA to become "islanded" from the rest of the NEM. "Had the generation deficit not occurred, AEMO's modelling indicates SA would have remained connected to Victoria and the black system would have been avoided," it said. "AEMO cannot rule out the possibility that later events could have caused a black system, but is not aware of any system damage that would have done this." But the causes that were most immediately obvious on the day itself were the tornadoes, with estimated wind speeds of between 190 and 260 km/h, that ripped through SA's mid north, damaging critical infrastructure. Indeed, the most enduring imagery from the blackout is probably that of giant transmission towers lying collapsed and contorted in fields. "Two towers had been taken down by a freak tornado or hurricane," Mr Koutsantonis said. "Any time you take out transmission lines … you're going to have a shock to the system. "That caused a sudden loss of power and the system reacted according to the laws of physics." Mr Price also pointed to the weather — but said there was a failure of preparation at market level ahead of a "one-in-50-year storm". "[There were not] any gas generators running, which is crazy to me," he said. "What they have been doing subsequently is what they should have done at the time, and that is to spin up the thermal generators that existed in the system that would have allowed some resilience, significant resilience." In a statement, AEMO's executive general manager of operations Michael Gatt described the blackout as a "cascading failure" that was the result of a "highly complex sequence of events". "The lessons learned from 2016 have informed industry-wide changes and risk reporting, which have strengthened the resilience of South Australia's power system and the broader National Electricity Market," he said. Universal constant of energy dispute Perhaps the most pressing question a decade on from the South Australian blackout is not whether such an event could have been prevented, but whether one could happen today. Loading... Mr Price — who believes renewables need the "big buffer" of thermal generation to ensure reliability — thinks it "very easily" could. "The system is more fragile than it was back 10 years ago. Far more fragile," he warned. "We are more dependent on intermittent sources of generation. "There's a lot more batteries out on the market but, as we know, they don't last very long and they cost a hell of a lot of money." Mr Koutsantonis agrees that a statewide blackout "could always happen again" — but departs company with Mr Price on the likeliest circumstances, and on the impact of batteries. "[A blackout's] probably more likely to happen in a jurisdiction that has more thermal power than renewables, because of the reliance on big suppliers from one big location," he said. "Battery storage is the obvious solution — and battery storage in the right places not only stabilises your grid, it saves consumers money [and] it allows you to put more renewables into the system." Those differences of opinion remain at the heart of Australia's energy debate. Much has changed in the electricity market since South Australia was left in darkness. But if there is a universal constant of the politics of power, it is surely that there is always friction over the question of what approach works best.

title: How a controversial scheme will fund Australia's largest koala park - abc.net.au
raw_text: The New South Wales government's plans for the country's largest dedicated koala national park have passed a key hurdle, but the plan to fund it has sparked debate over who should pay for conservation. The Great Koala National Park (GKNP) is planned to span 476,000 hectares running inland of Coffs Harbour, south to Kempsey and as far north as Grafton, and was a key promise from Labor during the 2023 state election. The state government plans to help pay for its costs by selling carbon credits generated from ending logging, and earlier this month the Senate rejected a bid to block the scheme, keeping the park on track for delivery by the March 2027 election. Supporters say the park may never have happened without the credits, but critics argue governments should not need a financial incentive to create national parks. What is a carbon credit? Carbon credits are generated by ending intensive farming practices, reforestation and other activities that take out more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere than they create. Through the Australian Clean Energy Regulator, projects are certified and the resulting carbon credit units can be sold on the market like shares on the exchange. Companies that either voluntarily want to lower their carbon footprint or are required by law to do so have the opportunity to buy the credits. The NSW government plans on generating carbon credits by ending logging in 176,000ha of state forests set to become part of the GKNP. Professor at the Crawford School of Public Policy at the Australian National University Frank Jotzo said many conservationists take issue with carbon credits because they do not encourage polluters to change their practices. "There's all manner of industrial companies as well as resource companies … who cover part of their emissions reduction obligation by paying for credits," he said. "You could take the opposing view and say these industrial and resource companies should be reducing their own emissions; that's where the fault line lies in the debate." Who's paying? Last year the NSW government finalised the boundaries of the GKNP and issued a moratorium on native logging in the proposed area. Instead of running the park at a cost to taxpayers, the upkeep would be covered by selling carbon credits, which would be prioritised to manufacturing industries and banned from fossil fuel companies. The plans needed the support of the federal government who runs the Clean Energy Regulator and decides on which projects are eligible to earn carbon credits. Conservationists who oppose carbon credits disapproved of the GKNP project, and three federal Greens senators crossed the floor to vote with the Coalition to unsuccessfully block it. Should national parks pay for themselves? While carbon credit schemes are not new, Professor Jotzo said Australia and China were both pioneering strategies to use them to encourage the preservation of forests. "There is nothing that incentivises or compels state governments to create national parks; there is really no push factor in that regard," he said. "I think there's probably a bona-fide argument here that, without the carbon credits, the park might not have gone ahead. "From that point of view, going ahead with [the GKNP] is unambiguously a good thing because we will see substantial carbon benefits and biodiversity benefits that flow from this." University of New South Wales senior lecturer in public sector management Megan Evans said having to cover the costs of creating a national park sets a dangerous precedent. "I just find it extraordinary that we are having a discussion about how we actually incentivise government [into] doing something that is actually their job," Dr Evans said. "The idea that a state government is poor or unable to find the resources to create a national park is just an absolute lie. "It's a lie that has been manufactured and socialised and normalised by these discussions around how do we make national parks pay for themselves." Dr Evans said the plans still have unresolved problems that are core to the ongoing debate about the efficacy of carbon credits offsetting polluting industries. "Offsets should only be a very last resort, and they should be very expensive in order to incentivise that behaviour," she said. "Spending tens or hundreds of millions of dollars on credits to ensure compliance is just spare change at the back of the couch [for many companies]. "We have a carbon credit regime that is in operation, but it's not actually facilitating the decarbonisation of Australia's economy." For and against Despite her disapproval of carbon credits, New South Wales Greens MP Sue Higginson said the scheme was the best option the NSW government had proposed to set up the GKNP. "This is the good method that actually sees the end of logging," she said. "The next method, the industry method, is nearly ready [and] would have seen carbon credits generated and logging continued." National Parks Association NSW Coffs Coast branch chair Grahame Douglas described carbon offsets as "very inappropriate" but argued the GKNP plans have integrity. "It's not perfect, but it does provide a very real way forward for the management of these areas for conservation," Dr Douglas said. Timber New South Wales president Andrew Hurford argued ending logging in the GKNP will have more harm on the environment than the predictions made by the carbon credits system. "We know that when we don't produce timber here in Australia, we import it to make up the difference," he said. "We replace things like timber power poles … with fibreglass produced with resins out of petrochemicals or steel produced out of coal and iron ore, much higher emissions than anything the timber industry would produce." What's next? NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe welcomed the approval by the Senate and said future parks, including the Great Southern Forest National Park currently being advocated for, were also on her radar. "Methods like [this] would create a framework that could make it easier to create projects like this," she said. The scheme still needs to be passed in the House of Representatives and approved by the Clean Energy Regulator before legislation for the GKNP will be introduced in the NSW Parliament.

title: Largest solar farm in any CBD in the Southern Hemisphere coming to Sydney - abc.net.au
raw_text: In short: The International Convention Centre Sydney (ICC Sydney) is to install 4,500 photovoltaic panels on its rooftop. Once completed, the ICC Sydney will be home to what is being described as the largest solar farm in any city centre in the Southern Hemisphere. The solar farm will cut carbon emissions by up to 2,000 tonnes a year. A solar farm heralded as the largest in any central business district (CBD) in the Southern Hemisphere is being built in the heart of Sydney. About 4,500 photovoltaic panels will cover the rooftops of the International Convention Centre Sydney (ICC Sydney) and produce enough electricity to power up to 400 homes. The rooftop generation, combined with purchased renewable electricity, will mean the government-owned site is powered entirely by green energy. Paul Scully, the minister for planning and public spaces, told the ABC that the upgrade would attract more events to Sydney. "Coming to one of the most environmentally friendly convention centres in the world is a big selling point," Mr Scully said. "This is showing how, as an urban community, we can do our part in the rebuild of our energy system, where we're using large roof spaces." The solar farm will cut carbon emissions by up to 2,000 tonnes a year, which the government has said is equivalent to the amount absorbed by a forest of about 100,000 mature trees. The ICC Sydney already had some solar panels installed, but the older technology was too heavy to be placed on certain sections of the rooftops. With lighter panels now available, the centre can increase the size of its solar footprint. '300 per cent more energy' Chris Jones is the head of asset management at Capella Capital, which leads the consortium that maintains the facility. Mr Jones said the newer, more efficient panels would allow the ICC Sydney to produce about 300 per cent more energy. "This facility running at full capacity is a big drawer of electricity," Mr Jones said. Battery storage was not an option as it would take up too much space. "The only logical way to do it is to use the grid as a synthetic battery, if you will," Mr Jones said. With power bills reaching $1.8 million a year, the centre was also trying to reduce consumption by upgrading appliances such as fridges. ICC Sydney chief executive officer Adam Mather-Brown said the facility sought to use less power each year. "We've just finished an entire re-bulbing exercise on the building, because being 10 years old, new technology has come in," Mr Mather-Brown said. "For thousands of lights that we have, we've reduced that already." The existing panels were dismantled this week and will be given to the Kindly Animal Sanctuary near Armidale in the Northern Tablelands for reuse. It is estimated they will last another 10 to 15 years. "They can reduce their energy bill and keep those rescue animals warm at the same time," Mr Scully said. More cities likely to follow In June, NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane pledged to create a renewable energy zone (REZ) in the cities of Sydney, Newcastle and Wollongong. The state's first urban REZ is being set up in the Illawarra, drawing from solar generated on the roofs of homes and businesses, and using home and community batteries. Mr Scully would not say whether the government was looking to establish a REZ in Sydney but hinted other areas of urban generation would follow the Illawarra. "We're looking to use that as the test bed to see what we might be able to take from that and scale up to other urban communities," he said.

title: ‘Who’s paying?’: Huge Albo project backfires - News.com.au
raw_text: ‘Hypocrisy’: Labor’s flagship net zero program expected to release 2 million tonnes of emissions It’s meant to help cut emissions, but new figures show a flagship net zero program will release millions of tonnes of carbon. An electricity grid overhaul central to the Albanese government’s net zero strategy is expected to generate more than 2 million tonnes of construction-related emissions. The Rewiring the Nation (RTN) program includes the planned VNI West project in New South Wales and Victoria, which alone would emit almost 1 million tonnes of carbon dioxide during construction. Meanwhile, the Central-West Orana Renewable Energy Zone currently under construction in NSW would release more than 600,000 tonnes of emissions. In total, the amount of carbon dioxide expected to be released during construction for five RTN projects across Australia would amount to just over 2 million tonnes. That’s equivalent to nearly half a million gasoline-powered vehicles driven for one year, or more than 400,000 homes’ electricity use for one year, according to the United States Environmental Protection Agency’s Greenhouse Gas Equivalencies Calculator. But it was small in the scheme of Australia’s annual emissions of 458 million tonnes, representing just 0.45 per cent. Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan reacted with dismay to the emission estimates released under Freedom of Information by the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (CEFC). Mr Tehan described the figures as “(Energy Minister) Chris Bowen’s hypocrisy writ large again”. “Are the CEFC required to offset these emissions, and if they are, who’s paying the cost - is it going to add further to the Rewiring the Nation bill?” he told news.com.au. “Rewiring the Nation is likely to put an extra $600 on everyone’s power bills as a result of Chris Bowen’s renewables rollout, which is using nearly 100 per cent overseas-sourced materials.” A March report from independent think tank Policy Institute Australia found east coast Australians could face a $600 per year increase in their household electricity bills by 2035 as a result of the energy transition. For small businesses, the figure was $10,000. “Chris never talks about the emissions of Rewiring the Nation, just like he doesn’t talk about the emissions of mass producing solar panels and mass producing wind turbines,” Mr Tehan said. “The big question is, who is paying for these emissions if they’re being offset - or are they not being offset, which is another story?” Chris Bowen hit back, however, arguing that the new infrastructure would drastically reduce emissions in future. “Dan Tehan misses no opportunity to show how badly he misunderstands our energy transition,” Mr Bowen told news.com.au. “Australia hasn’t invested in new transmission in decades. “Our energy system needs upgrading, and we need new transmission regardless of the type of generation. That’s why the previous Liberal (Energy) Minister Angus Taylor supported new transmission lines. “Getting these new lines built will see emissions come down over coming years by much more than any emissions generated by their construction.” The CEFC also defended the construction-related emissions, saying in a statement that the RTN program was expected to unlock 11 GW of renewable energy and storage capacity. “Like all major infrastructure projects, there are construction-related emissions associated with delivery,” the statement said. “Total emissions during construction of RTN projects financed by the CEFC is expected to be 2 Mt CO2-e (2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide) based on the estimates of project proponents. “While the CEFC is not required to directly offset these construction emissions, they are outweighed by the 11 GW generation and storage expected to be unlocked by these projects. ”The CEFC estimates that this could cut emissions by approximately 3 Mt (3 million tonnes) in 2035 alone, compared to grid average emissions at that time.” Green project triggers farmer fury The RTN program was a core feature of Anthony Albanese’s 2022 election campaign and, after introducing the program that year, the prime minister said its projects were “putting us on track to be a renewable energy superpower”. “Rewiring the Nation has always been about jobs in new energy industries, delivering cleaner, cheaper and more secure energy, and bringing down emissions,” Mr Albanese said. The program’s funding includes $19 billion of taxpayer-backed capital from the CEFC, which operates as a government-owned climate investor with total capital exceeding $30 billion, giving out loans that must be paid back with interest. Since the program launch, grassroots movements have opposed the new transmission infrastructure being built across the country. VNI West, one of the pillars of the RTN program, sparked confrontations between farmers and the Victorian government late last year. State agency VicGrid was trying to conduct surveys on farmland for the transmission line, designed to move renewable energy from wind- and solar-rich areas to population centres, but it ran up against staunch opposition from locals. Kanya sheep and grain farmer Ben Duxson, one of the landowners who denied VicGrid access along with a blockade of 400 other farmers, previously told news.com.au that he opposed VNI West because renewable energy systems were costly and inefficient. “This is a government-induced energy crisis, it’s nothing to do with farmers holding up the project,” Mr Duxson said. “It’s a bad policy and we’re not going to put up with it. That’s why people are standing at the gate, it’s on principle - it can’t work.” Mr Tehan said, “Chris Bowen doesn’t care that these communities and these farmers have been run roughshod all over”. “All he wants to do is pursue his ideological dream at any expense to Australians.”

title: Government admits fuel prices higher than they'd like | Evening News Bulletin 8 August 2026 - SBS
raw_text: The Federal Government admits fuel prices are higher than they'd like; residents in Ceuta providing shelter for migrant children; Australia prepares to take on Bangladesh in a five-day cricket test in Darwin. Listen to Australian and world news and follow trending topics with SBS News Podcasts. TRANSCRIPT - The Federal Government admits fuel prices are higher than they'd like - Residents in Ceuta providing shelter for migrant children - Australia prepares to take on Bangladesh in a five-day cricket test in Darwin Energy Minister Chris Bowen admits fuel prices are higher than the Government would like - but says it could be worse. Labor's Fuel excise discount came to an end this week. That's seen prices surge back over two dollars per litre across the country. Mr Bowen says the Government made it clear from the start this relief was vital, but temporary, to ensure Australians got through the worst of the international fuel crisis when it comes to fuel prices. "Of course, petrol is more expensive than we'd like it to be because of the international prices. But prices are about 50 cents less now than at the time that the government took the decision to halve the fuel excise." Chris Bowen says the Government's other work on cost of living relief continues. --- United States President Donald Trump says the US government will invest $4.2 billion in critical mineral and battery projects as part of a push to strengthen national security. The investments come as the US attempts to reduce its dependence on Chinese supply chains for critical minerals needed to replenish depleted weapons stockpiles. While the Trump administration denies reports of significant weapons shortages, defence officials warn replenishing some inventories could take years given existing production constraints. Mr Trump says part of the investment will go towards educating miners. "Accredited mining programs in the United States now graduate less than 170 mining engineers each year, while China graduates more than 3,000. And half of our current mining workforce is set to retire within the next three years, wow. That's why my administration is making an unprecedented financial commitment to our nation's mining schools. It's going to keep us nice and young and vibrant." -- The Australian Government is welcoming the Trump administration's announcement of a loan to Sunrise Energy Metals as part of a major investment in critical mineral and battery projects. The US Government announced it would provide the company with a $566 million conditional loan as it develops a scandium mine in New South Wales. Resources Minister Madeleine King says the project hosts the world's largest and highest grade known scandium resource, which has a range of aerospace, defence and clean energy applications. In October last year, Australia and the United States signed an $8.5 billion rare earths and critical minerals deal. -- Residents of the Spanish enclave of Ceuta are providing shelter for unaccompanied minors among migrants remaining in the city following a mass influx last week. It comes as Spain introduces tougher border controls on Italy, in retaliation for Italy introducing similar restrictions on Spain following the influx of migrants. The leftist government expects to transfer some migrant minors from overcrowded reception centres in the North African enclave to the mainland within weeks. Ceuta resident, Bilal Kadur, says they're doing what they can to help. “What we are doing here is providing accommodation for those who are on the streets, good people are always welcome, not those who are problematic. Always helping, we have been attentive since day one. We haven’t slept, there are people who have stayed alert and taking care of them because not everyone who comes is good, you know.” --- A new joint defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan is a sign countries in the region are searching for new regional security partnerships amid mistrust in US guarantees, according to an analyst. Senior Middle East Research Fellow at Chatham House, Galip Dalay, says it resembles NATO's article 5, with the countries to treat an armed attack against any one of them as an attack against all three. Türkiye has NATO's second-largest military, while Pakistan is a nuclear-armed state and Saudi Arabia is one of the world's biggest oil exporters. Galip Dalay says he thinks Iran will take a negative view of the new alliance. "The fact that this is a collective defence treaty, so it considers an attack on one as an attack on all. Probably now Iran has to think twice, or the Iranian-aligned group has to think twice the next time that they are attacking Saudi Arabia. And that will create quite a lot of dilemmas, not only for Iran, but also for the parties to this agreement as well. So, but definitely, clearly Iran will regard this negatively." -- Australia's mens cricket team is preparing to take on Bangladesh in Darwin from Thursday in the first of two tests this month. It will be Australia's first red-ball match since they ended the Ashes by winning at the Sydney Cricket Ground in January. Allan Border medallist Travis Head and Jake Weatherald will open the batting for Australia. The second test will be played in Mackay.

title: Under threat: Rising sea levels could threaten hundreds of thousands of properties - SBS
raw_text: A new report by the Climate Council has projected that sea level rise will threaten more than 267,000 Australian properties over the next century. Rising sea levels are forecast to impact every state and the Northern Territory, with researchers saying coastal Queensland is at particular risk. Listen to Australian and world news and follow trending topics with SBS News Podcasts. TRANSCRIPT The turquoise waters and white sands of the Gold Coast have long attracted Australians seeking a sea-change. But that proximity to the coast could come at a cost, according to the Climate Council's Rising Seas, Rising Bills report. It projects that coastal flooding will cost Australia more than $855 billion this century, including property losses and land use damages. The report also categorises the Queensland Gold Coast as the single most exposed urban area in Australia. “Many coastal communities around Australia are already experiencing the impacts of sea level rise. We've had around about 22cm of sea level rise over the past century around Australia but also right around the globe. And that is having a big impact upon communities already, especially when we get very high tides and when we get storm surges. So, storms forcing the water up against the coast as well.” That's Andrew Watkins, an adjunct professor at Monash University's School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment. He's also a co-author of the Climate Council's new report, which analysed the consequences of sea level rise based on a quote "conservative scenario" where countries only implement existing policies to cut pollution. Scientists say they are confident that sea levels will rise by at least 14cm by the year 2050. “As our sea levels rise, because of the warming oceans, but also because we're melting ice sheets in Antarctica and also Greenland as well. We've already seen many impacts along the coast already, with erosion in places like Lancelin in Western Australia, Robe in South Australia, Byron Bay in New South Wales, the Gold Coast during tropical cyclone Alfred and even Inverloch down here in Victoria.” The Gold Coast is considered the canal capital of Australia. It also features the largest constructed canal network in the Southern Hemisphere, with more than 400km of constructed waterways. Mr Watkins says that design puts the city at heightened risk. “Well, the Gold Coast is fairly low-lying; it's not very high above sea level there. It's also a soft coast; it's got a sandy coast that can easily be eroded away. Now, estuaries and canals are also another way that sea level rise and extreme sea levels can actually go inland and attack the coast from behind.” Those findings stirring a mixed response from locals in the community. Voxie 1: "If we did have a big flooding incident, I could well have problems in my area." Voxie 2: "It's just about being aware of it and doing the precautions, like the sandbagging out the front of the shop; it doesn't happen very often though. Voxie 3 & 4: "It completely eroded after the cyclone and after the tornado. Yeah, it was a mess, they've lost a lot of sand." Voxie 5: "I have been flooded out before, years ago.” Mark MacCabe has long resided in the Gold Coast, where he also works as a principal licensee and real estate auctioneer. “It's been this way for years. People are buying on the Gold Coast, they're buying on the northern end of the Gold Coast, they want to be surrounded by the water. They're aware that storm surges happen, they're aware of what the possibilities of disasters are. But the reality is, I've lived here for 26 years and I've never seen anything more than a little bit of water and a surging tide coming up onto the gutters.” Mr MacCabe says part of his job involves preparing new homeowners about higher insurance premiums associated with the region. “You know, obviously, being in a floodplain, insurance costs have more than doubled in the last five years. So, there's no doubt - there's no running away from that - but the fact is that buyers don't care. If you're buying on the Gold Coast now, there's a legislative requirement called a local law 17A, which says we need to make everyone aware for events where the water meets the land.” The Climate Council predicts that extreme sea level events considered rare today will become more frequent and more intense. And it's not just coastal communities, with sea level rise expected to hit every state as well as the Northern Territory. The report also specifies that most private insurers don't cover "actions of the sea", meaning property owners could bear the costs of flooding. Earlier this month, the United Nations warned the world is likely to pass the 1.5°C global warming threshold by 2030. “Humanity is speeding past the limit to avoid climate catastrophe. Ten years ago in Paris, leaders pledged to limit temperature rise to 1.5°C — the threshold scientists say is critical to avoiding the worst climate devastation. The latest report from the UN Environment Programme delivers a stark warning: The world is failing to keep that promise.” That's Antonio Guterres, the United Nations Secretary-General. Speaking on behalf of the UN Environment Programme, Mr Guterres called for urgent action to minimise the magnitude and duration of this overshoot. “That demands an overshoot of ambition: Accelerating the phaseout of fossil fuels and the renewables revolution; slashing methane pollution; and protecting land, forest and oceans. Governments must over-deliver on national climate plans, net zero commitments and beyond.” August was the joint-hottest month ever recorded, according to the European's Climate Service. Samantha Burgess is the strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. She says the Earth was one-hundredth of a degree Celsius away from the highest monthly global temperature recorded in July 2023. “So, it's extremely unusual to have August as the hottest month. The fact that August 2026 has matched the hottest month ever observed means the climate system, our climate system, is really operating well outside the range we would have expected just a decade ago. And this summer is also the warmest summer on record, so we've seen an exceptional few months.” The result was also compounded by El Niño weather patterns, which are being fuelled by warming waters in the Pacific. El Niño is forecast to intensify over the coming months and persist through to February 2027. Mr Watkins says his research contributes to a growing body of evidence about the impacts of a warming planet. He's calling on Australia to adapt and act now. “We really need to look at the climate change and the sea level rise that's locked in, and we need to adapt to those locked-in changes that we know are going to happen right through to the end of the century. In this report, we have put some dollar values on that to really highlight what's at risk if we don't make changes, if we don't mitigate the greenhouse gases and also, if we don't adapt.”

title: Andrews and Allan loyalists take their leave as Carroll attempts to set a new course - SMH.com.au
raw_text: The last of Daniel Andrews’ original ministers and one of Jacinta Allan’s most loyal supporters have resigned from cabinet and announced they will not contest the next election, as Premier Ben Carroll seeks to unshackle his government from Labor’s past 12 years. Climate Change Minister Lily D’Ambrosio, the last serving member of Andrews’ class of 2014 cabinet and Health Minister Harriet Shing, a staunch ally of both Andrews and Allan, made their respective announcements on Thursday as a tumultuous sitting week of parliament drew to a close. The cabinet resignations, along with that of Allan, open three vacancies for Carroll to fill with fresh talent chosen from a restless backbench. He is expected to announce on Monday the cabinet line-up he’ll take into the November 28 election. It comes as the new premier finalises one of his most important appointments – the chief of staff who will run the Premier’s Private Office and administer his political agenda. The Age on Thursday revealed he has approached Julie Ligeti, one of Labor’s most respected political operatives, to serve in the role. Shing said she had told Carroll of her decision on Tuesday afternoon, hours after he replaced Allan as premier. During her 12 years as an upper house MP, she developed a reputation as a serious policy wonk through a string of complex portfolios including housing, water, and the Suburban Rail Loop, and as a fierce political warrior of Labor’s Left faction. In her Facebook post announcing the news on Thursday, Shing mentioned her eclectic choice of pets – which includes a pair of woolly miniature donkeys – and thanked her partner Lissie Ratcliff, who previously served as Andrews’ chief of staff. “It’s always been my view that we are custodians of these roles for the time that we have them, and it’s now time for me to pass these opportunities and obligations on to the next person,” Shing said. “I have congratulated and wished Premier Carroll every success. He deserves the full support, solidarity, and respect of the cabinet, the caucus, and our entire labour movement as he takes the government forward and into the all-important contest against the Liberal Party and One Nation in November.” D’Ambrosio was elected in 2002, and entered cabinet in the final year of the Bracks/Brumby government in 2010. Since Labor’s election win in 2014, she has served as energy minister, playing a significant role in the state’s transition to renewable energy and its emission reduction targets. She was also a staunch loyalist of Allan. One of her final acts as a minister was to ring journalists and wavering MPs to assure them the premier still had enough support to keep her job. “Back in 2014 not a lot of people thought about energy too much,” D’Ambrosio said in her announcement on Thursday. “Of course, the decade that followed changed all that. Under Labor, Victoria has led the nation, paving the way for Australia’s transition to renewable energy. Where Victoria has gone, the rest of country has followed.” Environment Victoria lauded Australia’s longest serving minister for climate change. “When D’Ambrosio came to office, Victoria had the dirtiest power system in the country and many thought rapid decarbonisation was next to impossible,” chief executive Jona La Nauze said. “She not only proved the doubters wrong, her reforms saved Victorian households millions of dollars in the process.” Carroll paid tribute to both ministers on Thursday. “Over many years of dedicated service, they have brought compassion, determination and a strong sense of purpose to their roles, delivering outcomes that have improved the lives of Victorians and strengthened the communities they represent,” he said. “Lily D’Ambrosio has been at the forefront of Victoria’s response to climate change. Her leadership has made Victoria a national leader in renewable energy, driven ambitious emissions reduction targets and laid the foundations for a cleaner, more sustainable future.” Carroll’s revamped cabinet will need to reward those who backed him in this week’s leadership coup without disenfranchising the ministers who remained loyal to Allan. Members of the cross-factional delegation who precipitated Tuesday’s spill by urging Allan to stand down – which included Colin Brooks, Ingrid Stitt, Anthony Carbines, Lizzie Blandthorn and Luba Grigorovitch – will all have claims for promotion. Gabrielle Williams, the senior Left faction figure who led the delegation into Allan’s office on Monday, has already been sworn in as deputy premier and by convention will have her pick of portfolios. Stitt, who is also from the Left, has expressed an interest in the now vacant health portfolio. All three cabinet resignations are women from Labor’s Left faction. MPs Sheena Watt, Nina Taylor and Ryan Batchelor – who are associated with D’Ambrosio’s factional grouping – could be elevated to cabinet as part of the reshuffle. In selecting Ligeti for his chief of staff, Carroll brings into the fold a veteran of one of Labor’s most successful state governments and a survivor of the Rudd-Gillard wars in Canberra, with deep connections across the party and the broader labour movement. A former senior adviser in the Bracks government, chief of staff to former federal minister Brendan O’Connor and current federal Housing Minister Clare O’Neil, Ligeti was also a one-time housemate of former prime minister Julia Gillard. She is also well known to the two factional chiefs who helped orchestrate this week’s coup to topple Allan – former federal MPs Alan Griffin and Stephen Conroy. Ligeti would join Carroll’s deputy chief of staff, Bassel Tallal, an emerging political operative with strong ties to Labor’s Right faction. A source close to Carroll, speaking confidentially to The Age to discuss internal party matters, said the new premier hoped to complete the transition to his administration and shift into full campaign mode within three weeks. Although Carroll has spent his first few days in power outlining the policy areas where his approach will differ from the Allan government’s – the establishment of a royal commission into the building industry, a more constructive relationship with business and tighter controls on the use of public money – his campaign focus will be on the same cost-of-living concerns Allan was seeking to address. The government’s legislation to protect work from home rights in anti-discrimination laws will not be withdrawn from parliament, despite business calls for the policy to be abandoned. The fate of the Suburban Rail Loop (SRL), a project Carroll does not support, will be decided once his new cabinet examines the contracts the government is already committed to. title: Power companies need more homes to share control of their batteries - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Energy companies need to convince millions of Australians to hand over control of their home batteries to support the grid at critical times if the nation is to avoid major cost blowouts in its multibillion-dollar transition away from coal, the consumer watchdog warns. While home-owners are rushing to insulate themselves from volatile electricity prices by installing solar panels and lithium-ion batteries, authorities are concerned that too few are signing up to join “virtual power plants” — schemes offering customers bill credits in exchange for allowing their power providers intermittent access to their stored electricity. Because batteries can store cheap and abundant solar energy during the day and discharge it after sunset, a three-fold surge in battery uptake – triggered by the launch of large federal government rebates a year ago – has slashed power bills for those who have adopted the technology. It has also lowered wholesale prices in the evening peak demand periods across the wider grid by reducing reliance on coal and gas. However, these grid-scale benefits remained “incidental,” according to a new report from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), as too few individual home units were synchronised to charge and discharge at the most optimal times for the grid. Spreading the benefits further would require a significant expansion of aggregated networks known as “virtual power plants”, it said. Virtual power plants are cloud-based networks run by power retailers or tech companies, which offer customers financial credits to orchestrate thousands of their household batteries at once into a single, co-ordinated power source capable of stabilising the grid during supply imbalances. “Co-ordinated batteries can more reliably and efficiently respond to price signals and the needs of the energy system, resulting in further reductions in the need for grid-scale storage, enhanced system reliability and security, and lower costs for all electricity consumers,” the ACCC said. Under the Australian Energy Market Operator’s 25-year blueprint for the least-cost pathway to replace retiring coal-fired generators and cater for burgeoning electricity demand, around 26 per cent of households would need to have batteries installed by 2050, and more than half of those needed to be part of virtual power plants. Current participation rates sit well below that target. Only about 3 per cent of east-coast customers have batteries, and just 24 per cent of those owners are in a virtual power plant. Failing to lift sluggish enrolment rates would increase the need for investment in other grid-scale projects, such as gas-powered generators, known as “peakers”, said Robbie Campbell, chief executive of Plico, a company that installs batteries and operates a 5000-household virtual power plant in Western Australia. “A battery sitting in a garage doing its own thing doesn’t displace a gas peaker – a battery in a virtual power plant does,” he said. “Right now, most of them are sitting in garages.” Lagging uptake in virtual power plants was not because of any technology problem, Campbell added. “It’s a trust problem,” he said, and too many in the industry were not focused enough on ensuring consumers understood how the schemes operated and the potential benefits. “Households aren’t going to subsidise the grid out of goodwill,” Campbell said. “Show them the money, show them how it’s made, and they’ll stay in a virtual power plant.” Some experts, however, believe the energy market operator’s assumptions on how batteries were behaving outside the virtual power plant setting may be too pessimistic. Tristan Edis, the head of analysis at energy consultancy Green Energy Markets, said a growing number of retail offerings were being built to encourage batteries to absorb low- or no-cost midday electricity and discharge it in the evening peak periods for a premium feed-in tariff. “It would be great if more were in a virtual power plant, but we are probably too pessimistic,” he said. “Maybe we don’t need as many enrolled in virtual power plants as we previously thought, because we have now got these retail offers that are proving popular with battery owners.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. title: ‘We are not banjo-playing dimwits’: The deep rural resentment that will shape the election - SMH.com.au
raw_text: From the time he was a child, James Knight knew his future lay in rural Victoria. Although he grew up in Melbourne, Knight got a taste of life on the land during school holidays at his uncle and aunt’s beef and cropping farm. From that moment, his mind was made up. “I got hooked,” he says. Later, Knight worked in corporate agriculture for four years while living with his wife, Georgie, in Melbourne. And during that time, the land kept calling. The couple both wanted the farm life and experience of living in a close rural community. So, when the chance came to take over Georgie’s family beef farm in south-west Victoria, they took it. But when they moved there in 2016, Knight found a community simmering with frustration. There was a proposal at the time for a wind farm with more than 40 turbines. While some landowners agreed to host turbines, many in the community vehemently opposed them, including Knight’s father-in-law. It was obvious to Knight that the project consumed the lives of neighbours “and not for the better”. So he sided with his father-in-law, declining to host turbines on their farm. The renewable energy wind project proceeded anyway with 35 turbines, including one erected 200 metres from Knight’s title boundary and 1.5 kilometres from his house. Knight understands Victoria needs renewable energy. But he believes many regional communities feel corporate interests have forced renewable projects on them, while compliant governments allowed the benefits to flow to the cities. “How about we put 30 or 40 of these across the St Kilda foreshore and see how you go?” Knight says. “Because it’s the same for us out here. We don’t want them.” Knight says there are also frustrations with turbines and transmission lines hampering aircraft access, which can be required for firefighting and spraying fertiliser on farms. Anger about the wind farm is emblematic of broader frustrations taking root across regional Victoria. It’s not just the soaring transmission towers and lines stretching across the landscape throughout much of the state’s south-west. Or the wind turbines rising above farms where there was once uninterrupted sky. It is not only the absence of doctors forcing people to drive long distances on roads pockmarked with festering potholes that pose a daily hazard to cars and lives. Nor is it just the hangover of pandemic restrictions that damaged faith in government institutions. Or the patchy mobile and internet coverage. Or the fire services levy that enraged volunteer firefighters. It is these and more grievances compounding into deep-seated resentment, and driven by a perception that state and corporate interventions inflict more harm than solutions to problems. Many of these issues are specific to regional Victoria. Yet here’s why they matter to everyone else. In 1999, rural seats swung hard against the Liberal Party, booting then-premier Jeff Kennett from government in an election he was expected to win easily. The eight regional seats Labor flipped, and three regional independents backing them, were enough to secure Labor minority government. So began an era of political dominance that continues today. But the dynamic is shifting drastically. Labor now faces the prospect of losing government in November after accumulating heavy political baggage over three terms. Unlike previous state elections, Victoria is in uncharted political waters. Multiple polls indicate fed-up voters are warming to Pauline Hanson’s One Nation – a prospect that seemed all but impossible a year ago. Knight is not a member of any political party, but he understands Hanson’s appeal. When Hanson took aim at renewables in her recent address to the National Press Club in Canberra, Knight said the message cut through. “Any individual or organisation that’s going to call out renewable energy, you will get regional communities on board because I feel like we’re seeing it firsthand,” Knight says. In 2024, the Clean Energy Council reported that farmers could earn more than $40,000 a year per turbine on their property and $1500 per hectare annually for solar panels. Farmers are also reimbursed for transmission line easements on their properties. Justine Hide is also no stranger to state politics seeping into everyday life. The deputy mayor of Northern Grampians Shire spent the past year on a community reference group seeking government answers for landowners worried about the long-term impacts of the renewable energy transition. The meetings touched on solar, wind and power lines, but tended to be dominated by one particular $7 billion transmission project planned to snake through 235 kilometres of Victorian farmland: VNI West. For three years the shadow of this planned behemoth has loomed large over regional people’s lives, even if they support the project or aren’t farmers themselves. “I can’t go to the supermarket or my kids’ swimming lessons without either seeing affected landowners or people in that community, and they’ll talk about it if they see you,” Hide says. The rollout of VNI West drew criticism for being short on answers when the Australian Energy Market Operator first revealed its preferred route for the transmission project. Hide says anger and distrust ultimately filled this knowledge vacuum, to the point where people became afraid to talk openly about the project for fear of offending one another. In November, state government agency VicGrid assumed responsibility for planning transmission and renewable energy zones. VicGrid chief executive Alistair Parker says the government established the agency after recognising national arrangements for renewable infrastructure had not served communities well. VicGrid has introduced new guidelines, which Parker says will ensure communities in renewable energy zones are treated respectfully. Some nondisclosure agreements for landholders hosting renewable infrastructure will be scrapped. Previously, these contracts banned property owners from discussing their financial payouts with neighbours. Parker says 40 per cent of the 220 property owners along the VNI easement have allowed VicGrid access to their land under voluntary agreement. He expects compulsory easement acquisition will only be necessary for 2 per cent or 3 per cent of property owners once the process concludes, based on experience elsewhere. “So it doesn’t take the land off people, it just creates an easement across the land,” Parker says. He insists VicGrid now has better decommissioning processes in place when renewable infrastructure reaches its end of life. And he says VicGrid is also trying to better share information about renewable projects with communities. “We’ll come and talk to anybody about any aspect of this whenever it suits them,” he says. But Hide remains pessimistic about VicGrid’s attempts to make amends. “I think the damage has been done,” she says. The most recent community reference group meeting was abandoned after dozens of anti-transmission line protesters gatecrashed with signs and chants. In one video of the confrontation, a man can be heard saying: “You could have done this five years ago, and you didn’t bother.” A generally negative sentiment bubbling in regional Victoria has emerged clearly in opinion polls. The Age’s Resolve Political Monitor, which surveyed 1652 Victorians in April, May and June, found 46 per cent of regional and rural Victorians expect their personal outlook to worsen, compared with 32 per cent of respondents in Melbourne. Similarly, 51 per cent of rural and regional Victorians expect the state outlook to worsen, whereas 38 per cent of Melburnians responded the same way. Resolve founder Jim Reed says cost of living is the most pressing concern uniting Melburnians and regional Victorians. But now rising anger in the regions is flowing through to increased support for One Nation: according to polling, Hanson’s party has a primary vote of 31 per cent in the regions, compared with 19 per cent in Melbourne. Reed says voters are drawn to the One Nation leader’s unvarnished image and plain speaking style. Hanson’s decision to accept a plane from billionaire Gina Rinehart seemingly mattered little to her supporters. “They are willing to forgive her quite a great deal in terms of her candidates’ behaviour and getting airplanes because she seems to stand for them,” Reed says. Reed says critics once dismissed One Nation’s supporters as grumpy, old white men. But One Nation is increasingly drawing supporters from every demographic group. That includes, crucially, women aged between 30 and 50. “Once you’ve won that group you tend to get a snowball effect,” the pollster says. Natasha Miller is in that group. The fifth-generation Mildura resident already had something in common with Hanson, as the owner of a fast-food shop. But after years of watching transport and health issues in her community persist largely unabated, she’s now considering voting for One Nation. And Miller knows she’s not alone. “I have customers who have told me they will be voting One Nation,” she says, even though the party is yet to announce its candidates for November’s election. “I think government needs a shake-up, and if One Nation can at least do that – get some different ideas and different people in there – then that’s what I’m hoping for.” Miller’s experiences speak to the growing resentment for the extent to which decisions made in Melbourne affect regional Victorians’ lives. COVID and the associated lockdowns were a turning point for her. Miller spent hours navigating government bureaucracy so she and her staff could keep working, while watching jealously as, just over the border, regional NSW lived in relative normality. Four years on, Miller is serving one-third of the customer base she had before the lockdowns. “Everybody is talking about how slow business is – tradies tell me they’re waiting for the phone to ring,” she says. “We have not recovered at all, not even close.” In response to questions about sentiment in the regions, a government spokeswoman lists a raft of commitments. Her response ranges from 68,000 energy jobs across the state to $1.04 billion on roads, including 70 per cent for regional Victoria. “Only Labor will deliver cheaper power for all Victorians and $18 billion in wages for regional Victorian workers through our renewable energy transition,” the spokesperson says. ‘You can go to the emergency department, but why would you with a sore throat?’Penshurst resident Ama Cooke Alex Fein, research and intelligence principal at polling firm Redbridge, says regional Victoria is somewhat more susceptible to anti-establishment and populist sentiment than Melbourne. She believes social media also allows populist messages to be spread easily throughout the regions, where residents often face greater economic challenges and less access to services than their city counterparts. The conservative Sky News now broadcasts for free in regional Victoria and its evening hosts often invite Hanson on air for interviews. Meanwhile, television audiences for the ABC, which is required to be politically neutral, are declining. “Whatever is really difficult everywhere in Australia is doubly so in regional areas,” Fein says. “They have to drive longer distances and their services are strained. The cracks are wider to begin with.” A report by the OECD released in January supports the assertion that regional communities confront steep financial hurdles. It found Australians have experienced a marked decline in disposable incomes while inflation surged and mortgages soared. A series of major shocks have battered the Australian economy: the COVID-19 pandemic, energy and food price spikes due to war in Ukraine, and sharp interest rate rises. These economic blows hit the regions particularly hard. Furthermore, the OECD report said the concentration of house price gains in capital cities meant the economic disparity between urban and rural areas widened. Ama Cooke sees these challenges firsthand. She runs a newsletter for her community in Penshurst, just south of the Grampians. Like Miller, she points to myriad reasons why residents of rural Victoria feel let down by the political class. “I think people are sick of being lied to,” she says. When pressed to identify the most urgent problems in her community, Cooke nominates the shortage of doctors and the poor state of rural roads. The paucity of health services in the region means it can take up to three months to secure a doctor’s appointment. “You can go to the emergency department, but why would you with a sore throat?” Cooke’s priorities for change are entwined. The lack of health services force residents to drive long distances for medical attention. But deep and numerous potholes pose a daily danger to rural residents who have no option but to drive. “Why can’t they do decent repairs instead of a quarter-inch layer of tar and pretending that’s OK?” she says. In Benalla, tow company owner Harlen Black is well acquainted with potholes. His team is regularly called out to motorbikes and cars damaged by the road surface on the Midland Highway and Hume Freeway. Three weeks ago, his crews were called to a pothole about 70 centimetres long near a bridge on the Hume. It had damaged eight cars. “Most of them had the wheel or the rim itself destroyed, so it’s a fairly big pothole to do that,” Black says. Or the wind turbines rising above farms where there was once uninterrupted sky. It is not only the absence of doctors forcing people to drive long distances on roads pockmarked with festering potholes that pose a daily hazard to cars and lives. Nor is it just the hangover of pandemic restrictions that damaged faith in government institutions. Or the patchy mobile and internet coverage. title: What happens when your EV runs low on a regional road trip? I found out - SMH.com.au
raw_text: What happens if your electric vehicle runs out of battery? What happens if you’re, say, in the middle of country Victoria with no one for miles and your estimated kilometres remaining is ticking down faster than you expected, and your car at some point just comes to a halt? It’s not as if someone can turn up with a jerry can filled with electricity for you. Does a rescue vehicle arrive with a car-sized defibrillator to get you going for an extra 20 kilometres? I’m pondering this as I’m driving in the middle of country Victoria with no one for miles and the estimated kilometres in my EV is ticking down – and it’s ticking down fast. I had 90 kilometres left in the battery for a 60-kilometre journey, but it’s already showing 50 kilometres remaining and there’s still another 20 kilometres or so to get to Bright. I’m experiencing my first case of “range anxiety”, when you stress about your EV running out of battery because you’re not sure what really happens when it starts to dwindle towards empty, whether you really do have 5 per cent left or, actually, it’s just going to disappear instantly and your car will slow to a halt a few kays outside the town of Eurobin, population 239. This is the future of the great family road trip in Australia, I firmly believe that. EVs are already wildly popular, and they’re becoming even more so, thanks in part to rising fuel prices due to Middle Eastern unrest. EVs make complete sense, particularly if you have solar power in your home and can essentially charge your vehicle for free. Sign up for the Traveller newsletter The latest travel news, tips and inspiration delivered to your inbox. Sign up now. With an EV, you can go on a road trip without the guilt of emissions. You can travel free of the prospect of whopping fuel prices or the threat of no fuel at all. We can, and should, and I believe will, all be doing this. But is Australia ready for it? I don’t own an EV. Instead, I was lent one a few weeks ago for a family road trip from Sydney down to Falls Creek and Mount Hotham in Victoria. I’ve been driving a Zeekr 7X, a new entrant to the Australian EV market, a mid-size SUV from a Chinese manufacturer that is an absolute dream to drive, smooth and comfortable, with heated seats and a huge sunroof and all sorts of bells and whistles that the kids can play with in the back while my partner and I shoot through the countryside up front. But what’s it like taking a long-distance road trip in an EV in Australia? To begin with, it takes a completely different mindset. You can’t just fill up your car anywhere you go, and it won’t take 10 minutes from start to finish. A road trip in an EV takes planning. It means you have to know where you’re able to stop to recharge, and what you’re going to do (especially with your small kids) while that is happening. The Zeekr 7X has a range of about 600 kilometres, which is great, but it’s not enough to get through an entire day of driving, so a stop will need to be made, hopefully somewhere useful and interesting. You learn pretty quickly, on your EV journey, about superchargers and kilowatts and CCS2 v CHAdeMO plugs. You learn that charging points are not created equal: a point with four lightning bolt symbols on your Google Map search will charge your car in about 25 minutes; a charging point with only one bolt will take about three hours. You also learn that you have to pay for this service, and that a full charge of the EV will cost almost $70. That doesn’t seem much cheaper – if at all – than using petrol. Australia’s EV infrastructure, outside major cities at least, also appears nowhere near adequate for the wave of vehicles hitting our shores. That’s something I can tell you after two weeks on the road in rural NSW and Victoria. There’s very little signage for EV charging points – it’s up to you to find them on your GPS. Many of the points are stuck in the middle of nowhere with nothing else around, nowhere to sit, nothing to amuse travellers while your car gets its juice. We sat on a rock by a fence and ate McNuggets for half an hour in Sutton Forest because there was nowhere else to go. The key issue, however, is that there aren’t enough chargers. Certainly not if you’re driving in peak times such as school holidays or long weekends (which, fortunately, we weren’t). Our brilliant plan on the way down was to drive from Canberra to Beechworth, a lovely town filled with great shops and restaurants – and an Evie branded charging point – to juice up while making good use of our time at the bakery and a local wine shop before continuing the drive to Falls Creek. Only, we arrived in Beechworth and someone else had just pulled in and connected their car at that charging point’s one CCS2 plug. Great. The app told me that that car probably had about half an hour to go, so we drove down the street to have some lunch, figuring we would just have to wear the loss of an extra half hour. When that car was getting close to 100 per cent charge, I drove back to the charging point, only to find that another car had parked in the other space next to the charger, its owner hanging out by the front of his car, waiting for the cable. Ah ha. This is a thing you need to do. Queue. Now we faced the loss of at least another half hour, probably an hour, while this guy filled up. But we needed to make it to Falls Creek before dark and couldn’t afford to wait. My GPS told me there was a Tesla charging point behind the brewery in Beechworth, but it was very slow and often blocked by other cars. There’s a much faster Tesla Supercharger outside Ovens, though that would require registering on yet another app for our short holiday, and the internet seemed divided on whether our non-Tesla car would get full speed from it. So, we made the call to wing it to the next Evie charging point in Bright, trusting that the 90 kilometres of remaining charge really was going to take us 60 kilometres. We made it, with 4 per cent battery remaining. But the lesson was learnt: Australians, including me, are absolutely ready for the EV road-trip revolution. Bring it on. But Australian infrastructure is not. The writer drove a loan vehicle courtesy of Zeekr.

title: ‘Moving at light speed’: Plug-in solar and batteries are coming to Australia - SMH.com.au
raw_text: Households could soon be able to buy plug-in solar panels and batteries for energy storage as part of reforms that will broaden access to solar for renters and apartment dwellers. Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said all states and territories had agreed to look at how plug-in solar and batteries could work in Australia to give apartment dwellers and renters more control over their bills. “A third of Australians have a solar panel on their roofs. It’s more popular than the backyard pool,” Bowen said. “Now we’re taking the next step, by looking at how even more Australians can take advantage of free, abundant sunshine to cut their energy bills - even if they don’t have a roof.” As reported previously by this masthead, plug-in solar allows consumers to buy panels for about $500 each. The panels hang in an outdoor area and plug into a socket to power any appliances, charge a battery or feed into the grid. The devices do not need to be installed by an electrician, and owners can take them when they move homes. The technology is widely used in Germany and being increasingly used in other European countries such as France and Spain, as well as in many US states; it was also recently legalised in Britain. It is currently unlawful in Australia because of compliance with safety standards, although the market is growing anyway and a number of online retailers already sell systems here. The federal and state climate change and energy ministers agreed on Friday to progress legal and regulatory reforms that would enable widespread adoption in Australia, with a key deadline by mid-2027. New Zealand is separately working to enable plug-in solar. Glen Morris, director of Smart Energy Lab and a member of the Solar Standards Committee, said Australia had been lagging but was now moving at light speed given it usually took years to develop new standards. “It went from zero to 100 in one day.” Morris said. “I was prepared for a very long campaign to get it through … but obviously, when there’s political will, things can move a bit faster.” The main change required was an amendment to the Australian standard for inverter systems, which could be fast-tracked by copying international standards, he said. “The products designed for the European market already have the safety features we like – it’s important that we don’t turn it into a very complex process, so that it can be done swiftly. “To some extent, the horse has bolted because people can buy these and the only thing stopping them plugging it in is that it’s illegal. But it’s not very obvious – certainly if you don’t have solar panels and just have a plug-in battery system, no one would know.” The plug-in panel technology is often called “balcony solar”, and panels hanging vertically off balcony railings are a common sight in Germany. However, Francis Vierboom, chief executive of Rewiring Australia, said the panels would be most useful in backyards in the Australian context. “The sun is a lot lower in the sky in northern Europe, and solar that’s actually on sideways on your balcony is going to generate more energy than it does in Australia, where the sun is a bit higher in the sky because we are closer to the equator,” Vierboom said. The real game changer for apartment dwellers could be the portable “suitcase batteries” because the panels require outside space, but the batteries work even without any kind of solar, Vierboom said. In that scenario, a battery would charge up from the cheap daytime energy available on the grid, including three hours of free power available in the middle of the day on some plans, and then a household could use that energy in the evening peak. “The less we all lean on the grid in that evening peak, the cheaper the energy system stays, and the more we can be using solar energy instead of fossil fuel generators in the evening,” Vierboom said. Governments may need to look at strata law and tenancy law to consider whether owners’ corporations, strata managers and landlords could block plug-in solar and under what circumstances. Solar Citizens, a group that advocates for consumers to gain from renewable energy, has been lobbying Bowen to push for plug-in solar. Chief executive Heidi Lee Douglas said the group would push for a clear timeline with a target deadline of July 1 next year, and to ensure renters, apartment dwellers and low-income households could benefit. “Renters shouldn’t be locked out of cheaper, cleaner energy simply because they don’t own the roof over their heads,” Douglas said. “They should have a fair right to request solar, batteries and energy-efficiency upgrades, and landlords shouldn’t be able to unreasonably say no.” Tyler Peck, 24, rents an older home with his partner in Preston in Melbourne. While the home is affordable and close to transport, it is poorly insulated and the heating bills are high. Peck would like to have plug-in solar set up on his porch, which gets good sunlight, and says he is equally motivated by the electricity savings and the environmental benefit. But he would definitely wait for the official green light, rather than buying any of the systems already on the market. “With all the [public service announcements] that went out a while ago about dodgy scooter or e-bike batteries being fire hazards, I’m just very cautious about anything that isn’t official,” Peck said. Return on investment An 800-watt system with two panels would cost $450 to $850 based on German prices, which gives it a two to four-year payback with a 25-year warranty, Morris, of Smart Energy Lab, said. Adding a 1.6-2Kwh battery would be a combined cost of $1100-$1300, with a five to eight-year payback and batteries rated for 15 to 20 years of daily use. Morris said Australian prices would probably start higher than Germany and eventually fall. Bowen said on Saturday that if plug-in solar met safety standards, it would be automatically covered by the government’s existing rebates, the Cheaper Home Battery policy and the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme for solar panels, adding “but we’ll work those details through”. However, Vierboom said the government should consider a change to legislation, since the Cheaper Home Batteries program does not cover small batteries, or the installation of batteries without solar, and the rebates for panels required installation by an accredited electrician. Morris said he had been testing a small panel tilted 75 degrees from horizontal – only 15 degrees off being vertical – similar to how it was used in Germany. But to get a decent return on investment in Australia, it should be tilted more horizontally – from 37 degrees in Melbourne to 32 degrees in Queensland, with Sydney in the middle. On a balcony, “it would stick out a bit more, providing a bit more shade for your neighbour below”, Morris said. Other options for apartments Karin Aubrey will get a shared solar system on the roof of her apartment building in the Sydney beachside suburb of Maroubra in October. The building received a Solar for Apartment Residents grant from the NSW government to reduce the cost, and will use the Allume SolShare 2 technology to fairly split the solar power between apartments. Aubrey is happy about the panels and the grant, but said it took more than a year of advocacy to get everyone in the owners’ corporation on board given the cost of the panels and electrical rewiring required. title: ‘The sites are ready’: Power giant wants AI data centres built at its coal plants - SMH.com.au
raw_text: The owner of two giant coal-fired power plants in Victoria and New South Wales is pitching its sites as prime real estate for new data centres, saying their ready-made access to the electricity grid, water and industrial-zoned land makes them the ideal homes for the energy-hungry facilities. EnergyAustralia, the nation’s third-largest electricity and gas retailer, is pursuing plans to convert the Yallourn coal-fired generator site in the Latrobe Valley into a low-carbon energy hub that could support new “hyperscale” data centres once the power station is retired in two years’ time. EnergyAustralia is due to close the Yallourn generator on June 30, 2028, while its other coal-fired power station – Mt Piper in NSW – is to be retired sometime in the 2030s. Chief executive Mark Collette said coal-fired power plant sites offered the exact features required by data centres, including water and around-the-clock electricity to run their high-intensity computing and cooling systems, a skilled workforce and supportive communities. He said these sites would offer data centre developers the fastest track to getting new facilities built and plugged into the grid. “The sites are ready,” he told an Australian Energy Council event in Melbourne on Wednesday. “Coal power sites can connect big data centres within a couple of years – start from a greenfield paddock, and you’re [taking] most of a decade.” Plans to build dozens of new data centres – buildings filled with servers that store and transmit online data – are attracting intensifying scrutiny across Australia, partly due to the vast amounts of power they will require and the strain they threaten to place on the grid. Australia is already home to 165 operating data centres, which consume 2.8 per cent of total electricity demand on the eastern seaboard today. The Australian Energy Market Operator assumes that that figure could rise nearly seven-fold to 13 per cent of demand by 2035. Despite community pushback, the data centre investment boom is also coming at a critical time for Australia amid a period of sluggish economic growth. Investment analysts have put the local pipeline at more than $155 billion. Microsoft has committed $25 billion to Australian data centres, and Amazon Web Services another $20 billion – money which the government has welcomed at a time of slow growth, even as community opposition builds. However, securing access to enough land and renewable energy have emerged as two of the biggest potential roadblocks to further projects proceeding. Last month, state and federal energy ministers agreed to develop a set of national standards requiring data centres to source 100 per cent of their electricity from renewables, backed up by firming assets like batteries and fast-start gas power stations. EnergyAustralia has been in early-stage talks with potential investors and data centre companies about the opportunity to repurpose Yallourn as an “energy security precinct”, containing solar power, back-up gas power and battery storage. He said the company was not waiting “sitting on our hands” waiting for the Yallourn coal plant to close in 2028, but was actively planning for “what comes next”. “We are doing the work now, so when the day comes, there is something to walk into,” he said. Also on Wednesday, the head of Santos, one of the largest Australian oil and gas companies, pointed to burgeoning energy demand from data centres as a major reason that the world needed to continue investing in all forms of energy, including fossil fuels. “Last year, demand for every single energy source grew,” Santos managing director Kevin Gallagher told the National Press Club. “The world did not swap one energy source for another – it took more of everything.” Gallagher also confirmed Santos would throw its weight behind Labor’s domestic gas reservation scheme, requiring the nation’s liquefied gas exporters to set aside 20 per cent of their export volumes for the local market only from mid-2027, provided it ensures existing contracts with Asian buyers remain untouched and loosens a requirement for producers to not only offer, but sell, supplies into the domestic market. His call clashes with the demands of an alliance of unions, environmental groups and major gas users, which earlier this week argued the government must not cede to gas industry lobbying, and argued a forced oversupply of gas was necessary to get prices back below $10 a gigajoule – the level that manufacturers insist is necessary to prevent further factory closures.
