title: ‘We’re not remotely prepared’: Labour MPs fear party has gone soft on climate crisis - The Guardian
raw_text: Britain has experienced a summer of record-breaking wildfires, deadly heat and drought, with almost 2,900 heat-associated deaths recorded in England during May and June alone. Homes have been destroyed by fires in the West Midlands, and deadly wildfires have swept across Europe. Despite the ever more visible impacts of the climate crisis, there is widespread concern that there has been no big political push at the centre of British politics or a renewed case for net zero. Some Labour MPs believe the government’s caution is a huge mistake. One said the the approach was “a failure to recognise where our vote is”. Jeevun Sandher, the Labour MP for Loughborough and a parliamentary private secretary in the energy department, argues climate is an electoral dividing line Labour should embrace because the party’s voters remain strongly supportive of net zero, even though support has dropped on the right. “Climate is a fight that fires up our base, persuades the middle and splits our opponents,” he said, arguing Labour should combine a climate message with an affordability offer. Another Labour MP said: “We’re not remotely prepared for the fact that our voter base is radically changing. We’re trying to ride two horses. Half of our movement is based on net zero and left-leaning values and we’re still running scared of Reform.” The political pressure from the right has been clear this week. Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, prompted a big backlash from nurses, medical experts, politicians and campaigners for urging British people to enjoy the warmth of the recent heatwaves, while dismissing efforts to tackle the climate crisis. “When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it,” Tice said. “And if it means that English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic. That means we can take on the French – fantastic. Let’s celebrate some of these things rather than just be sort of doom and gloom about it.” Claire Coutinho, the shadow energy and net zero secretary, called for cheap electricity to take priority over net zero targets. In a speech on Wednesday, she said the UK should focus on bringing down the price of electricity and then let “consumer choice be king”, abandoning what she believes are expensive net zero policies in favour of a cheap energy system that will rely on more nuclear and gas. But people in Britain are not as divided on the issue as the political debate may suggest. Recent polling from More in Common found two in three Britons (67%) are worried about unbearably hot weather becoming more frequent in the UK, while 86% believe climate change was at least partly responsible for the recent heatwaves. This includes 73% of Reform supporters, 87% of Conservative supporters and 96% of Labour supporters. However, fear over the climate crisis is decoupling from support for net zero. Even as climate concern remains stable, and spiked during the recent heatwave, support for Britain’s climate targets is eroding. While two-thirds of people say they are worried about climate change, support for the UK’s net zero target has fallen from 68% in 2024 to 45% today. Opposition has almost doubled over the same period, from 12% to 23%. There are different positions on the right, too, with Max Anderson of the Conservative Environment Network saying “slowing climate change by reducing emissions remains essential, but we have to broaden climate debate beyond decarbonisation”. Luke Tryl, the executive director of More in Common, said: “The public are definitely freaked out. Two-thirds of the country say they are worried about the heat events. “There is definitely an opportunity here for Andy Burnham as support for net zero hasn’t changed at all among Labour 2024 voters, though it has dropped massively among the [much smaller number of] Tory voters. This is a clear example of elite-level consensus breaking down, leading to public consensus breaking down.” YouGov’s polling also shows a split on what should be done to address the climate crisis. The environment has risen to the fourth highest issue on the pollster’s salience tracker, with 25% of people listing it as one of their main concerns. But the usual summer increase in concern over climate breakdown has actually been lower than in previous summers, even as there has recently been an increase in the number of people saying the government is not doing enough to tackle it. Government figures reject the suggestion that Burnham’s Labour has retreated from net zero, pointing to the clean power 2030 target, large-scale investment in clean energy including nuclear power, the transition to electric vehicles and heat pumps, and the commitment not to issue new oil and gas licences. A Labour source said: “This government has the most ambitious energy climate agenda in British history. Labour MPs know that this is the right agenda for the country and is essential for uniting our electoral coalition.” A second source said: “Burnham’s wildfire video shows that this government is going to confidently make the case for climate action.” Figures say the issue is not that voters have stopped worrying about the climate crisis, but that net zero targets are increasingly becoming associated with personal sacrifice, especially during a cost of living crisis. They argue voters want action, but are less willing to accept higher bills or further costs just to hit targets. A source familiar with the government’s climate agenda argued that under Keir Starmer, No 10 allowed speculation about a rowback from net zero to grow despite those policy changes never materialising. But some parties have tried to force the climate crisis higher up the agenda. Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens, called for an emergency Cobra meeting before Burnham convened one and held a “reality check” conference on extreme heat. The Liberal Democrats have also argued that Britain needs to become “climate ready”, pushing measures to protect homes and buildings from extreme heat and being “unapologetic” about keeping action to cut emissions high on the agenda.

title: It is now almost certain the world will warm past 1.5C. But ‘net-negative’ emissions are still possible - The Guardian
raw_text: Anthony Albanese is in Palau this week for the annual Pacific Islands Forum and regional security is expected to top the agenda. China is testing nuclear-capable missiles in the Pacific, prompting talk of a new regional agreement. The United States-Iran war has exposed a reliance on costly fossil fuels that is undermining Pacific economies. And as the world comes perilously close to the Paris agreement’s 1.5C temperature goal, a record-breaking El Niño looms in the Pacific Ocean. But the forum will be missing key leaders – Solomon Islands’ prime minister, Matthew Wale, made a shock departure, flying out of Palau just hours after arriving, in order to deal with a looming leadership challenge back home. And the Kiribati president, Taneti Maamau, the Samoan prime minister, Laʻauli Leuatea Schmidt, and Vanuatu’s prime minister, Jotham Napat, are also not attending. It is unclear if Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, will be present. Pacific nations will want Albanese to address the world’s key security threat – climate change. As president of negotiations of the Cop31 climate talks in November, Australia can work with the Pacific to keep 1.5C within reach and secure much-needed finance for island nations at the climate frontline. China’s missile test Since the second world war, the United States has maintained fortified bases in the Pacific and an unrivalled deep-water navy (the US also regularly tests long-range missiles in the region). However, China’s investment in military capabilities has challenged the status quo. In July, China launched a nuclear-capable test missile that flew over multiple Pacific nations and hit waters close to Tuvalu’s exclusive economic zone. This sparked calls for a new regional security agreement: Wale said China’s missile test was “not the act of a friend”. Ironically, it was Solomon Islands that signed a security deal with China in 2022. This changed the security dynamics of a region long aligned with the US and Australia (notwithstanding concerns about nuclear testing and decolonisation). Since then, Canberra has pursued a web of bilateral deals to shore up Australia’s place as Pacific security partner – first with Tuvalu (2023), then Naoero (formerly Nauru) (2024), Papua New Guinea (2025) and Vanuatu (2026). Discussions are ongoing with Tonga and Solomon Islands. The most recent agreement, an Ocean of Peace Alliance signed with Fiji in July, is a mutual defence pact that is open to other Pacific nations to join. Canberra was already pursuing a treaty allowing for coordinated regional responses to disasters and other crises. China’s missile test may have opened the door for something more. Renewables the solution to fuel crisis The Middle East conflict has pushed the Pacific toward an energy crisis. About 80% of the region’s energy relies on imported oil products, much of which would normally transit the strait of Hormuz. Even before the US-Iran war, Pacific island countries spent an eye-watering percentage of GDP (between 10% and 25%) buying fossil fuels to run power plants, generators, boats and vehicles. This compares with a regional average of 8% spent on education and 6% on health. The Middle East conflict has only added to the bill. According to a new report, Fiji’s annual refined fuel import costs could rise by US$375m (A$520m) if high oil prices persist. This is more than Fiji’s entire healthcare budget. Renewable energy offers a clear solution. Replacing diesel generators with grid-scale solar and battery storage could save Pacific countries about US$700m (A$520m) each year in avoided fuel costs. The incoming chair of the Pacific Islands Forum, the Palau president, Surangel Whipps Jr, wants the region to become the first in the world 100% powered by renewables. He says investment of US$120m (A$ 166m) is needed for Palau to add 60MW of solar and battery storage, which would enable 90% of its power needs to be met by renewables. The greatest Pacific threat When climate change was first debated at the UN Security Council in 2007, Pacific countries argued the impacts of a warming planet were “no less serious than those faced by nations and peoples threatened by guns and bombs”. Since then, Pacific Islands Forum leaders have explicitly reaffirmed climate change is “the single greatest threat” to Pacific security. In 2025, Earth was 1.44C warmer than the long-term average. Pacific countries are reeling from stronger cyclones, dying reefs and ocean acidification. Without urgent action to shift away from coal, oil and gas impacts will get much worse. Just this week, the world’s oceans are the warmest on record, fuelled by climate change and a rapidly intensifying El Niño event. It is now almost certain the world will warm past 1.5C. Yet it remains possible, following a temporary “overshoot”, that countries can limit warming to 1.5C by the end of the century. This will require deep and immediate emissions reductions and some carbon dioxide removal to achieve “net-negative” emissions. Limiting global warming to 1.5C is a line in the sand for low-lying Pacific nations – “1.5 to stay alive” is the slogan. Pacific negotiators helped secure this temperature goal in the 2015 Paris agreement. Pacific nations expect Australia to reaffirm global commitment to 1.5C. Australia is helping Fiji and Tuvalu host a pre-Cop summit in October that will remind world leaders the survival of island nations is at stake. Pacific countries will also seek new finance for a Pacific-owned climate fund to invest in community-scale adaptation projects. Some argue collaboration with the Pacific in the lead-up to Cop31 is an expensive exercise. But climate action is crucial to Australian strategy in the region. Investing in renewables and adaptation in the Pacific is an investment in shared security, even as geopolitical competition sharpens between China and the US.

title: Reform says we need to choose between climate and economy. It’s wrong | Larry Elliott - The Guardian
raw_text: So now we know: the smart response to the UK’s summer of record temperatures is to do precisely nothing. According to Richard Tice, Reform UK’s deputy leader, the climate crisis is just one of those things. Nothing can be done about it, so we should simply bask in the sunshine. It is reasonable to assume Tice would not have said anything quite as crass had he been addressing people in Stourbridge who have seen their homes burn to the ground. Or the farmers whose crops shrivel in parched fields. Or the firefighters exhausted from battling wildfires across Britain. Yet Tice clearly thinks he is on to something. The cost of living crisis has put the government’s commitment to achieving net zero by 2050 under the spotlight. The assumption underlying Tice’s comments is that there is a trade-off between tackling the climate emergency and raising, or even maintaining, living standards – and that for the time being, the latter should take priority. The government has certainly been acting as if it believes this is the case. While the drought affecting most of England and Wales makes the strongest possible case for hastening the green transition, Andy Burnham’s focus has been on reducing prices for consumers, including by cutting VAT on electricity bills. It took the prime minister an awfully long time to use the words “climate change” to explain this summer’s heatwaves. He did so only after the devastating fires in Stourbridge and when prodded by a letter from green groups calling on him to end his silence. At one level, the emphasis on putting cash in people’s pockets makes sense. Traditionally, interest in the environment waxes during periods of strong economic growth and wanes when times are tough. Climate breakdown slips down the list of priorities for voters when they are worried about losing their jobs or struggling to pay their bills. Peaks in concern have tended to come at the end of long booms, such as the early 1970s or the late 1980s. But opinions are changing across the political spectrum. As the Conservative peer David Willetts has pointed out, 86% of Britons see climate breakdown as at least partly responsible for the recent heatwaves, and even 63% of net zero opponents make that connection. More than a third of Reform UK voters said tackling climate breakdown should be more of a priority in a recent poll. There are good reasons for the high level of public concern. The rate of food price inflation has also been coming down in recent months, but a poor harvest means that trend could well go into reverse soon. Meanwhile, a report by the German insurance company Allianz has exploded the myth that governments have a choice between growth and the environment. The study shows that extreme heat poses structural challenges to many rich countries because, as temperatures rise above 30C, workers struggle to do their jobs and their productivity suffers. The higher the thermometer rises, the greater the losses. For the most exposed countries – especially those in continental Europe – the hit to economic activity will be considerable: over a five-year period the impact of extreme heat could knock a cumulative 5-7% off GDP. According to Allianz, the UK has hitherto been below the 30C threshold and has not been one of the countries at risk from extreme heat. But on the basis of this summer, Britain may soon become a higher-risk country alongside France and Spain. To be sure, Britain is responsible for only a small fraction of the world’s CO2 emissions, and there is a legitimate debate about how to achieve net zero. But the warning signs are flashing red. Now is not the time to go slow on tackling climate breakdown. The longer that action – global as well as domestic – is delayed, the greater the risk that the climate crisis will eventually wreck the economy. A failure to invest in basic infrastructure needs to be remedied fast. People faced with hosepipe bans have the right to ask why Britain has not built a reservoir in 30 years. The electricity grid was designed and built for fossil fuels rather than renewables, and many green projects are held up by a lack of capacity. The UK’s housing stock is woefully inefficient. Household bills would be lower if existing homes were retrofitted with insulation. New homes should be subject to tougher building regulations to make mechanical ventilation – which keeps temperatures stable year-round – mandatory. None of this comes cheap. The state will have to invest in new infrastructure as well as making changes to the planning laws. Subsidies will be required to provide incentives for consumers to go green. No question, there are costs involved in the net zero transition, but they are outweighed by the benefits. These include cheaper running costs for electric vehicles and lower energy bills for homes where gas boilers are replaced by heat pumps. Governments can always find the money when the occasion dictates. When the security of the nation is at risk, ways to finance extra spending are found. To take one example, ministers have committed to raising defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 because of the perceived threat from Russia. But which is the greater threat? Is it Russia, bogged down in Ukraine after more than four years of attritional fighting, or is it the climate crisis? The answer should be obvious. - Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

As the Conservative peer David Willetts has pointed out, 86% of Britons see climate breakdown as at least partly responsible for the recent heatwaves, and even 63% of net zero opponents make that connection. More than a third of Reform UK voters said tackling climate breakdown should be more of a priority in a recent poll. There are good reasons for the high level of public concern. The rate of food price inflation has also been coming down in recent months, but a poor harvest means that trend could well go into reverse soon. Meanwhile, a report by the German insurance company Allianz has exploded the myth that governments have a choice between growth and the environment. The study shows that extreme heat poses structural challenges to many rich countries because, as temperatures rise above 30C, workers struggle to do their jobs and their productivity suffers. The higher the thermometer rises, the greater the losses. For the most exposed countries – especially those in continental Europe – the hit to economic activity will be considerable: over a five-year period the impact of extreme heat could knock a cumulative 5-7% off GDP. According to Allianz, the UK has hitherto been below the 30C threshold and has not been one of the countries at risk from extreme heat. But on the basis of this summer, Britain may soon become a higher-risk country alongside France and Spain. To be sure, Britain is responsible for only a small fraction of the world’s CO2 emissions, and there is a legitimate debate about how to achieve net zero. But the warning signs are flashing red. Now is not the time to go slow on tackling climate breakdown. The longer that action – global as well as domestic – is delayed, the greater the risk that the climate crisis will eventually wreck the economy. A failure to invest in basic infrastructure needs to be remedied fast. People faced with hosepipe bans have the right to ask why Britain has not built a reservoir in 30 years. The electricity grid was designed and built for fossil fuels rather than renewables, and many green projects are held up by a lack of capacity. The UK’s housing stock is woefully inefficient. Household bills would be lower if existing homes were retrofitted with insulation. New homes should be subject to tougher building regulations to make mechanical ventilation – which keeps temperatures stable year-round – mandatory. None of this comes cheap. The state will have to invest in new infrastructure as well as making changes to the planning laws. Subsidies will be required to provide incentives for consumers to go green. No question, there are costs involved in the net zero transition, but they are outweighed by the benefits. These include cheaper running costs for electric vehicles and lower energy bills for homes where gas boilers are replaced by heat pumps. Governments can always find the money when the occasion dictates. When the security of the nation is at risk, ways to finance extra spending are found. To take one example, ministers have committed to raising defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 because of the perceived threat from Russia. But which is the greater threat? Is it Russia, bogged down in Ukraine after more than four years of attritional fighting, or is it the climate crisis? The answer should be obvious. - Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

title: ‘Our operations are powered by solar’: meet the companies tackling energy hikes with technology - The Guardian
raw_text: When it comes to energy prices, the only thing that seems predictable is unpredictability. In recent years, global conflicts have disrupted supply chains and sent prices rocketing. For business owners managing costs it’s a daily rollercoaster. ‘I didn’t have to take a step out of my day job’ Jake Parry, general manager of the not-for-profit leisure centre RiversMeet in Gillingham, Dorset, has keenly felt the effects of fluctuating costs. After RiversMeet survived the pandemic lockdowns, the 2022 energy crisis saw its energy outlay soar. “We were experiencing a big increase in the cost of running the facility. Our electricity costs went from 11p up to 88p a kilowatt hour (p/kWh),” Parry says. Leisure centres are energy-hungry places: swimming pools require heating, gyms and fitness studios need air conditioning, and a soft play centre full of inflatables needs to stay inflated. It meant RiversMeet needed a way to insulate itself against the volatility of the global energy market or risk shutdown. “We looked at the numbers and at that point it was only three months before we closed the doors for good,” he says. “We had to take action and we started down the process of installing solar panels.” The centre started with an energy audit – which showed massive grid power reliance and outdated lighting. This audit and the actions alone helped them to reduce electricity consumption by half. Next came the solar panels – installed by Good Energy and funded through a Power Purchase Agreement with another party. For a business with the energy needs of RiversMeet, that meant a whopping 528 in total, along with 264 SolarEdge power optimisers (a device designed to maximise energy yield and increase safety), and two SolarEdge inverters (which convert the heat energy absorbed into usable AC power). The installation took place in two stages across 2022 and 2024. As Parry explains, the process was smooth and straightforward, with Good Energy’s expertise allowing him to focus on what he does best – running a leisure centre. “Working with Good Energy, they understood our needs as a business. They didn’t really require my input on anything, which made my life easy. I didn’t have to take a step out of my day job.” ‘Why haven’t we done this sooner?’ Solar has been a significant investment, but one that is already seeing returns. Parry says: “Solar panels have made a big difference to our business here, helping us reduce our running costs. It was one of those things where you think: ‘Why haven’t we done this sooner?’” RiversMeet is projected to generate 253,282kWh of power annually, which equates to a saving of £57,000 each year. This should lead to a return on investment from the solar installation in less than four years. Equally as impressive as the savings are the CO2 reductions (annually RiversMeet is saving 141 tonnes). RiversMeet is far from the only Good Energy solar success story, with others including smart home energy manufacturer myenergi, which is saving £62,000 annually. For myenergi, the benefits extend beyond lower bills. Emma Brigginshaw, head of sustainability and ethics, says the solar arrays make “a big impression” on visiting customers and partners, helping demonstrate the company’s sustainability commitments while enhancing its reputation alongside delivering a rapid return on investment. According to Mark Coyle, services sales director at Good Energy, this experience isn’t an outlier. It reflects a wider pattern playing out across UK businesses right now. “For many, the cost of energy is a critical factor in their financial viability and ability to invest for growth.” he says. “Yet UK energy prices remain among the highest in Europe for business.” Modelling for a typical large manufacturer using 3.54GWh of electricity a year shows just how much is at stake; not installing solar could cost around £2.1m more over the next decade than the investment itself. Compared with a larger system that includes battery storage, that gap widens to around £3.8m. Coyle says: “Every month that a decision isn’t taken, the higher energy costs remain, impacting the business. The question then becomes not should they install solar, but how they can afford to keep waiting.” With RiversMeet’s roof now working as hard as the rest of the leisure centre, the business is going from strength to strength, says Parry. “The charity now is larger than it’s ever been, with more social value than it’s ever had. We’re committed to sustainability, we’re committed to the future, we’re committed to creating a provision here that’s going to last the test of time. And by having renewable energy on the roof, it makes that possible.”

title: ‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre - The Guardian
raw_text: The datacentre revolt spreading across the US has reached the rolling hills of north Devon in an uprising against a planned hyperscale AI data campus in the middle of a globally protected landscape. Perched on an inland cliff, the town of Great Torrington has views that stretch for miles over the landscape of the Unesco biosphere reserve in which it sits, taking in the winding River Torridge and rolling acres of wooded valley and wildflower meadows. Pastoral and peaceful, its history was notably punctured by violence in 1646 when the royalists’ resistance in the first English civil war was brought to an end by the parliamentarian New Model Army in a battle fought out in the narrow streets in heavy rain and darkness. Today, a very 21st-century threat is rippling through the same country lanes as the AI boom reaches the pubs, churches and parish halls of Great Torrington and its surrounding villages. The countryside that makes up the biosphere has been selected by a British company, Xlinks, to house a 1.5GW AI datacentre, one of the largest in Europe, as well as a vast 1.8GW battery energy storage system, or BESS. About 344 hectares (850 acres) of countryside have been secured for the huge campus, with five vast buildings ranging in height from 50 to 130 feet. Listed buildings on the site, Xlinks says, will be relocated and transformed into a visitor centre. Such is the anger locally that the new campaign against the AI datacentre has drawn in tens of thousands of people, uncovered what campaigners say is evidence of secret deals and adopted tactics being used by activists in the US such as Erin Brockovich. A recent public meeting in Great Torrington was hosted by Elizabeth Humphreys of the US campaign group Not in My Valley. She was one of the forces behind achieving a permanent datacentre ban in Coachella, California, over concerns about air pollution, water and energy use. “We’re fighting the largest companies that have ever existed in the world, and that is scary but we are all fighting this together,” Humphreys said. “This is a global issue; we are all connected. People across the world are standing up and fighting back.” Today within the halls and pubs of Great Torrington and the villages of Huntshaw and Weare Giffard, the AI project is the main talking point. And the question being asked is: why here, in a protected UN biosphere, on productive farmland? The proposal was first announced to the public this summer with a call by Xlinks for a collaborative approach. But adopting the tactics of veteran campaigners like Brockovich, people from the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group took to their keyboards – researching, rallying and requesting more information in a series of freedom of information (FoI) applications. What they uncovered fuelled the rising tensions. Documents released under FoI revealed the company had been in closed discussions with council officials since March 2025. In April, the council issued a letter of “in-principle support” before any environmental statement or public consultation – and more than a year before the proposal was made public. Torridge district council told the Guardian the pre-application process was standard practice and was confidential. A spokesperson said it was not confirmation of any proposal and intended to offer guidance on whether a proposal was acceptable in principle in planning terms. In an email dated 18 December 2025, council officials and the developers discussed creating links with a sixth form college in Exeter and a stakeholder engagement plan. “Who do we all feel it is critical to get onboard and when both locally and further afield?” the email asked. Emily Clark, of the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group, said: “Email exchanges and private meetings spanning the past 18 months reveal some officers treating the project as a foregone conclusion. Community frustration is understandably at boiling point. “How can the largest and most costly infrastructure proposal in the nation be conducted almost exclusively in secret?” FoI requests also uncovered a detailed site plan not released to the public. It revealed the two largest buildings would measure 335 metres by 267 metres and cover approximately nine hectares (22 acres) of ground footprint each – both big enough to house Exeter Cathedral 18 times over, campaigners say. Xlinks said its proposals cover about 344 hectares (850 acres) but only a third would be developed; the majority of land would be open to the public or used for new habitat creation to support wildlife, they said. The campus would also house a 1.8GW battery energy storage system (BESS) involving 1,720 containerised units, dwarfing the largest operational BESS currently in Britain, such as the 100MW Bramley facility in Hampshire. The UK urgently needs vast BESS facilities to balance electricity supply and demand as wind and solar power generation increase. The government estimates the country requires 23-27GW of battery capacity by 2030 to meet its clean power goals, which it describes as a “very significant level of increase”. But according to research by the House of Commons Library, the government does not hold data on the projected land use required for the expansion, has no specific policies for their location, and has no definitive estimate of the number of operational BESS facilities or their current total capacity. Campaigners in Devon say this creates a “regulatory wild west”. Clark said: “We’re facing the biggest construction proposal of its kind in the UK, and for that matter, in Europe. It would not only annihilate 850 acres of prime north Devon farmland and breathtaking countryside – an ecological gem – but have massive repercussions for the entire region. “At their sole public town hall meeting in June, Xlinks assured residents they intended to work collaboratively with our community. Regrettably, genuine dialogue has been nonexistent.” Those rallying against the proposal cite its proposed location in a globally protected environment, water consumption, wastewater runoff potentially containing toxic Pfas, known as “forever chemicals”, air pollution, high background noise, safety and fire risks associated with the BESS and the industrialisation of open countryside. In the last few weeks 30,000 people nationally have signed a petition launched by Cheryl Cottle-Hunkin, the cabinet member for rural affairs for Devon county council, calling on the government to pause all datacentre and BESS plans outside designated AI growth zones. “Proposals like this outside AI growth zones are highly problematic, because they may seek to evade regulation and government scrutiny,” said Cottle-Hunkin. “We need an urgent national conversation on AI and associated infrastructure to make sure it’s on the right scale and in the right place.” After the hottest summer on record, north Devon remains under a hosepipe ban and the potential water usage of such a vast site is a significant concern. Xlinks says the data campus will be self-sufficient in water terms, recirculating it to absorb heat and topping up mainly from rainwater. But an FoI answer revealed that under extreme conditions, such as severe heatwaves and serious droughts, annual water consumption could reach approximately 2.9bn litres. Xlinks told the Guardian that the design on which that water consumption estimate was based had been superseded by a new design that would be released during public consultation and in the planning application. Community tensions erupted this week when protesters rallied and demanded answers about secrecy and due diligence outside a Torridge district council meeting. Doug Bushby, the chair of the council, responded by threatening to call the police over “unsubstantiated and unfounded allegations, abuse, harassment and intimidation”. When planning applications were received, he said, “they will be dealt with within the same legislative, professional and operational boundaries that exist for all planning applications”. Meanwhile, PR agents for Xlinks are contacting parish councils for private conversations. On 18 September, Monkleigh parish council said the PR company Coast Communications had sought a closed meeting. Councillors said the minutes should be made public, and a recording released, but this was refused. “As a result … Monkleigh parish council will not be accepting the invitation from Coast Communications on behalf of Xlinks to a closed meeting with them and therefore no meeting will be taking place,” the council said. Xlinks is no stranger to Great Torrington. The company was behind a plan in 2024 to bring wind and solar energy to the UK from Morocco through subsea cables that would come ashore on the north Devon coast, including the building of a new electricity substation. But the government said it would not support the project because it was not in the UK’s national interest and did not clearly align strategically with the government’s mission to build homegrown power. Xlinks said in a statement its £13.8bn AI and BESS project would bring significant economic investment, between 600 and 1,200 jobs and clean energy infrastructure to the region. “We will ensure that the Devon data campus is designed sensitively for local people and the environment,” the company said. “We are carrying out nature and wildlife surveys on site. We must legally improve biodiversity by at least 10%, and plan to exceed this by some margin. Buildings will be sited to minimise visibility, through topography, landscaping and the existing treeline.” An environmental impact assessment was under way and any mitigation required would be built into the design and secured through planning conditions, Xlinks said. A spokesperson for Torridge district council said Xlinks had planned to undertake a public consultation in July, but this was postponed until later in the year: “When any proposals are received these will be validated and details will be published on the council’s planning portal … We appreciate that this proposal will understandably continue to generate a lot of local interest.” A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Every battery storage facility we build helps protect families from future energy shocks. “We have commissioned the national energy system operator to develop the first ever strategic spatial energy plan, which will support a more actively planned approach to energy projects, to bring good jobs to communities and help to lower bills.”

title: World’s top 20 private equity firms produce more greenhouse gases a year than most countries, report finds - The Guardian
raw_text: The energy portfolios of 20 private equity firms produce 1.5bn tons of greenhouse gases a year, more than the annual emissions of any country except China, the US, India and Russia, according to a new report. Together, these firms manage $7.3tn in assets of all kinds, affording them the ability to shape the pace of the transition away from fossil fuels. However their energy investments include significant fossil fuel assets including natural gas and coal-fired power plants to provide electricity to datacenters. The analysis of the top 20 private equity firms invested in global energy infrastructure was conducted by the Private Equity Climate Risks Consortium. It found that the firms owned 15,000 miles of pipelines, 124GW of power generation capacity across 370 fossil fuel-powered plants and hundreds of oil and gas fields. Half of the top 10 US datacenter owners are backed by private equity, said Matt Parr, the communications director for Private Equity Stakeholder Project (PESP), one of the organizations in the Private Equity Climate Risks Consortium. “This industry doesn’t get enough scrutiny and credit for its contribution to global emissions,” Parr said. “It’s a very opaque business model.” The research team queried energy holdings with the private markets data provider PitchBook, drawing on additional details from company websites, press releases, news articles and regulatory filings. Because of gaps in the data, the researchers were unable to calculate how much the 20 private equity firms invested in fossil fuel assets. But an earlier analysis of data compiled on PitchBook shows that private equity has funded more than $1tn in fossil fuel assets since 2010, said Amanda Mendoza, senior research and campaign coordinator on the climate team at the Private Equity Stakeholder Project. While some public-sector retirement systems have been trying to limit their exposure to fossil fuel projects, the private equity firms BlackRock, GIP, Energy Capital Partners, EQT and Kayne Anderson increased the amount of fossil fuel companies in their portfolio compared with 2024, according to the report. The private equity firm EQT has positioned itself as a climate conscious investor, supporting the energy transition. But EQT, along with Blackrock’s GIP and the California Public Employees’ Retirement system could soon acquire AES Corporation, which owns more than 20 power plants. “It is alarming because if this deal does go through they will then be owners of a fleet of coal power and gas powered plants,” Mendoza said. “That’s significantly going to impact their transition. It seems like they’re transitioning to fossil fuels instead of away.” EQT did not respond to questions from the Guardian about the private equity firm’s fossil fuel investments. ArcLight also declined to comment on the report’s findings. Private equity firms’ growing role in energy infrastructure is increasingly intersecting with another major private equity bet: the buildout of datacenters to support artificial intelligence. Private equity firms have emerged as the largest datacenter owners outside of big tech. In June 2024, Blackstone invested $2.16bn in the Northern Indiana Public Service Company (NIPSCO) for a 19.9% stake in the utility, including a seat on the board. NIPSCO, which serves 1.3 million customers across Indiana, has since announced plans to build a 2,300 MW natural gas power plant to serve datacenters, with the potential to emit millions of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Asked to comment, Blackstone told the Guardian it is a minority investor in NIPSCO, does not manage the company’s day-to-day operations, and has no control over management decisions. Blackstone has also announced plans to invest over $25bn to support the buildout of datacenters and energy infrastructure in Pennsylvania. “The electricity infrastructure required to power the AI revolution requires a tremendous amount of capital. title: California and New York sue over Trump push to halt wind energy projects - The Guardian
raw_text: Democratic attorneys general from California and New York have sued the Trump administration over its plans to buy back offshore wind leases as Donald Trump seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels. California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, said he was suing over removal of a project off his state’s coast planned by Chicago-based Invenergy. The Trump administration said in June it was buying back the company’s US offshore wind leases for four wind projects on the east and west coasts. New York’s attorney general, Letitia James, meanwhile, led seven states in suits seeking to block the Invenergy deal and another proposal with Bluepoint Wind, which agreed in April to end a wind farm under development off the New York and New Jersey coast. The deals would hand energy companies $1.4bn in taxpayer dollars in exchange for the cancellation of multiple projects. In all, the Trump administration has pledged nearly $4bn to companies to walk away from projects across the country. The interior department started buying back offshore wind leases in March after federal courts thwarted Trump’s efforts to stop offshore wind development through executive action. In exchange for reimbursements of lease fees, companies are investing in fossil fuel projects and geothermal energy. Interior secretary Doug Burgum has said that companies “are shifting investment back toward dependable, secure energy infrastructure that can power our economy and lower utility costs”. James called the deals illegal and said they would ultimately increase Americans’ electricity bills by sabotaging states’ ability to meet growing energy demands. “Americans are facing increasing energy costs because this administration would rather pay off energy companies than let us build the new power sources we need,” James said in a statement. “These illegal backroom deals take money that should have gone toward lowering New Yorkers’ bills and hand it to fossil fuel projects in other states.” Bonta said that as a national and global leader in the fight against the climate crisis, California finds itself enmeshed in “avoidable and unnecessary battles with our own federal government” to advance climate action and move toward clean energy. Bonta, speaking at a Climate Week event in New York, said climate action needs to match the scope, speed and scale of the problem. “Because we have to go to court and block an unlawful action by the Trump administration each time, it takes time. It slows the process down and we know we are running out of time and we need to be urgent and aggressive,” Bonta said on Tuesday in remarks just before Trump addressed the UN general assembly. “We’re still all in, in California,” Bonta said. “No matter what the Trump administration does, we’re going to push to participate in the climate action that is needed to meet this moment and to rise to the occasion.” Later in the day, Bonta was among the California and New York officials participating in a Climate Week panel about state leadership on wind energy. California’s energy commission chair, David Hochschild, said at the New York City bar that the power to drive a transition away from fossil fuels still rests primarily with the states. While Trump, who often talks about his hatred of wind power, can slow it down and make it more expensive, Hochschild said, “he can’t put the genie back in the bottle”. Trump has said his goal is to not let any “windmills” be built. Doreen Harris, the New York state energy research and development authority president, said they are all confident they will ultimately succeed in court, however they need energy infrastructure in their states for a reliable grid. “The reality is, even if successful, the question becomes who is going to invest,” Harris said. She added: ‘“We just want to get back to building.” Attorneys general in Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Vermont joined New York’s suit.

title: Dining across the divide: ‘He suggested the Clacton byelection was a vanity project. Obviously I disagree’ - The Guardian
raw_text: Chris, 42, London Occupation Electrical supervisor of the maintenance team at an NHS hospital Voting record Labour Amuse bouche He used to play and referee mid-level community rugby until he got “too old and unfit” Alex, 42, London Occupation London Assembly member Voting record Conservative for most of his life, then during the pandemic he moved to Reform (in a move his still-Tory husband characterised as “throwing a strop”) because he didn’t agree with lockdown, masks or banning social gatherings of more than six people Amuse bouche He has two Brittany dogs, and one won a class at Crufts For starters Alex I didn’t know what to expect, though part of my job is talking to people with different views. Chris was really friendly. Chris We got on well. Alex is a really nice, personable guy, and it’s quite hard to question somebody belligerently when they’re so easy to talk to. Alex I had calamari to start, which was lovely. For the main course, I had fettuccine with lamb ragu and a glass of montepulciano, and for dessert I had my go-to: tiramisu. It was great. Chris I had the calamari to start, with a minty tartare dip. Then I had a spicy pepperoni pizza, a couple of bottles of beer, and for dessert a really nice lemon tart. The big beef Alex He suggested the Clacton byelection was a vanity project. Obviously I disagree, but it’s a perfectly understandable position. Nigel Farage clearly believes (and I support him) that ultimately his constituents should be the judge – and they gave him a resounding vote of confidence. Chris If constituents could be the judge, then why would there be another byelection later if he’s found to have breached parliament’s rules? In Clacton, you’d only need about 8,000 people to sign a petition to recall him, which seems likely because almost 10,000 people voted for a man with a bin on his head. Alex It was a lot easier canvassing for Reform in Clacton than in the local elections earlier this year in London. I got more abuse during that campaign than I had had in 27 years of politics. Chris I said, imagine how it is now for a canvasser who isn’t a middle-aged, white, Anglo-Saxon male. If you’re a woman, or from an ethnic minority, or if you’ve got a disability, you’re probably going to get a lot more abuse. Sharing plate Alex Hurtling towards an artificial target of net zero is counterproductive. We’re doing self-inflicted damage to the economy for what’s largely virtue signalling, in my view, because of the 1% of emissions we’re responsible for. Fundamentally, we need to keep the lights on and food on the table. I support more efficient use of our own natural resources, including oil and gas. Chris I’m in favour of investing in renewable energy; he’s more in favour of bringing energy costs down by extracting more fossil fuels. I said we can do that, but it’s going to make global warming worse. At our NHS hospital, we’re pretty much at maximum electrical capacity, and if we were to install loads of extra air-conditioning units, as people think we should, that would overload our electrical system. For afters Alex Andy Burnham is not willing to make tough decisions on things like welfare spending. My view would be that we need to look very seriously at things like Pip [personal independence payment] and foreign-born residents being able to claim universal credit. Chris He was all for shrinking the state a bit, but he didn’t really go into much detail on how he would do that. I think we should try to raise revenue in other ways, such as bringing capital gains tax in line with income tax, going after big corporations because they’re not paying proper tax, and reforming other taxes like VAT and council tax, because I believe those are regressive taxes that hit the people in the lowest income brackets the hardest. Takeaways Alex I think that just by having an interest in politics you’ve got more in common with someone else, even if they’re taking a contrary view. Even though we disagreed, we had that shared interest. Chris We swapped numbers. He was nice, personable and easy to get on with. I imagine he’ll stand as an MP in the next general election, so I’ll probably text him around then and see how he’s doing. Additional reporting: Kitty Drake Citro, London N6. title: ‘Negligent’ to talk about long-term risks to Australia without examining cost of climate crisis, experts say - The Guardian
raw_text: An Australian government snapshot of life in 40 years has been sharply criticised for underplaying the economic and social damage expected due to the worsening climate crisis. The government’s seventh intergenerational report, which projects out to 2066, finds the effects of global heating four decades from now are “highly uncertain”, pointing to the pace of the global energy transition as a key source of unpredictability. The report finds sea level rise from global heating will have the greatest effects on coastal and low-lying areas, while hotter temperatures could reduce productivity of workers, affect agricultural crop yields and damage tourism. “Over the next 40 years, increasingly frequent and severe natural disasters will pose a significant economic risk,” it finds. The deputy director of Melbourne Climate Futures at the University of Melbourne, Assoc Prof Ben Neville, said that while the report “connects demographic trends with threats on the horizon, it is negligent in ignoring the economic damage that the changing climate already is and will increasingly bring in the next 40 years”. The report mentions Treasury modelling which finds that a disorderly approach to the net zero transition results in a cumulative $2tn hit to the economy by 2050. “As the geopolitics show, we are clearly on this disorderly pathway,” Neville said, adding that – as highlighted by the national climate risk assessment – current modelling methods significantly underestimate economic impacts “as they don’t incorporate the recognised complex impacts of climate change”. “Not integrating this perspective when forecasting the next 40 years is a very disappointing miss, illustrating a government that just doesn’t seem to get it on climate change, all while it co-leads the world towards the next global Cop negotiations in Turkey.” Sarah Wheeler, a professor of water economics at Flinders University said that the issue of water scarcity was overlooked in the report. “One of the largest impacts [of climate change] will be on water security issues, with higher water variability meaning increased probability of more damaging flooding and severe droughts,” she said. “Without urgent action to address and manage these issues, the ramifications on Australian productivity and wellbeing will be huge.” Climate activist Anjali Sharma questioned the report’s utility. “Young people won’t be looking at this report to know their future. What use is a report forecasting the next 40 years by a government failing to tackle the greatest challenge of our time?” However, the report does highlight the benefits of embracing renewable energy. Prof Frank Jotzo, director of the Centre for Climate and Energy Policy at the Australian National University, said it “correctly points out the many economic advantages that Australia will reap from the transition to renewable energy, and from future clean energy-based export industries”. “The national vision of renewable energy based exports of green iron, green ammonia and carbon-neutral fuels is alive, despite some disappointment of early excitement not yet having translated into large investments.” The executive director of policy for the Investor Group on Climate Change, Francesca Muskovic, said: “The government needs a laser focus on making sure datacentres’ growing electricity demand is aligned to and supports investment and rollout of new, firmed renewable energy. “Runaway demand without securing a strong pipeline of additional, new clean energy supply will put immediate, acute pressure on the existing grid and could lead to increased energy prices for Australian households and businesses.” Addressing the intergenerational report at an event in Sydney on Tuesday, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said that at a time when “AI seems to have swamped discussion about everything else”, governments would have to contend not only with “the potential impacts of climate change”, but with “what we need to be doing to lean into the energy transition … and the investments that we need to make”.

title: Australia’s dependence on gas generation during evening energy peak falls by almost 70% - The Guardian
raw_text: Australia’s dependence on gas for power during the evening, when the grid is under the most pressure, has fallen by almost nearly 70% over the past year as batteries surged in, replacing the fossil fuel. Gas generation during the busy early evening, between 5pm and 8pm, fell by 67% in the year to August, as large-scale batteries continued to come online and 500,000 home batteries were installed under the government’s subsidy program, analysis by consultancy EnergyEdge found. The company’s managing director, Josh Stabler, said batteries big and small recorded their highest peak output on record, off the back of rapid uptake. “The rate of installation of batteries in Australia is the fastest uptake of any electricity asset ever – faster than solar, faster than wind,” he said. According to the EnergyEdge report: “batteries have taken the evening peak, and they’re not giving it back”. Batteries met 49% of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during the evening in August 2026, up from 0.4% in 2020. In contrast, gas fell from 65.9% to 20.6% over the same period. Wholesale electricity prices fell in response – a win for households – but potentially a problem for future investment in new dispatchable power. Recent quarterly data (April to June) from the Australian Energy Market Operator highlighted a similar pattern, with gas generation recording its lowest Q2 on average in more than two decades. Gas power declined in all regions, the AEMO said, with the fall “most evident” during the evening peak. The Grattan Institute’s energy and climate change program director, Alison Reeve, said utility scale batteries were increasingly mopping up surplus renewable energy in the middle of the day and displacing the role of gas during the peak. “Overall, this is super good news. title: UK shares findings of damning climate crisis national security report suppressed under Starmer - The Guardian
raw_text: The UK has warned countries around the world that the climate and nature crises and the coming El Niño threaten their national security and defence, presenting foreign ministries with the findings of a report suppressed under Keir Starmer. Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, made a presentation to the foreign ministers of the EU as well as Kenya and other countries on Wednesday night at a private meeting during the UN general assembly in New York, based on the report by the UK’s spy chiefs that found the collapse of natural systems around the world would lead to conflict, migration and food shortages. Miliband told the meeting, the first such discussion among foreign ministers, that the coming El Niño, which has been supercharged by climate breakdown, would test the world’s food systems as never before. “We face an El Niño that is already set to be the most intense in living memory,” he said. “This will intensify climate shocks that compound and cascade across borders, threatening food and water security, displacing communities, putting pressure on markets and scarring economies.” This year’s heatwaves, bad harvests and food price inflation showed governments what they were in for, he said, and must be dealt with at the highest levels. “Climate change and nature loss have never been issues for climate and environment ministers alone,” he said. “They are defining challenges for our citizens, our economies, our foreign policy and our national security.” With the backing of Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, Miliband presented the research that found the collapse of global ecosystems such as in the Amazon and Congo rainforests, driven by the climate crisis and the destruction of nature, would have impacts on national security around the world. The joint intelligence committee (JIC) report, revealed by the Guardian, was scheduled to be published last October, but was suppressed on the eve of its launch by Downing Street. A redacted version was issued in January under the Freedom of Information Act, but ministers have continued to resist calls for the full report to be made public. Richard Nugee, a retired general and security expert, told the Guardian governments must treat the climate as they would other threats to national security, such as sabotage by hostile states. “If a bridge is washed away, it has the same impact whether it’s done by [a foreign power] or the climate,” he said. “The climate crisis will affect food security, energy security, water security, and lead to migration and potentially the recruitment of farmers to [terrorist organisations such as] Isis. Countries should absolutely be treating this as a national security issue.” He said it was not surprising that the JIC report was suppressed and redacted, as it was “very rare” for security reports to be published. Miliband will appoint a new special representative for climate security, as well as a new ministerial taskforce on “the national security and resilience risks of a changing climate and nature loss”, with military and security experts as well as climate scientists. He also announced £330m for the Global Environment Facility, the main international fund for protecting nature, that will go towards protecting forests, oceans and other critical ecosystems in developing countries. The closed-door meeting among foreign ministers was convened after Miliband made a public speech on Monday at the UN general assembly that touched on the links between the climate and national security. Soon after taking office in July, the former energy secretary told the Guardian he would put the climate at the heart of UK foreign policy. On Wednesday night, Miliband said: “The countries fit for the future will be those that see climate and nature as intrinsic to economic and national security. Countries that anticipate risks and invest in resilience before crises hit. “Countries that seize the incredible opportunities the clean energy transition presents. Countries that don’t just see the connections but act on them.” He added: “That is why the UK is placing climate and nature security at the heart of our national security and foreign policy decision-making.” Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, who has campaigned for the JIC report to be made public, said: “It’s good that the foreign secretary is presenting the findings of this crucial report to ministers from other governments. “But it begs the question, why are MPs in this country still being denied access to the full report? And, most importantly, why has our government still not published its response to how it will address the stark findings?”
